## Outline of Books I and II

The Islamic world is not a monolith. Its religious identity is not the same thing as the political identity of the Arab world.

There is an Iranian Islam, just as there is a Turkish, Indian, Indonesian, Malay, and other forms of Islam.

Unfortunately, while readers interested in the archaeology and arts of Iran, both before and after the coming of Islam, have a wealth of literature at their disposal, few books answer a different question: what were the underlying impulses of Iranian consciousness that gave these forms their shape?

From the very beginnings of the Islamic community, the Iranian world formed a distinct whole.

Its defining characteristics and its calling can be understood only if we view Iran's spiritual world as a continuous whole, before Islam as well as after it.

Islamic Iran became, above all, the homeland of some of Islam's greatest philosophers and mystics.

For them, speculative thought could never be separated from what it brought to fruition or from its practical consequences.

And those consequences concerned not merely what we today call the *social* environment, but the whole concrete reality that human beings sustain with their very substance, beyond the limits of this life: their *spiritual* world.

It is by remaining faithful to this understanding that the author has built the work presented here, in seven books.

It is the fruit of more than twenty years of research in Iran itself, both in libraries and in the company of Iranian friends, combined with years of teaching in Paris and Tehran.

The method is fundamentally *phenomenological*, though it belongs to no particular school of phenomenology.

Its aim is to encounter the *religious fact* by allowing the *religious object* to reveal itself as it appears to those for whom it is a living reality.

This explains the essential subtitle of the work: *Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects*.

To speak of an *aspect* is to imply someone who sees it.

But here the observer—the phenomenologist—must become a spiritual guest of those to whom that reality appears, and must share with them the responsibility it entails.

Any *historical* account must therefore remain within the horizon of the religious reality itself, rather than impose some alien framework upon it from outside, dialectical or otherwise.

Only on this condition can we recognize, together, the many correspondences suggested throughout the work, for they are variations of the same reality.

The first two volumes contain Books I and II of the work.

*Book I* sets out to show several essential features of Twelver Shiism, also known as Imami Shiism. It took deep root in Iran from the earliest period and became the official religion in the sixteenth century.

These features are brought to light and examined through what the author has elsewhere called the “phenomenon of the Revealed Book,” as it appears to the people the Quran calls the *Ahl al-Kitâb*, the “People of the Book”—a community embracing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

In every branch of the Abrahamic tradition, interpreters of the Bible and the Quran have faced the same problems and the same task: discovering the *true* meaning of the Book.

On both sides, the search for that *true* meaning—the spiritual meaning concealed beneath the literal wording—has led to similar methods of bringing out the *esoteric*, or inward, meaning of divine Revelation.

The “phenomenon of the Book” lies at the origin of *hermeneutics*: the art of understanding and interpretation.

Those who have sought the inner meanings of the Bible and the Quran probably still have much to teach contemporary philosophers, who are themselves so deeply concerned with *hermeneutics*.

The technical name for the Quran's esoteric interpretation is *ta’wîl*: literally, to “lead back” something to its origin, to its archetype.

Shiite metaphysics is governed by the idea of a God who, in his Essence, is unknowable, inaccessible, and beyond all names, and by the idea of his *epiphany*—his manifestation—in the *pleroma*, the complete company of fourteen beings of light, who appeared on earth as the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”: the Prophet, his daughter Fâtima, and the Twelve Imams.

The inner meaning that Shiite *ta’wîl* draws from the Quran's literal words chiefly concerns this *pleroma* of fourteen.

In doing so, it also illustrates the distinctively Shiite understanding of prophecy, from which it follows that Shiism refuses to believe its future lies behind it.

In contrast to the majority Sunni understanding of Islam, according to which humanity has nothing further to await after the mission of the last Prophet, Shiism keeps the future open.

It holds that even after the coming of the “Seal of the Prophets,” something still remains to be revealed: the spiritual meaning of the revelations brought by the great prophets.

This was the task of interpretation entrusted to the holy Imams, whose teachings fill many volumes.

Yet this spiritual understanding will be complete only at the end of our *Aeon* (this world-age), with the return—the *parousia*—of the Twelfth Imam, who is now hidden and is the mystical pole of this world.

This way of interpreting revelation also implies a particular understanding of time, expressed in a division of history into periods: the age of the prophets' missions is followed by the age of spiritual initiation.

Here, too, the Shiite understanding of prophecy meets the aspirations of the Joachimite movement in the West, inspired by Joachim of Fiore and his proclamation of the coming reign of the Spirit.

Yet this division of history already belongs, in fact, to *metahistory*: its essentially eschatological dimension—its concern with the ultimate fulfillment of time—breaks through the limits of ordinary history.

Like the interpretation of revelation itself, the Shiite understanding of the Imams presented Shiite thinkers with problems similar to those that Christology had posed for Christian thinkers.

But Shiite thinkers consistently tended toward solutions that official Christology had rejected.

Perhaps it was in this way that Shiite *gnosis*—spiritual knowledge—escaped being secularized into a form of social messianism.

Shiite metaphysics and Shiite spirituality are inseparable: each is the very substance of the other.

A view of Islam confined to its Sunni majority has too long encouraged the assumption that Sufism and spiritual Islam are one and the same.

In reality, Shiite spirituality extends beyond Sufism.

There are, of course, Shiite Sufi orders, and the lineages of most *tarîqat*—spiritual paths or brotherhoods—likewise go back to one of the Imams.

But a Shiite seeker of inner meaning is already, by that very fact, upon the Path (*tarîqat*), without having to join a Sufi order.

At the summit of a mystical Sinai, knowing the Imam as his personal guide leads him to knowledge of himself.

*Book II* is devoted entirely to another feature of Iranian Islam, no less fundamental or distinctive in its philosophy and spirituality, and one that would from the outset become closely allied with the Shiism of many Iranian thinkers.

The word that best expresses it is *ishrâq*: the rising of the sun (*aurora consurgens*), its dawn, its “east.”

The philosophy of *Ishrâq*, understood as a “theosophy” or divine wisdom of Light, is therefore an “Eastern” theosophy; and the philosophers known as *ishrâqîyûn* are “Eastern” philosophers, in the metaphysical sense of the word *East*.

They are also frequently called “Platonists,” in contrast to the Peripatetic philosophers of Islam, who followed the Aristotelian tradition.

At the origin of these “Platonists of Persia” within Islam stands the heroic resolve of an extraordinarily gifted young thinker from northwestern Iran: Shihâboddîn Yahyâ Sohrawardî.

He would die in Aleppo, Syria, at the age of thirty-six, a martyr to his cause, in 1191.

His writings state his purpose quite plainly: to bring the wisdom of ancient Persia back to life—the philosophy of Light and Darkness; in a sense, to bring the Hellenized Magi home to Islamic Persia.

And he undertook this very work through the resources of interpretation (*ta’wîl*) made available to him by Islamic spirituality.

Some three centuries before the great Byzantine philosopher Gemistos Plethon, this Iranian thinker's work brought together the names of Plato and Zarathustra (Zoroaster) as heralds of one “Eastern” tradition reaching back to Hermes, the father of the sages.

Plato's Ideas are interpreted in the language of Zoroastrian angelology. This interpretation of being makes room for a third world, one whose existence philosophies confined to concepts had been unable to establish.

Between the intelligible world, grasped by the intellect, and the sensible world, known through the senses, lies the *mundus imaginalis*: a perfectly real world.

It is not the merely “imaginary” realm to which our philosophies of outward appearances reduce it. It requires its own word: the *imaginal*.

Sohrawardî understood that, by establishing the reality of this “third world,” he could also establish an objective reality for the prophets' revelations, the mystics' visions, and the events of Revelation. This theme would remain alive through centuries of Iranian thought.

A striking feature of this metaphysics of Light is that it identifies Light's primordial Source with what Zoroastrian theosophy calls *Xvarnah*, or the “Light of Glory.”

From this Source proceed the hierarchies of archangels, arranged here in a synthesis of Zoroastrian angelology and the celestial hierarchies of Proclus's Neoplatonism.

The image of *Xvarnah* opens out into inexhaustible echoes and possibilities.

In earlier research, the author has shown correspondences between the ways it manifests itself and the Holy Grail of Western tradition.

Indeed, the Grail itself—the mystical cup that mirrors the world—appears in the heroic epic of ancient Iran.

It is also present in Sohrawardî's work, where it marks the passage from heroic epic to mystical epic, one of the decisive developments in Iran's cultural history.

This same passage announces itself in a cycle of short tales of spiritual initiation, almost all written in Persian.

Their wealth of symbols enables Sohrawardî to lead his reader toward the fulfillment of the reader's deepest longing, even more effectively than his great systematic works.

The author gives particular attention to two of these spiritual tales: one set within the Iranian mystical epic, the other within the wider Gnostic epic.

Sohrawardî's “Eastern” tradition has remained active in Iran down to the present day. It also exercised a powerful influence in India during the religious reforms of Shah Akbar.

These first two books thus present two essential dimensions of Islamic *gnosis* as shaped by the spirit of Iranian Islam.

At a time when recent discoveries have given new momentum to the study of *gnosis*, both in ancient Gnosticism and in Jewish *gnosis*, this research comes at an opportune moment.

*In press.* Volume III will contain Book III of the work (*The Faithful of Love*) and Book IV (*Shiism and Sufism*).

Volume IV will contain Book V (*The School of Isfahan*), Book VI (*The Shaykhi School*), and Book VII (*The Twelfth Imam and Spiritual Chivalry*), together with a general index.

# Book II

## SOHRAWARDÎ AND THE PLATONISTS OF PERSIA

### CHAPTER ONE

#### A Life’s Great Undertaking

##### I. — Life and Martyrdom

In Iran, Sohrawardî is traditionally known as *shaykh al-Ishrâq*: the *shaykh*, or learned master, of *Ishrâq*.

That last word, both the name and the emblem of his teaching, has become inseparable from the name of the master himself.

Literally, it means the rising of the sun, *aurora consurgens*, the light of morning.

The adjective *ishrâqî* describes what belongs to the dawn or the East, what shines with the splendor of morning, like the sun as it rises.

*Ishrâqî-namâz* is the morning prayer, corresponding to “Prime” among the traditional Christian hours of prayer.

The *ishrâqî* teaching is a *theosophia matutina*: a wisdom of the morning. The *Ishrâqîyûn* are all the thinkers and spiritual seekers who embrace this teaching.

We shall soon see how Sohrawardî unfolds the different meanings of this East and makes it the emblem of Iranian spirituality.

We shall also see how and why his teaching has a deep affinity with Shiite theosophy[^EII2-1]—an affinity at first concealed, then openly acknowledged.

Many Shiite thinkers have belonged to the *Ishrâqîyûn*.

Their case illustrates, more clearly than almost any other, the fate of philosophical reflection in Islam.

After Avicenna (d. 428 AH / 1037 CE), there came, on the one hand, Ghazâlî's critique of philosophy (d. 505 AH / 1111 CE).

More than one Western historian, struck by superficial similarities, has compared this critique with Kant's.

Ghazâlî’s critique was taken to mean that metaphysics was no longer possible—as though the withdrawal of one philosopher, or several, were enough to persuade everyone else to abandon the questions that have always made metaphysics indispensable to human beings. Unfortunately, this understanding of what has been called the “philosophical adventure” was confined rather too narrowly to the horizons of the West. The consequences of Ghazâlî’s critique were sought in the ultimately fruitless efforts of Averroes (d. 595/1198) in Andalusia.

After Averroes, what for so long was called “Arabic” philosophy—a regrettable error of perspective—seemed to disappear into the sands, while Latin Averroism flourished in the West. This view lost sight of what else had happened after Avicenna: during Averroes’ own lifetime, and in striking contrast to him, the immense work of Ibn ’Arabî[^EII2-2] was taking shape, a work that would nourish the spirituality of the Islamic East down to our own time; and in Iran, Avicenna’s philosophy was being transformed into the “Eastern philosophy” that was Sohrawardî’s achievement.

The great undertaking of Sohrawardî’s life, as he understood it and as his disciples have understood it from generation to generation, was less the ambition of a “founder” than that of a man bringing something back to life. His purpose was to revive the spiritual vision of ancient Persia, and it was in pursuing this purpose that he would say he had had no predecessor.

We must be clear about what this means. Zoroastrianism still existed in Iran, as it does today. There was no need to “revive” it, and Sohrawardî never presented himself as a Zoroastrian, a convert, or a reformer of Mazdean religion. Born into Islam, he remained a *moslim* and a *mu’min*—a Muslim and a believer—for it was within Islam itself that he found the place from which to undertake his work.

As he himself makes clear, his calling and his role were first of all those of a philosopher. In Isfahan he encountered a philosophical world in which Avicenna’s memory was still alive. He does not tell us precisely when he came to know Sufism, though his treatises bear witness to his personal experience of it. Nor does he tell us exactly what he knew of Shiite theosophy and its understanding of prophecy, traces of which can be found in his writings and which, in the end, help explain why he was brought to trial in Aleppo.

What he does confide, in his principal work, is that a sudden illumination revealed to him the meaning and sources of ancient Persian wisdom. From that vision sprang the undertaking that would henceforth claim all his energies. It enabled him to bring together the names of Plato and Zarathustra—Zoroaster—some three centuries before the great Byzantine philosopher Gemistos Plethon (d. between 1450 and 1464) attempted a similar enterprise.

Yet Sohrawardî did not experience this undertaking as a struggle against Islam, even though it could not have been conceived within the limits of a strictly literal religion concerned only with outward observance. Quite the contrary: the energies of mystical faith, of the spiritual Islam alive within him, made it possible for him to embrace the undertaking and bring it to completion.

Inspired by the prophetic spirit of Islam, Sohrawardî came to see that *ta’wîl*—the interpretation that uncovers the hidden meaning of divine revelations—could also embrace the meaning of Zoroastrian prophecy, a meaning that only such an interpretation could disclose. We have seen how Shiite theosophy, through its idea of *walâyat*, the spiritual guardianship and authority entrusted to the friends of God, enters into the meaning of the missions of the prophets who came before the “Seal of the Prophets,” including the biblical prophets within its understanding of prophecy.

In a comparable way, Sohrawardî saw, in the radiance of the Light of Glory (the *Xvarnah*), glimpsed in turn at the “Lotus of the Utmost Boundary,” that the prophet and heroes of ancient Persia also belonged to the destinies traced out in the sacred history of the “Peoples of the Book.” In relation to the wisdom of ancient Zoroastrian Persia, he thus assumed something like the mediating role played by Salmân the Pure (*Salmân Pâk*, or Salmân the Persian, *Salmân Pârsî*) between the Iranian community and the Prophet’s Family (*Ahl al-Bayt*). As the Prophet himself is reported to have said, “Salmân is one of us, a member of our Household.”

The *Ishrâqîyûn*, the philosophers of illumination, would in their turn bring Sohrawardî’s themes into the family of Shiite theosophy. That is why his arrival in the philosophical and spiritual life of Islamic Persia mattered so profoundly, and left a mark that never disappeared. He too, while still young, was to seal the meaning of his cause with a martyr’s death, far from his native Iran, in Aleppo: the cause of the *’orafâ*, the mystical seekers of divine wisdom, ever vulnerable to the hostility of the doctors of religious law when those doctors become rather too closely allied with the ambitions of political power.

We have already had occasion elsewhere to sketch the course of his life and work. An admiration dating from our youth led us to edit the collected texts of his treatises.

But books become scarce, or escape the attention of readers who are not specialists in Oriental studies. We must therefore outline the essentials once more here.[^EII2-3]

Shihâboddîn Yahyâ Sohrawardî, who must not be confused with the Sufis who bore the same name,[^EII2-4] was born, as his name indicates, at Sohraward around 549 AH (1155 CE). The town of Sohraward, south of Zenjân and west of Soltâniyeh, in the province of Jabal—the ancient Media—in northwestern Iran, was still a flourishing and populous place at that time, before the Mongol invasions. In the section on physics in one of his works, while discussing instances of petrification that he had himself observed, he expressly refers to his birthplace: “As we have observed,” he says, “in our own country ... near the town of Sohraward[^EII2-5] ...”

While still very young he went to study at Marâgheh, in Azerbaijan, under Shaykh Majdoddîn Gîlî.

Another of Gîlî’s pupils was Fakhroddîn Râzî, a celebrated name in the history of Islamic philosophy. Sohrawardî and Fakhroddîn Râzî later exchanged views, and some trace of their exchanges survives,[^EII2-6] but the contrast between these two thinkers could hardly have been greater. Fakhroddîn Râzî remained a distinguished representative of Islamic scholastic theology (*Kalâm*), placing his rational confidence in the methods of argument inherited from the Greek philosophers.

Sadrâ Shîrâzî, in his turn, as an *Ishrâqî*, would emphasize this contrast. According to Shahrazôrî, Sohrawardî’s faithful disciple and biographer, our *shaykh* seems to have had reservations about Fakhr Râzî’s philosophical abilities. Fakhr Râzî, by contrast, admired Sohrawardî without reserve. We are told that after Sohrawardî’s death a copy of his *Talwîhât* came into Fakhr Râzî’s hands, and that he reverently kissed the book.

After his studies at Marâgheh, Sohrawardî went to Isfahan, where, as we know, Avicenna had been active for several years. It was there that Sohrawardî encountered the Avicennian tradition. He studied closely a work by ’Omar ibn Sahlân Sâwajî, which he discusses repeatedly in one of his major books. Ibn Sahlân had written a commentary on Avicenna’s mystical treatise, the *Epistle of the Bird*, which Sohrawardî would himself translate into Persian.[^EII2-7] Also in Isfahan, he wrote one of his earliest Persian treatises for a group of friends.[^EII2-8]

Then began his wandering life, spent visiting Sufi communities and seeking the solitude in which meditation can ascend the stages of the mystical Path. He stayed at Diyâr Bakr, in southeastern Anatolia, where he was warmly received at the court of the Seljuks of Rûm. To one of them, ’Imâdoddîn Qarâ Arslân, emir of Kharpout, he dedicated a work entitled *The Book of Tablets Dedicated to ’Imâdoddîn* (*Alwâh ’Imâdîyâ*).[^EII2-9] What he was seeking in these long wanderings he reveals to us himself on the last page of one of his major books.

He was thus moving toward a destiny that one of his closest friends, Fakhroddîn Mardînî, had already foreseen. Speaking of Sohrawardî with their companions, Fakhr Mardînî had said: “What fire, what brilliance of dawn shines from this young man! Never in my life have I met anyone like him.

“Yet I fear the very excess of his ardour, his lack of caution in protecting himself. I fear that this may bring about his destruction.” An all too accurate premonition, alas. When news of Sohrawardî’s murder reached him, the same *shaykh* was able to say to his disciples: “Did I not predict it, when I was so anxious for him?[^EII2-10]”

It was after a long stay with his friend Fakhroddîn Mardînî at Diyâr Bakr that Sohrawardî travelled to Syria, to Aleppo, from which he would never return. Aleppo was then governed by al-Malik al-Zâhir, one of the sons of Salâhoddîn—the Saladin of Crusading history. Some of our chivalric romances have surrounded Saladin with a halo that, unfortunately, fades when we look at him from the Eastern side of the story. His fanaticism brought him into violent conflict with his own son over our *shaykh al-Ishrâq*. A deep and lasting friendship had quickly grown between the two young men, al-Malik al-Zâhir and Sohrawardî.

A few years later the great mystical theosopher Mohyiddîn Ibn ’Arabî would likewise become a close friend of this same son of Saladin. Meanwhile Shahrazôrî, Sohrawardî’s biographer, preserves an echo of the fierce disputes between Sohrawardî and the jurists, the doctors of the religious law known as *foqahâ*. Our young *shaykh* seems to have abandoned all caution, including the salutary practice of *ketmân*, the prudent concealment of esoteric beliefs. He appears to have spoken his mind openly, without concealing even the specialized terms in which he expressed his thought.

The charge brought against him by the doctors of the Law is particularly revealing if we recall what we said in the preceding book about Shiite teachings on prophecy and the Imams (above, Book I, Chapter VI). A brief, sharply worded exchange, preserved by a historian who seems in no way inclined to favour our *shaykh*, makes the accusation perfectly clear. “You have said in your books that God has the power to create a prophet whenever He wishes?”—“Certainly. God has power over all things.”—“But not the power to create a prophet.”—“Is that an absolute impossibility, or not?”—“You are a *kâfir* [an unbeliever].”[^EII2-11]

Thus the *takfîr*, the judgment declaring a person guilty of unbelief or infidelity to Islam, fell abruptly upon him. Of course, the force of a *takfîr* is limited, just as the authority claiming the right to pronounce it here is limited. It would be misleading to compare it with excommunication, which presupposes an institution such as the Church and the authority of a pope. Had Sohrawardî quietly moved somewhere else, the consequences would probably not have been tragic.

But such a flight was contrary to his deepest nature: his sense of loyalty, his readiness to challenge others, and his conviction that he served a cause greater than his personal interests.

The accusation admitted no distinctions. But how could one expect distinctions from the men making it? In fact, I know of no passage in which Sohrawardî states in so many words that God can create a prophet—a *nabî*—whenever He wishes, even after the coming of the one who was the “Seal of the Prophets.”

What we do find, however, is the prologue to his great book of *Eastern Theosophy*, which speaks of the hidden succession of a sacred line of sages possessed of divine wisdom (the *silsilat al-’irfân*), originating in the *Qotb*, the mystical pole around whom they are gathered. This prologue presupposes the original Shiite idea of the cycle of *walâyat*. Sohrawardî’s idea of a hidden spiritual lineage immediately calls to mind a text particularly characteristic of that idea: the conversation between the First Imam and his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyâd (above, Book I, Chapter III). Sohrawardî’s commentators recognized the connection: in explaining the prologue they quoted that conversation in full.

Nor did the *’olamâ*, the scholars of religious law, fail to recognize what was at stake. They certainly did not see—and could not see—that the very succession of the cycle of *walâyat* presupposes the closure of lawgiving prophecy, and that there will be no more prophets sent to bring a new revealed law.

Nevertheless, something does continue afterwards, something that remains open to the future. It nourishes an entire spiritual life that refuses to treat religion simply as the observance of the Law, detached from its inward truth (*haqîqat*). This something is the “divine sap” that keeps the phenomenon of the sacred Book alive. Beneath the outer bark of the revealed text (*zâhir*), its hidden meaning (*bâtin*) continually rises and prepares new blossoms.

From this follow several ideas: that while the cycle of Revelation (*wahy*) given to lawgiving prophets is closed, the cycle of inspiration (*ilhâm*) remains open; that every outward form has an inward meaning and that *ta’wîl*, the interpretation of symbols, has a vital role to play; that concealed within the succession of *walâyat* is the continuation of a secret prophecy (*nobowwat bâtinîya*). This is no longer the mission of prophets sent to give laws, but is identical with the *walâyat* that, from the very beginning, from Adam onward, formed the inward dimension of every prophetic mission.

Finally, this inward meaning leads not, as has been superficially claimed, to the “relativity of all religions,” but to the integration of each religion in its own place within the *hexaemeron*, the “six days of Creation” of the religious cosmos as described by Nâsir-e Khosraw, one of the greatest Iranian Ismaili theosophers. The scholars of Aleppo may not have known all this explicitly, but they surely sensed enough of it to feel alarmed. In accusing Sohrawardî, they were by that very act identifying him as a representative of Shiism, or of a concealed Shiism, which at that time was more or less compelled to remain underground.

This was precisely the period when Saladin was fighting the Franks. Sunni power had also overcome the Fatimid dynasty of Cairo, which for more than two centuries had embodied the hopes of Ismaili esoteric Islam.

We have already recalled the paradox inherent in those hopes (above, Book I, Chapter II), and explained why the Twelver Shiite conception corresponded more closely to the metaphysical and spiritual essence of the Imamate, since it entailed the Twelfth Imam’s withdrawal into occultation (*ghaybat*) until the Last Day. It is equally certain that the sacred succession of the sages, and that of their Imam or mystical pole, are not worldly dynasties exercising political power in rivalry with other powers. Their relation to such powers resembles that of the dynasty of the guardians of the Grail to the official succession of the Apostolic See.

Yet perhaps a succession that is wholly hidden and spiritual seems, to the powerful of this world, not harmless but all the more threatening and alarming. For they can imagine no horizon beyond the one upon which the petty ambitions of earthly rule contend with one another.

It was therefore inevitable that a man like Saladin would listen closely to the reports of his *’olamâ*.[^EII2-12] “If he is allowed to live,” they wrote of our young *shaykh*, “he will corrupt al-Malik al-Zâhir’s faith. If he is released, he will corrupt the whole country.” Saladin accordingly sent his son an order to put Sohrawardî to death.

But al-Malik al-Zâhir struggled desperately against it. Refusing to comply, he tried to shield his friend from the fury of the fanatics. The scholars again pressed Saladin, who sent a second letter to his son, threatening to strip him of the governorship of Aleppo if he refused. Three times the relentless accusers had to renew their demands before they could tear the *shaykh* away from al-Malik al-Zâhir’s protection. His biographers have never established exactly what happened at the end.

We do not know precisely how the young *shaykh* died. It is even possible that he voluntarily refused all food “until his Lord should see fit to call him back to Himself.” The date most commonly accepted for his death in the citadel of Aleppo is 5 Rajab 587 / 29 July 1191. He would have been thirty-six years old, or thirty-eight by the lunar calendar.

To historians who felt no particular attachment to him, he was the *shaykh maqtûl*—the slain, killed, or executed *shaykh*. To his disciples he was the *shaykh shahîd*, the martyr, the “true witness on the path of God.” To philosophers, the *Ishrâqîyûn* and others alike, he remains, by tradition, the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*.[^EII2-13]

Brief though his life was, and despite the disruptions of constant travel, Sohrawardî worked with extraordinary energy and produced a substantial body of writing. His biographer Shahrazôrî compiled the most complete list: about fifty works and shorter treatises in Arabic and Persian, most of which have come down to us. We cannot reproduce the full list here.[^EII2-14]

Let us simply recall that elsewhere we have divided the writings into four groups, according to their structure and purpose.

1) First comes a *trilogy* of three large, systematic treatises. As Sohrawardî conceived them, their purpose is above all preparatory: they equip the reader to study and put into practice a fourth work, the one containing the *shaykh*’s central teaching, the *Book of Eastern Theosophy* (*Kitâb Hikmat al-Ishrâq*).[^EII2-15] All three share the same structure, treating logic, physics, and metaphysics. They examine in detail the fundamental doctrines of Peripatetic philosophy—the Aristotelian tradition—as it was then taught within Islam. Sohrawardî always believed that familiarity with this philosophy was the necessary foundation and starting point of a philosopher’s education, even though the spiritual seeker was obliged to go beyond it. The three works generally maintain the severe tone of technical argument. Yet more than once the writing bursts open under the pressure of a lyrical inspiration, denouncing the wretchedness of those who are spiritually blind or anticipating the secret entrusted to the *Book of Eastern Theosophy*. We shall have much more to say about that book.

2) Next is a group of *Opera minora*, some eight shorter works in Arabic and Persian. Like the writings of the trilogy, each generally begins with an account of theoretical problems and ends at the threshold of mystical experience.

3) A third group forms a cycle of about ten short Persian works, cast as parables or stories of initiation. Together with the *shaykh*’s great book, these are the writings most characteristic of Sohrawardî’s spirituality. They are no longer teaching manuals but genuinely *’irfânî* works, writings concerned with inward spiritual knowledge. The theoretical discussion has ended. Their purpose is to draw the reader into the movement of their “story,” to make it the reader’s own story, and so to lead the reader onto the Path. That is why we shall give them particular attention, translating two of them below.

4) Finally, standing apart, there is a collection of writings that together form a kind of “Book of Hours”: freely composed hymns that give liturgical expression to the *Ishrâq*. They include invocations addressed to archangelic powers, as well as exhortations and psalms inspired by visions of the last things. At times one can hear an echo of Manichaean devotion, as in this invocation: “Raise up the litany of Light, give victory to the people of Light, guide Light toward Light.”[^EII2-16]

##### 2. — The Lineage of the *Ishrâqîyûn*, or “Eastern” Theosophers

To understand fully what Sohrawardî intended and accomplished, one must read his great book, the *Kitâb Hikmat al-Ishrâq*. We have already devoted many years of work to this book, and we intend to publish a complete translation of it.

Yet such a translation cannot be separated from the work of the commentators who developed the *ishrâqî* doctrine in Iran, century after century. Inevitably, then, the translation as a whole will have to be extensive.[^EII2-17] Here we can only touch on the matter and recall why elsewhere we have translated the title as *Theosophy of the Orient of Lights*, or, more simply, *The Book of Eastern Theosophy*.

A few statements by the author are enough to convey the atmosphere of the book and suggest what our *shaykh* meant by the great family of *Ishrâqîyûn*, the “Eastern” theosophers, for whom he wrote the work that held the great undertaking of his young life. He closes it with these words: “Brothers, I entrust this book to your care.

“Watch over it; protect it from the unworthy, the profane. May it, by God, stand in my place among you as my successor [my ‘caliph’]. I finished composing it at the end of the month of Jomâdâ II in the year 582 of the Hegira, on the day when the seven planets were in conjunction in the sign of Libra.”

One of its commentators, Qotboddîn Shîrâzî (d. 710/1310–1311 or 716/1316–1317), observes here that the date was Tuesday the twenty-ninth of that month—16 September 1186 in our calendar—and that the appearance of this magnificent book on that very day was among the effects of the extraordinary conjunction. Sohrawardî continues: “The Holy Spirit inspired this book in my heart all at once, on a marvellous day, although because of the difficulties caused by my travels I was unable to put it into writing until after several months.”[^EII2-18]

This was not, then, a book composed in the comfortable quiet of a scholar’s study. It came from a long period of gestation: reading, meditation, conversations while travelling slowly along the long roads of Iran and Anatolia, where chance made possible so many encounters and discoveries. And then, suddenly, came the “marvellous day” when the entire book, still in the form of an idea, rose before Sohrawardî’s mind. In that book his whole undertaking to establish a new theosophical vision at last took definite form, “under the inspiration of the Holy Spirit”—that is, of the angel Gabriel, who for the philosophers of Islam is both the Angel of Revelation and the Angel of Knowledge.

Certain pages of the great *Trilogy* already refer to this book, suggesting that he must have been writing the works side by side. Several allusions help us understand what he sought so feverishly, and why he undertook the long journeys recalled in the account of his life, despite the obstacles they placed in the way of writing. In the third work of the *Trilogy*, at the end of a long discussion of the problem of being, directed chiefly against the school of the Avicennian Ibn Sahlân, already mentioned here, Sohrawardî says: “These people have no means of escaping the difficulty, for the arguments we have set out at length admit of no trickery.

“The experienced investigator will become certain that the constructions advanced by these philosophers are utterly futile, and that all they are doing is wasting time. It is through the emergence of such philosophical speculations that wisdom—theosophy (*hikmat*)—is interrupted, the higher sciences of the spiritual Journey are erased, and the road to the *Malakût*, the spiritual kingdom, is closed. In the end, all that remains is heaps of writings.

“Yet there are people who, putting on the appearance of philosophers, allow themselves to be seduced by these things. They think that merely reading books can give a man a place among those who possess wisdom, without his having to enter the path of the spiritual world himself, without personally experiencing the vision of the spiritual Beings of Light.

“As for us, we have set down in a book what God revealed especially to us concerning these sublime sciences—things of which our predecessors were indeed given an overall glimpse, but which we have been granted the ability to unfold in detail. Their exposition will be found in our book entitled *Eastern Theosophy*. We have even invented a special script for this book, so that no one may become acquainted with its contents except the person approved by the Maintainer of the Book (*Qayyim al-Kitâb*), after the latter has verified that the necessary conditions are fulfilled.

“‘To whom God gives no light, what light shall he have?’ (Qur’an 24:40). For just as a mystic who lacks philosophical ability is incomplete, so too a philosopher who does not possess, along with his philosophy, a personal vision of the Signs and of the *malakût* is incomplete—a person not to be greatly esteemed, a man to whom the spiritual world has never spoken.”[^EII2-19]

Already this passage sets out the guiding thought of Sohrawardî’s fundamental work and the basic teaching of *ishrâqî* spirituality.

Another passage, from the conclusion of that same work, confirms it: “If the road toward God had not been cut off in our time, we would not have endured so much sadness, nor suffered the irritation of such grief. I am now approaching my thirtieth year. I have spent most of my life travelling, investigating, searching for a companion fully initiated into these things; but I have found no one informed about the Higher Sciences, nor anyone who believes in them.

“Brothers! This is the testament I leave you: let every concern other than the divine world fall away from you; let your only concern be perseverance in the work of mystical detachment (*tajrîd*). The key to all these things is placed in my book of *Eastern Theosophy*. Nowhere here have we dealt with them as we have dealt with them there.

“We even devised a special script for that book, to prevent its contents from becoming widely known. We believe that, even if the beginner cannot recognize its importance, the experienced investigator will at least understand that I have had no predecessor in writing such a book, and that it contains hidden dwelling places.”[^EII2-20]

We have found a trace of this secret script, to which the author has just referred twice, in at least one manuscript. It bears a strange resemblance to a secret alphabet used by the Ismailis.[^EII2-21] Is that merely a coincidence? The *shaykh* speaks of his solitary years, spent searching for a companion who shared his initiation. The search, he says, was in vain, so thoroughly had the field of the Higher Sciences been laid waste.

Yet had not the “Great Resurrection,” inaugurating a purely spiritual Islam, been proclaimed at the fortress of Alamût on 8 August 1164, in the mountains southwest of the Caspian Sea that Sohrawardî must have known?[^EII2-22] Might there not have been a possible companion there? We have also noted in passing the expression “Maintainer of the Book.” Sohrawardî may well have been looking far into the future, imagining something like an “Order of the *Ishrâqîyûn*” that would survive him, headed by an “Imam” who would hold his teaching in trust and initiate others into the secret of his *Book of Eastern Theosophy*.

But here we encounter another strange correspondence. The expression “Maintainer of the Book” is precisely the one used in Shiite *hadith* going back to the holy Imams, where it names the Imam’s essential function as guardian of the sacred Book’s secret interpretation: “the Book is the silent Imam, and the Imam is the speaking Book.” So a Shiite reader encountering this expression in Sohrawardî’s text could quite naturally understand it as referring to the Imam.[^EII2-23] And a Shiite of Sohrawardî’s own day would have shared his grief at the devastation of the Higher Sciences.

We cannot fail to take these signs seriously; others will come to support them. Both passages seem to point toward a final secret, whose key must be sought from the person who maintains and guards the Book—as though the boldness of what the book already states concealed an undertaking reaching further still. Both passages show us Sohrawardî the wanderer, searching for his spiritual family, conscious of the lineage to which he belongs and whose sublime wisdom, he repeatedly declares, he has undertaken to revive.

Yet he is just as conscious that, in pursuing this particular undertaking, he has had no predecessor.

Whom, exactly, did Sohrawardî have in mind when he spoke of the *Ishrâqîyûn*, the “Eastern” philosophers or theosophers? The only fully satisfying answer must come from Sohrawardî’s writings taken as a whole, and from the mystical idea of the “Orient” that emerges from them.

But we should first ask whether this name was unknown before his time. In fact it was not entirely unknown; we can find traces of it. One brief and curious indication appears in a context that helps explain the reverence with which Sohrawardî brings together the names of Hermes and Zarathustra, or Zoroaster. Islam has a long Hermetic tradition, and Sohrawardî’s undertaking to “revive” the wisdom of the ancient Persians also belongs within it.

Moreover, traces of “Eastern” philosophers can be found in his illustrious predecessor Avicenna. Sohrawardî himself offered explanations of this that we must keep in mind, for they reveal the spiritual ancestry he claimed for himself and, through him, for the *Ishrâqîyûn*—the name by which the disciples of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* would subsequently be known.

A famous and prolific writer, himself something of a Hermeticist (d. 291/903), makes the following observation in an essay describing the different classes of Egyptian priests: “The third class of these priests were called *Ishrâqîyûn*, or the children of the sister of Hermes, who is known in Greek as Hermes Trismegistus. Their parables and allegories have come down to us.”[^EII2-24] This is precisely the Hermetic ancestry that Sohrawardî repeatedly claims for himself. He regards Hermes not only as the ancestor of all wisdom, but also as the archetypal hero of mystical ecstasy (below, Chapter VI). For its part, the Islamic Hermetic tradition identifies Hermes with Idrîs, and Idrîs with the prophet Enoch.[^EII2-25]

Another equally significant piece of information appears in the commentary written by ’Abdorrazzâq Kâshânî (d. around 730/1330) on Mohyiddîn Ibn ’Arabî’s famous manual of mystical theosophy, the *Fosûs al-Hikam* (*The Bezels of the Wisdoms of the Prophets*—the “bezels” are the settings of precious stones). In that book, each prophet is contemplated not simply as belonging to a particular period in chronological history, but as embodying a degree in the hierarchy of being and wisdom.

The commentator specifies that Seth, the son of Adam, is the prophet and initiator of the *Ishrâqîyûn*.[^EII2-26] Among the *Ishrâqîyûn*, Seth is traditionally identified with Agathodaimon; in Sohrawardî’s writings the name Agathodaimon is most often mentioned together with that of Hermes. This is all the more interesting because certain ancient Gnostics, called Sethians on account of their veneration of Seth, regarded Christ as a manifestation of Seth.

Seth, moreover, was identified with Zoroaster, who in a famous prophecy identified himself with the saviour to come—“I am he, and he is I”—the *Saoshyant*, who would be born of his line and would one day renew the world.[^EII2-27] All these indications are rich in meaning for a phenomenology of religion that seeks to discover the intentions through which these figures “show themselves” to consciousness and through which these connections are established among them.

Finally, if we turn to a classic reference work in the Islamic world, the *Book of Definitions* by Sharîf Gorgânî (d. around 818/1415–1416), we read: “The Peripatetic philosophers (*mashsha’ûn*) are those whose master is Aristotle. The *ishrâqîyûn* philosophers are those whose master is Plato.”[^EII2-28] Accordingly, in the prologue to his great book Sohrawardî speaks of “the Imam of wisdom, our master Plato.”

Hermes, Zoroaster, Plato: these three great figures dominate the horizon of the *Ishrâqîyûn*, the “Platonists of Persia” who followed Sohrawardî. Other figures would join them, drawn from Iran’s past or chosen from among the Greek sages, who also, it was believed, drew their light from the “Niche of the Lights of Prophecy.”

Together they would make up the *silsilat al-’irfân*, the “sacred lineage of gnosis,” or spiritual knowledge. The spiritual perceptions and visionary ecstasies of its great figures furnished so many precedents for the Prophet of Islam’s heavenly ascent (*Mi’râj*). Across the centuries, the story of that ascent, in its many versions and elaborations, became an archetype for the meditation of mystical theosophers in Islam.

And when the Platonists of Islamic Persia interpreted Plato’s Ideas in terms of Zoroastrian angelology, were they not intuitively rediscovering a situation known to us through the accounts of Eudoxus of Cnidus? For Eudoxus tells us of the interest, even the enthusiasm, that prevailed in Plato’s Academy for Zarathustra. We know, moreover, from a papyrus discovered at Herculaneum listing the members of the Platonic Academy, that during Plato’s final years the Academy included a “Chaldean”—that is, an Achaemenid subject from Mesopotamia. This person may have been the source of Eudoxus’s report, and of the edifying parallels it drew between Zarathustra and Plato.[^EII2-29]

Whatever the case, Sohrawardî’s great undertaking cannot be “explained” simply by collecting its antecedents. Rather, the reverse is true: ultimately it is Sohrawardî himself, his own person, who explains how those antecedents came together. For anyone convinced that a creative intuition is not something to be explained but is itself the source and principle of explanation, no accumulation of earlier influences could ever account for the birth of such an undertaking. It is the creative intuition that first makes those earlier things its antecedents.

We can already see how Sohrawardî understood his own position from the words he uses. He treats *Ishrâq* (the Orient as the moment when the sun rises, the illumination of dawn) and *mashriq* (the Orient as a place, the land in the East) as equivalent terms. So too with *Ishrâqîyûn* and *Mashriqîyûn* (the Easterners), and with *Hikmat ishrâqîya* and *Hikmat mashriqîya* (Eastern Theosophy). His disciples and commentators, generation after generation, did the same.

Yet long before Sohrawardî—who has remained almost unknown in the West down to our own time—his illustrious predecessor Avicenna, a name familiar to Western readers for centuries through medieval Latin translations, was himself said to have conceived a project for an “Eastern” philosophy (*mashriqîya*).

We must therefore ask Sohrawardî himself how he understood his relationship to Avicenna, for the answer is of decisive importance to the meaning of the present book.

We have already discussed this question at some length elsewhere, both in editing the works of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* and in a book on Avicenna. We do not intend to reopen the debate here. We have preferred to seek an answer in Sohrawardî’s own statements, because they seem to us far more directly relevant than the hypotheses proposed by various modern scholars.[^EII2-30]

Let us simply recall the broad outline. The question was needlessly tangled by a misreading made in the West during the nineteenth century, through ignorance of the state of philosophy in Iran, even down to our own day. Why, instead of reading *mashriqîya* (“Eastern”), did someone decide to read *moshriqîya* and give the word the meaning of “illuminative” philosophy? For many reasons, this latter word, even if theoretically possible, could never have been the name of a school of philosophers.

This was demonstrated by the famous Italian Orientalist C. Nallino in a paper published in 1925, whose arguments and conclusion everyone then contented themselves with repeating for a long time. The first misfortune was that this victorious demonstration proved what should never have been in doubt. Any Iranian *shaykh* teaching *hikmat ilâhîya*, divine wisdom, or any of his students, could have told us long ago, had anyone thought to ask, that no one in Iran had ever read the word as anything but *mashriqîya*, “Eastern” philosophy.

The second misfortune was that Nallino, neglecting the context of the gloss by Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî that had set him on the right path, wanted to go much further. He artificially separated the *Ishrâqîyûn* from the *Mashriqîyûn*. According to him, the former, whom he called “Illuminationists,” belonged exclusively to Sohrawardî, whereas the latter, the “Easterners,” were the philosophers Avicenna had in mind.

Now, he was right to think that Avicenna’s “Eastern” philosophy—announced in his great work, the *Kitâb al-Shifâ*, as the work that would contain his own philosophy—would, had it survived in full, have been something different from Sohrawardî’s *ishrâqî* philosophy. Without such a difference there would have been no *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, no distinct philosophy of Sohrawardî.

But it was wrong to declare that the *Ishrâqîyûn* were not *Mashriqîyûn*. How, indeed, could anyone make such a claim while holding the old Iranian lithographed edition of Sohrawardî’s *Eastern Theosophy*, where it is easy to see that both Sohrawardî and his commentators use *ishrâqîyûn* and *mashriqîyûn* interchangeably for the same idea? I can explain this insistence only as an extraordinary aversion to the Neoplatonists, especially Iamblichus and the great Proclus.

Nallino’s extreme rationalism allowed him to see nothing in the Neoplatonists but “extravagances” (*sic*). At all costs, heaven knows why, Avicenna had to be kept safe from such compromising company. It is true that the few surviving “notebooks” of Avicenna, believed to preserve his *Logic of the Easterners*, contain nothing *ishrâqî* in Sohrawardî’s sense.

But it would be altogether false to claim that Avicenna’s “Notes” in the margins of the so-called *Theology of Aristotle*[^EII2-31]—a text we now know to be a reworking of Plotinus’s *Enneads*—or an Avicennian mystical narrative such as the *Story of the Bird*, have nothing in common with Sohrawardî’s undertaking.

In short, from Sohrawardî’s point of view, and in keeping with his own statements, the situation can be summed up as follows. Avicenna wrote a large work entitled *Kitâb al-Insâf wa’l-Intisâf*, something like *The Book of Making Just Distinctions*. It was an extensive work in which he distinguished the “Easterners” from other philosophers. Unfortunately, the manuscript of this still unfinished work, which would have contained Avicenna’s “Eastern philosophy,” was lost—apart from a few fragments—during the sack of Isfahan in 1034.[^EII2-32] Avicenna did not live long enough to reconstruct it.

Sohrawardî refers, on the one hand, to fragments of this *Kitâb al-Insâf*, and, on the other, to scattered notebooks surviving from an incomplete and damaged whole. They contain a logic whose teachings Avicenna associated with the “Easterners.” Sohrawardî rightly observes that, despite this attribution, the notebooks contain little more than Peripatetic theses and belong to ordinary philosophy. Their authentic connection with the “Eastern source” has therefore not been established.

For Sohrawardî this is the central question. When he speaks of “Eastern philosophy,” he means the philosophy that springs from the “Eastern” teaching of the sages of ancient Persia, whom he calls the *Khosrawânîyûn*, for reasons we shall soon discover. His position is this: Avicenna was undoubtedly the first to attempt to establish an “Eastern” teaching distinct from Peripatetic philosophy.

But because he had no access to the “Eastern source” (*asl mashriqî*), he could not bring his undertaking to completion. Henceforth anyone wishing to be initiated into the philosophy and theosophy of the “Easterners” must turn to Sohrawardî himself.

This is not the place to reopen the problem of “Eastern philosophy” in Avicenna’s own writings. What concerns us is Sohrawardî’s position as a whole. For a closer examination, we can sum it up in three propositions. 1) As Sohrawardî conceived and realized it, the philosophy of *Ishrâq* considers itself to be Eastern philosophy. Precisely for that reason it is also a philosophy of illumination: it prepares the soul to receive “Eastern flashes,” the archangelic Lights that “rise and shed their light” upon it. It provides the ontological and phenomenological foundation for this “Eastern” experience—that is, an account of its reality and of how it reveals itself.

As we shall see again, it is “illuminative” because it is “Eastern,” and “Eastern” because it is “illuminative.” This is the true relationship, in Sohrawardî’s thought, between the meanings carried by the two terms *Ishrâq* and *mashriq*. 2) Avicenna’s idea of the Orient and Sohrawardî’s idea of the Orient have something in common insofar as the Orient is understood in its true sense: metaphysically, not geographically.

In Avicenna, this Orient appears in the *Story of Hayy ibn Yaqzân*, in the commentary on the Verse of Light (Qur’an 24:35), in the *Story of the Bird*, and in references found in the “Notes” written in the margins of the so-called *Theology of Aristotle*. In Sohrawardî, it is the Orient understood as the universe of archangelic Lights, arising from the “Light of Glory” (*Xvarnah*) and surrounding the Light of Lights with a radiance, with all the Orients that form its ascending degrees.

But 3) there is a profound difference in what each personally accomplished as a spiritual realization. Sohrawardî expresses it most clearly in the prologue to his *Story of the Western Exile* (below, Chapter VI). And the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* knew perfectly well the reasons for this difference. To bring the “Eastern source” back to life—the teachings and symbols of the sages of ancient Persia—was his own work, an undertaking in which he had no predecessor, since Avicenna, not knowing that source, had been unable to complete his.

He expresses this conviction repeatedly, for example in a treatise devoted specifically to Sufism. Sohrawardî writes: “Among the ancient Persians (*fî’l-Fors*) there was a community of men guided by God (*al-Haqq*) who therefore walked upon the straight path, eminent sages possessed of divine wisdom, unlike the Magi (*Majûs*). It is their precious theosophy of Light—the very wisdom witnessed in the mystical experience of Plato and his predecessors—that we have revived in our book entitled *Eastern Theosophy*. And in pursuing such an undertaking I had no forerunner.”[^EII2-33]

A passage like this widens the scope of our inquiry still further. Brief though it is, it has the force of a manifesto. It states the author's purpose plainly: to bring back to life the wisdom, or theosophy, taught in ancient Persia by a group of sages whose teachings and spiritual life were in harmony with those of Plato and the early Greek sages.

Two features tell us precisely what kind of sages these ancient Persians were. To establish the first, the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*—the Master of Illumination—uses *ta’wîl*, an interpretive reading that brings different moments of sacred history into relation.

A verse of the Quran says: “Among the people of Moses there was a community of men who were guided by God and followed the straight path” (7:159). Through this interpretive transposition, Sohrawardî applies to the sages of ancient Persia what the Quran says about a chosen group among the people of Moses.

The second feature completes the first. Because these Persian sages were guided by God, Sohrawardî is careful not to let them be confused with those commonly called the *Majûs*. In both Persian and Arabic, this is the usual name for the “Magi,” the followers of the ancient Iranian religion.

But how are we to reconcile these claims? At the very moment when Sohrawardî affirms his spiritual descent from the sages of ancient Persia, he expressly rejects the impiety of the “Magi.”

Yet for us, historically, that name designates the bearers of Iran's ancient Mazdean wisdom—the very wisdom Sohrawardî wishes to “resurrect.” What are we to make of this? The question matters, because the entire meaning of Sohrawardî's undertaking depends on the answer.

Put simply, the Magi whom Sohrawardî rejects are those who professed a radical dualism: the belief that the two Principles, Light and Darkness, have existed eternally alongside one another. This is not the doctrine he intended to revive.

We shall see later how he explains the metaphysical meaning of the opposition symbolized by these two Principles. His account agrees with what we learn from Shahrastânî (d. 1153), that outstanding early historian of religions.

Shahrastânî's account can be summed up in three points. 1) The Magi (*Majûs*) are the radical dualists. 2) The original Magi (*al-Majûs al-aslîya*), however, did not teach that two distinct Principles were equally eternal in their very being.

They differed instead over how Darkness came into existence, while preserving the primacy of Light. 3) Zoroaster himself belonged to these original Magi. They held that Light and Darkness came from one Principle, but “explained” evil as the result of Darkness becoming mixed with Light.

Zoroaster could thus be understood as another prophet of the One God, who has no partner, opposite, or equal. The outlines of Zoroaster's teaching found in Shahrastânî, in Sohrawardî, and much later in Qotboddîn Ashkevârî, a disciple of Mîr Dâmâd in the seventeenth century, agree with one another.[^EII2-34]

This picture of Zoroaster, the prophet of ancient Persia, and of his Magi presupposes a whole history of religious developments, above all the steady westward movement of Zoroastrian Magianism.

From Bactria, at the far eastern edge of the Iranian world, Zoroastrianism in its Sasanian and post-Sasanian forms came to be established in the western Iranian lands.

Zoroaster himself then came to be thought of as a native of Azerbaijan. The sacred geography of the Avesta was reversed, as though it had turned around an imaginary axis.[^EII2-35]

Yet this was only one stage of the movement “westward,” one part of a larger pattern whose coherence some future phenomenological study might reveal.

That study would have to follow the successive rebirths of Zoroaster and his Magi in human consciousness, asking in each case what conditions of consciousness made these figures appear as they did—from the great Byzantine reformer George Gemistos Plethon in the fifteenth century, all the way to Friedrich Nietzsche.

Although we can deal with these matters only in broad outline, we must recall a series of developments of enormous importance for the religious destiny of humanity. From its base in the western part of the Iranian world, Zoroastrian Magianism spread farther west along two routes.

One route ran southwest, toward Chaldea. Had Babylon not long served as the Great King's winter residence? The encounter with Chaldean wisdom gave rise to what we may call Magian-Chaldeanism, which passed through Syria to Alexandria. That city had become an intellectual center of Hellenism and, more immediately important to us, a center of Neoplatonism.

A shared religious and philosophical passion among kindred minds made possible an encounter between Platonism, Orphism, Hermeticism, and Magian-Chaldean thought.

The echoes of that encounter can still be heard in Sohrawardî's work, within Islam. It was from this spiritual setting that the famous text known as the *Oracula chaldaïca*, or *Chaldean Oracles*, emerged.

Gemistos Plethon, and probably others before him, attributed these oracles to Zoroaster. In fact, they were composed in the second half of the second century by two devout theosophers: Julian the Chaldean and his son, Julian the Theurgist.[^EII2-36]

Written in an obscure symbolic language, the *Chaldean Oracles*—“Chaldean” here being a rather loose ethnic designation—concern the knowledge of *noetic* beings: beings of the intelligible world who govern our own. The means of communicating with them are likewise noetic, that is, spiritual.

The text profoundly influenced the Neoplatonist philosophers. Iamblichus, Syrianus, Proclus, and others wrote extensive commentaries on it, treating its difficult sayings almost as though they belonged to a sacred scripture.

As these Neoplatonists understood and contemplated them—and we shall return to them in a few pages when discussing Sohrawardî's vocabulary—the *Oracula*, or *Logia*, present something like a “Hellenized Magianism.”

Yet this Magianism, fashioned by Neoplatonists drawn toward the East, no longer teaches the radical dualism of the *Majûs*, the Magi condemned by Sohrawardî. It accords instead with the picture of Zoroaster as a prophet of the One God, and with Shahrastânî's understanding of the “original Magi.”

Sohrawardî will prefer to call these sages the *Khosrawânîyûn*; we shall see why.

The other route led northwest, through Asia Minor—to Armenia, Pontus, and Cappadocia. The Magi of Asia Minor are commonly known as the Maguseans.[^EII2-37] They certainly acknowledged Zoroaster as the founder of their rites and mysteries, but Zurvanite doctrine predominated among them.

At the same time, Mithra and the mysteries devoted to him took the central place. In the Avesta, by contrast, Mithra is only one of the *Yazatas*, the divine beings created by Ahura Mazda, the “Lord Wisdom.”

As we know, the mysteries of Mithra eventually spread throughout the Roman Empire, reaching Britain, Gaul, and Spain.

Sadly, only the remains of monuments and fragments of ravaged literatures allow us to trace this extraordinary expansion of Iranian Magianism. Hermippus, a celebrated librarian of the great library of Alexandria, not only wrote a multivolume work *On the Magi*.

According to Pliny, he also compiled a catalogue of writings attributed to Zoroaster—or, more precisely, to the Magi of his school: works placed under his authority because they had been composed in the spirit of his teaching.

Altogether, they amounted to two million lines: an entire library in itself. Only scattered fragments and passing references survive. The *Oracula chaldaïca* mentioned above must have formed part of that literature.

But it has taken the immense labor of patient scholars to recover what remains of them—some four hundred verses, preserved as quotations scattered through the surviving writings of the Neoplatonist philosophers.

As for the Magi of Mithra, the Maguseans of Asia Minor, we owe to Dio Chrysostom (second century) a passage from their psalter: one of the hymns which, he tells us, “Zoroaster and the children of the Magi sang, having learned it from him.”[^EII2-38]

In this hymn, Zoroastrian teachings mingle with Stoic ideas. It tells the symbolic story of the cosmic chariot and its four horses, representing the four Elements.

We find something similar in the four pillars of the Throne described by Islamic gnostics, who had themselves learned, by one route or another, of the *tetramorph*—the fourfold figure in Ezekiel’s vision.

We shall also have occasion later to recall the text known as the “Liturgy of Mithra.”

Faced with so many losses, so much accumulated ruin, scholars of religion remain inconsolable even today.

But Sohrawardî's response was characteristic of the man. He would not be content simply to mourn. He would be a “resurrector,” one who brings a lost wisdom back to life.

And we see him setting about the task, certain of his path, once he has cleared away the misunderstanding concerning those Magi whose radical dualism had made them unfaithful to the true teaching of the ancient Persian sages.

His own spiritual experience will appeal to the testimony of Zoroaster's visions: visions of the blazing Light of Glory, of the Lights of the divine Heptad, and so on.

Now, in the “hieratic ascent” described by the *Chaldean Oracles*, the same imagery of Light and Fire predominates: the hymn of Fire, the flower of Fire, the paths of Fire, the most holy living Fire worshipped in the silence of the soul's sanctuary.

We may also sense an echo of the psalter of the Magi of Mithra in the hymns that Sohrawardî addressed to the Angel of the Sun and to the “Perfect Nature” (see below, III, 5).

Throughout his writings, in other words, we find scattered features of the same kind as those which led certain Neoplatonists, and later Gemistos Plethon, to recognize an affinity between the *Chaldean Oracles* and the theosophy of Zoroaster's Magi.[^EII2-39] It was the same intuition that led the Byzantine philosopher to bring the names of Plato and Zoroaster together.

We may even wonder whether his teacher, the mysterious Jew Elisha—who introduced him to the name of Zoroaster and was said to have been a disciple of Averroes—was not, rather, a wandering *ishrâqî* who had found his way to Anatolia.

Three centuries before Gemistos Plethon, Sohrawardî had already brought the names and teachings of Plato and Zoroaster together within Islam.

But the Byzantine and the Iranian philosophers pursued their work in very different circumstances. Through Gemistos Plethon, the “Hellenized Magi” would be carried still farther west, to his friends in the Platonic Academy of Florence.

Plethon's aim was to place a great philosophical and religious reform under Zoroaster's patronage: a religion of the future that would overcome, and make people forget, the antagonism between the religion of Christ and the religion of Muhammad.

Our *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, by contrast, feels no such opposition that must be overcome. For him, the spiritual resources of Islamic gnosis itself—*hikmat* and *’irfân*, wisdom and mystical knowledge—make it possible to bring about the rebirth of the sages of ancient Persia.

Seen in this light, Sohrawardî's work completes a magnificent circuit that began with the two migrations of Magianism to the southwest and northwest.

It is as though Zoroaster's Magi, having clothed themselves during their westward travels in Chaldean wisdom and the Platonism of the Neoplatonists drawn toward the East, now needed Sohrawardî to bring them home to Persia—but to the Islamic Persia of the twelfth century, carrying all the treasures of mystical theosophy that their disciples had gathered under their inspiration.

To bring them home was, above all, to reconnect this Platonizing Magianism with the Avestan tradition, of which Sohrawardî certainly knew a few authentic fragments—those concerning the *xvarnah*, the Light of Glory, and the world of angels—and with the heroic traditions of ancient Iran, preserved within Islamic Persia by Ferdawsî's *Shâh-Nâmeh*, the *Book of Kings*.

Through this rebirth, the heroic epic of ancient Iran begins to unfold as a mystical epic. It will be one of the most compelling aspects of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*'s vast and intricate work (see Chapter V below).

What sustains him is his sense of belonging to a spiritual family scattered across the earth, yet bound together by an invisible, unbreakable bond, as closely united as the branches of a single great tree. It is the great tree of Wisdom, whose branches never cease to grow and spread, nourished by a mysterious sap.

Sohrawardî gives this sap the form of an “Eternal Leaven,” a living ferment that passes mystically from spirit to spirit. No “sufficient reason” drawn from history can explain its movement if we look only at the machinery of demonstrable causes.

Strengthened by the certainty of his spiritual ancestry, by his gratitude for it, and by the duty it lays upon him, he can devote himself to his work as a “resurrector.”

Thus he writes: “We have entrusted the knowledge of True Reality to our book entitled *Theosophy of the Orient*.

“In it we have revived the ancient wisdom that the Imams of India, Persia (*Fârs*), Chaldea, and Egypt, and those of the ancient Greeks down to Plato, always took as their central point of reference, drawing from it their own theosophy. This wisdom is the Eternal Leaven (*al-Khamîrat al-azalîya*).”[^EII2-40]

It is this idea of the Leaven, like sap spreading through the branches of the tree of Wisdom, that leads Sohrawardî, on the final pages of his *Crossroads and Conversations*, to sketch the spiritual “family tree” of the *Ishrâqîyûn*, the philosophers of Illumination.

The outward opposition between Greek sages and “Eastern” sages disappears. Both are “guardians of the Logos” (*Kalimat*), one group on the “western side,” the other on the “eastern side.”

Sohrawardî's account allows us to picture this family tree as follows.[^EII2-41] At its root stands Hermes, the father of the sages. From him imagine two great branches.

On the “eastern side” stand the ancient Persian sages (the *Pahlawîyûn*): Gayomart, the primordial king, followed by two heroes whose deeds, belonging to an age before Zarathustra or Zoroaster, are already celebrated in the Avesta—the sacred kings Fereydûn and Kay Khosraw.

The ecstatic sages who came after them were called *Khosrawânîyûn*, after Kay Khosraw (see Chapter IV below). Sohrawardî sees their spiritual leaven reaching him through three Sufi masters: Abû Yazîd Bastâmî (the “wanderer” of Bastâm), Mansûr Hallâj (the *fatâ*, or “knight,” of Bayza), and Abû’l-Hasan Kharraqânî (the wanderer of Amâl and Kharraqân).[^EII2-42]

On the “western side” stand Asclepius, Empedocles, Pythagoras, and Plato. The leaven of the Pythagoreans then passes into Islam through Akhî Akhmîm (Dhû’l-Nûn Misrî) and Abû Sahl Tostarî.[^EII2-43]

At last the two sides come together, like the curved branches of a cypress meeting at its crown, in a community of spiritual seekers whose speech becomes the instrument of the Sakîna.

This last word calls for a long explanation. For Sohrawardî, its meaning reaches back to one of the most fundamental Zoroastrian ideas he brought back to life: that of the luminous Presence, the Light of Glory, the *Xvarnah* (see Chapter III below).

Here, too, we find the spiritual ancestry that, in Sohrawardî's thought and experience, links the mystics of Islam to the mystical theosophers of ancient Persia.

Let us gather a few essential points. For Sohrawardî and the mystics close to him, the Sakîna is above all the experience of a Presence made known by a sign, or by signs. These are not perceived through our ordinary physical senses, but through “spiritual senses” able to perceive the intermediate, or *imaginal*, world.

The Arabic word *Sakîna* corresponds to the Hebrew *Shekhinah*, a concept of great importance in the Kabbalah and one that, broadly speaking, can be understood in Jewish religious consciousness as the personal embodiment, or hypostasis, of God's Presence in the world.[^EII2-44]

More directly, the Arabic word suggests stillness, trust, and gentleness. Its root, *skn*, carries the idea of dwelling in a home, of resting in a presence that brings quiet, peace, and security.

Quranic verses evoking this idea have received extensive commentary. One of them says: “Those who believe, and whose hearts find peace in the remembrance of God—yes, it is in the remembrance of God (*dhikr Allâh*) that their hearts find peace” (13:28). Stillness, peace: *itmî’nân*.

Another verse answers it: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord” (89:27–28). It is precisely this *itmî’nân*—the soul's serenity as an unshakable certainty of faith in what it has itself seen—that the Fifth Imam, Mohammad al-Bâqir, invokes when commenting on yet another verse: “It is God who sends down the *sakîna* into the hearts of believers, so that they may add faith to their faith” (48:4).[^EII2-45]

He goes on to explain that those upon whom the *sakîna* descends are the people spoken of in this verse: “He strengthens them [inspires them, gives them strength] with a Spirit from Himself” (58:22). They are also those described in the *hadîth*: “In my community there are those who speak, and there are those to whom [the angels] speak”—the *mohaddathûn*.

The central idea, then, is of a Presence that comes to dwell within the soul. For Sohrawardî, that Presence takes a particular form: blazing Lights, all those luminous phenomena (*photisms*) and revelations of light that he experienced before Najmoddîn Kobrâ and his school would describe similar experiences.[^EII2-46]

When these Lights reach their greatest intensity, they become steady and remain for a time. This is what is called the *sakîna*.[^EII2-47] Sohrawardî speaks of “those who possess the greater Sakîna” (*al-Sakînat al-kobrâ*). His commentators explain that he means “those in whom the spiritual Lights and the flashing radiances remain as a lasting presence.”[^EII2-48]

That is also why the passage quoted above, where the two currents of mystical leaven meet and join in the community of the Sakîna, opens into an account of the different states of the Light of Glory, the Zoroastrian *Xvarnah*.[^EII2-49] It is in the form of Sakîna-*Xvarnah* that the two mystical traditions come together among the *Ishrâqîyûn*.

Sohrawardî's conviction that this union establishes their spiritual ancestry opens a path not yet explored by comparative theology and the study of mysticism.

For the luminous Presence that comes to dwell in purified souls is the same Presence that invested and guided the blessed kings Fereydûn and Kay Khosraw. It is also the Presence that revealed itself to Moses, when a voice called to him from within the burning bush for a secret encounter (28:30).

And Kay Khosraw's experience becomes the model for the illumination of a soul that has itself become the burning bush.

So the *ishrâqî* interpretation reads the Quranic Verse of Light: “God is the Light of the heavens and the earth. This light is like a hearth containing a lamp, a lamp within crystal ... and it is light upon light” (24:35).[^EII2-50]

Of course, when Sohrawardî traces the ancestry of the *Ishrâqîyûn* in this way, he is not writing an objective history of philosophy or mysticism. He is describing the history of souls as he perceives it within the history of his own soul, where that history takes place.

It would therefore be quite beside the point for a historian to object that his picture of the past is a construction of the mind, simply because it does not fit neatly with our historical records.

Such an objection would miss the only history Sohrawardî means to tell: the history he himself brings into being and *is*, not as an outward sequence of deeds, but as something lived in the innermost depths of his being.

It is when his spiritual perception brings that history into the present that the predecessors gathered in his family tree truly become the predecessors of the *Ishrâqîyûn*: Sohrawardî himself is both the witness and the evidence.

Time is turned around. It is from his own present, where these earlier figures become part of his living story, that they come to be the predecessors of the *Ishrâqîyûn*.

This is the whole difference—as we have already suggested in Book I—between *existential historicity*, the way history is lived from within, and what is ordinarily called *historical existence*. Unfortunately, the first is sometimes overlooked in favor of the second.

We shall return to the distinction.

Having established what the spiritual ancestry of the *Ishrâqîyûn* means, we may now hope to reach, with them, what Sohrawardî calls the “Eastern source.”

First, we must approach it by asking what this “Eastern” knowledge is, and what entitles its possessors to be called “Eastern” sages.

### CHAPTER II

#### “Eastern” Theosophy

##### 1. Hieratic Wisdom

As we have already had occasion to explain (in Book I), the words *hikmat* and *hokamâ*, though often translated as “philosophy” and “philosophers,” are not adequately rendered by either term. “Theology” and “theologians” would be no more suitable. *Hikmat* and *hokamâ* belong to a different order from scholastic theology (*Kalâm*) and the scholastic theologians of Islam (*Motakallimûn*). Nor is *hikmat* simply philosophy combined with theological debate. The closest translation would be “wisdom” (*sophia*), provided we understand wisdom in its deepest spiritual sense: a wisdom touched by direct mystical knowledge, such as the ecstatic vision of Kay Khosraw will reveal to us (see Chapter IV).

We must not understand it merely in the ordinary sense of practical wisdom or knowledge gained through life. Even the adjective “sapiential,” derived from the Latin *sapientia* (wisdom), no longer conveys clearly enough its original connection with *sapere*: to taste, savor, experience—the *dhaoq* spoken of in our texts. For the thinkers we are studying, knowledge draws upon three sources, each recognized as valid within its own sphere.

First comes tradition (*naql*), which nourishes theology. Second comes the intellect (*’aql*), the instrument of philosophical reasoning, whether in *Kalâm* or in *falsafa*, the Arabic adaptation of the Greek *philosophia*. Finally comes what we may broadly call “spiritual perception,” or direct knowledge of the sacred (*kashf*, literally “unveiling” or “discovery”). This last is the source of the knowledge that constitutes divine wisdom (*hikmat ilâhîya*) and mystical gnosis (*’irfân*). Naturally, mystical gnosis does not disregard the first two sources. It presupposes them, just as the inner, esoteric meaning (*bâtin*) presupposes the outward, exoteric meaning (*zâhir*).

When Sohrawardî and his companions speak of the *hakîm ilâhî*, the “divine sage” or “sage of God,” they are therefore using what is, as we should recall, an exact equivalent of the Greek *theosophos*. *Hikmat ilâhîya*, or often simply *hikmat*, is *Theo-sophia*—divine wisdom in the original meaning of the word.[^EII2-51] “Eastern Theosophy” (*ishrâqîya*) is the wisdom of someone who unites the highest speculative understanding with the deepest spiritual experience.

Indeed, that experience can itself be called “speculative” in the word's original sense: it transforms the sage into a *speculum*, a pure mirror in which the pure Lights rising from the East of the spiritual world are reflected and by which the sage is set ablaze. This is the foundation upon which the hierarchy of “Eastern” sages will be established (see § 2 below).

The perfect “Eastern” sage is a *hakîm mota’allih*. He is not simply a mystic whose experience resembles that of many mystics without philosophical training, or of those who believe such training unnecessary or even dangerous. Nor is he merely a philosopher, like so many others who know nothing of putting philosophy into spiritual practice, of realizing its truth in their own being.
