The complete spiritual experience of this “theosopher”—this *sophos*, or sage of divine *Sophia*—may be described as an experience of divine Wisdom itself.

We must now examine more closely the technical meaning of the terms Sohrawardî uses when he speaks of *ta’alloh*, the spiritual state of the *hakîm mota’allih*. The word *ta’alloh*—formed from the Arabic root *’lh* in its fifth verbal form—carries two related meanings. It denotes both becoming godlike, or assuming a divine form, and worship or devoted service to the divinity. In its first sense, it corresponds to *theôsis*, the term used by Byzantine mystics in Sohrawardî's own time.

Yet if we meditate carefully upon that particularly revealing part of his work consisting of his “tales of initiation” and his “Book of Hours,” we are led to understand his intentions by following a path he himself opened a few pages earlier, when we sought to clarify what he meant by the word “Magi.”

We can follow that path here because he refers to the teachings and exemplary experiences of Zoroaster and Plato. Within his “Eastern Theosophy,” these two names also point toward the Chaldaean Oracles and the Neoplatonic sages. What Sohrawardî calls *ta’alloh* seems, in fact, to have much in common with what the later Neoplatonists called *theurgy*. His *mota’allih*, the sage who has undergone this transformation, shares many characteristics with the figure they called the theurgic or “hieratic” sage. Indeed, the “hieratic” is a category that embraces Sohrawardî's entire vision of the world: in that vision, every species is the “theurgy,” the “hieratic work,” of its Angel.

The Greek word *theourgos* appears to have been coined by the “Chaldaeans” who composed the *Oracles*, toward the end of the second century. Proclus and his school use the name “theurgic sages” collectively for these “Chaldaeans”: all the members of the mystical community known by that rather imprecise name, whose teaching the Neoplatonists themselves brought back to life.[^EII2-52] Whereas theologians are “those who speak of divine things,” theurgists are “those who bring about divine things.” This distinction corresponds exactly to the one Sohrawardî so carefully establishes between the philosopher as such and the *hakîm mota’allih*. The “divine work” can be understood in several ways. Theurgy may be called a divine work because it confers a divine nature upon the human being through the “sacrament of immortality” at the heart of Chaldaean teaching and initiation.

Yet insofar as this making-immortal (*apathanatismos*) appears as the “offspring” of a deification (*apothéôsis*), the word *theurgy* also takes on the metaphysical meaning given to it by the Neoplatonic philosophers. For Iamblichus and Proclus alike, the human intellect is incapable of perceiving the supreme God in the perfection of his nature. Its power extends to the contemplation of the Ideas in their multiplicity, but not to their source: the undivided unity of the *Noêton*, the intelligible—or rather the supra-intelligible—in its absolute oneness. That supreme goal can be reached only through a higher faculty of perception, the “flower of the intellect.”

What takes place is no longer an act of intellectual reasoning. It is the result of a state beyond reason: a living flame kindled in the soul by divine Light, just as a flower is a flame drawn from the depths of the earth by the sun's warmth. As the philosopher Damascius observes, this gnosis, which must be apprehended through the “flower of thought,” is “not an impetuous knowledge; it does not struggle with its object; it does not hurry to seize possession of it; rather, it surrenders itself to it.”[^EII2-53] This *cognitio passiva*, this receptive knowledge, marks the state of union (*enôsis*) described by Plotinus. In different formulations, the gnostics and Sufis of Islam would say much the same thing in their attempts to express the moment when consciousness becomes aware of the presence of the divine Subject—the true subject of the activities taking place within that consciousness.

It is precisely a power of the same kind that enables Sohrawardî's sage to attain the supreme vision of the “Light of Glory.” The Neoplatonists call this power *theurgic*, and the Chaldaean Oracles present it as a necessary condition for the soul's ascent (*anagôgê*).

Thus, among the Neoplatonists, theurgy can mean both a practical method of active union (*drastikê enôsis*) with spiritual beings and the union beyond reason in which the Subject performing the “divine work” is the divine Subject himself. This “method” is also called hieratic, and those who practice it are the “hieratics.” For the Neoplatonists, Chaldaean theurgy was one hieratic method, though not the only one. Such a method always rests upon certain ascetic disciplines and presupposes a whole body of theosophical knowledge. Iamblichus seems to have borrowed the term *hieratic* from the Hermeticists. In any case, when he affirms the superiority of the hieratic life over that of the philosopher alone, he establishes exactly the same precedence that Sohrawardî gives to the *hakîm mota’allih* within the mystical hierarchy of sages whose ancestry goes back to Hermes.

The expressions in which the adjective “hieratic” occurs help us understand it more precisely. There is, for example, a “hieratic hope.” One of the Chaldaean Oracles declares: “Hope filled with fire shall be your nourishment.” Hope here is a faculty of spiritual intelligence, an instrument of knowledge. The same is true of everything in the *Oracles* qualified by a compound containing the word “fire,” for such expressions indicate a gift descending from the supreme Intelligence. This “hieratic hope,” like hope more generally in the language of the mystery communities, such as that of Eleusis, means the initiate's trust in a blessed life beyond death.[^EII2-54] It lies at the heart of the “sacrament of immortality” practiced by the Chaldaean Magi, and it accords entirely with the teaching of Sohrawardî and the “Neoplatonists of Persia.”

The theurgic or hieratic ascent of the soul (*anagôgê*) was therefore the central mystery of the sacramental community whose sacred book was the *Chaldaean Oracles*. Its teaching offered more than knowledge *about* a mystery. The purpose of the sacrament, the mystery (*teletê, mysterion*), and of initiation itself (*teleiôsis*), was to render the soul immortal. What Proclus and a few others tell us about the teaching of the “hieratics” is that they sought to separate the soul from its physical body before the final departure of death, before the *exitus*. The aim was to give the soul the capacity to break the bonds tying it to the body and to physical nature. Here we should recall the kinship between two Greek words: *teleutân*, to die, and *teleisthai*, to be initiated. The soul has descended temporarily into this world to fulfill the mission and role assigned to it as a soul. That mission can be completed only if the soul is capable of ascending once more to the place from which it descended.

But this requires the soul, carried by its subtle vehicle alone (*okhêma*), to have become accustomed to separating itself from its physical body while it still inhabits that body. Otherwise, it risks being overwhelmed by the violence of physical death. The Greek terms for the soul's double movement of descent and return (*kathodos* and *épanodos*) have exact equivalents in the terminology of Islamic mystical theosophy: the two arcs of *nozûl* and *so’ûd*. The conviction that mystical death must come before physical death, so that physical death may be rendered harmless, is so compelling that its commandment is placed upon the lips of the Prophet himself in a *hadith*: “Die before you die...” In the seventeenth century, the great Shiite philosopher and spiritual master Mîr Dâmâd would repeat Sohrawardî's own words: “No one is truly a *mota’allih*, a hieratic sage, until he has made himself capable of taking off his physical body as one takes off a tunic.” Whether one speaks in Greek of *khôrismos*, separation, or in Arabic of *tajarrud*, one is speaking of exactly the same thing.

We need not imagine that this necessarily involves phenomena we would today regard as “disturbing” or “abnormal.” We have only to consider how often the mystical theosophers of Islam quoted the famous account of Plotinus's ecstasy, which they knew through the Arabic text of the work called the *Theology of Aristotle* (the beginning of that account will appear later in this book). That is the kind of experience at issue. The soul's ascent is also described in several surviving fragments of the Chaldaean Oracles, each of which may be understood as an account of the “sacrament of the soul's immortalization.” What we encounter is a *drama mystikon*, a mystical drama that can be expressed only through narrative. The same is true of Sohrawardî's “tales of initiation”: that is precisely what they seek to convey.

We also find a remarkable form of it in certain traditions attributed to the Imams of Shiism, notably the *hadith* of the “White Cloud,” interpreted by Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî (see Book V, Chapter III). All this also resonates with the text known as the “Mithras Liturgy” and with Apuleius's account of the mysteries of Isis. The action of the theurgic sacrament seeks to represent the destiny awaiting the initiate's soul after its physical *exitus*. This is also the purpose of Sohrawardî's *Tale of the Western Exile*. It is the story of the soul's passion: descent and return, death and rebirth. As Proclus says, citing one of the oracles: “The souls that have known the works of the Father”—the Ideas and the spiritual worlds—“escape the fatal wing of Destiny.” “Theurgists no longer belong to the herd of men subject to Destiny.”[^EII2-55]

But we must not misunderstand: supreme salvation is not accomplished by the hieratic sage acting alone. It would take a profound ignorance of humanity's religious history to accept, as some contemporary theology would have us do, that Christianity differs from other religions because salvation in Christianity is God's work, while other religions supposedly represent humanity's efforts to secure salvation for itself. The entire spirituality of Islamic gnosis, and indeed of Islam generally, bears witness against so simplistic a contrast.

Moreover, the Neoplatonic piety whose affinity with that of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* we are considering also shows that the hieratic sage does not unite with spiritual beings without their assistance. This is all the more true when the theurgist—the one performing the “divine work”—is the divine Subject himself.

Proclus knows that “only someone possessing an angelic soul is capable of performing the hieratic operation,” although he keeps secret the nature of the sacrament that bestows this quality upon the soul. The reason is precisely that the quality is conferred by a ray of divine Light at the very moment when the soul's hieratic ascent culminates in mystical union with that Light. Proclus knows the hierarchy of Angels who “set the soul aflame with divine fire.” He speaks of the Angel who is the “guide of separation”: the guide who leads the soul out of the physical body. This Angel resembles the one who appears to Sohrawardî at the beginning of his *Tales*. For their part, the Chaldaean Oracles know the Angels as “beings of spiritual intelligence” who descend from the Empyrean at the supreme God's command to assist the hieratic soul. It is for this reason that the soul, as an “angel in potential,” has its dwelling among them after death, in the “angelic realm.”[^EII2-56]

Nevertheless, this hieratic operation—this ecstatic separation that anticipates the departure of death—can only announce itself and be experienced as the end of things and of time: as an individual event of the Last Things, an individual *eschaton*. This is exactly how it occurs in Sohrawardî.

We shall see it later in the account of Hermes's ecstasy, where Hermes appears as the hero of this ecstatic encounter with the end. This is why the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* so aptly describes the experience of the hieratic mystic, the *mota’allih*, by borrowing the expression “Great Upheaval” or “Great Shaking” (*al-tâmmat al-kobrâ*). In a Quranic verse, this expression announces the final hour, the *eschaton*. The theme is heard at the opening of the *Tale of the Western Exile* (see Chapter VI below), just as it appears in the visions of light described at the end of the *Eastern Theosophy*.

The preceding pages have tried to bring *ta’alloh*, mystical *apothéosis*, understood as the distinctive gift of the hieratic theosopher (*mota’allih*), into relation with the teachings of those whom Sohrawardî himself invokes in support of his own experience: the sages of Persia and Chaldaea, Zoroaster and Plato, as they appear within the traditions of Magian-Chaldaean spirituality and later Neoplatonism. We can now recognize in this *mota’allih* a spiritual companion of the theurgic or “hieratic” sage of the Chaldaean Oracles and the Neoplatonists.

But for our *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, this same theosopher is, by that very fact, the *ishrâqî* sage: the “Eastern” sage. This last characteristic marks the whole of his teaching and school. A Persian work written in seventeenth-century India, the *Dabestân al-madhâhib* (see also Book IV below), makes the point when it speaks of the *Ishrâqîyân-e Irân*, the “Eastern” theosophers of Iran—in other words, the “Platonists of Persia.”

We must now identify, in Sohrawardî's work, the qualities that distinguish the hieratic sage as an “Eastern” or *ishrâqî* theosopher. To understand the meaning and ideal of *Ishrâq*, we have briefly surveyed the spread of Magian spirituality westward and southwestward, in its “Chaldaean” and Neoplatonic forms. Sohrawardî's own explicit statements about *Ishrâq* will now allow us to recover, with him, the connection that was never entirely broken between the Chaldaean Magianism of the “Eastern-minded” Neoplatonists and the specifically Iranian Zoroastrian tradition stemming from the Avesta, its sacred book. The path of *Ishrâq*, of “Eastern” knowledge, is the path by which Sohrawardî invites us to rediscover with him the “Eastern Source”: that Light of Glory (*Xvarnah*, *Khorrâh*) which is the key to Zoroastrian cosmology and spirituality. For our *shaykh*, the Light of *Ishrâq* (*Nûr ishrâqî*, *Lux orientalis*) is identical with that Light of Glory.

##### 2. “Eastern” Knowledge

For Sohrawardî, the word *ishrâqî*, “Eastern,” describes both the highest form of spiritual knowledge and the community of sages and theosophers—the “hieratics”—whose aim and vocation is to attain it. The word carries many layers of meaning. “East” and “Eastern” are not simply geographical or ethnic descriptions. Above all, they refer to something that cannot be located on the maps in our atlases.

We must therefore find a way to pass from the literal meaning of “East” to its spiritual meaning. What opens that passage is the idea of illumination: the appearance and vision of light, the experience of light itself.

Yet “illumination” alone is not enough to convey the reference to the Eastern source. Conversely, whenever we use the words “East” and “Eastern,” we must guard against a geographical misunderstanding. From the *ishrâqî* point of view, especially today, we must acknowledge that the geographical East is populated by great numbers of “Westerners,” while a few genuine “Easterners” still survive in the West. We should take our guidance from the statement quoted earlier: “Among the ancient Persians there was a community of chosen people guided by God.” In saying this, Sohrawardî had given a new application to a Quranic verse. If we can repeat this transformation of meaning, it will provide us with a criterion not only for recognizing the ancestors of the *Ishrâqîyûn*, but also for recognizing their successors: the “Eastern” tradition that alone entitles these sages to be called “Eastern.”

Let us begin with the passage in which the word *Ishrâq* first appears in Sohrawardî's great work, a passage that his two principal commentators, Qotboddîn Shîrâzî and Shahrazôrî, expand upon in almost identical terms.[^EII2-57] Sohrawardî has just mentioned how insistently his friends, his “brothers,” urged him to commit to writing this “Eastern Theosophy,” whose inspiration, as he tells us at the end of the work, came to him “all at once, on a wonderful day.” Qotboddîn pauses over the two words that form the book's title. “These words,” he writes, “mean the theosophy founded upon the East of the Lights (*Ishrâq*, the light of the East), which is spiritual perception (*kashf*); or else the theosophy of the Easterners (*mashâriqa*), meaning the inhabitants of Persia (*Ahl Fârs*).

“In fact, the two meanings amount to the same thing, since the theosophy of the ancient Persians was a spiritual perception experienced through inward tasting (*kashfîya dhawqîya*). It therefore originated in the East of the Lights (*Ishrâq*), the East that is the manifestation (*zohûr*) of the pure Lights or pure Intelligences. It arose from their radiance and from the outpouring of the illuminations (*ishrâqât*) that dawn upon souls withdrawn from their physical bodies. The foundation of the ancient Persians' theosophy was inward experience and spiritual perception. The same was true of the ancient Greek sages, with the exception of Aristotle and his school, who relied upon rational debate and logical demonstration, and nothing else.”

Three lessons emerge from this passage.[^EII2-58]

**1)** The first concerns the spiritual meaning of the word *East*. The East, the light rising in the East, the hour of *Ishrâq*, is the primordial manifestation or revelation of being. It is the spiritual perception that takes place within consciousness when this Light flashes forth, disclosing the mystery of how being shines through into appearance. In the same way, the rising sun reveals the presence of things through the light of its dawn. The heavenly body rising in the physical sky, and the hour of its rising, correspond within the physical world to the moment when Knowledge dawns—and when the subject of that Knowledge awakens to itself, rising at its own East. The term *ishrâq* thus has a precise technical meaning that sets “Eastern” theosophy apart from every other kind. Just as, in the world of the senses, it names the splendor of morning, the instant when the sun's first brilliance unfolds in the crimson of the rising dawn, so, in the spiritual heaven of the soul, it names the revelatory moment of self-knowledge.

**2)** In a second sense, we may understand it as the theosophy of the *Easterners*: people whose home lies in the geographical East. We are told that these were the ancient Persians, the people of Fârs, of Persia.

Yet this involves no ethnic privilege whatsoever. Living in the East, or even being Persian, is not enough to make someone an “Easterner.” What qualifies the “Eastern” theosopher, the ancient Persian sage, is a different kind of investiture. It is announced by the words “East” and “Eastern” when these, like *Ishrâq* itself, are understood at the level of their spiritual meaning: the level at which the rising sun in the physical sky corresponds symbolically to the sun rising in the spiritual Heaven.

For as Qotboddîn observes, if the theosophy of the Easterners and Eastern theosophy amount to the same thing, it is because the wisdom of the ancient Persians was precisely that higher mystical theosophy known to us through the visionary perceptions of Kay Khosraw and Zarathustra, and through their teachings concerning the *Xvarnah* and the world of the archangelic Lights. Without this, the two expressions would not mean the same thing. The ancient Persians were therefore “Easterners” because their knowledge arose from that East. In other words, it is “Eastern” knowledge that makes a sage an “Eastern” theosopher; belonging by birth to the geographical East is not enough to make one's knowledge “Eastern.” Once their spiritual calling is understood in this way, the ancient Persian sages can rightly be regarded as the ancestors of the “Eastern” theosophy that Sohrawardî explicitly set out to revive.

**3)** These spiritual “Easterners” also happened, in the persons of the ancient Persian sages, to be geographically Eastern. It would therefore be especially absurd to separate what is supposedly the theosophy of *Ishrâq*—an “illuminative” theosophy—on the one hand, from the theosophy of the Easterners on the other (see p. 27 above). Our philosophers never made such a division. Avicenna himself had pursued an “Eastern philosophy.” Sohrawardî, who was better placed than we are to judge, explained why Avicenna's attempt had failed and why it was he, the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, who had brought this Eastern philosophy into being. There is more. As we have already seen in tracing the spiritual genealogy, there is no reason to set the Greeks against the “Easterners.” The ancient Greek sages were also “Easterners,” because they too had access to the sources of higher mystical theosophy. The real opposition is between the “Easterners” and the Peripatetics of Aristotle's school, especially the “modern” Peripatetics of the Islamic world. These, together with the scholastic theologians of *Kalâm*, were Sohrawardî's principal adversaries.

The two terms *East* and *Eastern* (*Ishrâq* and *Ishrâqî*) bring three distinct visions together in a single culminating vision. There is the rising sun, with the hour and place of its rising. There is illumination, the morning splendor pouring forth from that East. And there is the rising sun itself. We may therefore speak of a knowledge that is Eastern because it is itself the East of knowledge; a knowledge that is illuminative because it is Eastern, and Eastern because it is illuminative. This is because such Knowledge is the very dawning of Knowledge, its morning, its hour of *Ishrâq*. It is the primordial place of Knowledge, the East from which all knowledge rises.

And finally, it is Knowledge that constitutes the very essence of the knowing Subject: the Subject's self-knowledge, which causes everything knowable to rise at its own East. The “Eastern” theosopher is an *ishrâqî* because to know is, for him, to be present to himself—and thus, by that very fact, to be present at the morning, at the East of knowledge. Conversely, his knowledge is “Eastern” because that presence makes his own self-present being the East from which the knowledge dawns. “Eastern” describes both a way of being and a way of knowing, each inseparable from the other.

We could multiply expressions in an attempt to make up for the inadequacy of any single translation. We might think of Jacob Boehme's *aurora consurgens*, the rising dawn, or of expressions found in Hegel: Eastern light, dawning light, the substance of dawn; or again, the essence of the rising sun, emerging light—Eastern light!—the substance of the East, the pure luminous essence of dawn.[^EII2-59] All this is contained in *Ishrâq* and “Eastern” theosophy. These expressions also harmonize with one already found in Latin Hermeticism: *cognitio matutina*, knowledge “at morning.” Everything before that morning is merely groping and illusion in the Darkness.

Thus, in its very title, Sohrawardî's theosophy gives form to its most beautiful symbol, one that brings with it the whole traditional symbolism of Light and Darkness. All the sages of the “Eastern” lineage have accordingly spoken in a language of signs and symbols (*romûz*). When we use the word “symbol” here, however, we mean neither an emblem or abstract sign nor an innocent allegory. We mean the forms assumed by an intermediate world, through which alone we can begin to apprehend the worlds above it. More precisely, we must speak of worlds that symbolize one another. In such a relationship, the symbol receives its truth from the higher reality it symbolizes; and what is an inner, esoteric spiritual truth at one level of meaning becomes an outward, exoteric truth at a higher level of being. The essential function of the symbol here is to initiate us into the mysteries.

“For everything I set forth concerning knowledge of the pure Lights—or beings of Light,” writes Sohrawardî, “and for everything founded upon that knowledge, as indeed for the rest of my teaching, I have the support of all those who have walked upon the path of God. For this higher knowledge was the inward experience (*dhawq*) of Plato, the Imam and leader of wisdom, a man endowed with great spiritual strength and inner light. Long before him, from Hermes, the father of the sages, down to Plato himself, it had also been the experience of other eminent philosophers, pillars of theosophical wisdom, such as Empedocles, Pythagoras, and others.

“Now the doctrines of those ancient sages were expressed in the language of symbols; arguments directed against them therefore do not refute them. Even when someone claims to argue against the outward, exoteric appearance (*zâhir*) of their doctrines, that person has not reached their true intentions at all, for symbols cannot be refuted in that way. It was precisely upon symbolism that the original Eastern doctrine of Light and Darkness was founded. This was the highest teaching of the sages of ancient Persia, such as Jâmâsp,[^EII2-60] Frashaoshtra,[^EII2-61] Bozorgmehr,[^EII2-62] and others before them. It was not the doctrine upon which the impiety of the dualist Magi (*Majûs*) was founded, nor was it the deviation of Mânî.”[^EII2-63]

This passage, particularly its final qualification, confirms what we have already seen. The book's two great commentators, Qotboddîn Shîrâzî and Shahrazôrî, who here largely repeat one another, expand upon it in the following terms:

“It was upon symbolism that the doctrine of the Easterners (*ahl al-Sharq*) was founded—that is, the doctrine of the sages of ancient Persia, who professed the existence of two principles (*asl*), one Light and the other Darkness. These are, in fact, the respective symbols of necessary being and non-necessary being. Light stands for (*qâ’im maqâm*) Necessary Being; Darkness stands for non-necessary being. This does not mean that the absolutely First Principle divides into two principles, one Light and the other Darkness. No penetrating mind has ever maintained such a thing, least of all the elite of the Persian sages (*fozalâ’ Fârs*), who explored the depths of the sciences of being. That is why our Prophet, Mohammad, said in their praise: ‘Even if knowledge were suspended from the Pleiades, there would be men of Persia who would reach it.’[^EII2-64] It is precisely their higher sciences and teachings that the author, Sohrawardî, has brought back to life in this book.

“The same was also the inward experience of the elite of the Greek sages, for the two communities, Persian and Greek, agreed upon the principle. Among the Persians were, for example, those named by the author: Jâmâsp, the disciple of Zoroaster; Frashaoshtra; and, most recently, Bozorgmehr. Their predecessors included King Gayômart, Tahmuras, Fereydûn,[^EII2-65] Kay Khosraw, and Zoroaster, among the great kings and prophets of high rank. It is true that the changing fortunes of history destroyed their higher sciences. The most disastrous blow was the loss of their sovereignty and Alexander's burning of most of their books.

“But the author succeeded in discovering certain aspects of their teachings. Finding that these agreed with what spiritual perception and intuitive vision (*kashfîya shohûdîya*) disclose, he recognized their excellence and worked to bring them to completion.”[^EII2-66]

This was how Sohrawardî's commentators assessed his work in the thirteenth century. The final remark in the passage they have just commented upon, with its reference to the Magi and to Mânî, is especially significant. Because Sohrawardî's concern is an “Eastern” knowledge, for which he claims an “Eastern” ancestry identified with that of ancient Persia, he found it necessary to guard against confusion. An earlier statement of his already gave us occasion to clarify which Magi he wished to distance himself from (see p. 29 above). They were, above all, the Magi who professed a radical dualism, and especially those among them who had entered into alliance with Ahriman.

We shall see in Chapter III that the great event of Sohrawardî's spiritual life was a visionary experience that transformed both his consciousness and his understanding of reality. It shattered, for him, the overly restrictive framework of the Aristotelian theory of the Intelligences. It was also the source of his interpretation of the Platonic Ideas through the language of Zoroastrian angelology. He appeals to the ecstatic visions of the prophet of ancient Persia as confirmation of his own vision, because he is convinced that Zoroaster did not belong to those who professed a radical dualism: the doctrine of two coeternal Principles, existing from the very beginning and on the same level of being, one a primordial Power of Light, the other a primordial opposing Power of Darkness.

We have just seen how Sohrawardî and his commentators tell us the true meaning to be given to the duality of principles in cosmogony and cosmology. The *shaykh al-Ishrâq* would maintain this interpretation consistently, for it is inseparable from the declaration whose significance we previously described as that of a manifesto: “Among the ancient Persians there was a community of chosen people guided by God, who walked upon the right path: eminent sages and theosophers bearing no resemblance to the Magi.” For our part, we can use the word “Magi” if we qualify it carefully enough to remove the associations that make it suspect.

Writing in Arabic, Sohrawardî could hardly give the word *majûs* any meaning other than the one current in the Islamic world. He therefore preferred another term, speaking of the *Khosrawânîyûn*. Earlier we encountered the “Platonic Magi.” Thanks to Sohrawardî, the connection between them and their Iranian ancestry was restored. By bringing about this “resurrection” of ancient Persian theosophy, he could, by that very act, claim an Iranian ancestry for his own theosophy, which he accordingly named *ishrâqî*, “Eastern.” From his time onward, the past was no longer what it had been: time had become reversible. That is precisely what the word “resurrection” implies.

Thus the resurrection of Zoroastrian theosophy within *ishrâqî* spirituality became conceivable in Islam through, and for, Sohrawardî—a thinker who himself professed the esoteric *tawhîd*, the affirmation of the One as uniquely One, and for whom the shadow of Ahriman was experienced as definitively overcome. Symbolic interpretation (*ta’wîl*) brings the two Principles back to two ontological aspects of being: on the one hand, Necessary Being, which possesses its full positivity by its very nature; on the other, non-necessary being, whose degree of potentiality measures its negativity.

Certainly, Sohrawardî's symbolic interpretation (*ta’wîl*) presupposes a modification of classical Mazdean dualism, if it does not itself accomplish that modification. But this change had precedents. The passage from Sohrawardî quoted above, together with his commentators' elaboration, invites us to extend our inquiry in three directions. Here we can do no more than indicate them briefly: **1)** the efforts to overcome metaphysical dualism; **2)** the figure of Zoroaster; and **3)** the case of Mânî.

**1)** The classical Iranian form in which radical dualism appears to have been overcome is known as Zurvanism. Zervân, Unlimited Time, is understood as the original absolute divinity, from whose thought two “sons” proceed. Ohrmazd, the principle of Light, is born from Zervân's triumphant thought; Ahriman, the principle of Darkness, is born from the doubt, the negativity, that obscures Zervân's thought.

Yet this way of overcoming dualism still places two antagonistic Principles on the same level of being. Light and Darkness remain equal; indeed, it may even give Ahriman an immediate precedence, postponing Ohrmazd's reign until the end of the cosmic cycle. Such a solution was unacceptable to the gnostics of Islam. Consequently, when we detect traces of Zurvanism in their thought, what we actually find is something like a “neo-Zurvanism.” It is achieved through a radical alteration of the original Zurvanist drama, preserving the supremacy and primordial priority of the Principle of Light. Zervân is no longer the Supreme Principle but one of the beings of Light, one of the highest-ranking Angels of the Pleroma, the fullness of the angelic world. Darkness is therefore born not from the original Light itself, but from a being derived from that Light.

Nevertheless, one characteristic feature of Zurvanism is retained. A thought of doubt, a kind of vertigo before nothingness, takes hold of the Angel Zervân and, through him, gives birth to the Other, to Ahrimanian Darkness. This is how Shahrastânî describes the cosmogony of the Gayômartian gnostics, named after Gayômart, who appears sometimes as the Primordial Man and sometimes as one of the legendary rulers of the Iranian epic.

The same dramatic alteration appears, with the necessary differences, in the cosmogony and cosmology of the *Oracles*, or *Logia*, of the Chaldaean Magi (already discussed above, p. 32), and in their interpretation by the Neoplatonists. Once Evil and Darkness are understood as originating in a catastrophe within the angelic Pleroma, there is no longer any need to profess a radical metaphysical dualism. The principle of metaphysical monism—the ultimate unity of reality—is preserved. By accepting the Platonic principle that matter is divinely created, the Chaldaean Magi accepted the principle of a single-source explanation of the world's origin. They were not the *Majûs* whose impiety Sohrawardî condemned.

Yet once the catastrophe is admitted, whether the chief of the demons is called Ahriman or identified with Hades, and insofar as these demons correspond to the lower, irrational part of the soul, dualism at the human level becomes all the more powerful. The opposition between the faithful of Ohrmazd and the followers of Darkness reaches its greatest intensity in the struggle between the devout theurgists—the “hieratics,” assisted by the Angels, the Avestan *Yazatas*—and the *goêtes*, the Ahrimanian magicians assisted by demonic powers, the *Devs*.[^EII2-67] There can be little doubt that these Magi, reduced to the status of magicians who exploit the ambiguity of dualism, belong to the category of *Majûs* whose impiety Sohrawardî condemned, and who had made the very name *Majûs* suspect.

Hence the need, through vigilant moral conduct and ascetic discipline, to protect the conditions of the “hieratic ascent” against the snares of their demonology. Otherwise there is the danger of another catastrophe, traces of which can be found even in Wolfram von Eschenbach's *Parsifal*. There we read that Klingsor, the fallen knight who turned to black magic, had been initiated “in Persia” into the *ars magica*, the magical arts.[^EII2-68]

We must also recall that the “neo-Zurvanist” cosmology of the Gayômartians corresponds, point for point, to the “drama in Heaven” described in Ismaili Shiite cosmogony. Here too the Angel Zervân is represented as the third Intelligence of the Pleroma, the *Spiritual Adam*. His vertigo of doubt causes him to fall to the rank of tenth Intelligence, whereupon he becomes the demiurge of our world, creating it so that those who belong to him may find in it a means of salvation.[^EII2-69]

There is more. This characteristic seems to express so deeply and persistently a concern of the Iranian soul that we find it again in a major Twelver Shiite thinker of seventeenth-century Safavid Persia, Sayyed Ahmad ’Alawî. He was the student and son-in-law of the great Mîr Dâmâd (d. 1631), the intellectual master of several generations of Iranian philosophers. Using a commentary on Avicenna as his starting point, he constructed a monumental work entitled *The Key to the Book of Healing* (*Miftâh Kitâb al-Shifâ’*). He explicitly explains his choice of title by referring to Avicenna's mention of his “Eastern philosophy” in the prologue to that great book. For Sayyed Ahmad ’Alawî, the key is precisely this “Eastern philosophy.” When he comes to explain Avicenna's theory of multiplicity, he invokes the Pythagorean principle, “When the One emanates from the Cause, the non-One emanates from it also,” and immediately refers to “the teaching attributed to Zoroaster.” This teaching is, in fact, the very “neo-Zurvanism” discussed above. We have examined this *ishrâqî* testimony elsewhere and shall not dwell on it here.[^EII2-70]

**2)** We have seen how carefully Sohrawardî and his commentators distinguish Zoroaster and the sages of ancient Persia from the dualist Magi. We have also considered the spread of Iranian Magian spirituality toward the southwest, where it encountered “Chaldaean” wisdom and, ultimately, Neoplatonic wisdom. Although the Neoplatonists recognized an identity, or at least a definite affinity, between the doctrine of the *Chaldaean Oracles* and the doctrine believed to have been professed by the Magi of Zoroaster,[^EII2-71] some ancient authors were struck by differences suggesting two distinct personalities. They were therefore led to distinguish Zoroaster, the Persian prophet, from Zaratos—or Zoradès, or some similarly named figure—the Chaldaean Magus. Traces of this distinction appear in Clement of Alexandria, Pliny, and even certain Manichaean Homilies.[^EII2-72] We should also note that it appears in the work of one of the most important Ismaili thinkers, Abû Hâtim Râzî (fourth/tenth century).[^EII2-73] For him, Zaratosht, the Persian Zoroaster, was a *dâ’î*, a dignitary within the esoteric hierarchy, during the fourth period of the cycle of prophecy, the period of Moses.

Yet despite differences of spelling that merely register variations in pronunciation, the names are, strictly and etymologically speaking, the same. Moreover, the historian Agathias explicitly affirms that Zoroaster and Zaradès are two names for one and the same person.[^EII2-74] This was also the position of Sohrawardî and the *Ishrâqîyûn*, to whom the idea of dividing Zoroaster into two separate figures never occurred. Here we encounter a particularly striking kind of perception and representation whose positive meaning escapes us as long as we cannot distinguish what is *historically* true, in the sense we give that word today, from what is *phenomenologically* true—true to the way a reality is experienced and disclosed to consciousness.

**3)** The case of Mânî seems rather more straightforward. We have seen that Sohrawardî speaks of Mânî's “deviation.” Yet several features of his own doctrine and spirituality of Light bear a Manichaean imprint. Perhaps this judgment was, in part, a personal safeguard against those within Islam who knew no more about Mânî's teaching than certain commentators today who indiscriminately speak of “Manichaeism” in matters that have nothing to do with it. Sohrawardî's position is not without parallel. Elsewhere, we have noted the unmistakable and profound traces of Manichaean gnosis within Ismaili gnosis,[^EII2-75] even though Mânî's name is never mentioned there.

We must always take account of *ketmân*, the “discipline of secrecy,” the practice of concealing esoteric knowledge. The example of Shahrazôrî, a commentator who was an *ishrâqî* to the depths of his heart, illustrates this especially well. On the one hand, in the book's prologue, Shahrazôrî summarizes the information then circulating about Mânî: originally a Mazdean, Mânî proposed to combine the Mazdean and Christian religions; he claimed a prophetic mission and preached an asceticism supposedly destined to ruin society. In short, this was the whole stock of conventional opinion, as poorly informed about Manichaeism as Western opinion long remained about the Cathars.

On the other hand, in the section of the *Eastern Theosophy* dealing with the Last Things, we find an extended discussion by the same Shahrazôrî, in which he presents the teaching not of the impious Mânî but of *Mânî the sage* (*al-Hakîm Mânî*), concerning the *Column of Light* and the *Earth of Light*. Shahrazôrî relates this teaching to Sohrawardî's doctrine of the *imaginal* world of the “eighth climate”—the middle or intermediate East, to which we shall shortly return—and concludes: “If this is indeed what the sage Mânî intended by these symbols, as we have just explained them, then his teaching is true.”[^EII2-76] Otherwise, naturally, it would be false. But Shahrazôrî does not entertain that possibility.

All this seems to complete our understanding of the nature and content of “Eastern knowledge,” by revealing the figures who upheld it in the past. Meanwhile, the frequent use of the words *East* and *Eastern* within the technical vocabulary helps to clarify their meaning still further. The esoteric geography of the spiritual worlds places the *Jabarût*, the universe of the pure cherubic Intelligences (the *Angeli intellectuales* of Latin Avicennism), above the *Malakût*, the universe of the Angels-Souls. The latter comprises the higher *Malakût* of the *Angeli caelestes*, or heavenly Souls, and the lower *Malakût* of human souls.

We shall later distinguish the many worlds within these universes (Chapter III). For the moment, let us note that Sohrawardî calls them, respectively, the *Greater East*, or the farthest spiritual East (*al-sharq al-akbar*), and the *Lesser East* (*al-sharq al-asghar*).[^EII2-77] The physical, bodily world (*molk*), the world of visible phenomena (*shahâdat*), is the West, where souls decline. This will be the central theme of the mystical *Tale of the Western Exile* (see Chapter VI). It is a spiritual geography already familiar to Avicenna.

In the descending procession of being, the Intelligences “rise” at the East, the horizon of the Godhead, the Light of Lights. The heavenly Souls “rise” at the East that is morning for them: the world of the Intelligences. Human souls descend toward the West of the physical world, into the Darkness of Matter, the “land of exile,” where they must temporarily govern a body of flesh. Conversely, in the ascent back toward the origin (*so’ûd*, *ma’âd*), the soul's manifestation outside the physical body—through profound meditation, ecstatic vision, or death—constitutes its rising dawn, its *Ishrâq*, and its manifestation (*tajallî*) after a complete *katharsis*, or purification.

The world of Souls is then revealed to it as its “East.” The soul “rises” at that East by revealing itself to itself, lifting itself above the horizon of the body, which had been its West. Then the world of the Intelligences is revealed to it: the *Greater East*. The soul “rises” there by ascending beyond the world of Soul, which now becomes like a West in relation to the “Eastern Intelligence” (*al-’Aql al-mashriqî*).

Besides these two Easts, there is also a “middle” or “intermediate East” (*al-sharq al-awsat*).[^EII2-78] This “Middle East” is simply another name for what our philosophers, in contrast to the “seven climates” of traditional geography, call the *eighth climate*. It is the “second world,” where all the forms, figures, and colors of our own world appear, in even greater richness and diversity, but in a state beyond sensory perception. Here lie the mystical cities of Jâbalqâ, Jâbarsâ, and Hûrqalyâ. This is the whole universe of the *Malakût* as it “rises” within the world of the Soul. It is therefore the intermediate East between the East of the Soul and the West in which souls had been plunged into darkness. We have already devoted so much attention to this universe elsewhere that we would prefer not to repeat ourselves here.[^EII2-79]

The essential point is this. Each of the three universes has its own corresponding faculty of perception. The *Jabarût* is apprehended through intellectual intuition; the *Malakût* through imaginative intuition; and the physical world through sensory perception, the empirical knowledge provided by the five external senses.

We must emphasize once again that the imaginative faculty, or imagination, directed toward the *Malakût* must not be confused with what we ordinarily call *fantasy*. It is a genuine faculty of knowledge, with its own distinctive power of understanding, and the world it perceives possesses reality in its own right. Sohrawardî appears to have been the first to establish systematically the particular ontology, the distinct order of being, proper to this intermediate universe.[^EII2-80] This obliges us to abandon the adjective “imaginary” when referring to the *mundus imaginalis* (*’âlam al-mithâl*). Elsewhere, we have proposed calling it the *imaginal* world.

Thus the *jism mithâlî*, the subtle body, is an *imaginal* body, not an “imaginary” one. Knowledge of the *imaginal* world, or intermediate East, is itself an “Eastern” knowledge. Sensory perception, by contrast, and the fantasy that produces what is merely “imaginary,” are “Western” forms of knowledge.

The *imaginal* world fulfills an indispensable function. It frees us from the dilemma so often posed today when spiritual events are discussed: *myth or history?* The events of the intermediate East are neither one nor the other. They belong to a world with events of its own. It is in this intermediate East, this “eighth climate,” that the Revelations given to the prophets come into being, that the events of sacred history unfold, and that the happenings described in visionary narratives take place. There too occur the manifestations of the *Xvarnah*, the Light of Glory, and finally the event of the Resurrection (*qiyâmat*), the prelude to future renewals of life. Sohrawardî rightly observes that no philosophy which denies itself this intermediate world can understand the language of *Ishrâq*.

We shall have occasion to return to this point in discussing his mystical *Tales*, as well as the mysterious country where the Hidden Imam resides—the Green Island and other such places (see Book VII).

Thus there is a succession of *Easts*. As the human being rises out of the Western exile, one East after another dawns before the soul, from world to world, in a “hieratic ascent” through successive mornings and illuminations. This is *istishrâq*, literally the “quest for the East.” The *mostashriq* is the mystical pilgrim “in search of the East.” There is a certain humor in the fact that modern Arabic uses this very word for scholars called Orientalists. The vocabulary of *Ishrâq* might confront such scholars with obligations they had never expected.

The “quest for the East” undertaken by the *Ishrâqîyûn* is a pilgrimage through the Easts that dawn from vision to vision, from ecstasy to ecstasy. Each ecstasy is a “lesser death,” until the final ecstasy arrives: the “greater death” to the “Western” world, when the soul rises definitively into its Heaven. This is not merely a growing intellectual certainty, but a spiritual union with the successive ranks of a hierarchy of beings of Light, up to the threshold of all thresholds. It is deeply significant that Sohrawardî made Hermes the first hero of these ecstatic encounters with the Last Things, or this ecstatic eschatology (see Chapter VI): the archetypal hero of the pilgrimage leading back to the East.

We shall also see that Sohrawardî's Hermeticism contributes to the theme of the Quest. Unfortunately, this contribution has been overlooked by recent studies that have traced the Hermetic origins of the Quest for the Grail as presented in Wolfram von Eschenbach's *Parsifal*.

“Eastern knowledge” (*’ilm ishrâqî*) is therefore both the goal and the means of the pilgrim's Quest toward the East. That is because it is not theoretical knowledge but a transformation of being. It is knowledge that is *real Presence*, literally *knowledge by presence* (*’ilm hozûrî*). As such, it stands opposed to representational knowledge, the kind assumed by the Peripatetic theory of knowledge. In that theory, knowledge reaches its object only through an intervening form of knowing, which is not the being of the object itself but a *representation* of that being (*’ilm sûrî*).

Even before composing his great work, Sohrawardî had described “Eastern” knowledge in his *Book of Elucidations*.[^EII2-81] He did so by recounting a dream—or, more precisely, a visionary conversation that took place in the state between waking and sleep. At that time, he tells us, he was obsessed with the problem of Knowledge. He meditated upon it incessantly but remained overwhelmed by difficulties, unable to glimpse a solution. Then, one night, he suddenly felt himself enveloped in great joy and radiant light. Gradually, a human figure took shape before him. He studied it attentively and soon recognized the *Primus Magister*, Aristotle, appearing in a form of astonishing beauty. In another of his books, Sohrawardî would refer back to this conversation and specify that it had taken place in Jâbarsâ,[^EII2-82] one of the cities of the intermediate East, the “eighth climate.” That is the *imaginal* world discussed above; this one example alone would be enough to show that our understanding of the worlds cannot dispense with it.

Is there a touch of humor in the Platonist language spoken by Aristotle in this vision? Or does it simply reflect the conviction that the author of the *Theology*—in reality, an adaptation of Plotinus's writings—had always been a Platonist in his inner teaching, and that only his successors were responsible for Peripatetic philosophy? At the end of their conversation, Sohrawardî asks Aristotle whether the philosophers of Islam, Fârâbî and Avicenna, have come close to Plato's rank. Aristotle replies: “Not even one degree in a thousand!”

Sohrawardî then turns his thoughts to Abû Yazîd Bastâmî and Sahl Tostarî, two Sufi masters whose names have already appeared in our genealogy of the *Ishrâqîyûn*. Bastâmî transmitted the spiritual leaven of the *Khosrawânîyûn*, while Tostarî transmitted that of the Pythagoreans. Aristotle reads the visionary's thoughts and declares, joyfully and with approval: “Yes, those are the philosophers and the theosophers in the true sense (*al-falâsifa wa’l-hokamâ haqîqan*). They did not content themselves with ordinary knowledge. They went beyond it and attained *knowledge by presence, knowledge through union*. They began where we ourselves began, and they spoke the truths that we ourselves spoke.” “Then,” the author continues, “the Sage left me, and I remained weeping over our separation. Ah, what grief and tears over this wretched condition!”

Unfortunately, we can give only a few indications of this conversation, whose narrative extends over several pages and is further enlarged by the commentators. The visionary lays his difficulties before the philosopher, whose first reply is: “Return to yourself, and the difficulty will be resolved for you.” This is the starting point, the very starting point recalled, as we have just read, at the end of the conversation. The entire exchange is, in essence, a progressive initiation into self-knowledge as something inherent in, and necessary to, all knowledge.

The initiation seeks to awaken the soul to a knowing that is neither the product of abstraction nor a representation of its object: a knowing that does not require the intervention of a form or *species*, a mental likeness. No: this act of Knowing is not something added to the knowing subject. It is the subject's very essence, the essence of the soul itself, of personal, existing subjectivity (*anâ’îyat*). For that subjectivity is, by its very nature, life, light, manifestation, and self-awareness (*hayât, nûr, zohûr, sho’ûr bi-dhâti-hi*). All these terms also describe the pure Essences that are separate from matter, whether they are entirely free of it, like the archangelic Intelligences, or charged with governing a body, like the heavenly Souls and human souls. This is not knowledge of a logical universal.

In contrast to the knowledge of abstract universals, called representational knowledge (*’ilm sûrî*), Sohrawardî calls the first kind *knowledge by presence*: unitive, intuitive knowledge (*’ilm hozûrî, ittisâlî, shohûdî*). It is knowledge of an essence in its absolutely real, individual existence, freed from every reference both to logical abstraction and to embodiment in a sensory phenomenon. When every veil has been lifted and removed, and because the soul's being is a being of light, an illumination emanates from the soul: the dawn of its presence (*ishrâq hozûrî*) upon the object of its vision. From that moment, the soul knows the object because the object itself is present to it and through it—not merely represented before it by a form or an idea. The object is present in its very being. And this presence consists in the soul's “rising” over what is present, making it present through the soul's own presence. Its manifestation is the presence of that presence. This is what constitutes *Eastern presence* (*hozûr ishrâqî*): presence at the very East of knowledge.

Yet this power of “making present” (*istizhâr*) is proportionate to the degree of separation (*tajarrud*): the degree to which the knowing subject has freed itself from the matter of this world, and thus the degree of its presence at the East, or at the successive Easts. At the same time, this freedom from matter determines the degree of the Dominion of Light over matter and darkness (*tasallot ishrâqî*). For the soul may descend until it becomes a wavering shadow at evening twilight, sinking into the abyss of what Sohrawardî calls the *Western Exile*. Presence, then, is proportionate to this Dominion of Light, and knowledge is proportionate to Presence.

We can begin to see why Sadrâ Shîrâzî, whose metaphysics of *existing* culminates in a metaphysics of Presence, belongs firmly to the “Eastern” (*ishrâqî*) tradition. We can also see how “prophetic philosophy,” centered on the teachings of the holy Imams of Shiism, led this *ishrâqî* tradition toward a metaphysics of testimony: testimony understood as the presence of the eyewitness (*shâhid, shahîd*; see Book V).

Furthermore—and here we reach the heart of “Eastern Theosophy”—it is through this idea of the Dominion of Light, inseparable from “Eastern Presence” and determining the hierarchy of degrees of being and knowing, that a fundamental conception of Mazdean theosophy asserts itself anew in philosophical life: the Light of Glory, the *Xvarnah*.

When Sohrawardî uses the characteristic expression *tasallot ishrâqî* to describe the victorious Dominion of Light rising at its East, the dominion revealed at morning, or the term *Anwâr qâhira* to designate the archangelic order of the overpowering, victorious Lights, we can hear behind the Arabic words the Middle Persian and Persian *pêrôz* and *pêrôzîh*. These convey the idea of the victorious one's victory, the power of being victorious (compare the Latin title *Angelus victor*, given to the Archangel Michael; see Chapter III, § 3). These Sohrawardian expressions all correspond to the manifestations and powers of the Light of Glory, the *Xvarnah*, celebrated in the Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrianism (see Chapter III). Ultimately, it is in this vision of the *Xvarnah* that Sohrawardî's vision of *Ishrâq*, of the Light of the East, originates. Its forms of manifestation—the illuminations (*ishrâqât*)—establish the succession of the dawns and mornings of being.

In an eternal dawn,[^EII2-83] at the summit of the hierarchy of Light or being, shines the Light of Lights (*Nûr al-Anwâr*), whose transcendence, whose freedom from matter (*tajarrud*), surpasses every other immateriality. Its absolute, victorious Dominion (*tasallot wa qahr*) calls all existence into being: that is, it makes all existence present to itself in an absolute Presence. From this Light of Lights, whose essence is what the ancient Persians called the Light of Glory—the Avestan *Xvarnah*, the Persian *Khorrâh*—emanates the first of the “archangelic” or “victorious” Lights (*Anwâr qâhira*). Sohrawardî gives this first Light the name it bears in Zoroastrian angelology: *Vohu-Manah* in the Avesta, *Bahman* in Persian. It is the first of the Zoroastrian Archangels, the Ahmaraspands,[^EII2-84] or “Holy Immortals.” From the illumination and reflection that constitute the relation between the Light of Lights and the First Archangel, a new Light proceeds: the second Archangel, and so on.

For this original relationship is the source and archetype of all the others, the source of successive irradiations, of the successive *Easts* of being. Illumination and reflection; the sovereign power of Light and the loving longing that answers it, because the Light itself awakens that longing (*qahr wa mahabbat*): at the dawn of being, this original relationship is the relationship between the first Beloved and the first Lover. The Power of this radiance beyond the senses holds together the being of every being, arranges all the beings of all the worlds in pairs, and causes the original relationship of love between the Light of Lights and the First Archangel to be repeated endlessly among them. This is not dualism but *duality-in-unity*, an essential polarity within every being. Beings discover that polarity by being present at the East, at the “morning,” of one another, just as every being is present to the Angel who is the lord of its species.

Thus, from one rank to the next, the whole hierarchy of archangelic Lights illuminates every lower rank with Presence.

Sohrawardî's original and fundamental intuition—the intuition of *Ishrâq*, of the *Xvarnah*—already contains within it all the moments through which it will later unfold. What we have sketched in a few lines will be completed and developed in the angelology (see Chapter III, §§ 3–4). This also explains why the expressions of Sohrawardî's technical vocabulary form such characteristic harmonies: Eastern vision; contemplation at the East (*moshâhadat ishrâqîya*); Eastern knowledge by presence (*’ilm ishrâqî hozûrî*); the East of a Presence (*ishrâq hozûrî*).[^EII2-85] This is a vision that brings about the “morning” of its object, making that object present. For the seeing soul, itself illuminated by the archangelic Intelligence nearest to it, is itself the light of that “morning.” Its knowledge of every “object” is brought back to the knowledge through which it knows itself.

“Eastern Presence” (*hozûr ishrâqî*) makes every entity separated from Matter, and freed from matter's potentiality, into an *East* for things and beings, at each degree of the hierarchy of existence. Here is an absolute knowing whose truth no longer depends on any temporal qualification attached to the object—“will be,” “has been,” and so forth. It is knowing *in the present*, presence itself establishing the specifically “Eastern” relationship (*izâfat ishrâqîya*) with everything known, known within that very Presence. These are the “Eastern sciences” (*’olûm ishrâqîya*). And this relationship lies so profoundly at the foundation of both being and knowing that all the terms by which we try to express it become interchangeable and reciprocal: it is the dawn of substance, but also the very substance of dawn; the vision of essence, but also the essence of vision.

This is why “Eastern knowledge” cannot be attained without satisfying a rigorous requirement. Sohrawardî formulates it in a passage so striking that many who followed the tradition of *Ishrâq* after him quoted it in their turn: Mîr Dâmâd, for example, whom we mentioned earlier, and Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, both among the greatest mystical theosophers of Safavid Persia (see Book V). Sohrawardî himself appealed to exemplary precedents: the ecstatic vision of Plotinus, which he knew through the so-called *Theology of Aristotle*; the visions of Hermes and Zoroaster; and the visions of the Prophet of Islam. The passage is the very one to which we referred earlier, where our *shaykh* traces the spiritual ancestry of the *Ishrâqîyûn* back to Hermes. After naming those through whom the two spiritual leavens—that of the sages of ancient Persia and that of the Pythagoreans—were transmitted, he concludes:

“In short, the theosopher who truly possesses hieratic experience (*hakîm mota’allih*) is one for whom the material body has become like a tunic, which he sometimes takes off and sometimes puts on again. No one can be counted among the mystical theosophers so long as he knows nothing of this sacred leaven, so long as he has not experienced the taking off and putting on. After this, he ascends toward the Light if he wishes. He appears, if it pleases him, in whatever form he chooses. The power that enables him to do so is brought into action within him by the Light whose dawn embraces his person (*al-nûr al-shâriq ’alay-hi*).

“Do you not see how iron, heated until it glows by the action of fire, comes to resemble the fire itself, shining with its brightness and burning with its heat? So too the soul, spiritual in its essence, when it undergoes the action of the Light and puts on the robe of rising dawn, produces the effect and action of the Light. It gives a sign, and the thing occurs at its signal. It imagines, and what happens accords with the image it has imagined. Impostors, the *goêtes*, seduce people through tricks and sleight of hand.

“But the Illuminated One, the Perfect One, whose love is attached to the order that is innocent of evil, acts with the spiritual assistance of the Light, because he himself is a child of the Light.”[^EII2-86]

Finally, our *shaykh* makes an important clarification: these allusions can truly be understood only by reference to the events that take place in the “intermediate East”—that is, in the *imaginal* world whose reality and ontological status, as we indicated above, Sohrawardî was the first to establish systematically.

##### 3. The Hierarchy of Spiritual Sages and the Mystical “Pole”

When Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî (see Book V) describes *ishrâqî* spirituality as an intermediate reality (*barzakh*) that brings together the method of the pure Sufis, directed essentially toward inner purification, and the method of the philosophers, directed toward pure knowledge, he expresses with complete fidelity to the inspiration of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* what constitutes the essence of “Eastern Theosophy.” There is, indeed, a form of Sufism that has deliberately set aside, even despised, all philosophical teaching, suspecting it of delaying the spiritual seeker on the way to the goal. And there is a philosophy that has forgotten this goal altogether, contenting itself with theoretical problems. For an *ishrâqî*, an “Easterner” of Sohrawardî's school, a mystic without philosophical training runs a serious risk of going astray. Conversely, a philosopher who fails to understand that philosophy must blossom into a personal spiritual realization wastes his time in a fruitless pursuit.

Neither of these figures is the intended reader of the *Eastern Theosophy*. The work presupposes, first of all, a serious philosophical education. Its reader should already have studied Peripatetic philosophy, discussed throughout the works that constitute Sohrawardî's threefold philosophical preparation.

But there is a second condition: the reader must not wish to stop there. The *ishrâqî* school is neither a Sufi *tarîqat*, an organized spiritual brotherhood, nor a philosophers' club. It has no need of an organization or archives; nor does anyone belong to it merely by professing this or that opinion. Our authors have traditionally repeated that *Ishrâq*, “Eastern Theosophy,” stands in relation to the philosophers' theoretical philosophy as Sufism stands in relation to the scholastic theology of *Kalâm*. This is an analogy between relationships, not an identification of the things being compared, and it conveys the situation particularly well. Someone may be both a Sufi and an *ishrâqî*, but not because of membership in any particular *tarîqat*. It is because of a whole lifetime of effort directed toward inner, “esoteric” truth. In this same sense, we shall see Haydar Âmolî (Book IV) explain why there is a Sufism that is true Shiism.

Yet one may also be a Sufi without being an *ishrâqî*, just as one may be a Sufi without being Shiite—unless, perhaps, one is a Shiite without knowing it. This is why we shall find Sadrâ Shîrâzî, speaking as an *ishrâqî*, denouncing a certain “obscurantist” Sufism. We shall also find a fully committed Shiite theosopher, a man of profound spiritual experience such as Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î, rejecting Sufism as well. These are some of the dividing lines within the spirituality of Iranian Islam, lines that the present book hopes to help us discern and encourage us to explore more deeply.

The preceding pages have shown us something of Sohrawardî's ideal of the mystical sage; the pages that follow will define it more precisely. We have heard him lament the sadness of his times: the higher sciences have disappeared, and the road to theosophical wisdom has been cut off. He has spoken of his ceaseless search for a companion who would share his love of the higher sciences, and we wondered whether it was possible that he had never found one. He certainly had companions.

But insofar as they were truly his companions—the “brothers” to whom his books are dedicated—they probably shared his pessimism. On the one hand, that pessimism is explained by the conditions necessary for the realization of the complete theosophical sage. The union of philosophy and mystical experience is rare, perhaps exceptional. The relative development of these two qualities in a single person is precisely what determines the hierarchy of the “Sages of God.”

On the other hand, this pessimism expresses itself as a despair that never ceases to hope in spite of itself, because it knows why it can trust in spite of itself. This *desperatio fiducialis*—to borrow once again Luther's expression, a despair sustained by trust—is not only characteristic of the Shiite spiritual outlook. The reason Sohrawardî gives for it is exactly the reason professed by Twelver Shiism. Here we encounter something more than an affinity: a deep understanding between *Shiism* and *Ishrâqism*. It explains why Eastern theosophy found itself so thoroughly “at home” in the hearts of so many Shiite thinkers.

This reason is stated at the very point where Sohrawardî describes the hierarchy of the mystical sages. It appears in the prologue to his great work, in the passage quoted earlier, immediately beside the lines where he sketches the ancestry of the *Ishrâqîyûn*, the line through which the “spiritual leaven” was transmitted. It is a declaration that, from the outset, quietly undermines the radical pessimism inspired by the ruins of the vanished higher sciences.

“Do not imagine,” writes our *shaykh*, “that mystical theosophy existed in a period not so distant from our own and has since disappeared. No! The world has never been, and never will be, without mystical theosophy. There will always be someone who preserves in the world its proofs and testimonies. That person is the *khalîfe*, the representative of God upon this Earth, and so it will remain for as long as the Heavens and the Earth endure.”[^EII2-87]

This is exactly what Twelver Shiism professes concerning the Imam who is presently hidden: the Pole. To human eyes, everything is hopeless.

Yet because “the matter now belongs to God alone,” pessimism never ceases to overcome itself. The commentators develop this theme at length. They know that around the “hidden” Pole there is an entire group of men who are, in truth, “the pillars that still uphold the world.” It is through them that the outpouring of divine grace continues to reach this world. If an age were ever deprived of them, the world would perish in a final catastrophe. Who are these men? Into what categories do they fall? Once again, we encounter the theme of the esoteric hierarchy already made familiar to us by the Shiite tradition (see Book I, Chapter III, § 4).

Sohrawardî divides this hierarchy into five degrees, with the central degree, the third, forming the summit of the pyramid. We may distinguish five cases.[^EII2-88]

In the first case, the theosopher, the “sage of God” (*hakîm ilâhî*), has penetrated deeply and extensively into mystical experience—*ta’alloh*, *theôsis*—but that experience is not accompanied by philosophical work. The commentators point out that this was the case with the prophets and with the “Friends of God” among the Sufi shaykhs: Bastâmî, Sahl Tostarî (whose places in the genealogy of the *Ishrâqîyûn* we should recall), and Hallâj.

In the second case, the reverse of the first, the sage is a master of philosophical speculation but lacks mystical experience. This is the case with the majority of the Peripatetic philosophers who form the school of Aristotle.

In the third case, the sage possesses both perfect philosophical knowledge and perfect mystical experience. The commentators observe that such a person is rarer, and more extraordinary, than the philosopher’s stone or the alchemists’ elixir. They add that this achievement required the technical structure of philosophy to have reached completion, something owed to Aristotle.

Yet among the “moderns”—that is, in the Islamic world—they know of no one before the author of *Eastern Theosophy* who combined these two forms of wisdom, philosophical and mystical.[^EII2-89]

There are, finally, fourth and fifth cases. In one, the sage has a sound grasp of speculative philosophy but only middling spiritual experience; in the other, the balance is reversed, with fairly developed mystical experience but limited philosophical training.

To these five ranks of fully initiated sages, or theosophers, Suhrawardi adds three ranks of seekers, aspirants, or beginners. These correspond to the three basic paths into which the first five ranks can be grouped: those who seek mystical experience alone; those who seek philosophical knowledge alone; and those who seek both. The hierarchy envisaged by the theosophy of Illumination thus has eight ranks in all.

Some important distinctions follow. Without question, it is the sage of the third kind who is God’s true *khalifa*, or representative, on earth. If such a sage is unavailable, to whom does spiritual authority pass? We are told that even a mystic without philosophical training takes precedence over a philosopher who, however accomplished, has no mystical experience. As Suhrawardi and his commentators explain, a minister must receive his appointment directly from his sovereign.

But what claim to such direct appointment could philosophers who rely on reason alone possibly make? How could they vouch for a world they have never truly encountered? How could they answer *on its behalf*? Suhrawardi himself made clear that he first experienced the realities described in his book and only afterward undertook to justify them philosophically.

In the end, though, the question of succession is theoretical: the perfect sage is never absent from this world, even when hidden from it. Here the *Shaykh al-Ishraq*, the Master of Illumination, comes so close to the Shiite belief in the Hidden Imam that the religious scholars of Aleppo, who tried him, did not miss the implication.

“In truth,” he writes, “the earth is never without a sage who possesses the highest mystical experience. A sage who was a consummate philosophical thinker but had not entered deeply into mystical experience would, no doubt, have no claim to authority on God’s earth. For the world is never without a sage who possesses the highest spiritual experience, and such a sage has a stronger claim to authority than someone who is merely a philosopher. The office of *khalifa*, of God’s representative, requires direct investiture.

“But when I speak of the authority (*ri’yasat*) belonging to the perfect sage, I do not mean the triumphant exercise of worldly power. Far from it! The Imam endowed with sacred mystical experience (*al-Imam al-mota’allih*) may reveal himself openly and have his authority publicly acknowledged, but he may equally remain hidden. Even then he is the one called the **Pole** (*Qotb*), and the authority is his, even if human beings know nothing of him. When power actually rests in his hands, the age is an age of light.

“But when an age is bereft of all divine guidance and ordering (*tadbir ilahi*), darkness prevails.”[^EII2-90]

The Shiite resonance of these words is immediately apparent. In the sixteenth century, Mohammad Sharif Harawi, who translated and commented on *Eastern Theosophy* in Persian, stressed that the authority in question was essentially *spiritual* (*ma’nawi*), not an outward authority exercised over the temporal affairs of the visible world.[^EII2-91]

Shahrazuri, for his part, observes: “Conversely, many of those who actually wield visible power are not even worthy of the name, so wretched are their souls and so boundless their ignorance. How, then, could they deserve the name that denotes authority in its true sense? No: that authority can mean only the realization of human perfection, whether attained through mystical experience together with philosophical knowledge, or through mystical experience alone.”[^EII2-92]

On the rare occasions when worldly authority did belong to the perfect sage, these were exceptions: in ancient Iran, for example, Gayomart and the blessed kings Fereydun and Kay Khosrow. As for the prophets and their spiritual heirs, our commentators evoke a sacred history that brings us back to the “cycle of prophecy” already familiar from Shiite teachings about the prophets. Every age has had its company of perfected beings, but only one among them possessed the qualities that made him the Pole. Our authors understand that each prophet sent by God was followed by twelve Imams.[^EII2-93]

Yet neither the group as a whole nor each Imam individually was necessarily known to ordinary people, let alone acclaimed by them. Quite the contrary: “ages of light” have been exceptional. We need not even invoke the sage who governs Plato’s ideal city. That sage descended from contemplation to involve himself in human affairs.

Here the demand is the reverse, and far more radical. It is the entire human community, whose Pole is the Imam, the sage of God, that must rise beyond its present condition to fulfil a destiny lying beyond the horizons of earthly history. From prophet to prophet, the Call has been heard. The interval between one prophet and the next was a time of interregnum.

But now the cycle of prophecy has ended. “Because the age of the prophets has passed,” Qutb al-Din writes in his commentary, “fools and the ignorant seize power in triumph. Such is an age like ours, when religions have lost their strength, disasters follow one another, the paths and ways of wisdom have been so thoroughly erased that not a trace remains, and the ranks and degrees that make up the hierarchy of Intelligence have been abolished.”[^EII2-94]

Things, it seems, have always gone very badly indeed. Qutb al-Din Shirazi wrote these words in the thirteenth century, the age of the Mongol invasions. Does the person living in “modern times” need any *ta’wil*—any spiritual interpretation—to read them as a description of the present? Yet their meaning eludes us unless we recognize the time “between times” that Shiite thought about the Imams calls the time of *occultation* (*ghaybat*), the time of the Hidden Imam. His role as the Pole is first and foremost metaphysical and mystical.

It follows that he has no need of public recognition. Whether known or unknown to the multitude, the Imam remains the Imam. His imamate does not depend on fashionable opinions, human whims, or human favour. This is a fundamental teaching of Shiism.

Suhrawardi’s text, however, allows two interpretations. One would accord with the view of many Sufis who hold that their *khirqa*—the ceremonial mantle signifying their initiation as Sufis—derives from one of the twelve Imams. They recognize that the Twelfth Imam was the mystical Pole “in his own time.” After him, they believe, came successive Poles, generation after generation, from a line of Sufi masters whose names and number are known to the initiated. This assumes that the Twelfth Imam, too, departed this world through death. Semnani, for example, seems to profess something of the kind (see below, Book IV).

But despite its apparently Shiite recognition of the Imams, this conception is incompatible with Twelver Shiite belief.

Shiite followers of Illumination, the *Ishraqiyun*, therefore had to read the passage differently. The Twelfth Imam’s occultation did not result from his death. It remains a mysterious event, which can be imagined in several ways, but every account must preserve the meaning of his continued presence in this world: the Imam is “hidden from the senses but visible to the hearts of his faithful.” When it is said that he dwells in the “eighth clime,” the “middle Orient”—a realm bordering our world and, unlike the higher universes, still in communication with it—this is what is meant.[^EII2-95] His ways of appearing during the “Great Occultation” cannot, indeed, be understood apart from this eighth clime.

The Twelfth Imam therefore remains the *mystical Pole* until his return, which will announce the Resurrection. He has no successor and will have none. This remains “the time of the Hidden Imam.” Even when the title *pole* is applied figuratively to some outstanding Sufi master, the Imam remains the *Pole of Poles* (*Qotb al-aqtab*). We should notice how discreet Suhrawardi is here. Nothing in the few lines where he affirms the existence of the mystical Pole requires us to read them in any way that conflicts with Twelver Shiite theosophy.

Around this Pole is gathered the mystical hierarchy of the “Eastern” sages. It is an entirely spiritual hierarchy, unknown to humanity, just as its leader is invisible to human eyes. It is founded on a criterion that cannot be recognized by ordinary observation, but only by the “spiritual senses.” The Imam alone knows its members. No one joins it by selection among peers, by election, or through a competitive examination. The service they render humanity goes infinitely beyond anything we now call “social.”

The human world owes its continued existence to them, yet human beings do not even know it. Because the law governing their vocation is the same, we have already called them, and shall call them again, “knights of the Grail.” For if one of them were to claim publicly a spiritual rank that he might indeed possess in the secrecy of his consciousness—a rank known to the Imam alone—he would lose his power. By announcing what he was, he would, in that very act, cease to be it.

We have encountered the idea of the Pole and the mystical brotherhood surrounding him before (see above, Book I, Chapter III), at the end of the First Imam’s conversation with his disciple Kumayl ibn Ziyad. There the Imam said everything essential. Shahrazuri, Suhrawardi’s disciple and commentator, knows this so well that, when explaining his master’s teaching, he quotes at length the very conversation translated earlier in this work.[^EII2-96]

Thus the hierarchy of the *Ishraqiyun*, the sages of Illumination, leads us back to the hidden spiritual hierarchy taught by Shiism. We have already examined its principal sources.
