We shall meet this hierarchy again in Ruzbihan, where its members are those through whom God still “looks upon”—still concerns himself with—our world (on this theme, see also Book IV, Chapter IV, and Book VI).

It would take an entire book to assemble the Shiite and Sufi texts bearing on this essential theme. We have already pointed out some of the differences among the traditions describing the structure of the mystical hierarchy; a few are recalled in a note here.[^EII2-97] Certain connections and resemblances emerge only dimly, in a half-light, and perhaps they will never become clearer.

Consider, for example, an Ismaili tradition reported by Hasan Sabbah, the famous founder of Alamut, which gives the Imam the name Melchizedek. This suggests a connection between Shiite teachings about the Imam and a school of Christian religious knowledge known to theologians as the “Melchizedekians,” whose teachings developed between the third and fifth centuries CE. One can readily see the interest of such a link for comparative research.[^EII2-98]

Another example comes from Kaf'ami, a Twelver Shiite author of the ninth/fifteenth century, who identifies the Pole with the Twelfth Imam by drawing an analogy between the hidden spiritual hierarchy and the structure of a cosmic tent: the Imam is its axis, the central pillar, and the four *Awtad* are the pegs set at its four corners, and so forth. This analogy once inspired a learned Zoroastrian theologian to compare the idea of the Pole with its counterpart in Taoism.

In the Taoist tradition, the region around the Pole Star is represented as the dwelling of an “angel” of holiness, and the highest achievement of holiness as reaching the celestial North Pole. The comparison therefore concerns, on the one hand, the numerical and symbolic arrangement of the mystical palace of Ming-Tang, which determines the structure of the Taoist spiritual hierarchy, and, on the other, the spiritual hierarchy described by Shiite and Sufi sources. This comparison becomes all the more fruitful when it brings to light an important figure of Zoroastrian spirituality: the angel Sraosha (Persian *Sorush*), whose heavenly dwelling lies precisely “on the polar axis.”

From the standpoint of the study of religious experience, this angel of the Avesta may be seen as corresponding to the *Pole* of Shiism and Sufism.[^EII2-99] The name of Sraosha, moreover, appears in some of Suhrawardi’s own writings. There is more. Since every species—including every moral or spiritual species—has its own “angel” (*Rabb al-nu’*), a Shiite thinker such as Qazi Sa'id Qommi, deeply influenced by the theosophy of Illumination, will show, through his analysis of a famous sermon, that the Imam, the Pole, is the “angel” of a “species” called spiritual vigilance (*taqwa*; see below, Book V).

Finally, we should not omit the mysterious “Order of Philosophers” whose liturgical calendar, ceremonies, and festivals are described in detail in the encyclopedia of the “Brethren of Purity” (*Ikhwan al-Safa’*). Their choice of the Pole Star as their *qibla*, the direction toward which they turn in worship, suggests an affinity with the Sabians, and thus with Hermeticism: the “prayer of Plato” and the “prayer of Idris,” that is, of Hermes, recited during the last third of the night.[^EII2-100]

I can only apologize for passing so quickly over these details concerning the mystical Pole. Even without the space to pursue them, it was important at least to draw attention to them.

What prompted this discussion was the affinity between the doctrine of Illumination and Shiite theosophy. Evidence of that affinity appears throughout the history of philosophy and spirituality in Iran. Let us bring together three particularly telling features.

The first is one we have already noticed: Suhrawardi’s use of the title *Qayyim al-Kitab*, “the Sustainer of the Book.” In Shiite traditions attributed to the Imams, this title also designates the Imam’s defining responsibility. The expression *al-Qayyim* appears again in the closing pages of the *Book of Elucidations*, without its meaning being explicitly explained.

The second appears near the end of that same book, in a series of commands addressed to the mystical pilgrim: “Rise step by step to the family of *Ta-Sin*; perhaps you will behold your Lord upon the great road along which you are advancing.”[^EII2-101]

The two Arabic letters *Ta-Sin*, like the letters *Ya-Sin*, are among the mysterious, isolated letters that stand at the beginning of certain surahs of the Quran. There are fourteen such letters. They have been interpreted sometimes as names of the surahs, sometimes as a cipher for the Supreme Name of God, and in other ways. *Ta-Sin* occurs at the opening of surah 27; *Ya-Sin* opens surah 36, to which it gives its name—a surah recited for the dying and the dead.

Moreover, verse 130 of surah 37 says: “Peace be upon the family of *Ya-Sin*.” Shiite commentators understand *Ya-Sin* as a name for the Prophet Muhammad, and “the family of *Ya-Sin*” as a reference to the holy Imams. Suhrawardi’s commentators, for their part, cite a tradition that identifies “the family of *Ya-Sin*” with “the family of *Ta-Sin*.”[^EII2-102]

Put very briefly, in the spiritual science of letters practised within Islamic gnosis, the fourteen letters placed like a supporting framework at the openings of certain Quranic surahs are “letters of light.” They represent the hidden Spirit, and also correspond in number to the invisible stations of the Moon and the northern signs of the zodiac. The other fourteen letters of the alphabet are “letters of darkness”: they represent the body and correspond to the Moon’s visible stations and the southern signs of the zodiac.[^EII2-103]

The fourteen “letters of light,” which may be combined and rearranged, thus point to the hidden, inward meaning of revelation—to the Imamate as the inner dimension of prophecy. They form a cipher for the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones.” From this perspective, identifying the “family of *Ta-Sin*” with the “family of *Ya-Sin*” presents no difficulty. As Shahrazuri rightly observed, Suhrawardi’s command to “rise to the family of *Ta-Sin*” carries a Shiite resonance. It invites the mystic to join “the perfected Souls who belong to the Family of prophecy”—that is, the Twelve Imams.

The command given to Hermes during an ecstatic vision of the midnight sun—“Climb to the battlements of the Throne”[^EII2-104]—then takes on further hidden echoes. It too appears in the closing pages of the *Book of Elucidations*, and brings Hermeticism, Illumination, and Shiism into resonance with one another. Other examples will follow.

The third feature is the person of the mystical Pole, the Hidden Imam, who possesses the only authority that cannot be called into question: the authority of the Spirit. No doubt this idea can be found elsewhere, in other religious and mystical traditions. Certainly it can, and we shall return to such parallels in the pages ahead, for they confirm the idea’s universal significance. We might even say that Twelver Shiite theosophy, in the work of Qazi Sa'id Qommi for example, found in the idea of the Imam the foundation of a general theology of religions.

Seen in this light, how inadequate is the explanation that an unhappy community, having suffered worldly defeat, naturally invented the idea of the Imam and the expectation of his return as a consolation. Such explanations are generally advanced by people who remain complete strangers to the *spiritual reality* of lived faith. In any case, as we have already asked, how convincing is this explanation when applied to Persia since the Safavid period? Shiism there was certainly not the faith of a persecuted minority.

No: neither Suhrawardi’s statements about the Pole nor Shiite thinkers’ statements about the Hidden Imam depend upon historical accidents. They express an essential truth, a claim that never ceases: the sovereignty of the Spirit alone. As for worldly rule, we have already noted how insistently Qazi Sa'id Qommi reminds his readers that the Prophet Muhammad chose to be a servant-prophet, not a king-prophet. He had no reason to pass on to the Imams a power he had refused for himself.

We can now understand what Suhrawardi intends when he tells us for whom *Eastern Theosophy* was written. “This book of ours is addressed precisely to those who seek both mystical experience and philosophical knowledge. Neither the philosophical disputant who knows nothing of mystical experience nor the aspirant whose search is not directed toward that experience will find anything here meant for him.

“Indeed, in this book and in its symbols, our discussions are addressed only to the accomplished seeker (*mujtahid*)[^EII2-105] who possesses sacred mystical experience (*ta’alloh*), or at least to the seeker who aspires to it. The minimum required of anyone who would read this book is that he should already have been struck by the divine Lightning Flash,[^EII2-106] and that the irruption of this lightning should have become a settled habit of his soul. Anyone else will gain absolutely nothing from our book. Whoever seeks only philosophical knowledge, pure and simple, should go and study with the Peripatetic philosophers. This is an excellent and reliable path when one’s aim is rational inquiry alone.

“But we, for our part, have nothing to say to such a person, and nothing to debate with him, concerning the fundamental teachings of Eastern theosophy. No, the undertaking of the ‘Easterners’ (*Ishraqiyun*) cannot be accomplished without the flashing forth of the Lights. Some of its teachings have no other source than those Lights. So much so that, if these ‘Easterners’ should come to doubt those sources, their doubt would disappear the moment their souls withdraw into solitude from their bodies.

“Just as we observe sensible things and establish how they exist, and then use those observations to build reliable sciences, such as astronomy and others, so we observe certain spiritual realities and, on the basis of our direct observations, construct the metaphysical and theosophical sciences. Whoever cannot make this path his own will have no share in mystical theosophy and will be left at the mercy of every doubt.”[^EII2-107]

Our *shaykh* could scarcely be clearer or more explicit in setting out these enduring conditions. Everyone must judge for himself—beginning, alas, with this book’s own editor and translator—whether he has been reckless in attempting to read it! The preceding pages have allowed us to explore the approaches to the “Eastern source” and to learn what qualities are required of those who set out on the pilgrimage toward it.

Suhrawardi has now told those who are not called to this path, without softening his words, that they would do better not to take it. So we must ask how this “Eastern source” revealed itself to him and to others. Here, above all, we shall see how he came to live for himself the spiritual experience of the wonder-working sages of ancient Persia. Many traditions will echo one another. There are crossroads where “companions of the Quest” arriving from different horizons meet.

We shall then see how Suhrawardi, by creating magnificent symbolic narratives, became a *mystagogue*: a guide leading the initiate toward the “Eastern source.”

### CHAPTER III

#### The Zoroastrian Light of Glory (*Xvarnah*) and Angelology

##### I. The Light of Glory as the “Eastern Source”

We now come to an idea as distinctive as it is fundamental to the religious world of Zoroastrianism. No single word in a Western language can cover every aspect of this heavenly Light of Glory, this “victorious Fire,” which belongs first and foremost to the divine beings of the Avesta, the celestial *Yazatas* (the “Worthy of Worship”). One aspect of it appears in a visible form—visible in religious images, at least—as a halo or flame: the *Aura Gloriae*, the radiance surrounding the princes of Iranian dynasties that lie beyond, or outside, our historical chronologies, such as the Kayanids, whom we shall encounter later.

The *flammula*, the little flame or golden battle-standard from which the word *oriflamme* derives, may also be regarded as a symbol of this *Aura Gloriae*.[^EII2-108] This sacred Glory is made visible in the stylized halo that passes from images of the *Saoshyant*, the Zoroastrian Saviour, into Western depictions of Christ and the saints, Eastern images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and even Shiite Islamic representations of the holy Imams.

In Suhrawardi, the imagery is precise enough to attest a direct line of inheritance. Because this reality is alive within him, he claims the wisdom of ancient Persia as the ancestry of his own teaching. He believes himself entitled to say that he has brought that wisdom back to life, without anyone before him having travelled the same path.

We have already emphasized that this undertaking did not conflict with spiritual Islam as it has always been understood by the *‘urafa’*, those possessing spiritual insight. Far from it: it presupposed their spirituality, and especially their practice of *ta’wil*, the inward interpretation of revelation, as an exercise in spiritual life. The Prophet of Islam had himself been enabled to participate personally in the exemplary experiences of the prophets who preceded him, reliving the scriptural events that anticipated his own revelations.

Consider, for example, his visits to the prophets during the *Mi‘raj*, his heavenly ascent. From this comes the idea of the “cycle of prophecy” that we have already drawn from the traditional teachings of the Shiite Imams. The *Shaykh al-Ishraq* followed the same exemplary path. When he extends the privilege of *ta’alloh*—the experience of becoming godlike, or *theosis*—to all the “sages of God,” he knows that his own experience has repeated visions personally lived by the prophets and by the sages endowed with sacred mystical knowledge, whose inheritance he deliberately assumes. He refers with particular affection to the visions of Kay Khosrow and Zoroaster.

But that preference in no way diminishes the exemplary importance he attaches to Hermes, the ecstatic hero and father of the sage-theosophers. Similarly, when he recalls Plato’s vision of the “Spheres of Light” (more accurately, Plotinus’s vision), he also recalls the Prophet’s vision of the “seventy-seven veils of Light,” an earlier instance of the same experience.[^EII2-109] The task of uniting this spiritual lineage of ecstatic visionaries presupposes *ta’wil*, the practice of spiritual interpretation. And it was Islam—more precisely, Islamic gnosis—that placed the resources of *ta’wil* at the disposal of the Master of Illumination.

The key to that interpretation lies here in Suhrawardi’s own person: it is in him that Islamic spirituality demonstrates its capacity to embrace the exemplary visions of Hermes, Zoroaster, and Plotinus. Suhrawardi has confided to us the personal secret of that capacity: the access, granted him by divine grace, to the “Eastern Source.” That Source is precisely what he means by the term *Khorrâh*, the Persian equivalent of the Avestan *Xvarnah*: the Light of Glory, the blazing radiance of heavenly Light, the source of “Eastern knowledge.”

Access to this source enabled him to build his *Eastern Theosophy*. As he has emphatically warned us, this theosophy does not arise from theoretical knowledge. It is drawn from an experience of Light: the calling of the “Easterners,” the *Ishraqiyun*, and of everyone to whom that name can rightly apply. The idea of *Ishraq*, or Illumination, whose essential features we have already explored, ultimately coincides with the idea of *Xvarnah*. Suhrawardi insists that the sources (*yanabi’*) of *Ishraq* are the very sources of *Xvarnah*.

The Orient of Light, Eastern Light, and the Light of Glory are different names for one and the same source of all sources. And that is indeed what is at stake: the source of sources. Suhrawardi repeats throughout his writings that the experience of these Lights is not theoretical knowledge about an object, not the formation of a concept, and not an image constructed from a concept. It is what makes all the knowledge of Eastern theosophy possible and gives that knowledge its foundation. Light is not itself the object of vision; Light is what makes vision possible.

This is not the place to attempt a linguistic history of the word *Xvarnah*, a task in any case beyond our competence.

But a few indications are needed to situate the principal texts in which Suhrawardi uses its Persian form. As noted above, *khorrah* is the Persian form derived from the Avestan *Xvarnah*, corresponding to the northern Middle Persian, or Pahlavi, form *Xvarrah*. The same term also appears in Persian as *farr*, derived not from Avestan but from the Old Persian of the Achaemenids (*farnah*), through the southern Pahlavi form *farrah*. This element appears in the names of certain Iranian rulers, preserved in Greek transcriptions such as Artaphernes, Pharnadates, and Gondophares.[^EII2-110]

Since Anquetil-Duperron, Iranologists have proposed at least twenty descriptions, definitions, or translations of the word.[^EII2-111] In practice, much the same terms recur: glory, radiance, splendour, sovereignty, blazing majesty, supernatural and victorious fire, halo, and so on.

In short, they evoke light, glory, and sovereignty: a radiance beyond the senses that nevertheless shows itself through certain signs in the world of the senses. There have, of course, been attempts to demonstrate that “originally” the word had a purely practical meaning, without mystical significance. I strongly suspect that explanations of this kind always conceal some unacknowledged—or unconscious—philosophical assumption. At any rate, they are of no use to us here. Supposing lead has been transformed into gold, it is the gold that interests us. In Suhrawardi, his commentators, and his disciples, the word *khorrah* has a perfectly clear and precise meaning, entirely faithful to the tradition.

The best way to sum it up is to preserve both its tangible and its mystical meaning. We may say with J. Darmesteter that *Xvarnah* is “the halo of light and divine inspiration that descends upon the saints; it is the heavenly principle that gives the person invested with it power, virtue, genius, and happiness. It is divine good fortune.”[^EII2-112]

We must also emphasize, as Émile Benveniste does, the connection between *Xvarnah* and the very principle of being and life. *Xvarnah* is “a luminous sign of heavenly favour and of power delegated by the gods”; it symbolizes “radiant prosperity,” but is also “an inner agent of vitality, the force that binds a being to existence.”[^EII2-113] This connection is essential if we are to understand the meanings gathered over time under the name *Xvarnah*, and how the idea entered Islamic gnosis—not only in Suhrawardi’s *Eastern Theosophy* but earlier still in Ismaili gnosis.

It brings together the Light of Glory (Greek *doxa*) and personal Destiny (Greek *tykhê*). Their fusion was chiefly the work of Zurvanism, the religious tradition centred on eternal Time. We have already seen this tradition reappear, in dramatically altered form, in Ismaili accounts of the origin of the cosmos. We may even say that the fusion is symbolized in the Aramaic ideogram used to represent *Xvarnah* in the Pahlavi texts of Zoroastrianism.

We must now briefly review several facts bearing on this point.

In different Greek texts, *Xvarnah* is rendered by two words: *doxa*, meaning glory, and *tykhê*, meaning destiny or fortune. For anyone studying how religious realities are experienced and manifested, the pairing is already full of meaning. It helps explain the forms in which *Xvarnah* appears, the distinct personal figures it can take, and the qualities attributed to it. It also helps us understand how *Xvarnah* can be encountered as a person belonging to the world of Light. We should not be too quick to call this “mythology.”

What is at issue is a reality beyond the senses, yet entirely concrete and individual. We need to bring out these features now so that we can recognize them when they reappear in Suhrawardi’s *Eastern Theosophy*.

Zoroastrian books written in Pahlavi employ a curious system known as *uzvaresh*. Probably surviving from a time when documents of the Persian imperial chancery were written in Aramaic, this system writes certain words in Aramaic rather than Pahlavi. Readers see the Aramaic word but pronounce its Pahlavi equivalent. Aramaic words enclosed in this fashion thus function as ideograms—there are about six hundred of them—and scholars of Pahlavi know how much labour they have caused. Now the Pahlavi word *xvarnah* is written with the Aramaic word *gaddeh*, meaning destiny or fortune.[^EII2-114]

The connection we have just described is therefore already present in the written sign itself. This Glory-Destiny (*xvarnah-tykhê*) appears on certain coins from Bactria, personified sometimes as a male figure and sometimes as a female one. Compare the Syrian god Gad, the Roman *Dea Fortuna*, and the Greek *Agathê Tykhê*.[^EII2-115] The aspect of radiant Glory is also represented on these coins, sometimes by a halo and sometimes by flames rising from the shoulders.

This personification is itself rooted in a characteristic capacity of Zoroastrian thought: the ability to perceive beings and things by encountering them in the person of their “angel,” their heavenly archetype. In other words, to perceive *what* they are in their essence by perceiving *who* they are.[^EII2-116] This is how *Xvarnah* itself is apprehended as one of the personal figures inhabiting the subtle world of Light, one of the *Yazatas*, the beings “Worthy of Worship.” Like every being of that subtle heavenly world, *Xvarnah* possesses a *Fravarti* (Persian *foruhar*): its archetype or “angel,” known as “Infinite Light.”

And like the other figures of Zoroastrian angelology, *Xvarnah* can remain a spiritual being in its own right—a distinct reality in the spiritual world (*menok*)—while being wholly present in each of the individual forms through which it comes into relation with the materially manifested world (*getik*).[^EII2-117] The heavenly Figure is both itself and the energy it unfolds and invests in a being of the material world.

Already in the Avesta, we find three forms in which *Xvarnah* takes shape in the earthly world: (1) the Light of Glory of the Aryans (*Airyanem Xvareno*), belonging to the knights of the Iranian epic and to the heroes and heroines of the Zoroastrian faith; (2) the royal Light of Glory (*Kavaem Xvareno*), belonging to Vishtaspa, Zoroaster’s protector, and to the kings of the Kayanid dynasty; and (3) the Light of Glory of Zoroaster himself.[^EII2-118]

We shall find all three categories faithfully represented in Suhrawardi, enriched with shades of meaning that had gathered around the term during the centuries before it reached him.

The accounts of Zoroaster’s *Xvarnah* are especially illuminating for the study of religious experience. In one version, *Xvarnah* descends as a Flame from Infinite Light and enters Zoroaster’s mother at the moment of her own birth. In another, Zoroaster’s *Fravarti*—his “heavenly being”—and his *Xvarnah* unite to form the child Zoroaster. Or else the *Amharaspands*, the “archangels,” place them in earthly substances—*hom* and milk—that will nourish his parents.[^EII2-119] Later, Zoroaster’s *Xvarnah* is preserved in the waters of Lake Kansaoya, from which rises the mountain of dawns, *Mons Victorialis*, the Mountain of Victory.

A multitude of *Fravartis* keep watch over it. At the end of our cycle, our *Aeon*, a young woman will enter the waters of the mystical Lake. The Light of Glory will become present within her body, and she will conceive “the one who is to subdue all the evil spells of demons and human beings.”[^EII2-120] None of this, of course, belongs to the anatomy or physiology of the physical body. As an element of Zoroastrian understanding of the human being, *Xvarnah* belongs to the “body of light,” or, to use a simplifying expression, the “subtle body.”[^EII2-121]

The nature of *Xvarnah* as the blaze of primordial Light; its transmission through the archangels; its anticipated reappearance in the future *Saoshyant*, who will bring our Aeon to a close—all of this calls for comparison with the motif of the “Muhammadan Light” (*Nur Muhammadi*) contemplated in Shiite teachings about prophecy (see above, Book I). That Light is transmitted mystically from the heavenly fullness of divine beings, the Pleroma, to Adam; then from prophet to prophet until Muhammad; and finally to the last Imam of the Muhammadan era.

There is more: the supernatural process leading to the birth of the child Zoroaster corresponds closely to the process that precedes the birth of the holy Imams. Here we can do no more than point out these striking parallels.

Some years ago, however, we were able to identify equally clear traces of the *Xvarnah* motif in a fourth/tenth-century Ismaili theosopher, Abu Ya'qub Sejestani. He invited us to treat the Arabic word *jadd* by reading it as the Persian *bakht*—destiny, allotted fortune—just as the Aramaic ideograms in Pahlavi require a reader to do. In Pahlavi commentaries on the Avesta, *xvarrah* is likewise interpreted as *bakht*.[^EII2-122] The way forward was then clear, for Abu Ya'qub’s descriptions allow us to recognize in the three archangels of Ismaili gnosis—Gabriel, Michael, and Seraphiel—three distinct manifestations of *Xvarnah*: the *Aura Gloriae*, or *Doxa-Sophia*, Glory-Wisdom.[^EII2-123]

We cannot repeat the details here.

Let us simply note that, because Abu Ya'qub is speaking of the spiritual gift bestowed upon prophets and Imams, his account corresponds particularly closely to what Suhrawardi says (as we shall see below) about royal *Xvarnah*: the Light of Glory that invests the “representative of God on His earth.” Since this is the source of the sacred gift that makes the Pole or Imam what he is, it matters little, to Suhrawardi as to Shiite thinkers, whether the Imam is hidden or openly present and recognized. Worldly authority is not what makes him the Pole and the Imam. His spiritual gift endures, whatever human beings may do.

Yet the Light of Glory has manifestations and individual forms other than the full royal and priestly spiritual gift. We recalled above that it is the power that constitutes a being of light and holds that being together. In this sense, the Glory means the soul itself: the soul as pre-existing in one way or another, as the eternal archetype and standard of an earthly individual.[^EII2-124] It is the pre-existing energy that makes this being an individual and spreads a protective radiance around it. It cannot be detached from that being without placing the being in danger; nor can the being seek to go beyond it or deny it without destroying its own existence.

Thus the Glory takes on the features of an eternal Companion of light, who appears both as the goal and as the guide toward that goal. The “Glory” allotted to a being is therefore truly that being’s “Destiny.”

All at once, a whole group of images and ideas associated with Zurvan—as absolute Time, eternal Time—begins to reveal how they fit together. More precisely, we might speak of a play of figures shining through one another, attested by texts from different traditions. Zurvan appears at once as Light of Glory and as Destiny,[^EII2-125] making him, so to speak, the ideal meeting place of the two meanings whose fusion concerns us here.

Put very briefly, the Greek equivalents of these ideas tend to bring this interplay into focus around a particular Figure: the *Agathos Daimon* of Hermeticism, the Good Spirit, who in each instance becomes a guardian Angel or heavenly counterpart. This appearance of one figure through another agrees with an identification we can already discern in Zurvan: he is also Wisdom-*Daena*, at once the divine Wisdom of the Zoroastrian religion—its Sophia—and the heavenly Self of the believer. For Zurvan is essentially many-formed. He is the *Aeon*, eternal Time, the *pantomorphos theos*[^EII2-126], the God who assumes every form.

It follows that each figure in which the Aeon reveals itself is supremely fitted to say to the initiate: “I am your eternity”—your Aeon.

Here lies the secret of the image that brings together the Light of Glory and Destiny in a single Form, a single Figure. We find the same union when Destiny (*tykhê*) is identified with the Figure that dominates the religious horizon of Hermeticism: *Agathos Daimon*. He is at once *Nous*, the divine Intelligence of Hermeticism, and the personal good *daimon* of Hermes and of the Hermetic initiate. He is the *daimon paredros*: the heavenly companion or counterpart, the guardian “Angel” of the person who is his earthly counterpart.[^EII2-127] It is precisely this *Agathos Daimon* whom Suhrawardi knows and invokes as the “Perfect Nature” (*al-Tiba’ al-tamm*). That is the name of the “Form of light” which, in the tradition of Islamic Hermeticism, appears to Hermes and “casts knowledge into him” (see below, Section 5 and Chapter VI).

Let us also note here that a trace of this “Perfect Nature” can be found in a Shiite *hadith* concerning the First Imam.[^EII2-128] We may recall, too, the “Form of light” that joins the Ismaili initiate during initiation, which we have shown elsewhere to be a reminiscence of Manichaean teaching.[^EII2-129]

Set out so quickly, these ideas may seem hopelessly entangled. Certainly, the ways in which these religious worlds overlap and meet in such images form one of the most complex chapters in the study of religions. So long as we are content to speak too easily of “syncretism,” everything may appear arbitrary and confused.

But if we try to discover what a person’s faith intends, and how it gives shape to an entire world, then that faith itself—the thing supposedly “inexplicable”—becomes the explanation. Hermeticism and Zoroastrianism meet in Suhrawardi’s personal faith in a way whose ultimate secret lies in Suhrawardi himself. Their meeting is announced by his use of two distinctive ideas: the Zoroastrian Light of Glory and the Hermetic “Perfect Nature.”

Suhrawardi bears witness to the first by recounting a vision, and to the second in one of the most beautiful psalms in his “Book of Hours.” They come together through an underlying idea that emerges fully into view when the Light of Glory is identified with personal Destiny.

To sum up the facts we have reviewed: (1) In Zoroastrianism, Zurvan is the infinite Time of Ohrmazd’s Religion (*Daena*, Persian *Din*). That Religion is Ohrmazd’s path, eternally vibrating in the Light.[^EII2-130] It is divine Wisdom or Sophia, the “robe” and eternal Time of Ohrmazd. It is also the Figure that, after death, presents itself to the Zoroastrian soul that has fought and won its battle, as the soul’s heavenly Self, its Self of light.

Thus the soul embodied on earth recognizes its heavenly partner or counterpart in a Figure through whom the Figure of eternal Time shines.[^EII2-131] (2) In the *Corpus Hermeticum*, the Aeon, eternal Time, likewise appears as a distinct divine reality, a Power of God identical with Wisdom-Sophia, the active, creative Soul of the world.[^EII2-132] This World Soul is the mother of *Anthropos*: the initiate who has been reborn and has brought forth his “immortal body” (*athanaton soma*). This assurance of immortality is bound precisely to attaining, or receiving, the *daimon paredros*: the heavenly “Angel” or companion, a free gift obtained through prayer and initiation.

The parallel is striking. Zurvan and the Aeon each take the form of personal Destiny. In Zoroastrianism, this is the angel Daena-Sophia, who is at once a distinct manifestation of the Zoroastrian religion and the personal “angel” of the Zoroastrian believer. In Hermeticism, it is *Agathos Daimon*, who is at once a divine manifestation and the *daimon paredros*, the personal angel of every initiate.[^EII2-133]

We can thus see how Zoroastrianism and Hermeticism meet in a single fundamental image.

The common element, in Suhrawardi’s thought, is what binds the vision of the *Xvarnah*, the Light of Glory, to the form of light called the “Perfect Nature”—a person’s own destiny, since it is at once the initiate’s “father” and “child.” And this union opens onto a vast horizon.

Later we shall consider the studies that have connected the Zoroastrian idea of the *Xvarnah* with the Holy Grail of Western tradition, and the figure of Kay Khosraw with that of Parsifal. Other studies, meanwhile, have traced the sources of Wolfram von Eschenbach’s *Parsifal* to the *Corpus Hermeticum*. What emerges from these lines of research is the idea of a meeting of traditions—a meeting that, in Suhrawardi’s *Eastern Theosophy*, has already taken place.

That meeting is already apparent in the imagery of the *Xvarnah*, whether imagined or actually depicted. Its triumphant visions are precisely what will find expression in the language of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, the master of Illumination. The figures shine through at the threshold between the visible and invisible worlds, surrounded by an aura of victory: the victory of the believer, the initiate, or the mystic undergoing the rebirth inscribed in his or her destiny. The victorious power inherent in the *Xvarnah*—at once Light of Glory and Destiny—becomes an attribute of the person it invests.

In Mazdean theosophy, this *Gloria victrix*, or conquering Glory, appears in the person of the angel Ashi Vanuhi, “daughter of Ohrmazd, sister of the archangels, Spirit of wisdom.” A majestic and proud figure, she is, in the language of sacred imagery, a sister to the Nikai, the winged figures of Victory in Greek sculpture. Those figures, chiefly through Gnostic influences, were among the sources of the earliest Christian images of angels. Ashi Vanuhi both possesses and bestows the *Xvarnah*; yet she is also Victory itself, its triumphant Fire.

Glory and Destiny converge in her person: the *Aura Gloriae* of a being of light. Mithraism, too, understood her as *tykhê*, destiny, in the sense of *Fortuna victrix*, victorious Fortune—Glory and Fortune as one. Her meeting with Zoroaster in Erân-Vêj, a famous episode of the *Avesta* (*Yasht* XVII), is an exemplary event taking place “at the centre of the world.” As such, it prefigures—and makes possible—the believer’s meeting after death with her sister Daênâ, who is the believer’s own “victorial power.”[^EII2-134]

We have recalled these images and scenes because they embody the qualities of the *Xvarnah* that give Suhrawardi’s vocabulary its characteristic tone. Central to them is the idea of victory, of triumphant power (Pahlavi *pêrôzih*), inherent in beings of light. Persian and Arabic texts offer many equivalents: greatness and beauty (*’azamat o zibâî, bahâ’*), light (*nûr*), radiant joy (*bahjat*), and others.[^EII2-135] (Here one might recall Repanse-de-joie, the name of the Grail queen in Wolfram’s poem.) When writing in Arabic, Suhrawardi chiefly uses *qahr*, meaning to triumph, prevail, or subdue (Persian *pîrûzî* or *fîrûzî*), and *qâhir*, the corresponding name for one who does so (Persian *pîrûz* or *fîrûz*).

The “archangelic Lights” that arise from the “sources of the Light of Glory and of the sovereignty of light” are called *Anwâr qâhira*: ruling or “victorial” Lights.[^EII2-136] (Recall the Greek Nikai mentioned above, and the Christian title *Angelus victor*, the victorious Angel, applied to the archangel Michael.)[^EII2-137] But an important distinction is needed here. The terms *qahr* and *qâhir*, together with their derivatives, also belong to the vocabulary of Arabic astrology, where they can even suggest the violence or domination exerted by a harmful star. Suhrawardi’s concept of *Xvarnah* certainly contains astrological allusions.

Yet in the vocabulary of *Eastern Theosophy*, these terms carry no harmful or evil implication.[^EII2-138] We generally translate them with the adjective “victorial” rather than “victorious.” By “victorial” we mean an enduring quality of a being, a permanent capacity for triumph; “victorious” more readily suggests a victory already won. The word “victorial” was suggested to us by the Latin name *Mons Victorialis*, the “mountain of the dawns” from which, according to one Christian interpretation of Zoroastrian prophecies about the coming Saviour, the Magi set out on their journey.[^EII2-139] To designate this whole idea of “victorial power,” Suhrawardi may use the phrase *al-amr al-qahrî*: something like *res victorialis*, the reality or principle of victory.

Perhaps we have now assembled the minimum background needed to understand the allusions, meanings, and implications of the texts in which the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* describes, in his turn, the different forms and appearances of the Light of Glory. These include the visions granted to the kings and prophet of ancient Persia, and the archangelic hierarchies that eternally “rise” from this Orient—from the highest Archangels down to the form of light nearest to each mystical pilgrim: his or her “Perfect Nature.”

At the end of the metaphysics of his great *Book of Crossroads and Conversations*, between the pages where he sets out the spiritual lineage of the *Ishrâqîyûn* and those where he alludes to events taking place in the mystical cities of the “intermediate Orient,” Suhrawardi gives a long account of the *Xvarnah* as both Light of Glory and personal Destiny. His threefold distinction corresponds to the three forms of manifestation described in the *Avesta* (see above, p. 86). He writes: 1) “If what is to predominate in the soul’s innermost being is the *res victorialis* (*amr qahrî*), then the effect of the dawning Light (*shorûq*) is to make the victorial powers (*omûr qahrîya*) prevail within it, powers arising from the configurations of the stars and from the Angels for whom those stars are the theurgies.

“For the subtle reality that the ancient Persians (the *Pahlawîyûn*) called the Light of Glory (*Khorrah*, *Xvarnah*) has its source in the radiance of heaven, and its imprint upon the human soul is felt as victorial strength (*qahr*). The person invested with it thus becomes a hero, one who rules and triumphs. — 2) If the dawning Light springs from the sacred radiance of the pure spiritual Lights, in proportion to the soul’s capacity for ardent longing and love, then the imprint of the Light of Glory upon the soul makes its bearer find joy and happiness in things of delicacy and refinement.

“Other souls feel spontaneously drawn towards such a person and come to love him, while peoples sing his praises, because the radiance investing him is transmitted from Angels whose theurgies are magnificent, worthy of reverence and love. — 3) Finally, if there is equilibrium, and the different forms of Light are abundantly present through the mediation of the lord who is the Sublime Luminary, then the person who possesses it is a revered king, one who inspires respect and is filled with knowledge, virtue, and happiness. This alone is called the ‘royal Light of Glory’ (*Kayân-Khorrah*). At its fullest, this last category is the most distinguished of the three, for it entails a perfect balance of Light; moreover, the Sublime Luminary is the gateway to all great ecstasies.”[^EII2-140]

Despite the particular nuances of *Eastern Theosophy*, we can recognise in this classification the three kinds of Light of Glory already distinguished in the *Avesta*. Suhrawardi’s first category corresponds to the *Xvarnah* of Iranian chivalry and legendary heroes.

The second is the priestly spiritual gift of sacred souls, of men of God such as the prophet Zoroaster.

The third is named directly in Persian: the royal *Xvarnah*, the “Glory of the Kayanids” (*Kevaem Xvarenô*). This is the *Xvarnah* in its fullness, bringing the other two together and tempering each with the other in a perfect balance of light.

Three groups of observations may be offered:

1) In each case, the Light is transmitted through an intermediary, an idea belonging to astrology or to theosophy concerned with the stars. It is as though a flame were shining in heaven at the birth of the person to whom the *Aura Gloriae* is allotted and whom it invests. In the second and third categories, the “spiritual Lights” are specifically named as the intermediaries of the *Xvarnah*. In no case do the patterns of the stars or the heavenly bodies themselves act through some kind of mechanical causation. The active agents are what Suhrawardi’s angelology calls the Angels governing the theurgies (*tilimsât*)—that is, the bodies of every kind, whether in the earthly world or among the stars. These Angels mediate the “oriental source” (*shorûq*), the Light of Glory, from which they themselves arise and which belongs to the world beyond the senses. The royal *Xvarnah*, being the *Xvarnah* in its entirety, is mediated by the “Sublime Luminary” (*al-Nayyir al-a‘zam*), the sun. Once again, it is not the physical mass of the sun that acts in its own right, but the Angel who works through it, whom we shall later see Suhrawardi call by his Iranian name, *Hûrakhsh*. The sun is the gateway (*pîshgâh*) to the great ecstasies: *Sol invictus*, the unconquered Sun. We can thus discern a trace of Mithraism within the *Ishrâq* (see below, § 5, the psalm to the archangel of the Sun, and Chapter IV, 1).

2) The three kinds of *Xvarnah* can readily be related to the three kinds of spiritual person, or philosopher-sage, mentioned in the prologue to the *Book of Eastern Theosophy* (see above, pp. 69 ff.). The first would be the *Xvarnah* of philosophers concerned solely with knowledge, heroes of the intellect. The second would belong to heroes of “theurgic piety,” or of pure mystical experience unmixed with philosophical knowledge. The third would belong to the person who combines both: the hero perfected alike in philosophical wisdom and in mystical and theurgic experience. Such a person is the *Khalifat Allâh*, God’s representative on His Earth (called precisely the *Gubernator Terrae*, “Governor of the Earth,” in the *Corpus Hermeticum*). The blessed king Kay Khosraw, as Suhrawardi contemplates him, was such a person. We might therefore see the passage from the first category to the third as the movement from heroic epic to mystical epic, a theme we shall develop later (Chapter IV, 4). The sages who follow in the footsteps of Kay Khosraw, the ecstatic king, are called the *Khosrawânîyûn* after him (the Persian adjective carries the general sense of royal or imperial). Kay Khosraw withdrew from this world into concealment after renouncing temporal rule. And Suhrawardi has expressly warned us that by “caliphal” authority he does not mean the exercise of worldly political power (see above, p. 71). The *Xvarnah* also invests the spiritual Pole when he is the “Hidden Imam,” invisible to the mass of humanity, although his light illuminates the hearts of the faithful and mysteriously guides them to the threshold of his dwelling in the “eighth clime” (see below, Book VII). Such are the *Khosrawânîyûn*. Suhrawardi’s vision gathers into one lineage of sacred figures the royal sage of ancient Persia and the mystical Imam (*mystikos* means “hidden”) of Shiite Persia. These features tell us much about the intentions of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*.

3) Elsewhere, too, Suhrawardi insists that the Lights encountered by the spiritual seeker, whose source is the Light of Glory, are not matters of theoretical knowledge or conceptual representation. Known in that way, the “oriental Source” would cease to be the Source; it would become simply one item of knowledge among others, an accidental property arising in the knowing subject. But this Source is the Orient of Knowledge itself, and its revelation touches the very depths of the being who encounters it. Suhrawardi makes this point at the end of one of his works written in Persian, the *Partaw-Nâmeh*, or *Book of the Ray of Light*,[^EII2-141] in a passage that concludes by clarifying once again the effects of the royal *Xvarnah* upon the soul.

“These flashes and lights,” he says, “are not theoretical knowledge, nor are they representations formed by the intellect. No: they are sacred irradiations, emanating from the spiritual world. The spiritual world comprises all Lights existing apart from matter, and pure souls share in this splendour of light. There is no limit to the power and radiance of the light of the Necessary Being and of the Intelligence.

“For souls in the other world, that light is more evident than anything visible to the eye in this world; it is more splendid than every splendour of light. The light of spiritual beings is not something added to their essence. No: they *are* Light, Light existing apart from matter, as the sages of Light have said on the strength of their own visionary experience.

“Every sovereign who has been initiated into wisdom and perseveres in the worship and adoration of the Light of Lights is given the royal Light of Glory (*Khorrah-e kayânî* = *Kayân-khorrah*) and receives the royal splendour of Light (*Farr-e nûrânî*). The divine radiance clothes him in a robe of majesty and beauty. He is the natural leader of the world. He receives triumphant aid from the higher universe; his dreams and his inspiration attain perfection.”

We can now begin to understand the claim made by the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* when he bears witness to the vision granted to him, like the visions of Kay Khosraw, Zoroaster, and others—a vision upon which he would subsequently build his *Eastern Theosophy*.

##### 2. The Visions of Kay Khosraw and Zoroaster

Suhrawardi alludes to the event that decisively changed the course of his spiritual life in a brief personal confession—one might even say a moment of self-criticism—at a crucial point in his *Eastern Theosophy*. He speaks of a direct vision that shattered both his doubts and the narrow limits within which he had confined himself in the company of the Peripatetic philosophers, the followers of Aristotle. It overturned the views he had favoured at the beginning of his career.

As his commentators point out, he is referring to his adolescence, when he was taking his first steps in philosophy. The Peripatetic doctrine he then defended was a cosmology that limited the number of angelic Intelligences moving the celestial Spheres to ten, or at most fifty-five.

Now he clearly understands his youthful error.

However wonderful the order and relationships governing the world of bodies—the world of night and darkness—those governing the world of the noble and pure Lights must be prior to them and higher than them. What can the Peripatetic philosophers possibly do with a plenitude of Intelligences restricted to such a paltry number? No: the relationships and proportions reigning in the world of Light are infinitely more wonderful, more real, and more complex than those we discover in our world, which is only their projected shadow.[^EII2-142]

The first thing Suhrawardi rejected, then, was a cosmology that knew nothing of worlds inhabited by countless beings of light. The conversion of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* was bound up with a revelation of the world of angels. As he would repeatedly recall, it was above all this angelic world that inspired the thought and shaped the worship of the ancient Persians.

We should note something else: Suhrawardi had an intuition of the unfathomable wonders of the “Heaven of the Fixed Stars,” a term that also encompasses all the star systems and galaxies beyond our solar system. His discovery of angelology went hand in hand with an astronomical revolution that burst open the limited heavens of Aristotelian and Ptolemaic astronomy. In the West, by contrast, the astronomical revolution came at the expense of angelology. This is no small indication of the difference between our cultures.[^EII2-143]

Suhrawardi knows that the pure spiritual Lights have been contemplated by all those who, at one time or another, have shed the dwelling of their physical bodies like an outer skin, and have then put their testimony into writing to guide others. This is what all the accounts of ecstasy describe: those of Hermes, Empedocles, and Plato. Plato, too, recounted his own experience and testified that, having cast off the darkness, he had directly beheld the world of Light.

We already know, of course, that under Plato’s name Suhrawardi is referring to the celebrated ecstasy of Plotinus. He knew it through the account from the *Enneads* embedded in the work called the *Theology of Aristotle*, a paraphrase of Plotinus. Throughout his *Eastern Theosophy* he returns repeatedly to this famous account: “Plato” (that is, Plotinus) said, “When I was separated from my material body, I saw Spheres of light.”

The commentators explain that these words refer to the highest archangelic Intelligences. Those of more intense light encompass those whose light is weaker, just as the heavenly Spheres in traditional astronomy are nested one within another. Suhrawardi then sums up the Plotinian account: “Plato related of himself that, in certain spiritual states, he seemed to be stripped of his body and separated from the material condition. Then he contemplated Light and Beauty within himself.

“Next he rose towards the divine Cause that embraces all things. He felt as though he had been placed within it, suspended from it, and he contemplated the Sublime Light on the highest divine summit.” This is the substance of the account, down to its conclusion: “But then conscious reflection came to place a veil between me and that Light.” For his part, the prophet who gave the law to the Arabs and Persians (the prophet Muhammad) declared: “God has seventy-seven veils of light; if they were lifted from before His Face, the radiance of His Face would set ablaze everything His gaze encompasses.”[^EII2-144]

A few pages earlier, Suhrawardi had already invoked the ecstatic testimonies of Hermes and Plato, and concluded: “The sages of Persia and India, too, are unanimous on this point. Well, if in astronomy we take account of observations made by one or two people, how can we fail to take account of the explicit testimony of those who were pillars of wisdom and prophecy, concerning something they themselves had seen directly in the course of their spiritual observations?”[^EII2-145]

For Suhrawardi, this is the decisive argument, and a modern phenomenologist could hardly put it better. We recognise that the first condition for a phenomenon—*that which shows itself*—is the capacity of *the person to whom* it shows itself. The objectivity of the vision is inseparable from this relationship.

Those to whom the phenomenon remains hidden have only one possible course: to discover the conditions under which it becomes visible to those who see it. That is why something like our word “phenomenology” may long have existed in the Arabic expression *kashf al-mahjûb*, the act of unveiling or disclosing what is hidden. The phrase appears in the titles of many works of mystical knowledge and experience. Any other criticism of the visionary object fails to reach that object and prejudges the manner of its existence.

All attempts to explain away the reality of what was seen by giving it a causal “explanation,” reducing it to a meaning that falls short of the reality *that shows itself*—none of this interests Suhrawardi. He will always counter with the prior question: by what right can those who have *not seen* reject the testimony of those who have? In his *Glosses* on these pages,[^EII2-146] Mulla Sadra Shirazi recalls the existence of an otherworldly faculty of sight (*hiss basarî okhrawî*), the organ that perceives the *Malakût*, the angelic world.

Those who lack it can always deny what others see, but their denial carries no weight. Drawing strength from the testimonies he invokes, especially those of the sages of ancient Persia, whose theosophical wisdom he sought to revive, the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* explains himself in these words:

“The author of these lines” (that is, Suhrawardi himself)[^EII2-147] “began as a staunch defender of the Peripatetic doctrine that denied these things, because he was excessively attached to their teaching. And he would have persisted in that position if he had not himself seen the decisive proof given by his Lord.” As the commentators emphasise, this was indeed a direct vision, a visionary perception of the pure Lights.

The author *saw* that all the forms, figures, and species existing in our world are icons or images (*asnâm*), shadows and silhouettes (*ashbâh*), of immaterial forms of light existing in the world of Intelligence. Suhrawardi continues: “If someone refuses to believe this testimony and finds this proof insufficient, let him undertake spiritual exercises in his turn and become a pupil of masters gifted with visionary perception.

“Perhaps an ecstatic vision will come to him, showing him the Light that pours forth in the world of the *Jabarût* (the world of the cherubic Intelligences). Perhaps he will see the celestial beings of the *Malakût* (the world of the Angels who are the ‘lords of species,’ or archetypes; see below). Perhaps he will contemplate the Lights contemplated by Hermes and Plato: the spiritual splendours, sources of the Light of Glory and of the Sovereignty of Light, which Zoroaster proclaimed and towards which the most truthful king, the blessed Kay Khosraw, was carried in an ecstasy that allowed him to behold them directly.

“The sages of ancient Persia were so unanimous about this that, according to them, Water has an archetypal Angel (*sâhib al-sanam*) in the world of the *Malakût*, whom they called *Khordâd* (Avestan *Haurvatât*). Plants have an Angel, whom they called *Môrdâd* (Avestan *Ameretât*). Fire has an Angel, whom they called *Ordibehest* (Avestan *Arta Vahishta*). These are also the Lights to which Empedocles and several other sages alluded.”

We have emphasised the characteristic expression “sources of the Light of Glory and of the Sovereignty of Light.” Suhrawardi combines two Persian technical terms in an Arabic phrase, *yanâbî’ al-Khorrah wa’l-Rây*. The first is already familiar to us (Avestan *xvarnah*, Pahlavi *xvarrah*).

The second, *rây*, represents an Avestan term (*rayi*) suggesting royal greatness, splendour, and magnificence.[^EII2-148] The pairing of the two terms, or of the adjectives derived from them, is both traditional and characteristic in the *Avesta* and the Pahlavi texts.[^EII2-149] Their appearance here is therefore evidence that Suhrawardi is not inventing anything. He is following a tradition that, by one route or another, had reached the man who would “revive the wisdom of ancient Persia.”

Elsewhere in the book, other expressions likewise allude to these “sources of the Light of Glory.” As we have said, *Eastern Theosophy* begins with a radical reform of Logic and ends with something like a reminder of ecstasy, interrupted by two lyrical psalms. There we hear of “wanderers who come knocking at the gateway of the lofty halls of Light.”

The “Angels who draw them towards the Orient” come out to meet them and pour upon them Water flowing from the “Source of Beauty” (*Yanbû’ al-bahâ’*).[^EII2-150] We have already noted (p. 92 above) that *Xvarnah* can also be translated into Arabic as *bahâ’*, meaning beauty, radiance, or splendour. Here, then, the “Source of Beauty” is equivalent to the *Yanâbî’ al-Khorrah*, the Sources of the Light of Glory, in the great passage of Suhrawardi’s personal confession.

The description of the Angels in that same passage makes it especially clear that, in his thought, *Xvarnah* and *Ishrâq*, Light of Glory and Light of the Orient, Source of the *Xvarnah* and oriental Source, can express the same reality. Water and Light, too, are traditionally interchangeable symbols of the sources of Life and Knowledge.[^EII2-151] Elsewhere we encounter the expressions “Sources of Life” and “Sources of Light and Life.”[^EII2-152] The Source is not itself an object of knowledge; it is what makes knowledge spring forth.

Naturally, these passages particularly engaged Suhrawardi’s earliest commentators, Shahrazuri and Qotb Shirazi. Their explanations show us what they knew of ancient Persian spirituality. Both specify that the “spiritual splendours” Suhrawardi speaks of—these heavenly irradiations—are those proclaimed by the prophet, “the wise, excellent and perfect Imam Zoroaster of Azerbaijan.”[^EII2-153] In his “Zend Book,”[^EII2-154] Zoroaster declares that the world is divided into two realms: *mînôvî*, the world of Light, the spiritual world, and *gêtî*, the dark, bodily world. These are indeed the two great cosmological categories of the *Avesta*: *mainyava* and *gaethya* (Pahlavi *mênôk* and *gêtîk*).[^EII2-155]

From the world of Light, a Light streams over the souls of the Perfect. It supports them, granting splendour and strength (*ta’yîd* and *rây*); their souls are filled with its radiance, and over them rises a dawn more brilliant than the rising sun. “It is this Light that is called *Khorrah* in Pahlavi, as Zoroaster also says: the *Khorrah* is a Light streaming from the divine Essence. Through it, creatures are ordered in a hierarchy in which some take precedence over others, while its aid establishes each creature in its proper action and work. The *Khorrah* belonging to sovereigns is called *Kayân Khorrah*.”[^EII2-156]

Thus a fundamental idea of Mazdean theosophy re-entered the stream of Islamic mystical knowledge and theosophy. From generation to generation, the *Ishrâqîyûn*, heirs to the *Khosrawânîyûn*, would pass on what Suhrawardi and his commentators had bequeathed to them.

Alongside the prophet Zoroaster, the “blessed king Kay Khosraw” is named here once again. Kay Khosraw is indeed the dominant and final figure of the Kayanid dynasty before the appearance of Vishtaspa, Zoroaster’s protector. Each of the Kayanids has particular traits and a distinctive story, rich in heroic and turbulent detail.

Yet none can be fitted into our chronologies. They belong forever to their own time—a time which, through Kay Khosraw, also belongs to all the *Khosrawânîyûn* sages. A few pages from now this commanding figure will reappear, his “history” passing beyond history into the “eighth clime.” That clime beyond all climes is the *place* where the heroic epic secretly passes into the mystical epic. It is also the place where a meeting becomes possible between the mystical chivalry of Iran as Suhrawardi understands it—the initiated *Khosrawânîyûn*, that is, the *Ishrâqîyûn*—and the chivalry of our own Grail tradition (see below, Chapters IV and V).

A passage Suhrawardi devotes elsewhere to Kay Khosraw[^EII2-157] shows us the sacred character he sees in the Iranian sovereign, placed in the line of ecstatic heroes stretching from Hermes to Empedocles. All the commentators, naturally, reproduced this passage. “It happened,” writes our *shaykh*, “that Kay Khosraw the Blessed remained absorbed in prayer and long inward meditation.

“Then the Wisdom (*Sophia*) of the most holy Father[^EII2-158] came to him and spoke with him of the world of Mystery (*ghayb*, the unmanifest). He was carried away into the highest world; his soul received the imprint of divine *Sophia*; the archangelic Lights appeared to him face to face, and in that encounter he understood the nature of the subtle reality called the royal Light of Glory (*Kayân-Khorrah*): it is the casting (*ilqâ’*) into the soul of a victorial element (*qâhir*) before which heads bow down.”

Kay Khosraw’s visionary ecstasy is therefore of the same kind as the ecstasies that brought Zoroaster face to face with the divine Heptad during his conversations with the “Archangels,” the Seven Most Holy Immortals. Kay Khosraw’s conversations with heavenly Wisdom also recall the conversations of the sage recorded in the Pahlavi book entitled *Mênôke-Xrat* (*Heavenly Wisdom*).

Yet the long passages Ferdowsi devotes to Kay Khosraw’s exploits in the *Shâh-Nâmeh* fall far short of what Suhrawardi writes about the ecstatic hero’s calling. The same is true of the other heroes of the Iranian epic who appear in his *Mystical Narratives* (see below, Chapters IV and V). That, precisely, is the mission of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* as the bearer of ancient Persia’s spiritual inheritance: to lead its heroes to the fulfilment of their vocation, to become their history himself, and to decipher the mystery concealed from us by Kay Khosraw’s final disappearance.

Without crossing the threshold of death, Kay Khosraw vanishes from the sight of the people of this world, just as the twelfth and last Imam of Shiism will later become invisible to them, thereafter to be known as the Awaited One.

Kay Khosraw is the figure of the initiate who has become a perfect Sage, initiated by Wisdom—heavenly *Sophia* herself. This investiture consecrates him as the mystical King of the world, endowed above all with what the Neoplatonist Iamblichus called the “sacred virtues.” It is when Kay Khosraw becomes invisible to human eyes that he is truly the mystical sovereign. “Casting a victorial element into the soul”: the Form of Light that is the Perfect Nature also casts forms of knowledge into Hermes. And the Hermetic initiate likewise became *Gubernator Terrae*, Governor of the Earth.

How is the initiate—who, according to Suhrawardi’s deepest wish, seeks both philosophical knowledge and mystical experience—to reach the fulfilment of his desires? Suhrawardi teaches him what oriental knowledge is and points out where its oriental Source lies.

But how is all this to become an event for him, *his own* event? This is what Suhrawardi will describe in symbolic stories that unfold the great themes of the mystical epic. Their settings and their *dramatis personae*, the characters who take part, presuppose that he has introduced his disciple to the hierarchy of being and, with it, to the hierarchies of beings of light.

Of these, the one nearest the disciple will become his guide, if he proves worthy, for that being too has its origin in the Orient of the Lights (*origo-oriens*), at the sources of the Light of Glory and of the Sovereignty of Light. In broad outline, then, what is at issue is Suhrawardi’s fundamental angelology: fundamental because it provides the structure through which being is understood and through which being reveals itself to consciousness.

##### 3. The Archangelic Lights and the Platonic Ideas

Ideally, we would set out the whole of Suhrawardi’s angelology here. We must confine ourselves to its essential features. We need to keep in mind the order in which its figures arise, and remember what Suhrawardi means by the world of Darkness.

We must clarify the words he uses for the beings of light that he identifies with the Platonic Ideas. In fact, however, his Ideas are no longer quite the same as Plato’s, because Suhrawardi understands them through an angelology explicitly related to that of Zoroastrianism. The later Neoplatonists, on the other hand—Proclus and Damascius, commentators on the *Chaldean Oracles*—would have recognised much that was familiar.

We must then sketch the structure of the hierarchies of Light that eternally proceed from the Light of Lights.

Finally, we must grasp what this angelology means for the spiritual life actually lived by the visionary theosopher, for his sacred way of being—his “hieratic” *ethos*.

As we have already explained, visionary perception identifies the *Xvarnah*—the Light of Glory, flaming Majesty, the Energy that holds together the being of every creature and surrounds it with its fire beyond the senses, its “personal angel” and its “destiny”—as the source of the Light that is identical with being itself, the Orient of all Light and the Light of every Orient. From this Light of Glory comes the name given to the highest Lights, which proceed immediately from it and mediate its power to the weaker Lights. They are the *Anwâr qâhira*, the “victorial” Lights.

The Arabic *qâhira* corresponds to the Persian *pîrûz*; it indicates that their being unites the two qualities called *xvarrômand* and *râyômand* in Pahlavi (see above, p. 100), qualities belonging to beings invested with the Light of Glory and the sovereignty of Light. We also often call them “archangelic Lights,” because the dawning Lights—the primordial *Ishrâqât*—which proceed directly from the Orient of the Lights are literally Archangels (*Ru’asâ’ al-Malakût al-Qâhira*).[^EII2-159] In the word *archangel*, the Greek *arkhê* evokes both beginning or first principle and command or supremacy.

Moreover, the very idea of an archangelic order completes an image that accords with the chivalric ethic developed, on different planes of existence, by Zoroastrian angelology. There is the struggle of the powers of Light supporting Ohrmazd, who is Wisdom-Light. There is also the struggle of the *Fravartis* (Persian *forûhar*), heavenly beings who are the archetypes of every creature of light. Their name means, literally, “those who have chosen”: those who chose to descend into the material world to fight the opposing Ahrimanian powers.

We find the same indication even in the name Suhrawardi chooses for the Lights that govern bodies. He calls each one a Light (*Nûr*) *Espahbad*,[^EII2-160] using an ancient military title whose very sound recalls the deeds of Iran’s chivalry (see also Chapter V below). Earlier we recalled how the traditional Christian image of the Angel derived, chiefly through Gnostic intermediaries, from the representations of Nike, or “Victories,” in Greek sculpture.[^EII2-161]

*Angelus victor, Lux victorialis, invicta*: the “archangelic Lights” thus manifest the same quality expressed by the name *Mons Victorialis*, the mountain rising from Lake Hâmûn in Sistan. For this lake—the Kansaoya Lake of the *Avesta*—is a receptacle of the *Xvarnah*, and its image is associated with the *Saoshyant* to come, the Saviour who will be “victorious.”[^EII2-162]

We also recalled earlier (p. 65 above) how the first illumination and the first reflection of the Light of Lights, or Light of Glory, gave rise to the original relationship of the First Beloved and the First Lover. This twofold relationship is inherent in the eternal phenomenon of Light, in which the revelation of being itself takes place, since being and light are ultimately the same.

If being, in its depths, means Light and the Sovereignty of Light, its disclosure and its various forms can occur only through a hierarchy of degrees, a progressive diminishing of Light. It is because Light is not only the source of all sovereignty but is sovereignty itself that some beings have power over others, and the latter are subordinate to the former. Such predominance and subordination express—and are fundamentally determined by—one thing: the relationship between different intensities of Light, stronger in some beings and weaker in others. This relation provides the pattern by which the Many proceed from the One. It is the very pattern of the fundamental angelology of the *Ishrâq*, of Suhrawardi’s philosophy, replacing the Peripatetic and Avicennian schemes.

At every level it is essentially a relationship of love. Each more intense Light has power over a less intense Light—reigning over it like a beloved who commands love, through the attraction it exerts—while the lesser Light longs for it and turns towards it. These are the two “dimensions,” *qahr* and *mahabbat*, reflected in Suhrawardi’s rich vocabulary: sovereignty of Light (*tasallot nûrî*), dominion through manifestation (*Qahr zohûrî*), divine radiance (*bâriq ilâhî*), and so on.

All these images arise from the concept of the Light of Glory (*Xvarnah*) revealing itself in the many *Ishrâqât*, the dawning Lights or illuminations. This is the relationship we find at the eternal dawn of being, between the Light of Lights and the primordial Archangel whom Suhrawardi calls by his Zoroastrian name, Bahman (Avestan *Vohu Manah*, Good Thought; Greek *Eunoia*).

That is why, as we have already pointed out, when Suhrawardi invokes “the sage Empedocles,” we must be careful not to confuse *qahr* and *mahabbat*, as understood by the new Empedocles known to Islamic Gnostics, with “love” and “strife” in the classical Empedocles.[^EII2-163] For Suhrawardi, *qahr* is fundamentally the dominion, the hold the beloved has over the lover, so richly explored in the mystical poetry of Persia. *Mahabbat* is the movement of love that directs the lover towards the beloved and places the lover in dependence upon the beloved, just as an effect is ordered towards and dependent upon its cause. For it is the cause’s illumination, dawning upon the effect, that raises the effect into being.

“Know,” writes Suhrawardi, “that every cause whose nature is light feels towards its effect both love (*mahabbat*) and sovereign superiority (*qahr*), while the effect feels towards its cause a love inseparable from a sense of dependence (*dhill*). That is why all being appears arranged in pairs, corresponding to the differing degrees of light and darkening, dominion and love: the superior rank that belongs to the power of dominion over what is lower, and the sense of dependence inherent in love towards what is higher. As God Most High says: ‘Of every being We have made a pair; perhaps you will take heed’ (51:49).”[^EII2-164]

How, then, does the universe appear to the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, beginning with the physical world? As an immense succession of dwelling places and steps marking the stages in the diminishing of Light, down to its burial in pure Darkness. Every movement of love, at whatever level and in whatever form, is the longing of a being to rise again out of this fall, calling upon the power of the Light that precedes and rules over it. So, step by step, the redemption of Light takes place through love, which is also the anguish of Light in exile—an anguish that only the “victorial” strength of the higher Light can overcome, calling the exiled Light back to itself.

In broad outline, the physics of *Eastern Theosophy* teaches us the following.[^EII2-165] Some things are, in their fundamental reality, Light, brightness, and splendour; others are, in their fundamental reality, Darkness, obscurity, and night. Light can be an accidental quality of something other than itself—a thing of which it is, precisely, the light.

Or it can be a substance existing in and through itself, as do the archangelic Lights of the different orders and the Souls governing bodies of various kinds. Similarly, Darkness may refer to the degree of darkness present in a thing, or it may mean bodily substance itself, which as such is inert and devoid of light and life. For this Suhrawardi uses the term *barzakh*,[^EII2-166] suggesting an in-between space, a screen, or an interval.

For the *Ishrâqîyûn*, a body is neither an assembly of atoms nor a compound of matter and form, as it is for the Peripatetic philosophers who follow Aristotle’s matter-and-form theory. Broadly speaking, a body is anything that forms a screen, anything that obstructs the Light and can, by that very fact, receive it and become a place where it appears (*mazhar*). A “body,” then, is whatever remains as pure, inert, undifferentiated Darkness once the Light has withdrawn from it.

We should note that for Suhrawardi there is no “neutral state,” no condition that is neither Light nor Darkness. Here his physics differs from that of the Peripatetics. For the latter, the withdrawal or absence of Light is not enough to make a thing dark. The thing must also possess the potential to receive Light. Air, for example—meaning cosmic space—cannot be called dark. It is transparent: it lets light pass through without stopping or reflecting it, as a *barzakh* does. Light simply cannot belong to it as a quality.

The *Ishrâqîyûn*, on the other hand, extend the meaning of Darkness beyond even the concept of *barzakh*, insisting, on the authority of the ancient sages, that Air or cosmic space must be called dark. For anything that is neither Light in itself nor a receptacle of Light is Darkness. This includes a *barzakh* once the Light has left it, and Air, which cannot even receive Light in the relevant sense.

We can only say that there are some *barzakhs* from which Light never withdraws—the sun and stars—and others from which it withdraws, temporarily or for good. It follows that *barzakhs* can never, of themselves, be the cause of anything. They differ from one another only through the Light that comes to them like a stranger living in exile. That Light owes none of its existence to their dark substance, since nothing can bring into being something higher than itself.

However closely we examine things, we find nothing other than Light as either their remote or their immediate cause. Motion and heat, for example, are two ways in which Light manifests itself (*mazhar*).[^EII2-167] Light causes them, not the other way around. Motion and heat “prepare” a receptacle for Light to become actual within it. That Light, flowing from the “victorial Light” (*Nûr qâhir*), will correspond to the capacity that has developed in the receptacle—a capacity whose original cause is, again, none other than Light. For Light brings heat and motion into existence. By its very essence it is active and pours itself forth (*fa’âl, fayyâz*). Light needs only to exist in order to illuminate; no new agent has to intervene.

Thus every quality of the *barzakhs*—every aspect and form appearing in bodies—is an effect of Light. The source that gives Light (*Dator Luminum*, the Giver of Lights) cannot itself be a *barzakh*. It must be something outside all dark substances and qualities.

A difficulty would remain here if Suhrawardi had not taken care to distance himself from the “dualist Magi,” and if the ancient Persian sages whose theosophy he sought to revive had not been so close to the “Chaldean” sages of sacred rites whom the Neoplatonists had adopted (see above, Chapter I, 2 and Chapter II, 1–2). For the *barzakh*, being essentially Darkness, continues to exist as such after the Light that is foreign to it has withdrawn. This dark substance, then, is neither sheer non-being nor merely a lack of being.

What is it? Where does it come from? Suhrawardi cannot answer as one of the “dualists” would, since he has explicitly rejected radical dualism as impious. He writes: “It belongs to perfect Light to be the cause of an imperfect Light.”

We can now see what this implies. As Light spreads and pours itself forth, it declines by stages until it reaches the West of its total extinction. The material body, the *barzakh*, is extinguished, dead Light, which another Light, exiling itself there, will temporarily bring to life. In governing that body, the exiled Light finds the means of its own redemption, the point from which it can rise in its “sacred ascent” and attain its transformations into glory.

What is now Darkness was therefore once itself a light, but a light that, in clinging to the furthest point of its own decline and fall, seems to have denied itself. This implies that if some Souls of Light tear themselves free from exile, there must have been a more profound and radical catastrophe, the one that degraded Light into its own pure negation. The Ismaili sacred drama presented this admirably as a catastrophe occurring at the level of the fullness of Light (see above, Chapter II, § 2). Its resolution was already assured when the “spiritual Adam” cast out his own Iblis-Ahriman.[^EII2-168] Here everything unfolds as a metaphysical process.

Suhrawardi will allude to the implicit drama that occurred in the soul’s pre-existence in some of his *Mystical Narratives* (see below, Chapters IV and V).

Yet no causal explanation of what appears through dark, inert, lifeless substance—whether the appearance lasts or is fleeting—can be based on that substance itself.

Consider two examples.[^EII2-169] If the oil in a lamp rises towards the flame, nothing has been explained, in Suhrawardi’s view, merely by invoking a physical law, whether the *horror vacui*, nature’s supposed abhorrence of a vacuum, or some active property of fire. Likewise, declares the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, the sages of ancient Persia found it strange that anyone should suppose the marvellous colours of a peacock’s plumage to result simply from the bird’s bodily constitution, from some mixture or combination within its feathers, without any definite purpose or personally acting intelligence at work.

No: in both cases what is revealed is an intelligent ordering, the work of the Angel who is the “lord of the Species.” In the first case this is the guardian Angel of the cone of flame, the very Angel the Persians called *Ordibehesht* (Avestan *Arta Vahishta*). For the bodily species is like a shadow, a projection, an icon (*sanam*) of its Angel, a theurgy (*tilism*, Greek *telesma*) that the Angel works in the *barzakh*, which of itself is dead, absolute night. “The ancient Persians,” Suhrawardi reminds us, “were supremely expert and diligent in matters of angelology (*fî arbâb al-anwâ’*).

“Thus they gave special worship to the Angel they called *Hômâ Izad*, the Angel of *haoma*, the plant that played such a major role in their religious rites.”

So, too, throughout Suhrawardi’s writings we encounter, one after another, the names of the six Zoroastrian archangels—the *Amâhraspands*, the “Holy Immortals.” With Ohrmazd, their prince and source, they form the divine Heptad of Light and Wisdom. The commentators Qotboddin Shirazi and Shahrazuri draw attention to each of these names and add their own explanations. They carefully describe the relations between the group of three “masculine” archangels and that of three “feminine” archangels, and the particular theurgies through which each acts.

We are told again that the sage Zoroaster was admitted to contemplate them, to enter into union with the divine Heptad, and to receive initiation into higher knowledge from each of the Seven. All proceeded one from another “as one lamp is kindled from another without the light of the first being diminished in any way.”[^EII2-170]

We have already learned that the first Light to proceed from the Light of Lights is the sublime Light the ancient Persians called *Bahman*, identified with the First Intelligence in both the Avicennian and the Ismaili worlds of divine Intelligences.[^EII2-171] From this sublime Light proceeded *Ordibehesht*, the Angel of Fire. Next came *Shahrîvar* (Avestan *Xshathra Vairya*, “Desirable Dominion”), the Angel of the sun and the metals (see also § 5 below, on the sun as the theurgy of the Angel).

Then came *Esfandarmoz* (Avestan *Spenta-Armaiti*), the archangelic Light (*Nûr qâhir*) whose theurgy is the Earth, and whom the Mazdean texts hail as the “daughter of Ohrmazd.” The role of “mistress of the household” (*kadbâ-nû’ya*) that Suhrawardi recognises in her preserves a precise memory of this tradition.[^EII2-172] Elsewhere we have tried to show the importance of this figure in the spiritual life of ancient Iran and of Islamic Persia, even where she bears another name.[^EII2-173] In her person the Earth is transfigured.

Finally come the two archangels already named: *Khordâd* (Avestan *Haurvatât*), the Angel of Water, and *Mordâd* (Avestan *Amertât*, “Immortality”), the Angel of plants.
