Our *shaykh al-Ishrâq* knows that these beings of light are also those whom Hermes, Agathodaimon, and Plato spoke of or were themselves allowed to contemplate. This, he says, is why they did not support their claims with rational proofs. Instead they laid claim to direct personal vision and offered their testimony. If they did so, our *shaykh* believes, it is not for us to dispute with them. His position, which we already know, remains consistent. In astronomy, the Peripatetic philosophers trust the observations of Ptolemy and those of the Chaldean astronomers.

Yet those very same Chaldean sages, like the sages of ancient Greece, claimed to have seen the realities of the spiritual world for themselves. Why trust their experience when it concerns observations of the physical world, but reject their experience when it concerns the spiritual world? What counts in one case must count in the other.[^EII2-174]

Here we truly have a vision of the world embracing the entire heavenly universe known to the sages of ancient Iran; it is also the meeting place of all the mystical theosophers invoked by Suhrawardi. We should not speak of “syncretism.” It is too easy a word, too often used either to discredit a teaching or to avoid examining it further. Anyone who considers only opinions combining or merging with other opinions will find it easy to speak of syncretism. Anyone who considers instead *what those opinions are about*, as it appears to the people who hold them, will be much more cautious.

Suhrawardi is not attempting a harmonious synthesis of philosophical opinions that happen to resemble one another. He starts from what he regards as an objective finding: the agreement of testimonies concerning the same reality. The spiritual world witnessed directly by the theosophers of different traditions is, for him, indeed the same world. That is what matters to him, and it is what matters to us here.

Bringing together a body of testimony is not “syncretism.” It does, however, presuppose that one “believes” in this spiritual world. Once that condition is recognised, we can see the meeting that takes place here between Zoroastrian angelology and the “Magian” wisdom of the Chaldean sages, those of the *Oracles* interpreted by the Neoplatonists. This is the meaning we sought earlier to bring out in Suhrawardi’s undertaking. Research should therefore examine the transformations Plato’s *Ideas* had already undergone in Chaldean-Neoplatonic theosophy, a considerable undertaking in itself.[^EII2-175]

The encounter between Chaldean practitioners of sacred rites and the metaphysics of Middle Platonism and Neoplatonism had already begun to work out the great solution Suhrawardi develops in full, adding the testimony of his own experience. That solution identifies the Platonic Ideas, the archetypes of Light (*mothol aflatûniya nûriya*), with the archangels and archangelic beings of Zoroastrianism. This identification is the major *spiritual fact* of his *Eastern Theosophy*.

A phenomenologist can only begin from that fact, seek to understand it, and uncover the intentions at work in it and the reality towards which they are directed. If one proceeds instead by arguing from abstract concepts, the difficulties become insoluble. Already in the eighth Islamic century (the fourteenth century CE), an unfortunately anonymous thinker had explained, in a learned dissertation, that Suhrawardi’s position no longer corresponded at all to the problem Plato had originally posed.[^EII2-176]

Suhrawardi’s angelology reflects the same vision as that of the Neoplatonists who interpreted the Chaldean sages. In this respect, the *Khosrawânîyûn* sages whose testimony he invokes are indeed the “Neoplatonists of Persia.”

We can already see this in the names given to the archetypal Angels. Each is the Angel or lord of a Species (*rabb al-nû’*), of its image or icon (*sanam*), of its theurgy (*tilism*). The bodily species itself is that theurgy, since it is the Angel’s own action. The concept of the archetype is no longer quite the one that posed a problem for us in classical Plato.

Instead, it shapes the whole religious devotion and spiritual life of the *Ishrâqîyûn*. This angelic interpretation of the Platonic Ideas—the *ta’wîl*, or spiritual interpretation, of the theory of Ideas—is, in effect, what Suhrawardi regards as the most precious inheritance from the theosophy of the ancient Persians. Every decision he makes in physics, psychology, cosmology, and metaphysics is directed towards preserving it.

But a difficulty remains: what kind of participation in being (*methexis*) connects the heavenly reality that is the Angel of a Species with the individuals that make up the material or earthly existence of that Species? In short, what foundation in being allows both Angel and species to share the same name?[^EII2-177]

Suhrawardi himself sums up his position in three propositions:

1) The Angel of each Species is a reality existing in its own right: a distinct spiritual individual, existing in and for itself.

2) There can be no question of an indwelling presence that would merge the Angel and its species into a single collective whole. Since the Angel of the Species is an Intelligence belonging to the world of Light, how could that Intelligence both exist as an individual in its own right and be present within the species and its many individual members?

3) Nor can we accept that the Angel of the human Species, for instance, exists *because of and for the sake of* what is beneath it. (The same applies to the “Pole,” the Imam as conceived in Shiism. As we know, his being the Imam depends in no way on whether human beings recognise him. The parallel is all the more compelling because a Shiite thinker such as Qazi Sa'id Qommi, who understood the Imam through the angelology of the *Ishrâq*, would describe him as the “lord of the Species” in relation to his faithful.) If an archetype meant no more than a *model* whose only purpose was to serve what exists below it, the archetypal Angel could no longer be called the “lord of the Species.” But Suhrawardi knows that the ancient sages never made that mistake.[^EII2-178]

For every species of plant, for example, there must be a spiritual being, separate from Matter and therefore endowed with knowledge and consciousness, which protects that species and cares for it as its guardian Angel. According to Suhrawardi, this is the being whom the ancient sages of Persia called the Angel or lord of that species (*rabb al-nû’*).[^EII2-179] The claim, of course, concerns every species that has a substantial existence of its own, not accidental or partial things.

All events in the life of plants, and likewise everything that occurs within a human being without the knowledge of the thinking soul, are governed by the Angel of the respective Species. This Angel must not be confused with the soul: a soul and its body together form a single individual. The higher a species stands in the hierarchy of being, the more intermediaries there are between it and its Angel.

In the human case, for example, there is the thinking soul and the subtle organs constituted by the three kinds of *pneuma*, or vital spirit. Suffering and injury to the body affect the soul that animates it, but they cannot affect the Angel. Neither the Angel of plants nor the Angel of fire, nor any of the other angelic lords, is injured by the violence inflicted on the species it governs. Their compassion for their respective species is not a matter of *suffering* but, essentially, of *acting*, as befits an Intelligence that is by nature fully actual and active.

Everything within a species that contributes to its coming into being and its continuing to exist proceeds from the activity of that Intelligence—from its acts of understanding and contemplation through which the species emanates. It is because the species is thus the contemplative activity of this Intelligence, its Angel, that the species is called the Angel’s theurgy.

It follows that the Angel of a Species, as archetype, appears as an *archetypal person*. Yet if its activity of understanding and contemplation causes a bodily species to emanate, that is in no way because the Angel needs the species. Such a need exists only for souls that must pass through the education of sensory knowledge—that is, through earthly existence—in order to attain their perfection.

But the law governing the descending hierarchy of being is strict and unchanging. A higher level does not find its perfection in a lower one. On the contrary, every level finds its perfected state in the Principle from which it emanates and which is its first cause. The species governed by the Angel is not the Angel’s ultimate purpose; rather, the Angel is the ultimate purpose of the species it governs, because the Angel is, *in person*, that species in its perfected state. This is the sense in which the Angel is its archetype. Its luminous nature is not something added to its essence, to its very selfhood, something it could acquire from below.

Certainly other Lights are continually added to its Light through the eternal manifestation of what is above in what is below. Human souls, too, are in their essential nature separate Lights and receptacles of sacred Lights; sensory perception merely prepares them to receive those higher Lights. The sages of ancient Persia knew this, unlike the “exotericists”—those concerned only with outward teachings—who remain bound to their books and never rise to the point of direct personal vision.[^EII2-180]

What, then, do the “Eastern” theosophers, the Khosrawânîyûn, mean when they speak of the Angel of a Species as the universal of that Species? They certainly cannot mean the universal as logic understands it: the general concept of a species, a concept whose very generality allows a multitude of individual beings to share in what it expresses. Such a concept is defined precisely by being negatively conditioned (bi-sharti lâ): it excludes any particular determination that would prevent all individuals of the same kind from falling under it.

But Eastern Theosophy understands the Angels of the Species as independently existing realities of Light, each possessing its own distinct spiritual identity, in which no other being can participate.

Thus, when we grasp the concept of a Species, it does not follow that we have grasped the Angel of that Species. In what sense, then, can the species be said to participate in its Angel?

We can understand this participation only by recognizing that the Angel, as a distinct spiritual reality, brings forth the material species through its thought, through its contemplative activity, as an act of theurgy—a spiritual act of creation. All the natural relationships and proportions observable in the embodied species are the shadow, image, or icon (sanam) of the spiritual relationships and forms of light existing within the Angel's own being, its own “person,” and its activity of thought. The individual material being is short-lived; it is the species as a whole that preserves this Image continuously.

The Angel is therefore universal—a metaphysical universal—in the sense that it is the “Mother of the Species” (Omm al-nû’). As such, it stands in the same relationship to the species as a whole and to each of its members, because it is the “Lord of that Species” (rabb al-nû’): the being that bestows its perfections and guides the species by guiding its countless individuals.

The Angel is determined only by what it is in itself, by the being it receives from its Principle. It is determined neither by the generality of the concept of the species nor by one particular feature of fleeting material existence rather than another. That is why the Angel of humanity appears to each human being in a form individual to that person: as that person's own Perfect Nature, their own guardian Angel.

If, then, the Angel of a Species is called its universal, and if the same name is applied to both the Angel and the species, this is because their relationship resembles that between the image appearing in a mirror and the person standing before it. Here again we encounter concepts fundamental to all Islamic gnosis, as we have already seen in Shiite teachings concerning the Imam: mazhar and mazhariya, the form in which something manifests itself—as in a mirror—and that form's power to make a higher reality appear.

It follows that the Angel is the universal of the species over which it presides because its care extends equally to the whole species and to each of its members.

Moreover, as an absolute archetypal person—absolute in the sense that nothing determines its luminous spiritual identity except the Principle from which it derives—the Angel presents to the whole species, and to every one of its individuals, the goal toward which they tend: their complete and perfected state. The Angel of the Species is the being in whom everything required by its nature is already fully realized, the being whose ever-renewed desire is forever fulfilled by the presence of what it desires.[^EII2-181]

This explains the Hermetic designation “complete,” “fulfilled,” or “perfect” (tâmm), given to the “Perfect Nature” that appears to Hermes in a vision and to which Suhrawardi dedicates one of the psalms in his “Book of Hours.” Compare the designation “Perfect Man,” Insân kâmil, Greek anthrôpos teleios. It also explains why Suhrawardi so firmly rejects the idea that the primary purpose of the archetypal Lights is merely to serve as models for the creation of species and individuals. That would make these higher beings subordinate to the lower existences they govern—beings that are themselves the products of their theurgic activity and the images in which they appear.

The relationship is precisely the reverse. The lower beings owe their existence to the archetypal reality of the higher Light, and from that Light they receive both the dignity and the purpose of their own existence: to become the image and expression of their Angel, insofar as they strive to attain its “perfect state.”

In short, the relationship between a species and the Angel that is its Perfect Nature becomes clearest if we return to the words of the psalm Suhrawardi dedicates to that Angel, translated below in § 5, or if we recall the “prayer of the heliotrope,” so beautifully described by Proclus.[^EII2-182]

When these Lights are called “Platonic Ideas or archetypes of light” (mothol aflatûniya nûriya), Species existing in a state of light (Anwâ’ nûriya), each possessing the nature of an angelic spiritual reality, Suhrawardi may not be expressing precisely what Plato himself intended. His thought is, however, entirely in harmony with that of the Neoplatonists. At the same time, it brings us close to the Avestan and Zoroastrian concept of the ratu, a term designating the guardian Angels of beings in heaven and on earth. We have already noted that Suhrawardi gives Esfandarmoz, the Angel of the Earth, the specifically Avestan title kadbânû, “mistress of the house.”[^EII2-183]

But there is more. As we shall shortly recall, the Angel of humanity is none other than Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, the “Active Intellect” of the philosophers. When this Angel's relationship to a particular human being takes on an individual form, the Angel appears to that person as their “Perfect Nature.” Now, as we noted earlier, Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî, a great seventeenth-century Shiite theosopher, makes a striking comparison in his commentary on a famous sermon of the First Imam. He sees the relationship between the Imam and each faithful believer as corresponding to the relationship between the Holy Spirit, Lord of the human Species, and the soul of each initiate, for whom the Spirit is the “Perfect Nature.”

The philosophical devotion of the Ishrâqî tradition and Shiite devotion to the Imam thus share a fundamental feature of Iranian Islamic spirituality, whose roots we can also discover in certain forms of ancient Gnosis. The multiplication of theophanic relationships—relationships through which the divine becomes manifest—expresses a mystical devotion that seeks neither emptiness nor formlessness, but a unifying relationship between persons. In doing so, it is equally concerned to preserve tawhîd, the oneness of God and the absolute transcendence of the One beyond all others.

##### 4. The Hierarchies of the Archangelic Lights

This broad picture, briefly sketched, allows us to understand the structure of Suhrawardi's angelology and to see exactly where it breaks with the Peripatetic or Avicennian system. Suhrawardi himself revealed the decisive moment of that break in his account of the vision of the Light of Glory (above, p. 99).

In Avicenna's system, the emergence of multiplicity begins with the first of the Cherubic Intellects (Karûbîyûn)[^EII2-184] and with the three acts of understanding that constitute its being. It understands its Principle; it understands its own existence as made necessary by that Principle; and it understands that, considered apart from its Principle, its own existence is merely possible and could just as well not be. These three acts of contemplation take on distinct realities respectively as a second Intellect, a first Angel-Soul that moves the outermost celestial sphere, and that first Heaven itself.

In fact, Avicenna seems to have hesitated for a long time over the structure of the angelic world that ought to be inferred, after the fact, from astronomical observations. Whether one accepted Aristotle's celestial physics or Ptolemy's theory, should one posit no more than ten Intellects? Or, following Aristotle, should there be somewhat more than fifty, corresponding to the additional celestial spheres needed to explain the irregularities in planetary motion?[^EII2-185]

It was the inadequacy of this scheme that Suhrawardi's vision of the “Sources of the Light of Glory” revealed to him.[^EII2-186] From then on, rather than confining himself to our solar system and deriving from it a set of nested celestial spheres—whether Aristotle's concentric spheres or Ptolemy's epicycles and eccentric circles—he directed his contemplation above all toward the “Heaven of the Fixed Stars,” whose explanation had already created more than one difficulty for celestial physics. He reflected on the almost infinite multitude of individual stars suggested by this eighth Heaven—that is, all the worlds beyond our solar system—and came to see that the mystery of how being becomes multiple must be sought among these wonders.

Earlier philosophers had failed to make sufficient use of the contemplative and loving activity of the Intellects to explain the emergence of these innumerable beings. Even the two intellectual “dimensions” recognized by the Peripatetics in each Intellect, necessity and possibility, were inadequate when considered in terms of desire. Suhrawardi even sensed that beyond the “Heaven of the Fixed Stars” there must be other universes, more marvelous still. The angelology whose necessity he grasped by intuition, a priori, could have matched the staggering dimensions calculated by modern astronomy. This stands in contrast to what happened during the astronomical revolution in the West, which did away with angelology.[^EII2-187]

Suhrawardi's angelology takes shape in three stages:

1\) From the eternal coming-into-being of the Firstborn Light, proceeding from the Light of Lights—a Light he identifies with Bahman, the first of the Zoroastrian archangels proceeding from Ohrmazd—Suhrawardi abandons the two or three intellectual “dimensions” available to Peripatetic angelology. In that earlier system, three acts of contemplation repeat themselves from one Intellect to the next as each proceeds from its predecessor.

In their place, Suhrawardi introduces a plurality of “dimensions” that inform his entire “Eastern Theosophy.” There are the dimensions called qahr and mahabbat, dominion and love, arising from his very conception of the Light of Glory. There are independence and dependence; there are the specifically “Eastern” dimensions of contemplation and illumination—contemplation that “rises toward” a higher Light and illumination that “rises upon” a lower one. There are also irradiation and reflection, and so on. Through these many-sided relationships, the multiplication of distinct beings of Light rapidly becomes innumerable.

At the highest, invisible level, these dimensions seem to enact the laws of optics: they combine with one another, and the ways in which they participate in one another, together with the proportions of that participation, produce a complexity without limit. Each individual Light, arising from these multiple irradiations and reflections, receives them from every Light that precedes it and communicates them to every Light that follows it, both directly and through the mediation of all the others.

The increasing complexity and accelerating rhythm defy the imagination's efforts to follow or measure them. In this way the universe of “Primordial Archangelic Lights” proceeds eternally. Because these Lights give rise to one another in a hierarchy of causes, they form a descending order, which Suhrawardi calls the Longitudinal Order (tabaqat al-Tûl). This is the universe of archangels he calls the Sovereign Lights, the Supreme Sources (al-Osûl al-A’âlîn), or the “World of the Mothers” (al-Ommahât).[^EII2-188]

2\) The hierarchy of the archangelic “World of the Mothers” gives rise to two distinct orders within the fullness of the world of Light. This results from the two categories of “dimensions” that constitute the archangels' being. One category may be called positive. The other expresses a lack: the dependence inherent in every Light whose being does not belong to it by its own right but comes from its Principle.

From the first category—dominion, independence, active illumination, and contemplation—proceeds a second order of archangels, or “Victorious Lights.” These no longer cause one another's existence or stand in a relationship of subordination. Instead, they correspond to one another and stand on equal terms. They form the Latitudinal Order (tabaqat al-’Ard). These are the archetypal archangels, the “Lords of the Species”—either masculine, arbâb al-anwâ’, or feminine, rabbât al-anwâ’—the Angels whose spiritual activity brings forth all the Species of the sensible and imaginal worlds.

We have already examined their manner of existence. They are in no sense abstract concepts treated as though they were independently existing things. They are genuinely independent angelic realities, existing in and for themselves. Their universality consists in the outpouring of their light upon all the beings that make up the Species born of their contemplation, and in the care they extend to every one of those beings.

From the second category of intelligible dimensions within the primordial archangels of the “World of the Mothers”—those expressing dependence, such as love and longing for the higher Light, reliance upon it, and the illumination received from it—proceeds the “Heaven of the Fixed Stars,” which serves as their common form of manifestation. The countless individual stars and constellations are emanations that give material form, in celestial matter—a still-subtle materia prima, or primary matter—to the element of non-being contained in those archangels' existence, if we imagine that existence separated from the Light of Lights, which eternally establishes its necessity to be.

For Avicenna's followers, the motion of the Heaven of the Fixed Stars arises from the longing of the single Soul that moves this Heaven for the single Intellect from which that Soul proceeds. The subtle matter of this Heaven marks the distance between the Soul's longing and the object of its longing. For Suhrawardi, the innumerable wonders of the Heaven of the Fixed Stars already demand a corresponding multiplication of Intellects and Souls.

3\) From the second order of archangels, the Latitudinal Order—the Lords of the celestial Species in the starry universe and of the elemental Species in our sublunary world—proceeds a further Order of Lights. Through these Lights the archetypal Archangels govern the Species. Whereas the Lights of the first two categories are called “Victorious” (Anwâr qâhira), those of the third are called “Governing Lights” (Anwâr modabbira). They are the Angel-Souls.

More significantly still, as we have already noted, the shaykh al-Ishrâq gives the Lights of this hierarchy an ancient Iranian title of command and knighthood: the Espahbad Lights. The name calls to mind the Stoic hêgemon or hegemonikon, the ruling principle, but the setting in which Suhrawardi places it is still more revealing. It evokes the heroic epic of Iranian chivalry and also the battle that has raged since the beginning of the world, described in the first chapter of the Bundahishn, the Mazdean book of Genesis.[^EII2-189]

The Espahbad Lights are thinking, governing souls; they are guides and interpreters—compare the Greek exègètès, meaning both a guide and an interpreter, a hermeneut. Each human soul is such a Light. So too are the Lights that move the celestial spheres and govern the Species present within those spheres, serving as intermediaries of the archetypal Archangel of which each Species is the icon or theurgic manifestation.

Each Species is at once the instrument and the setting of the “battle” undertaken by its Espahbad Light so that the power of the Light from which it proceeds may triumph. In Suhrawardi's system, the Espahbad Light thus assumes the role of the Zoroastrian Fravartis (forûhar), who “choose” to descend into the material world to fight against Darkness. When the outcome of this struggle—fought “for the Angel”—takes the form of the “rising” of the Espahbad Light, triumphantly emerging from its “West” and returning upright to its “East,” the heroic epic becomes a mystical epic.

We shall see later (Chapter IV, § 3 onward, and Chapter V) that this transformation may be the deepest meaning of ta’wîl, spiritual interpretation: the act that restores the world of ancient Persia's Light to Islamic gnosis. It may be the very meaning of Suhrawardi's work.

Such, in broad outline, is Suhrawardi's angelology. There are, in summary, three great orders of Lights, the “Victorious” or Dominating Lights (Anwâr qâhira, al-Qawâhir) being divided into two orders.

First comes the Longitudinal Order of archangels, which forms the “World of the Mothers”: transcendent Lights without any direct relationship to the world disclosed by sensory perception.

Second comes the Latitudinal Order of the theurgic archangels, the archetypal persons or Lords of the Species, of which the Species are images, icons, or theurgic manifestations. One might think that the manner of existence of these two hierarchies, resembling as it does that of the Neoplatonic Dii-Angeli, the God-Angels who mediate the hidden Godhead, differs from that of the angels of the Bible and the Quran.

But such an impression would be entirely foreign to the understanding of the Ishrâqîyûn philosophers.[^EII2-190] Third and finally come the Angel-Souls: the celestial Souls that move the planetary spheres, and human Souls—the Espahbad Lights.

Several observations should be made here. To begin with, the single order of supreme Intellects or “Cherubim” known to Avicennian philosophy has been divided into two. More precisely, it has unfolded into a double hierarchy whose names and functions were not anticipated by Avicenna: on one side, the “World of the Mothers”; on the other, the “Lords of the Species,” or archetypes.

Secondly, the boundary between the celestial and material worlds is no longer marked, as in Peripatetic philosophy, by the sphere of the Moon. Already the Heaven of the Fixed Stars marks the boundary between the angelic universe of Light (Rûhâbâd) and the universe of the barzakh, the intervening realm. The barzakh is the boundary, the dividing line between the West and the East of being; even the celestial spheres, however subtle their matter, already belong to the West. This was something Avicenna's story of Hayy ibn Yaqzân already understood.

A third observation concerns the transformation undergone here by Zoroastrian angelology. Suhrawardi names all the Amahraspands by their Persian names, and they perform in his theosophy the same roles they perform in Zoroastrian theology. When he identifies the archangel Bahman with the first Intellect proceeding from the Light of Lights, one might therefore expect the other Amahraspands to proceed immediately after him within the “World of the Mothers.”

But this is not what happens. Between the archangel Bahman and the Latitudinal Order of archetypes, where Suhrawardi places the names of the other Zoroastrian archangels, lies the Longitudinal Order, the hierarchy of the “World of the Mothers.” The Zoroastrian group of seven—or six—is thus, as it were, stretched apart. No doubt this enlargement was necessary to accommodate hierarchies corresponding to the Neoplatonic Dii-Angeli.[^EII2-191]

Yet it gives rise to a further consequence. Between the supreme archangels, who are the first Principles or the “World of the Mothers,” and the archetypal archangels, who bear the very names of the Zoroastrian archangels, there exists a relationship of imitation and embodiment comparable to that between a Species and its Angel. The latter archangels arise, in fact, from combinations and exchanges of light occurring in ever-increasing proportions among the supreme archangels.

Should we then speak, in some sense, of archetypes of archetypes? The question remains open, especially because it accords with the Mazdean conception of the Fravartis as heavenly archetypal beings corresponding to all beings of Light. Even the Amahraspands and Ohrmazd himself, as well as the multitude of the Yazdân—the Dii-Angeli—have their Fravarti. The way is open here for meditations that explore.

Finally, the Latitudinal Order of Lights, composed of the Angels of the Species, includes the Angel who is specifically Lord of the human Species, the Angel of humanity (Sâhib tilism al-Nu’ al-nâtiq, Rabb al-Nu’ al-insânî).[^EII2-192] This is also the Angel of Knowledge and the Angel of Revelation: Gabriel, identified with the Holy Spirit in the Quranic tradition, and with the “Active Intellect” in the philosophical tradition. This figure does not belong to the group of Amahraspands, but shares certain features with the Avestan angel Sraosha (Persian Sorûsh).[^EII2-193] By incorporating this Angel into the fullness of the archetypal Archangelic Lights, Suhrawardi brings together biblical and Quranic angelology with the angelology of the “Zoroastrian Neoplatonism” of Eastern Theosophy.

The Angel's role as a guide through spiritual initiation is crucial, both in Suhrawardi's writings and in the devotion he personally practiced. We noted above that the way Suhrawardi addresses this Angel as his “Perfect Nature” reveals, at the very least, how he understands the relationship between the Angel of a Species and every individual belonging to it. The same can be said of the other personal liturgies collected in his “Book of Hours.” Any account of his angelology would be incomplete without mentioning them. Their inspiration closely resembles the “Chaldean” spirit of the hymns composed by the Neoplatonist Proclus.

##### 5. Psalms to the Archangel of the Sun and to the “Perfect Nature”

We have already mentioned this group of highly original compositions, which together form something like a “Book of Hours.” Manuscripts are extremely rare,[^EII2-194] and the text is difficult.

Nevertheless, Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, the great seventeenth-century master of Ishrâqî philosophy, knew these compositions well. In his Glosses on the Book of Eastern Theosophy, he quotes them at length, bearing witness to the persistence, across the centuries, of this liturgical form in which the sacred, ritual devotion of the shaykh al-Ishrâq finds expression. The “Book of Hours” contains, on the one hand, a series of sermons with an eschatological character. Here eschatology concerns the individual's final destiny: the moment when the initiate's soul rises definitively into the world of Light, ascends to its “East,” and thereby disappears from this world, which is its “West.”

On the other hand, the “Book of Hours” contains a series of hymns of praise—doxologies—in honor of the Angels of the seven planets. Sadrâ Shîrâzî describes it in terms entirely consistent with what we know of the work: “For each of the seven days of the week, the shaykh al-Ishrâq had a particular hymn of praise in which he celebrated and invoked one of the Seven Angels. Each liturgy contains a hymn followed by a prayer, both so complete that nothing could be added to them.”[^EII2-195]

This “Book of Hours” brings us back to Suhrawardi's fundamental conviction: the perfected mystical theosopher, the hakîm mota’allih, cannot separate philosophical knowledge from spiritual experience. Suhrawardi's “Book of Hours” represents precisely the outcome that Neoplatonic metaphysics found in the theurgic or “hieratic” devotion of the Chaldean Oracles and Orphic hymns—texts that the Neoplatonists interpreted and that, in turn, inspired hymns of their own (above, Chapter II, § 1 onward).

However faithful and exact descriptions of the mystic's sacred experience may be, they remain descriptions. For the experience to be shown in action, to become an event, two paths are open. One is the visionary narrative told in the first person, using mystical symbols; Suhrawardi composed several such accounts (below, Chapters V and VI). The other is prayer, above all what is called monâjât, an intimate psalm in which the person praying addresses another as “you.” Only at this moment is the whole of philosophical knowledge transformed into a divine work, an act of theurgy involving personal spiritual realization.

When a thinker such as Suhrawardi succeeds, on the one hand, in giving form to symbols that are truly his own, and, on the other, in finding the Prayer that only he could have formulated—the “Prayer taught him by his own Perfect Nature,” as the Hermetic tradition would put it—he surely tells us more about himself and about the objective reality of the worlds present to him than a thousand pages of theoretical exposition could ever reveal. Suhrawardi addressed the figures of the heavenly fullness, the Lights of divine beauty glimpsed in fleeting visions, in the language of the “theurgic psalm.”

We shall translate two of these psalms below. Here his devotion comes closest to the “hieratic” method of a Neoplatonist such as Proclus, a thinker capable both of the most intricate metaphysical speculation and of composing hymns in honor of the divine beings to whom his personal devotion was directed. Suhrawardi, for his part, knew that he stood in profound harmony with the tradition of the ancient Sages of Persia and Chaldea.

He makes this especially clear when he recalls why these sages and theosophers revered the Flame.[^EII2-196] Just as every species is the theurgic manifestation and image of one of the Victorious Lights, a Light from which it proceeds and by which it is governed, so Fire—meaning luminous Fire (nâr dhat al-nûr), not the fire of Hell[^EII2-197]—is the theurgic manifestation of the archangel Ordîbehesht, one of the seven Amahraspands, called Arta Vahishta in Avestan.[^EII2-198]

As we have already seen, motion and heat are forms in which Light manifests itself (mazhar); they have no cause other than Light. Nowhere do motion and heat reach a higher degree than in Fire. Fire is closest to life, and it is a defense against Darkness. Far from being simply one of the four elements of classical physics, it is “the brother of the human Espahbad Light.”

Thus, if the human soul is entrusted with a greater khalifat, a greater vicegerency or delegated spiritual authority in this world, Fire assumes a lesser khalifat as the representative of the celestial Lights in the world of bodies, or barzakh.

What is honored in Fire, therefore, is the image and particular theurgic manifestation of one of the Archangelic Lights. Because Fire performs in our world the same function of revealing a higher reality that the invisible Lights perform in the higher worlds, the ancient Persians had every reason to take the Flame as the qibla, the point toward which they turned in prayer. Suhrawardi's commentators recall the liturgical institutions attributed to the rulers of ancient Iran—Hûshang, Jamshîd, Fereydûn, and Kay Khosraw—and finally given their definitive form by the sage Zoroaster.

Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî understood this perfectly. In the Gloss cited above, he emphasizes that the ancient Persians took the Flame as the qibla of their religious services because “they called the Flame the daughter of the sun (bint al-shams). For them, therefore, it was like the sun's representative or deputy (nâ’ib), by virtue of the strength of its being and its manifestation at every time and in every place, even when the sun was absent, just as the Moon represents the sun at certain times during the night.”[^EII2-199] This account of the veneration of the Flame thus provides a natural transition to the texts in which Suhrawardi gives us more than a mere echo of ancient solar theologies. What we hear is a psalm whose whole character is shaped by his “Eastern Theosophy.”

Nothing in the starry universe is dead or inert, for every Sphere is governed and animated by a thinking Soul. That Soul communicates its energy through the heavenly body set within its Sphere, which serves as its principal organ, its heart. Through this organ, the energies received from the Anima caelestis, the celestial Soul, flow into the sensible world.

So it is with the Sun, which Suhrawardi calls by its Iranian name, Hûrakhsh (Sol splendidus, the splendid Sun),[^EII2-200] and which the Avesta greets as “the most beautiful manifestation of Ohrmazd.” Suhrawardi describes it as the theurgic manifestation of the archangel Shahrîvar, one of the seven Amahraspands—the Avestan Xshathra Vairya, “Desirable Dominion,” whom the Avesta specifically describes as “having the appearance of the sun.”[^EII2-201] In Suhrawardi's hierarchy of Archangelic Lights, Shahrîvar belongs to the Latitudinal Order of archetypes. The Ishrâqî tradition, the tradition of the “Eastern” theosophers, therefore gives special honor to this brilliantly shining heavenly body, the “bringer of Day and prince of Heaven.”

The reference here to the “Eastern” theosophers has a precise purpose. The Sun's incandescent mass is certainly marvelous, and the continuation of life on Earth depends upon its radiance.

But Suhrawardi has something more fundamental in mind: everything implied, for him, by the notions of “East” and “rising Sun” (above, Chapter II, § 2). There is a way of perceiving sensible things simultaneously in this world and in the malakût, the invisible spiritual world: of perceiving, together with the Sun of this world, the spiritual Sun of the world beyond the senses. What matters to “Eastern Theosophy” is the rising of that spiritual Sun. This is the meaning suggested by a lengthy passage in the Book of Crossroads and Conversations,[^EII2-202] indispensable for understanding the psalm translated below.

Suhrawardi explains there that, were it not for the obstacle of the material body, our souls would receive the impressions of knowledge directly from the celestial Souls, the Animae caelestes. He then mentions certain inferior practices of divination that have nothing to do with the spiritual elite. This is the same distinction that the “Chaldean Magi” insisted upon between the wise practitioners of theurgy and those engaged in sorcery.

As for the “hieratic” sages, both their knowledge and their spiritual practices are “expressed in symbols” (marmûza), some of which are to be found in his Book of Eastern Theosophy. He goes on to describe the ways in which an encounter with invisible realities (al-amr al-ghaybî) may occur: sometimes as though one were reading a written text; sometimes through hearing the voice of an unseen speaker, a voice that may sound sweet or terrifying, or may be no more than a faint rustling.

At other times, the speaker appears in a visible form. This may be a figure associated with the stars, or one of the heavenly Princes manifesting in a form suited to the visionary's spiritual state. Such experiences are always real events, although they do not take place in our ordinary world, but in the mystical world of Hûrqalyâ, the mundus imaginalis, or “intermediate East.”[^EII2-203]

Suhrawardi then adds: “The gateway (pîshgâh) to all authentic ecstasies in the mystical world of Hûrqalyâ is precisely that of the magnificent Lord Hûrakhsh, the most magnificent of beings who have assumed a material body (motajassidîn), the Most Venerated, who is the supreme Face of God in the language of Eastern Theosophy, the language of Ishrâq. For he is the one who watches over meditation by dispensing light to it, and who is its witness in contemplation.”

These explanations make it clear that we are dealing with something other than the physical star, the incandescent mass of the Sun perceived by our ordinary senses. When the psalm translated below addresses Lord Hûrakhsh, the “gateway” to ecstasy, as “the most luminous of beings endowed with life and thought,” and speaks of “the splendor of his thinking soul,” it is unmistakably addressing a higher spiritual being. The entire psalm calls to mind the text known as the “Liturgy of Mithra,” which is actually less a liturgy than a personal rite of initiation, the celebration of a mysterion, a sacrament of immortality.

We know that in the Avesta, Mithra is the lord of heavenly Light and therefore of all the heavenly lights. Neither in the mysteries bearing his name nor in the Avesta is Mithra himself the Sun; rather, the Sun is his chariot. In Suhrawardi's psalm, the hymn of praise celebrates the “body of light” of Lord Hûrakhsh, while the invocation addresses him as the thinking Soul of that luminous body. The scheme of angelology described above is thus confirmed.

Addressing Lord Hûrakhsh, the psalm asks him in turn to pray to his “father,” the one who causes “his thinking soul to rise at its East,” that is, in the heaven of Hûrqalyâ. The Sun's incandescent mass is indeed the theurgic manifestation, the form through which the archangel Shahrîvar becomes visible. The Anima caelestis governing that mass, the Soul “moved by the ardor of love,” is Lord Hûrakhsh himself: the celestial Soul, the Espahbad Light that moves its Heaven through the longing drawing it toward the Intellect from which it proceeds.

The name “father,” repeated throughout the invocation, corresponds to its symbolic use among the Neoplatonists and in the Chaldean Oracles.[^EII2-204] It also suggests another reminiscence of the “Liturgy of Mithra.” Initiates who attained the highest rank in the mysteries of Mithra were called “fathers”; those at the rank immediately below them were the “sons” of these “fathers.” Their bond was far stronger than that between father and son by physical birth. It was a spiritual bond, for all were together the sons of Mithra, their “father.”

Under this name, and in this capacity, Mithra is invoked at the beginning of the Liturgy as the “father” who alone can impart—and can impart only to his “son”—what belongs to his own substance: that power (dynamis) whose birth or “initiation” within the human being is the sacramentum of the initiate's elevation to divine life.[^EII2-205] The final invocation of Suhrawardi's psalm aims at this same end. Suhrawardi will use the term “father” again in the Hermetically inspired psalm he addresses to his “Perfect Nature.” In the present psalm, the term reappears at every rank of the angelic hierarchy, joining all those ranks through a bond whose very name recalls the spiritual relationship uniting initiates in a brotherhood.

Suhrawardi's psalm begins with a doxology, a hymn praising the beauties of the visible heavenly body, the luminous body of Lord Hûrakhsh. The invocation itself follows. Notice how it unfolds through an ascending series of mediators. It is addressed first to Lord Hûrakhsh; through him to the archangel Shahrîvar, whose theurgic manifestation is that luminous body; through Shahrîvar to all the Victorious Lights; through them to the primordial archangel Bahman; and through Bahman, finally, to the “Light of Lights,” the “God of Gods”—a term that also appears in the encyclopedia of the Brethren of Basra. This liturgical ascent corresponds to the “hieratic” ascent proposed by the Angel of initiation in several of Suhrawardi's visionary narratives. Here is the translation of the “Great Invocation to Hûrakhsh.”[^EII2-206]

“Blessed be the most luminous of beings endowed with life and thought, the most manifest of persons, the most radiant of heavenly bodies. Peace be upon you! May God's greetings and blessings rest upon you, sublime Luminary, most august of the wandering stars; you who obey the One who brought you into being, you who move through the ardor of love for the inaccessible majesty of your Creator.

“You are Hûrakhsh the Mighty, Conqueror of Darkness, prince of Heaven, bringer of Day, by command of God Most High. You are king of the heavenly bodies, prince among the persons of the world above. By divine power and strength, which all obey, you reign over the Lights embodied in material forms. You are the body that dispenses Light, the Conqueror, the Radiant One, the Wise, the Supreme. In the incandescent splendor of your rays, you are the most magnificent of the children born of the spiritual world.

“In the world of bodies, you are the vicegerent of the Light of Lights, who sets you ablaze with a Light that reaches the summit of its victory. You are an image of His greatness, a visible expression of His beauty, His sign before the eyes of His faithful. Glory to the One who gave you your form and your light, who made you a wanderer through burning desire for His inaccessible majesty, and who placed you in the fourth Heaven.

“O most holy Father! I beg you to pray to the One who causes the splendor of your thinking soul to unfold at its East, the One who is your father, your cause, the object of your love, and the source of your motion—the One whose shadow and theurgic manifestation you are, the archangel Shahrîvar.

“And I beg you to pray with him to all the Archangelic Lights, the immaterial Intellects, that they too may pray—in the manner of prayer proper to the eternal world, free from change and alteration—to the One who is their Father, their cause, and the object of their love: the most august of beings brought forth at the beginning, the Light nearest to the Principle, the Intellect of the universe, the archangel Bahman. May he, in the same manner, pray to his God, the God of Gods, the Eternally Subsisting, the Light of Lights, God of every Intellect, every Soul, every body of ether or of the elements, whether simple or compounded, the Necessary Being.

“May he ask Him to illuminate my soul with flashes from the spiritual world, with knowledge of divine wisdom, and with the higher virtues. May he ask Him to count me among those who long for His Light, to protect me from every infirmity of soul and body, and to grant victory to the faithful of the Light and the mystical East. May He bless them and consecrate them, and us with them, for ever and ever. Amen.”

This psalm, so expressive of Suhrawardi's particular devotion and so faithful to the inspiration of “Eastern Theosophy,” contains a symbolism whose key may perhaps be found in the psalm to the “Perfect Nature.” Certainly this symbolism is bound up with a conception of the universe, an astronomy and a physics, that are no longer ours.

Yet it seems scarcely necessary to point out that, at the deepest level of mystical consciousness, whether one accepts a geocentric or a heliocentric account of the heavens is beside the point. Both theories stand equally far from what is really at issue. Or, to use Suhrawardi's own word, each is only a “gateway” that must be crossed. And we know very well that no satellite, no Sputnik, no rocket of the future will ever be capable of passing through that gateway. For the force of gravity from which the soul, the inner human being, must free itself in order to cross it has nothing whatever to do with the gravity overcome by the forces, however extraordinary, discovered in the laboratories of our time.

The ascending sequence of mediators invoked in the psalm suggests another observation. This liturgical progression presupposes a structure that we find in a strange dialogue. Its speakers are said to be the celebrated ninth-century Orthodox Christian physician Constantine, son of Luke (Qosta ibn Lûkâ), and his disciple ’Amâlaq the Greek, whose identity remains mysterious to us. Significantly, Ismaili theosophy seems to have adopted this dialogue, for we have found it in an Ismaili work that has not yet been published.

We shall quote only a very short passage here. The disciple asks his master: “Will you not make my God known to me?” The master answers: “Do you know the one who makes you known to yourself [...] the one who frees you from sorrow, who brings forth within you something whose intimate sweetness you taste while also feeling its power, and who makes you independent of everything that is not himself? If you know that one, you can know him only as a part of yourself.

“Then, yes, you have found your God; then you are a true believer.” When the disciple asks, “What lies beyond my God, so that I may be among those who have attained everything?” the sage replies: “Beyond him is the one who stands in relation to him as he himself stands in relation to you: one Unique to another Unique, and so onward until the threshold of the One in whom all the Uniques are contained.”[^EII2-207]

This dialogue opens up a “monadological” perspective—a vision of spiritual reality ordered through individual beings and their relationships—which belongs as much to Ismaili gnosis as to Ishrâqî theosophy. The sage's final words are in perfect harmony with what we hear at the end of several of Suhrawardi's narratives of initiation. His opening reply likewise implies what Suhrawardi calls the “Perfect Nature,” which the entire Ishrâqî tradition associates with the memory of Hermes' mystical experience. Since we cannot discuss Suhrawardi's entire “Book of Hours” here,[^EII2-208] or trace its connections with the Chaldean and Orphic devotion expressed in Neoplatonic hymns, or with the astral liturgies of the Hermetic Sabians of Harran, we shall at least give further attention to the psalm addressed to the “Perfect Nature.”

This psalm is addressed to the spiritual being whose name comes directly from Hermetic revelation as Suhrawardi and his school understood it: the “Perfect Nature” (al-Tibâ’ al-tâmm). We have already seen that this being is the philosopher's “Angel” (above, pp. 89 and 117), his tadaghât, in Arabic. In its own person it brings together the two meanings of the Xvarnah: it is both Light and the personal Destiny of the one whose “Angel” it is. Its significance for the soul's final destiny is already apparent in the fact that the ecstasy in which it sometimes reveals itself, as it revealed itself to Hermes, is a foretaste of the individual's ultimate spiritual fulfillment.

We have already mentioned its presence even within Shiite teachings on the Imam.[^EII2-209] The commentators sometimes identify it with the Angel of humanity—Gabriel, the Holy Spirit—because it gives an individual form to that Angel's relationship with each human being. In every case, the Perfect Nature is what this Angel becomes for each person. And above that Angel there is another being who stands in relation to it as the Angel itself stands in relation to the human species. This is what we meant by a “monadological” perspective.

In the preceding psalm, Suhrawardi asked the Angel of the Sun to ask all the Archangelic Lights to pray together to the First among them. Similarly, in his visionary narratives—for example, The Rustling of Gabriel's Wings and The Tale of the Western Exile—a mysterious figure appears, either at the beginning or later in the story. Referring to those who stand above him, he declares: “I am their tongue; beings like you cannot communicate with them.”[^EII2-210]

Likewise, in the writings of the Neoplatonist Proclus, there are Angels who serve as interpreters, revealing and explaining to human souls what would otherwise remain the Silence, the Unspoken reality of the Angels and gods belonging to the higher hierarchies.[^EII2-211] Anyone who impatiently claims to have no need of such mediators forgets a simple truth about experience itself. Whatever form the supreme divinity may take in appearing to someone, that form necessarily corresponds to the person's own manner of being.

The divine cannot appear to that person in any way other than one suited to their capacity to receive and understand it. At the same time, the form reveals the limits of that capacity and, through the very act of its presence, points beyond those limits. This is the meaning of the Angel: what Suhrawardi expresses through the Angel of humanity, and what he himself experiences when the Perfect Nature appears to him.

Here we should recall the original relationship that the shaykh al-Ishrâq places at the “dawn” of being, at the “East” from which all lights arise: the relationship between the first “beloved” and the first “lover.” Repeated at every level of existence, this relationship arranges the beings of every universe into pairs. It recurs between an Angel and the Species that is its “theurgic manifestation,” proceeding from its light. It recurs, too, wherever a being is joined by love to the heavenly cause from which it proceeds.

Every being, our shaykh tells us, has a beloved in the higher world toward whom its longing is directed. This beloved mediates between it and the Being who exists by His own right (al-Haqq), and through this mediator it contemplates the divine Archangelic Lights. Suhrawardi therefore uses the word “father” here in an entirely symbolic sense, for the birth in question is the birth that the lover owes to the beloved. If the lover, precisely as a lover, owes his birth to the object of his love, this is because love reveals his own spiritual origin to him in the beloved, the higher being from whom he proceeds. The beloved is his higher “I,” whom he addresses as “you,” not an object about whom he speaks in the third person.

Yet through this very revelation the lover, in turn, brings the beloved into being as beloved. This explains the striking reversibility of the terms, which we shall find in the very first words of the psalm below.

“Among these Archangelic Lights that mediate the One who is Being in His own right (al-Haqq),” the shaykh writes in the Book of the Temples of Light, “there is one who stands toward us in the relationship of a ‘father.’ It is the archetype, the Lord of our Species, the Giver from whom our souls proceed. It is called the Holy Spirit; the philosophers call it the Active Intellect.”[^EII2-212]

In the Book of Eastern Theosophy, the shaykh explains further: “It is the Archangelic Light of which the thinking species is the theurgic manifestation: that is, the archangel Gabriel. It is the ‘father’ of the human race, the Near One among the supreme archangels of the Malakût, the Giver from whom our souls proceed (Ravân-bakhsh), the Holy Spirit (Rûh al-Qods), the Giver of knowledge and inspiring grace, the one who bestows life and excellence. From this Angel there emanates, upon the most perfect bodily constitution—the human constitution—an immaterial Light. This is the Light entrusted with the government of a human body, the Governing Light called the ‘Espahbad of human reality’ (Espahbad al-nâsût), the Light that refers to itself by saying ‘I’ (bi’l-anâ’ya).”[^EII2-213]

Thus the tenth spiritual being of the Avicennian heavenly fullness is incorporated into the world of archetypal Lights described by Ishrâqî theosophy. More precisely, it belongs to the Latitudinal Order of the theurgic Angels, the archetypes of the Species, following the Zoroastrian archangels (Amahraspandân) named by Suhrawardi. It comes last because the radiance of all the preceding archetypal Lights converges within it, just as all the powers and radiations of the cosmos converge within the human microcosm.

Suhrawardi's names for this being establish its identity: Holy Spirit, Angel Gabriel, Active Intellect. Particular emphasis should be placed on the purely Persian name Ravân-bakhsh, “the one from whom our souls proceed.” We have suggested elsewhere how this term may have originated in the Manichaean metaphysics of Light.[^EII2-214] Traditional Persian dictionaries merely confirm the meaning it came to have without explaining its origins: “It is the name of the Angel who possesses knowledge and wisdom; in Arabic, it is called the Holy Spirit.”[^EII2-215]

Suhrawardi gives the theme of the Ravân-bakhsh, the Giver of our souls, a striking visionary form at the beginning of one of his narratives of initiation. The Angel Gabriel, we are told, has two wings. The right wing, turned toward being, is pure and absolute light; from it our souls proceed. The left wing, turned toward non-being, bears a dark imprint, the shadow from which arises the world of mirage and illusion.[^EII2-216]

There is more. This Angel, the Holy Spirit and Angel of humanity, is also identified with the Paraclete, and that identification is full of meaning. We have already recalled (above, Book I) how, in Shiism—for example, in the thought of Haydar Âmolî—the “Hidden Imam,” the “Expected Imam,” was also identified with the Paraclete.

Once again we encounter the path that enables an eminent Shiite thinker such as Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî to see a correspondence between two relationships: that of the Archangelic Light called the Holy Spirit to each soul of light, and that of the Imam to each initiate, each soul left “orphaned” or “widowed” from the world of Light. Such convergences between the theosophy of Ishrâq and the theosophy of Shiism are characteristic of Iranian Islamic spirituality. Just as Haydar Âmolî explicitly refers to the Gospel of John, Suhrawardi quotes these words of Jesus: “I am going to my Father and your Father, so that He may send you the Paraclete, who will reveal to you the meaning of the symbols” (Gospel of John 14:16, 26).[^EII2-217]

Finally, let us recall that in Suhrawardi's writings, the symbol of the dove of the Holy Spirit has its counterpart in the symbol of the sîmorgh (below, Chapter V).

As for the relationship between this Angel of humanity—the Holy Spirit or Paraclete—and the Perfect Nature, a relationship so close that one may take the place of the other, we shall try to clarify it later (Chapter VI) in connection with a visionary experience of Suhrawardi's. For now, let us say only that the Perfect Nature is to each human being what the Angel of humanity is to the human species as a whole. A being of light that exists before a person's earthly birth, it stands in such a relationship to that person that it is their protecting Angel, with whom they are finally reunited through death.

Above all, however, it is significant that in Suhrawardi's teaching, every evocation of the Perfect Nature is associated with the name of Hermes. Suhrawardi recalls—and all the Ishrâqîyûn after him will recall—the vision Hermes describes in these words: “Then a being from the spiritual world inspired me—‘cast into me’—the higher forms of knowledge. I asked it: Who are you? It answered: I am your Perfect Nature.”[^EII2-218] Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî and others would frequently invoke this account.[^EII2-219] Elsewhere, too, the dangers Hermes faced during an ecstatic vision are recalled, dangers that caused him to cry out: “You who are my father, save me!”[^EII2-220]

There is something in these accounts that recalls the Poimandres of the Corpus Hermeticum. Together with the parallels we have just noted, they enable us to understand the ardent, lyrical invocation found in Suhrawardi's “Book of Hours.” It follows the hymns or psalms he composed to be recited on each day of the week. Its title is Invocation (da’wat) to the Perfect Nature. Here is its translation:[^EII2-221]

“O You, my lord and prince, my most holy Angel, my precious spiritual being! You are the father who gave birth to me in the world of Spirit (ab rûhâni), and You are my child in the world of thought (walad ma’nawî). You are the one who, by divine permission, is devoted exclusively to the guidance of my person. You are the one whose fervent intercession before God, the God of Gods, makes up for all that I lack.

“You who are clothed in the most radiant of divine Lights, You who dwell at the summit of the degrees of perfection, I implore You by the One who has filled You with such sublime nobility and poured out upon You such immeasurable grace. Ah, may You reveal Yourself to me in the supreme Epiphany! May You show me the light of Your dazzling Face! Be my mediator before the God of Gods in the outpouring of the light of the mystical Secrets. Remove from my heart the darkness of the veils. I beg this of You in the name of His rightful claim upon You and of His rank above You.”[^EII2-222]

It seems clear that the Mithraic ritual—the so-called “Liturgy of Mithra”—knows a spiritual situation corresponding to that expressed at the beginning of this psalm. There, too, the initiate experiences the opening of the “field of consciousness” belonging to the higher Self, the heavenly pole of the self, the Self addressed as “you,” which is the “father” of the earthly person.

Yet although this higher, heavenly Self is our “father,” and although in one sense we are born from it, we must also, here below and in another sense, give birth to our higher Self if we are to establish any conscious relationship with it: a relationship between “I” and “you.” This, according to the Neoplatonic commentators on the Chaldean Oracles, is what it means to “act according to the archetype.” It is the fruit of the “theurgic” virtue that distinguishes initiates who have attained the highest spiritual rank.[^EII2-223] As anticipated above, The Tale of the Western Exile (below, Chapter VI) will give us occasion to bring together other texts concerning the Perfect Nature. Several sources of inspiration—Hermetic, Neoplatonic, Zoroastrian—can certainly be identified in Suhrawardi's thought.

Yet they come together in his devotion to the “person” of the Perfect Nature, as that being is present to him and as he invokes it. And perhaps the entire mysticism of the “Faithful of Love” (below, Book III) is simply another way of reaching the manifestation of the Perfect Nature.

We observed earlier that the decisive moment in the work—or, more precisely, in the inner life—of the shaykh al-Ishrâq comes when doctrine ceases trying to speak of the Ineffable and instead becomes an event. This is the moment when knowledge of divine wisdom and spiritual, “hieratic” experience come together.

We now understand that it is because of this event that the mystical East gives its name to “Eastern” Theosophy. The event may take the form of a psalm in which the spiritual seeker addresses another as “you.” Or it may take the form of a narrative in which the seeker recounts, in the first person, an event experienced as happening to himself in the eighth clime, the imaginal world. Suhrawardi's visionary narratives form a cycle. When the protagonists of the event are heroes of the Iranian epic, as in the narrative translated later, they undergo an “Eastern” transformation. That is why what emerges above all in Suhrawardi's work is the passage from heroic epic to mystical epic (above, pp. 95, 102), a passage whose exemplary hero is King Kay Khosraw.

Today we find ourselves trapped in a dilemma that seems to leave us no choice but between myth and history, or between the unconscious and rational consciousness. We have already suggested that this may be the result of a more or less agnostic understanding of being, one that can no longer recognize the real existence that properly belongs to the imaginal world, or distinguish that world from what is merely imaginary.

In Suhrawardi's narratives, as in many accounts from the Shiite traditions, everything takes place on a level that rises above both sides of our false dilemma: neither myth nor history in the ordinary sense of those words. The same is true of the initiate's encounter with the Paraclete, or Perfect Nature. It is therefore all the more precious to recognize that the Iranian mystical epic crosses paths with the cycle in which the West may have deposited its deepest mystical secret, at a time when human beings had become incapable of bearing it: the cycle of the Holy Grail.

We are dealing with something far more precise than similarities of folklore or recurring archetypes of the collective unconscious. We are dealing with shared “hieratic” Presences, with the Presence of a world common to both traditions. These Presences demand that the reality of their existence be fully acknowledged. This, of course, requires an understanding of being that has overcome the separation of thought from existence—a separation that so many minds in the West seem to find so difficult to abandon.

We have already alluded several times to the knighthood of the Grail when discussing the Shiite Imam and his faithful, and there will be further occasions to return to these connections. That something is shared, that there is a common Presence: this is among the most fascinating things the Iranian spiritual world can reveal to us. And it is no less significant that certain correspondences between the world of Iranian chivalry and that of Western mystical knighthood have been brought to light in our own time by a Zoroastrian scholar.

### CHAPTER IV

#### The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail

##### I. Hermetica and Mithriaca

The two Latin adjectives in this section's title refer to the spiritual treasures of two of humanity's great religious traditions: Hermeticism and Mithraism. I have brought them together because of two scholarly investigations. The more recent seeks the origins of the Western mystical understanding of the Holy Grail in the *Corpus Hermeticum*—more precisely, the understanding found in the German Grail cycle, in the work of Wolfram von Eschenbach.

The earlier study seeks the origins of the Grail and its devoted knighthood in the Zoroastrian *Xvarnah*, the Light of Glory, and in the images and beliefs surrounding that Light. Neither an *Ishrâqî*—a follower of the philosophy of spiritual illumination—nor a scholar devoted to the tradition of *Ishrâq* can afford to overlook investigations of such exceptional interest.

First, Suhrawardi's “Eastern theosophy,” which brings the ancient Persian world of light back to life while invoking Hermes and the Hermetic tradition, seems to us the ideal meeting place of these two lines of inquiry.

Second, Suhrawardi's own understanding of what counts as evidence allows us to assess, from within the philosophy of illumination, the different degrees of credibility reached by the two investigations.

We have already referred to the Grail, and to the role of its knights, on several occasions, and we shall return to them. They have arisen both in connection with Suhrawardi's revival of ancient Persian themes and in our discussion of the esoteric hierarchies of Twelver Shiism (Book I, Chapter III).

We have also seen the idea of the *Xvarnah* appear in the triad of archangels belonging to Ismaili theosophy; in Suhrawardi it becomes explicit and fully conscious. To the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, the master of illumination, the *Xvarnah* reveals itself as the very source of the mystical “East.” For him, the idea is inseparable from a hidden spiritual lineage: guardians of a secret treasure, headed by the being who is the mystical Pole of the world.

In this company of companions, faithful through every trial, we recognise a recurring theme. In Zoroastrianism it is the band surrounding the *Saoshyant*, the Saviour who will appear at the close of the twelfth and final millennium of our Aeon and work with them to transfigure the world (*frashkart*). In Twelver Shiism it is the chosen companions of the presently hidden Twelfth Imam, who are even now preparing with him for the dawning of the Resurrection (*Qiyâmat*).[^EII2-224]

We have also noticed echoes of Iranian chivalry when Suhrawardi calls the beings of Light who have descended into this world—the Zoroastrian *Fravartis*—the “Espahbad Lights of human reality,” or the commander-lights within the human being. Some among their elect are granted a vision of the sources of the Light of Glory. A modern Zoroastrian scholar has set out to demonstrate the proposition that this Light of Glory, the *Xvarnah*, and the Holy Grail are expressions of one and the same image.

On the other hand, Hermes is, for Suhrawardi, the father of the sages and of all wisdom. Suhrawardi's Hermetic affinities are unmistakable, as is the kinship between certain of his psalms and the astral liturgies of the Sabians, who themselves revered Hermes and Agathodaimon.

The visions of the Light of Glory experienced by Kay Khosraw and Zoroaster, and Hermes' sacred ascent to the world of Light “at the hour when the column of dawn bursts forth”—the hour of *Ishrâq*, of the mystical “East”—are two similar forms of the Event that fulfils the initiate's spiritual destiny: descent into this world, forgetfulness of one's origin, hearing the call, setting out upon the path of return, rebirth and final glorification. And the more recent of the two studies we shall discuss traces the spiritual meaning of the Holy Grail back to Hermeticism.

The two investigations were carried out independently. The more recent scholars were unaware of the earlier Zoroastrian study, making it all the more interesting to compare their findings. Both, moreover, overlooked Suhrawardi's “Eastern theosophy” and the Iranian tradition that follows from it—the tradition he “resurrected”—which to us seems their natural meeting place.

For within that tradition Hermes, Kay Khosraw and Zoroaster stand as equal heralds and guides into the mysteries of the same Light of Lights: the Light of Glory, which Suhrawardi names by its ancient Iranian name (*Khorrah*, *Xvarnah*), and in which the Zoroastrian scholar recognises an image identical to the Holy Grail. The studies matter profoundly to us for two reasons.

First, the vision of this Light as a return or passage to the “East”—the initiate's goal—helps us understand that part of Suhrawardi's work in which philosophical teaching becomes a story of initiation.

Second, it establishes a connection between Suhrawardi's tradition of *Ishrâq* and the Grail cycle, in which the West may have entrusted its deepest mystical secret. Through that connection, Suhrawardi's work, and with it a whole dimension of Iranian Islamic spirituality, comes unexpectedly close to us. The Grail leads us back to Hermeticism; the Iranian character of Suhrawardi's wisdom leads us back to the Grail. The circle closes, enclosing a vast spiritual realm: that of *Ishrâq*.

These are the outlines of the circle that the two major studies allow us to draw. Their methods, and the rigour with which they apply them, differ.

We shall consider them in reverse chronological order. The recent work is by two scholars at the University of Illinois, Henry and Renée Kahane.[^EII2-225] The other, some thirty years older, is by Sir Jahangir C. Coyajee, a Zoroastrian scholar in India.

Unfortunately, it appeared on the eve of the Second World War in a journal with very limited circulation in France. These fascinating investigations invite a far longer discussion than we can offer here; we must be content with an outline. The Kahanes' study stands out for its painstaking comparison of the *Corpus Hermeticum* with Wolfram's *Parzival*, its deep knowledge of the Romance languages of the twelfth century, and its judicious scholarly caution. It suggests and proposes more than it asserts.

Indeed, its restraint may make it stronger, because it opens the way for further research. Our chief concern is with three questions: how the Kahanes believe Hermetic teachings reached the West and entered the Grail tradition; how they identify certain proper names whose distorted forms have long perplexed scholars; and how the climax of Wolfram's epic brings us to the very place where Suhrawardi leads the disciple of *Ishrâq*, the pilgrim of the “East.”

The Kahanes' exceptionally close examination reveals similarities and correspondences between the doctrines, episodes and vocabulary of the *Corpus Hermeticum* and those of Wolfram von Eschenbach's *Parzival*. This immediately raises the question of historical transmission. How could knowledge of Hermeticism have reached Wolfram? The course of the Hermetic initiate's life and that of Parsifal[^EII2-226] agree so closely that, in the scholars' view, direct knowledge alone can explain the resemblance—and can also unlock Wolfram's allusions to his “sources.”

The authors distinguish three stages.[^EII2-227] **(a)** First, the preservation of Greek Hermetic material in Syriac and Arabic literature. **(b)** Next, the survival and further development of the Arabic- and Persian-language Hermetic tradition within medieval Islamic civilisation. Here a leading role clearly belongs to the Sabians of Harran (ancient *Carrhae*, in Mesopotamia), who survived within the Islamic world until the eleventh century, though not without difficulty.

They never wholly succeeded in being recognised among the *Ahl al-Kitâb*, the communities possessing a scripture revealed by a prophet, despite having their own “Book” and their own “prophets,” Hermes and Agathodaimon.[^EII2-228] Their devotion to Hermes, their astral liturgies, their teaching on Light and Darkness—the affinities with Suhrawardi's teaching deserve fuller treatment than we have so far been able to give them—and their particular familiarity with the fourth treatise of the *Corpus Hermeticum*, entitled “The Mixing Bowl,” all help us place this community in its spiritual setting.

Thabit ibn Qurra, a distinguished ninth-century scientist and philosopher, founded a new branch of Sabianism in Baghdad and wrote, among other works, a book on the “Liturgical Institutions of Hermes.” We also know that a very large number of Arabic treatises attributed to Hermes remain unpublished.[^EII2-229]

**(c)** Finally, we must consider the transmission to the West of this Greek-Arabic Hermetic material.

From this point the inquiry turns first to identifying the name by which the *Corpus Hermeticum* designates the Grail, then to tracing the people who carried the tradition westward, and finally to answering the question: what should we understand by the *Urparzival*, the supposed “original” *Parsifal*?

The central idea is this: the mysterious *krater*, or mixing bowl, which gives the fourth treatise of the *Corpus Hermeticum* its title, is none other than the Grail, both in meaning and in the very history of the word.[^EII2-230]

“God filled a great mixing bowl with intellect and sent it down to earth. He appointed a herald and commanded him to proclaim to the hearts of men: Immerse yourself in this bowl, you who are able, you who believe you will rise again to the One who sent the bowl to earth, you who know why you came into being. All those, then, who heeded the proclamation and were baptised with this baptism of intellect shared in knowledge (*gnosis*), and became perfect human beings, because they had received intellect.”[^EII2-231]

We shall meet the theme of the messenger from beyond in Suhrawardi's initiation stories. The herald invites all who are capable of understanding the bowl's purpose to enter the baptism it offers. Human beings thus fall into two groups, according to whether they possess the intelligence—and with it the awareness of divine mystery—that makes this possible: those whom spiritual knowledge transforms into “perfect human beings,” and those who will never know why they came into this world.

To connect this with Wolfram's text, let us follow the clues our scholars have identified. The Greek word κρατήρ (*kratēr*, a mixing bowl) is, they argue, the same word as *graal*, already used by Chrétien de Troyes in a form based on the Latin. The Greek became Latin *crater* and *cratera*; the development into *gradale* and *graal*—words for a cup, dish, vessel or basin—presents, in their account, no difficulty.

We leave the details of their philological argument to the authors and turn instead to the *astral* meaning of the vessel. An ancient tradition imagined two bowls traced among the stars, one holding wisdom and the other forgetfulness. Before entering earthly bodies, souls bathe in or drink from one or the other. The theme already appears in Macrobius (fourth–fifth century) and in the well-known Coptic Gnostic book *Pistis Sophia*.

Now, in Book IX of *Parzival*, at the heart of the poem and the culmination of Parsifal's instruction by the hermit, we read that Flegetanis—the learned “pagan,” descended from Solomon, who first wrote the history of the Grail—“discovered, while studying the constellations, profound mysteries of which he spoke only with trembling. There was, he said, an object called the Grail. He had clearly read its name in the stars. A host of angels had brought it down to earth and then flown away, far beyond the stars. Those angels were too pure to remain here below.”[^EII2-232]

The mixing bowl and the Grail are therefore, in their symbolic pattern, “something” brought from Heaven to Earth. Following his “sources” and the tradition known to Macrobius, Wolfram derives the name not from an earthly vessel but from a constellation, which the Kahanes identify as the constellation Crater. The Holy Grail is associated with that constellation as a *vas mysticum*, a mystical vessel.

We shall also encounter the Grail as a mystical bowl or cup in the Iranian tradition.

But does that conflict with the image of the Grail as a *stone*, which appears elsewhere in Wolfram's *Parzival*? Here again the Kahanes seem to us to have offered a sound solution to a problem often treated as an insoluble riddle.[^EII2-233] At the close of the Hermetic treatise on the Mixing Bowl comes a comparison whose crucial image is the “magnetic stone” (*magnētis lithos*): “This, then, O Tat, is the image of God that I have drawn for you as best I can.

“If you contemplate it carefully and picture it with the eyes of your heart, believe me, my child, you will find the way to the things above. Or rather, the image itself will show you the way. For contemplation has a power of its own: it takes hold of those who have once contemplated, and draws them to itself, just as, they say, the magnetic stone draws iron to itself.”[^EII2-234]

Wolfram seems almost to paraphrase this final exhortation when he says that “by the power of this stone the phoenix burns and turns to ashes; yet out of the ashes life is born again. Through this stone the phoenix sheds its old nature and returns in all its splendour, as beautiful as ever.”

Wolfram continues: “No man is so ill that, if brought into the presence of this stone, he is not certain to escape death for the whole week following the day on which he saw it.
