At each level, the literal meaning proper to that level is true and is at the same time a spiritual meaning; that literal-and-spiritual meaning is, in turn, the esoteric meaning relative to the level immediately below it. The visionary landscapes that open before the soul in the *mundus imaginalis*, and the figures who appear within them, are therefore *real* with the reality proper to supersensible beings.

But this reality is far more than the reality of a mere literal narrative whose esoteric meaning would be supplied by theoretical doctrine.

We can now understand why a theosophy expressed through dramatic action passes beyond the level at which it could, or should, furnish the “dialectical proofs” available to theoretical reason. Its grounds of certainty and its proofs are essentially those of directly tasted wisdom: *dhawq*, related here to the Latin *sapere*, knowledge that actually savours what it knows.[^EII2-321] And this knowing, a spiritual knowledge that saves, is inseparable from the movement of faith; it is that movement itself.

We can only be astonished by certain sweeping, categorical claims made today against gnosis—for instance, the assertion that it tries to provide faith with a second set of truths carrying the same kind of certainty as the exact sciences. Such a claim betrays a very limited acquaintance with gnosis. We have expressly rejected any idea of knowledge running alongside faith as a duplicate of it.

But if one begins by separating *pistis* (*îmân*, *fides*), faith, from *gnôsis* (*’irfân*), spiritual knowledge, one will obviously never succeed in bringing them together again in the unity of *theosophia* (*hikmat ilâhîya*), divine wisdom.

Let us now use these principles to examine the themes of the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel.” The tale begins with an important *prologue*. At its close, seven themes are announced, which the Angel will then develop in the teaching through which he initiates his disciple.

##### 2. The Prologue to the Tale

The prologue itself unfolds in several stages.

**a)** A question put to the author by a friend provides the opening: the pre-existence of the soul. Here the reader will recall the magnificent image in Plato’s *Phaedrus* of souls following the gods in a heavenly procession, and of the fall of some among them.[^EII2-322] The soul’s wings naturally suggest the form of a bird.

Hence the first motif: the “language of the birds” (*Mantiq al-tayr*). The Quran speaks of this language (27:16), saying that Solomon, as a prophet, had received the gift of understanding it. To understand the language of birds is to understand the language of all created beings as they speak through their very existence. Each thing is then alive and has a voice; each reveals its secret. To understand that language is to possess the key to symbols. This precious gift is therefore associated with the state of the soul before its fall into our world.

Moreover, *Mantiq al-Tayr*, *The Language of the Birds*, is the title of one of the best-known Persian mystical epics, by Farid al-Din Attar (twelfth century), whose culmination is the episode of Simorgh. We have already encountered that name here, and shall meet it again, for Simorgh is of great importance in Suhrawardi’s tales.

**b)** The soul’s pre-existence leads naturally to the next theme: its fall into captivity. We hear of the hunters called “Decree and Destiny, spreading the net of predestination.” Proclus, too, speaks of hunters, those who “together with the *daimones*, pursue souls and imprison them in bodies.”[^EII2-323] More immediately, Suhrawardi’s theme here closely resembles Avicenna’s visionary tales.

The “Tale of the Bird,” originally written in Arabic by Avicenna and translated into Persian by Suhrawardi, begins in a similar way. It speaks of searching for a friend to whom one might entrust a secret, and makes a moving appeal to the “Brothers of Truth.” Then the narrative begins: “When the hunters caught sight of us, they gave a whistle so pleasing that it lured us into uncertainty […] and suddenly we fell into the nets.”[^EII2-324]

Suhrawardi develops the same theme in the mystical rhapsody called “The Language of the Ants,” from which we earlier drew his “Tale of the Grail.” Elsewhere in that work, in its eighth chapter, he returns to the image of a captive bird. This time it is not a falcon, but a bird whose plumage reflects the colours of paradise: a peacock. “A king had a garden that was never, in any of the four seasons, without sweet herbs, greenery, and places of delight […]. Every joy the mind could conceive, every beauty the imagination could picture, was present in that garden.

“Moreover, a flock of peacocks of the utmost grace, beauty, and delicacy had settled there, and the garden had become their homeland. One day the king took a peacock from among them and ordered it to be sewn inside a skin, so that none of the colours of its plumage remained visible and, try as it might, it could no longer see its own beauty […]. The peacock lost all memory of itself; it forgot the king, the garden, and the other peacocks.”

Thereafter the bird’s whole horizon was reduced to the slit in a little basket through which food was passed to it, “and the conviction took root in its heart that no country could be larger than the bottom of the basket.”[^EII2-325] Once again, the peacock sewn into a covering of skin recalls the Grail buried inside its leather sheath. For the Grail to appear, or for the bird’s true form to become visible, each must be freed from the covering that conceals it.

In either case, its reappearance means reappearing *in its own world*, the world from which it descended only to be hidden here under an enclosing skin. To become visible again in its own world is to become invisible to this one. This is one of the ruling themes of Illuminationist gnosis, and indeed of spiritual gnosis in general.

We shall encounter another version at the beginning of the “Tale of the Western Exile.”

**c)** Captivity and the fall are followed by escape. This theme recurs in the other mystical tales. Each time, the author evokes a state in which the senses are “bound,” thereby releasing the person from subjection to the world of sensory perception. The state can be represented by “night”: when night conceals the world of the senses, the soul’s powers of higher understanding awaken. It is the moment when the Grail is drawn out of its covering and hidden from the sight of this world.

The initiate is not a schizophrenic; he knows perfectly well that he is between two worlds, that his liberation is not yet complete. The bird in our tale says: “Struggling all the while with my bonds, I finally made my way into the desert.” The same detail appears in Avicenna’s “Tale of the Bird.”[^EII2-326] The “desert,” the solitary open country—evoking the lonely expanses of the Iranian plateau, where infinite variety is gathered into a few essential tones—is always the first place reached by the soul escaping the turmoil of the outer world’s perceptions.

Another tale, the “Epistle on the State of Childhood,” likewise opens in the desert.

**d)** The escape into the desert leads immediately to the encounter with the Angel. The prologue to another tale, “The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings,”[^EII2-327] already shows us the Child—the heavenly human being—freed from the bonds imposed on the children of Earth. These bonds are the limitations of knowledge gained through the senses, which keep earthly human beings in servitude, sunk in the sleep of their soul’s death. It is therefore night for the senses.

The active Imagination is left entirely free to perceive the realities of the world belonging to it, the *mundus imaginalis*, which begins at the summit of Mount Qaf. At the coming of the mystical dawn, the hour of *Ishrâq* or illumination, the visionary opens the door of the *khângâh*, the Sufi lodge, leading out into the countryside. In other words, at the threshold of his innermost awareness, his “transconsciousness,” he opens the secret door onto an unexplored wilderness.

Crossing it will take him to the country from which he came into this world. “It was a night when … darkness … had spread to the furthest limits of the lower world … I took a torch in my hand … and walked until daybreak … I closed the door that led toward the town … I wanted to open the door that led into the countryside … I saw ten Sages with radiant faces …” These Sages stand in a hierarchy of ranks. Their beauty fills the visionary with amazement. He approaches the nearest with reverent awe, and his initiation begins.

This is not an initiation into cosmology; Suhrawardi had already set out his cosmology in his major works. It is an initiation into the angelology that gives cosmology its inner meaning. There are three orders of Angels: the *Karûbiyûn*, the Cherubim or cherubic Intelligences, who are the greater *Logoi*, the greater divine Words; the intermediate *Logoi* or Words, the heavenly Souls that move the Spheres; and finally the lesser *Logoi* or Words, human beings, who are potentially angels or demons.

Here, again, the angelology is not a matter of theory but of an event. The visionary really does find himself, *in actu*, before the one among the greater Words who stands closest to him. Who is this being? The text leaves no doubt: Gabriel, or the Holy Spirit, the Tenth Intelligence in the angelic hierarchy, the Angel of humanity.

To human beings, he is the interpreter of the higher worlds. Without him, those worlds, lying beyond the limits of human perception, would have nothing to offer but eternal silence. The relationship of this Angel with each individual human being takes a personal form: that *Perfect Nature* to which Suhrawardi dedicated one of his most beautiful psalms (see above, p. 138). In the end it is this Perfect Nature that undertakes the initiation, for it sometimes speaks of Gabriel in the third person. Gabriel the Archangel has two wings.

The right wing is pure, absolute light; across the left lies a shadowy mark, like the reddish darkening that veils the face of the moon as it rises full. The world of illusion, the world of becoming or *genesis*, is a shadow cast by Gabriel’s left wing; from his right wing emanate the souls of light. With the revelation of the “heavenly Self,” the horizon of a human existence beyond ordinary existence opens. When the “day” of sensory perceptions and their certainties rises once more, the vision ends.

Keep in mind this brief account of the prologue Suhrawardi placed at the beginning of “The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings.” In the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel,” the soul is in the same circumstances and encounters the same Figure, recognizable by the same features. No sooner has the visionary entered the desert than he sees a mysterious person approaching, a youth whose appearance enchants him. And yet, as he learns, this young man is “the eldest of the Creator’s children.”

To grasp exactly what this statement means, we must recall the distinction we have already encountered between the “world of the Divine Command” (*’âlam al-Amr*), which comprises the *jabarût* and *malakût*, and the “world of created beings” (*’âlam al-khalq*), embracing the whole world of becoming, to which human beings presently belong. As the “Angel of humanity” (*Rabb al-nû’ al-insânî*), Gabriel can call himself the “eldest” of the Creator’s children.

The distinguishing feature of this vision is its red or glowing crimson colour. That colour gives the tale its title, and makes the title difficult to translate in a way that speaks for itself. The Persian title is *’Aql-e sorkh*. The word *’aql* (plural *’oqûl*) is the traditional name for the cherubic Intelligences, whose ten hierarchical ranks we have just recalled.

In the Latin Avicennian tradition, these are the *Angeli intellectuales*, the intellectual Angels, while the *Angeli caelestes*, the heavenly Angels, form the intermediate hierarchy of Souls that move the Spheres. The last of the cherubic Intelligences is Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, the Angel of knowledge and revelation for humanity, the philosophers’ *Active Intelligence*, the *Madonna Intelligenza* of the Faithful of Love in Dante’s circle.[^EII2-328] *Sorkh* means “red.” We feared that translating the title simply as “The Red Intelligence” would mislead readers, if indeed it conveyed anything to them.

Moreover, when the Angel explains his “colour” to the disciple, he speaks of the purple-red glow of twilight. Since the *’oqûl*, the Intelligences, are also called archangels, the title suggested itself at once: *Tale of the Crimson Archangel*. The Angel’s explanation tells us that this colour, crimson red, comes from the mingling of light and darkness, of white and black. This is precisely what the symbolism of Gabriel’s “two wings,” recalled above, is meant to convey. From the standpoint of our physics, the explanation may seem surprising; if we wished to account for it experimentally, we might think of a ray of light passing through stained glass.

But an optical phenomenon is not what matters here. The colour has, above all, a meaning beyond the senses and a symbolic function. The closer a being is to the source of being, the more it tends toward whiteness; the closer it comes to the world of *genesis*, the more it tends toward black.

This striking feature of Suhrawardi’s visionary tales must therefore be understood in relation to the symbolism of colours in Islamic theosophy. The theme has so far received very little study. It is initially organized around the image of the Throne, which plays a role in Islamic gnosis comparable to that of the *Merkabah*, the divine chariot-throne, in Jewish Kabbalah.

The Throne’s four “pillars,” representing the foundations of being, correspond to the four archangels—Seraphiel, Michael, Gabriel, and Azrael—each appearing in a colour of his own. The arrangement varies somewhat from one author to another. Qazi Sa'id Qommi, in particular, gave a remarkable analysis of the metaphysical meaning of the gradual “diminution” of white light: it passes through yellow, red, and green as it descends toward the world of Darkness. We cannot pursue the subject further here.

Let us at least note how the same theme appears in the work of several other great Iranian spiritual masters. In the visions of Najm al-Din Kubra (d. 618/1221), among the perceived lights that lie beyond the senses—the spiritual *aura*—a glowing crimson announces the Angel-Intelligence in a double form: in the great world, the macrocosm, as the Angel-Logos, a manifestation of the Inaccessible; and in the small world, the microcosm, as the heart, a consciousness made of light.[^EII2-329] Later, in Book IV, we shall encounter Semnani (d. 736/1336) and his account of the seven subtle organs or sheaths (*latîfa*) that constitute the subtle body of mystical physiology.

Each makes itself known to the mystic’s supersensible perception by a particular colour, and each is represented by a prophet. The *latîfa* corresponding to the heart—the “Abraham of your being”—is red. We should also recall the predominance of red light in the visions of Ruzbihan of Shiraz (d. 606/1209), discussed in Book III. “One night I saw something enveloping the heavens. It was a sparkling red light. I asked: What is this? I was told: It is the mantle of magnificence.”

Finally, in the last century, Shaykh Muhammad Karim Khan Kermani, the second successor of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i (see Book VI below), composed, among many other works, a long treatise on the colour red. He considered it from its optical appearance, essence, and nature through to its symbolic and mystical meanings.

Of these examples, and others we could add, the essential point to retain is the connection between the heart as the dwelling place of knowledge and Gabriel as the Angel who mediates that knowledge. Here, as in similar tales by Suhrawardi, the Angel performs the same function as *Poimandres* in the first treatise of the *Corpus Hermeticum*. The *Nous*, the Intelligence, appears to Hermes as his initiator. We have already traced this figure in Suhrawardi’s “Perfect Nature” and in the Illuminationist tradition.

An angel who serves as the human being’s shepherd (*poimên*) also appears in *The Shepherd of Hermas*, that delightful little book so rich in symbolic visions, which for a time formed part of the canonical Scriptures. Hermas’s “shepherd” is the angel personally entrusted with his care. In each instance, the personal angel—the Hermetic “Perfect Nature”—appears under similar circumstances. Just as Hermas’s angel is sent by the glorious Angel, the “Most Holy Angel,” whom the context suggests is Michael the Archangel, so the Perfect Nature expresses for the Illuminationist initiate his own individually distinct relationship with the Angel of humanity.[^EII2-330]

We should also remember that the great Iranian poet Hakim Sana'i of Herat (d. 545/1150), who died a few years before Suhrawardi’s birth, had already written a poem called “The Journey of Souls to the Place of Their Return,” in the form of a first-person narrative. It describes a journey through the Neoplatonic cosmos under the guidance of the Active Intelligence, appearing as a personal angel or guide. Even so, Suhrawardi’s initiatory tales *in prose* remain unique in Persian literature.

Finally, his tales ought to be considered alongside the theory of spiritual knowledge developed in Shia teaching on prophecy, based on the words of the holy Imams. This theory distinguishes between actually seeing an Angel while awake, seeing an Angel in a dream or intermediate state, and merely hearing the Angel’s voice without a vision. According to these distinctions, it establishes degrees of sacred knowledge, from prophetic revelation to mystical inspiration (see Book I above). We have, indeed, already seen that the accusation brought against Suhrawardi at his trial was directed at the understanding of prophecy implicit in his entire teaching.

**e)** Once the disciple has identified the Angel, he wants to know more: where does the Angel come from? From beyond Mount Qaf, he answers—from the place where he dwells and where his disciple, too, *once dwelt*, before falling captive into this world. The disciple has lost all memory of that home because his awareness is confined within the limits of the very world that holds him prisoner. The whole purpose of the initiatory tale is to teach him to recognize the stages of the journey that will carry the exile across Mount Qaf and out of the cosmic crypt.

We have already said enough about Mount Qaf, the cosmic mountain, not to need another lengthy account. We know that at its summit, or in its heart, begins the “eighth clime”: the “Middle East,” the *mundus imaginalis*, the Earth of emerald cities, the “Land of No-Where” (*Nâ-kojâ-Abâd*). It is called “No-Where” because it lies beyond the spatial coordinates contained beneath the Sphere of Spheres. The Angel will point toward it only from afar, as if by a gesture. The pilgrim himself will enter it, for a moment, only at the end of the following tale.

But before setting out, he must learn the stages of the road. These are what the Angel will reveal through the seven wonders he has observed in his ceaseless travels through the world. This perpetual wandering is also a feature of Hayy ibn Yaqzan in Avicenna’s tale of that name.[^EII2-331] Every human intelligence the Angel illuminates marks another stage of his journey. The very nature of the seven wonders, which will become the seven themes of the tale proper, makes clear what he means by endless travel: he goes from soul to soul, awakening each through his illumination from its torpor.

##### 3. The Seven Themes of the Tale

**I.** The first of these “wonders” is Mount *Qaf* itself, which the Angel names first when he says where he comes from. We already know that this mountain belongs both to the cosmos and to the inner cosmos of the soul. Traditional accounts that speak of it in a literal sense agree in identifying it with the mountain range encircling the world, formerly known as *Alborz* (Elburz; in the Avesta, *Haraiti Bareza*). Geographically, that name now designates the mountains stretching across northern Iran.

But visionary geography is not concerned with this measurable feature of the Earth’s terrain when it speaks of a mountain surrounding the world, and of the wondrous race inhabiting its cities. More precisely, this is a “cartography of vision,” a mapping that locates and names places according to the visionary experiences corresponding to them. At that level, the true meaning of Alborz appears in its “visionary calling.”[^EII2-332]

As the cosmic mountain surrounding our earthly world, Mount Qaf, or Alborz, is described by the Angel as actually consisting of eleven mountains. Their succession of peaks and valleys represents the nine heavenly Spheres—from the heaven of the Moon to the Sphere of Spheres—together with the spheres of the Elements: the cold region of the sphere of Water and the hot regions of the spheres of Air and Fire.

The Angel’s listener is concerned above all with one question: how can he get out? How can he cross these mountains and finally reach the summit of Mount Qaf? The hardest task is to escape the first two mountains, representing the earthly human condition: bondage to the Elements, to the physical body composed of them, and to the kind of perception that this condition imposes.

The Angel proceeds through hints and veiled suggestions: “However far you travel, and however long you keep going, you will arrive once more at your point of departure.” This is because the spiritual person’s “place of return” (*ma’âd*) is also the place of his origin (*mabdâ’*). It is in no sense a matter of setting out from oneself only to arrive, quite simply, back at oneself. Between departure and return, a great event will have transformed everything. The *self* found up there at the summit of Mount Qaf is the higher self, the “self in the second person,” encountered face to face by the pilgrim in the “Tale of the Western Exile.”

Consider closely the Angel’s understated lesson when the questioner proposes using great physical force to cross the mountains. If you pour a drop of balm into the hollow of your hand and hold your hand in the sun *until it grows hot*, the balm will pass through to the other side of your hand by virtue of its own natural power. The same symbol will return at the end of the tale: *the one who has bathed in the Spring of Life*, on emerging from its waters, has acquired the capacity that makes him like the drop of balm. Such a person is Khezr, and can pass through. It then takes only an instant to cross these mountains.[^EII2-333]

This is the *leitmotif* governing the whole tale, for it states, in veiled language, the secret way out of the cosmic mountain. Most people, of course, will never pass beyond the first two mountains. Others will reach the third, fourth, or fifth, but go no farther.

The third mountain represents the inner, spiritual heaven of the Moon, just beyond the elemental Spheres. Here one already enters the “desert.” This is the deeper meaning of the traditions that tell of the infant Zal abandoned in Alborz; in the present tale the author will simply say “in the desert.” At this boundary, the encounter with the Angel takes place.

If the disciple fails to understand the Angel’s hints, he will indeed get no farther than the third mountain. If he understands them, he will cross them all and reach the Spring of Life. Having become like the drop of balm, he will then have passed from the world of outward, natural appearances to the world of the inward spiritual realities hidden within those appearances, as an almond lies concealed within its shell.

Yet, paradoxically, to pass into the *inner* world is to find oneself *outside*—or, in the language of our authors, “on the convex surface of the Ninth Sphere.” That is to say, one finds oneself at the summit of Mount Qaf, and thereby beyond every mountain range. One has left the space of perceptible dimensions by way of the *quarta dimensio*, the fourth dimension, without needing to “dig a tunnel,” as the questioner naively supposed at the outset. We might think here of knot theory, or of twisting a circular ring into the shape of a figure eight, so that something moving along the inner surface of the eight, from any given point, eventually finds itself on the outside.

**II.** The second “wonder,” furnishing the second theme of initiation, is the “Jewel That Lights the Night,” a traditional Persian metaphor for the Moon.

But neither here nor in the two following themes are we really dealing with astronomy. To understand what is at stake, it helps to recall a passage in Proclus explaining why Timaeus calls himself “the most astronomical” of the three speakers in Plato’s dialogue bearing his name. Proclus brings in one of the “Chaldean Oracles.” Timaeus, he says, does not describe himself in this way “because he had scrutinized the speeds of heavenly movements or measured the course of the sun by means of a collection of tables … but because he studies the stars above Heaven itself, in accordance with the *leader* mentioned in the *Theaetetus*, and contemplates the invisible causes which are stars in the true sense.”[^EII2-334]

Suhrawardi, too, has these “stars in the true sense” in mind when, for example, in his “Epistle of the High Towers” (*Risâlat al-Abrâj*), he speaks of Hallaj, Bastami, and other Sufis as “Moons in the heaven of *tawhîd*”—the realization of divine unity. In that same epistle, written in Arabic rather than Persian, the Moon (*qamar*, masculine in Arabic) appears as the lover of the queen of the stars, the Sun (*shams*, feminine in Arabic). The lover never lingers. He presses onward from the lowest point of the new moon to the height of the full moon.

Then, at the fullness of the lunar cycle, the rays of his “queen, the Sun,” are reflected in him, setting his whole being ablaze, though in himself he was nothing but Darkness. Looking within, the lover, stripped of his separate being, can see nothing that is not filled with that light. And so he cries out: “*Anâ’l-Shams*—I am the Sun!”[^EII2-335]

Exactly the same lesson appears in the mystical rhapsody “The Language of the Ants,” in its ninth chapter. There we hear the answer the Moon gave to the prophet Idris—whom, as we know, the tradition identifies both with Enoch and with Hermes Trismegistus—when he asked why her light sometimes wanes and sometimes waxes. “Know that my body is dark, but smooth and pure. Of myself I have no light at all.

“Yet when I stand opposite the Sun, and precisely to the degree that I face it, an image of its light falls upon the mirror that is my body, just as the forms of other bodies appear in mirrors […] until, when I look within myself at the moment of encounter, it is the Sun that I see […]. Then, whenever I look at myself, I find that everything is Sun.

“Do you not see that when a mirror is placed before the Sun, the form of the Sun appears in it? If, by divine decree, the mirror had eyes, and looked into itself while facing the Sun, it would find that everything within it was Sun, even though it was made of metal. *I am the Sun* (*Anâ’l-Shams*), it would say, because it would see nothing within itself but the Sun. And if it went so far as to say *I am God* (*Anâ’l-Haqq*) … even then, we would have to accept its plea in excuse.”[^EII2-336]

These two passages seem to make any further explanation of the “Jewel That Lights the Night” episode in our tale unnecessary. The Moon represents the mystic journeying through the heaven of *tawhîd*, divine unity. Her phases represent the successive stages and repeated encounters face to face that bring the mystic’s inner being to a state of incandescence.

At such a moment, the Light that wholly possesses him becomes the active Subject within him. Absorption, or *fanâ’*, into this Light does not mean the destruction of the mystic’s being or personhood. It means a transformation of consciousness, in which the illusory ego is transfigured in the real Self, the true subject of thought and action. “When my servant draws near to me, I become the eye through which he sees, the ear through which he hears,” and so on.

The more the real Self comes to the fore, the more the lower ego of ordinary consciousness fades and disappears; and the reverse is equally true. This is the meaning of the Angel’s teaching, illustrated by the Moon’s phases, by the little sphere floating on the surface of a bowl, and by the approach to the Tuba tree. Taken to its limit, the second passage quoted above lets us hear the ecstatic declaration of al-Hallaj: *Anâ’l-Haqq*, “I am God.”

But is that, without qualification, the position professed by the Master of Illumination?

Notice the progression in the two passages just quoted, leading to the final cry: “I am the Sun.” Hallaj’s declaration, “I am God,” appears only as an extreme case. There can be no doubt that the Tuba tree, whose light sets the Moon ablaze, here represents the Sun (compare theme IV)—not, of course, the incandescent body visible in the astronomical heavens, but the “star in the true sense,” the spiritual Sun.

We should therefore return to the psalm dedicated to the Archangel of the Sun (see above, III, section 5). There the author describes that archangel, who is the gateway (*pishgâh*) to every ecstasy in the spiritual world, as the vicegerent of the Light of Lights. He is its image because it sets him ablaze with its own light. In the present tale we are told, on one hand, where he stands among the eleven mountains: in the fourth Heaven, the Heaven of the Sun, which in Jewish gnosis is the heaven of the Archangel Michael.

On the other hand, we are told that “whoever is familiar with paradise beholds this tree whenever he walks there.” Yet Suhrawardi held, like every spiritual master within Islam, that God Most High and any created being, at whatever level, cannot belong to the same order or species of being. This is precisely the great problem facing these thinkers.

Must we then agree with the rationalist theologians of *kalâm*, who declare any direct relation between the divine Essence and human nature impossible? Must we assume that such a relation would inevitably mean either a Manichaean “mingling” or the Christian idea of Incarnation? That would be to forget entirely—and the West has forgotten it more than once—the very way forward opened by Shia teaching on the Imam. It is profoundly significant that both the Tuba tree and Simorgh have been understood, in Twelver Shiism and Ismailism alike, as symbols of the Imam.

For the Imam is the Sun, the Face, the Perfect Human Being, the form of divine manifestation (*mazhar*) who can fill a believer with the Light manifested within himself without dissolving that believer’s created existence. The *walâyat* of the faithful—their standing as “friends of God”—is a lunar *walâyat* in relation to that of the Imam.[^EII2-337] The present tale does not explicitly speak of the Imam; it speaks instead of the Tuba tree and Simorgh.

The Angel’s hint is discreet, given in half-spoken words. Without pressing those words too hard, we may observe that the relation between Moon and Sun in the heaven of the *malakût*, the world of the Soul, establishes the very conditions of the *hikâyat* recalled earlier. In that threefold unity, the person telling the tale, the mystical epic, and the one whose deeds are recounted become one. At its limit, the situation finds expression in *Anâ’l-Shams*: “I am the Sun.” At the end of our tale, the initiate will be called upon to decide whether he can say, “I am Khezr,” and, by that very fact, whether he can cross Mount Qaf.

**III.** The third “wonder,” and the third theme of initiation, grows directly out of the preceding one. It gives rise to a long exposition of particularly dense and allusive meaning, forming the centre of the entire tale. The Angel’s teaching now concerns the Tuba tree and Simorgh. Mention of the mysterious bird itself leads to an extended digression on two heroes of the Iranian epic: first Zal, then Esfandiyar.

We have just recalled the *situs*, the symbolic location, of the Tuba tree: at the centre of the mountains making up Mount Qaf and, correspondingly, at the centre—and therefore also at the summit—of the *malakût*, the world of the Soul, or “paradise.” This symbol recurs throughout the mystical traditions. In Ismaili gnosis it represents the Imam as unconditioned existence (*wojûd motlaq*). A ray from the light of his knowledge is projected into the nature or substance of every inhabitant of paradise, every faithful follower of the Imam. Traditions shared by the whole of Shiism tell us that the branches of the Tuba tree hang down from the highest region of paradise.

This means that whatever the people of paradise desire appears immediately upon its branches, because for them knowledge, desire, and the effective power to bring something about are simultaneous. Similarly, the statement that one of its branches hangs before the window of every place of prayer in paradise means that all its inhabitants share in the tree, each according to the measure of their desire.[^EII2-338] This simultaneity is also the law of the *mundus imaginalis*, the imaginal world. Our text seems to refer us to this understanding, while also making the Tuba tree the symbol of the spiritual Sun of the *malakût*.

Next comes Simorgh, whose nest is “at the summit of the Tuba tree.” We know that the name of this mysterious bird already occurs in the *Avesta* as *Saena meregha*, which eventually became the Persian *Simorgh*. Since the Avestan form is feminine, and Persian does not distinguish masculine and feminine grammatical gender, we prefer to preserve the feminine form of the Avestan name. The Persian form made possible the brilliant play on words by which Attar brings his great mystical epic, *Mantiq al-Tayr*, *The Language of the Birds*, to its conclusion.

The name can be read as *sî-morgh*, “thirty birds.” Under that name, Attar encodes the double mystery of identity within difference and difference within identity, between the eternal Simorgh and the *thirty birds*, the only ones among thousands to have completed their long and painful quest.[^EII2-339] We have already referred to the mystical secret encoded in the name Simorgh (see above, Book I, Chapter VII, section 4).

Naturally, the interpretation of this symbol varies among the authors in whose works it reappears.

For example, in Shams al-Din Lahiji (d. 918/1506), the commentator on *The Rose Garden of Mystery* (*Golshan-e Râz*), the great poem by the celebrated Azerbaijani mystic Mahmud Shabestari (d. 720/1317), Simorgh represents the absolute divine Selfhood. Mount Qaf, where she dwells, is the spiritual reality of the Human Being, the *Anthropos*. This is the perfect form of divine manifestation (*mazhar*), the Form through which the divine Being reveals its Names and Attributes.

For the Ismaili commentator on the same mystical poem, Simorgh is the name of the Spirit, and the mountain where she dwells is the body. Since Simorgh names the Spirit, it also names the Imam: the Imam is spiritual truth and resurrection, in contrast to the body, which is the outward letter of the *sharî’at*, the religious law, within which that truth is presently concealed.[^EII2-340]

Attar’s understanding offers us the best guidance through Suhrawardi’s difficult text. At first Simorgh appears as the eternal Simorgh: she who cares for Zal, and whose Image carries Esfandiyar away in supreme ecstasy, just as the thirty birds stand overwhelmed before the revelation of Simorgh.

Yet later we learn that the name Simorgh can also designate each Simorgh among a multitude of Simorghs. Here we may recall the celebrated theological conception of the “members”: the World Soul is at once identical with its members and, as a distinct spiritual reality, different from them.[^EII2-341]

In another of Suhrawardi's mystical treatises, appropriately entitled *The Incantation of the Simorgh*, the prologue describes what happens to each hoopoe when spring comes. It leaves its nest, takes flight toward Mount Qaf, and strips itself of its own feathers with its own beak. Once Mount Qaf has cast its shadow over the bird for a period measured in the time of the *Malakut*, the spiritual kingdom (compare Quran 22:46: one day with your Lord is equal to a thousand years by your reckoning), the hoopoe becomes a Simorgh, whose song awakens those who sleep.

The Simorgh flies while remaining motionless; it takes flight without crossing any distance; it draws near without traversing any interval. All colors are within it, yet it has no color of its own. Its nest is in the East, yet it is not absent from the West. Everyone is concerned with it, yet it depends on no one. All forms of knowledge arise from this bird's song, as does the sound of every musical instrument. Its food is fire.[^EII2-342] (More than one feature of this description was taken up by a Christian theologian to describe the dove, the mystical symbol of the Holy Spirit.[^EII2-343])

Here, then, we meet the image of the hoopoe becoming a Simorgh. Its flight in the spring coincides with the moment when Kay Khosrow held the Grail toward the rising sun—the hour of *Ishraq*, the dawn of illumination. The circumstances in which the lower self is cast off correspond, in turn, to the mystical significance of the moon's phases, when it reaches the fullness of its light on the side facing the Tree of Tuba. This is also the moment when the mystic draws the Grail from its tunic of skin.

The Simorgh feeds only on fire—the fire that is the Grail itself (see above, IV, 5). It thus takes on the attributes of the phoenix mentioned by Wolfram von Eschenbach (see above, IV, 1). Through the Grail, “the phoenix is consumed and reduced to ashes.” Yet life is born anew from those ashes, and the phoenix, having undergone its transformation, reappears in all its splendor.

These details from the prologue are invaluable if we are to understand—or at least begin to sense—the Archangel's answer in *The Tale of the Crimson Archangel*: only an ignorant person, he says, would dare claim that there is just one Simorgh. On the contrary, a Simorgh is continually descending from the Tree of Tuba to the earth, while the one that was there before disappears. Without this ceaseless coming and going, nothing in this world could continue to exist, for nothing in the visible world can endure without the life-giving influence of the spiritual world.

The suggestion that there are many Simorghs recalls the many birds in Attar's mystical epic: the thirty birds (*si-morgh*) who reach the presence of the eternal Simorgh. What the Archangel says in Suhrawardi's tale would imply that the eternal Simorgh stands in relation to all these birds as each individual Simorgh stands in relation to the human being to whom it belongs. That, indeed, seems to be the suggestion at the end of the fourth theme.

Within the human being, the Simorgh is the mystical “moon,” whose encounter with the sun sets the human being ablaze like a mirror catching the light. It is the heavenly Self and the protecting Angel, the imperishable Face of that being. It corresponds to the Perfect Nature, which is both the mystic's *father* and *child*: it feeds upon the flame of the mystic's Grail, and this feeding requires the human being to die to the lower self. When the burning is complete, the human soul—the hoopoe—has become the phoenix-Simorgh. Rising again from its ashes, it takes flight “in springtime” toward the East, the summit of Mount Qaf.

All this is suggested so delicately, through hints and allusions, that we must not weigh it down with an elaborate argument designed to force it into a rigid system of concepts. Here we have to think in images (compare our remarks above, pp. 194 ff.).

But if we keep in mind the twofold character of the Simorgh, as Suhrawardi suggests it and Attar develops it, we can begin to understand—still only through hints—the episodes of Zal and Esfandiyar that appear at this point in the tale. For clarity, we shall examine them separately below (§4). Here, above all, the Simorgh takes on the full mystical meaning bestowed on it by Iranian Sufism. By that very fact, the image gives the heroic epic its “Eastern destination.” The deeds of the heroes of the *Shahnameh* find their fulfillment in a mystical epic.

**IV.** The fourth “wonder” consists of twelve workshops, followed by seven further “workshops,” each presided over by a master. Each of the seven masters also has charge of either one or two of the twelve higher workshops. Behind the language of craftsmen and their guilds, we readily recognize an astronomical symbolism: the twelve signs of the zodiac and the seven planetary heavens, each governed by its Angel. Each planet has two “houses” among the signs of the zodiac, except the sun and moon, which have only one each.

Yet, as we observed earlier when referring to a particularly revealing statement by Proclus, this is not intended as a lesson in astronomy. These are spiritual stars in the heaven of the *Malakut*. The ultimate meaning of the symbolism is therefore clear: the seventh master (the Angel of the moon) borrows his “robe of honor”—that is, his light—from the fourth master (the Angel of the sun). We are brought straight back to the second theme, the “Jewel That Illumines the Night.”

The point is that the “moons” in the mystical heaven, set ablaze like mirrors by the spiritual sun of the *Malakut*, can exclaim: “I am the sun.” The final sentence leaves no doubt: “As I explained to you in speaking of the Simorgh”—the Simorgh “whose nest is at the top of the Tree of Tuba,” a tree that is itself the symbol of the spiritual sun of the *Malakut*. This, I believe, makes clear the meaning of the Simorgh that we have tried to bring out in our analysis of the preceding theme.

**V–VII.** The meaning of the last three themes is almost self-evident. The “coat of mail” is the elemental body, “woven” in the workshops just mentioned. It is the leather sheath, the covering of skin that encloses Kay Khosrow's Grail. The Sword belongs to the Angel of Death. With a single blow it breaks open the coat of mail when that armor has served its purpose. For the uninitiated person, who has not devoted a lifetime to undergoing the ordeal of mystical death, the blow causes unimaginable suffering.

But for someone who has discovered the Fountain of Life and bathed in its waters, the coat of mail has become so supple that the blow of the Sword is no longer felt. Thus the last and seventh “wonder” is precisely this: the “Fountain of Life” in the darkness, reached by the mysterious prophet Khezr (Khidr), companion of the prophet Elijah, or perhaps identical with him. The Archangel's final instructions are intended to initiate his disciple into the search for the Fountain of Life—that is, into the passage through Mount Qaf to its heart or summit.[^EII2-344] His final words are: “If you are Khezr, you too can pass through Mount Qaf without difficulty.”

Once again we hear the image of a drop of balm passing through to the back of a hand heated by the sun, as a piece of iron is made incandescent by fire. “If you are Khezr”: in other words, if the condition of the *hikayat*, the mystical telling of a tale, is fulfilled, and Khezr is not merely someone whose story the narrator relates from the outside, as an “objective” event. No: in the act of mystical recitation, the narrator, Khezr himself, and Khezr's journey to the Fountain of Life become one and the same reality—as they did in the “Tale of the Grail,” and as they will again in the “Tale of Exile.”

##### 4. From the Birth of Zal to the Death of Esfandiyar

These episodes may well be the key to the meaning of *The Tale of the Crimson Archangel*. Yet they may also be the hardest to interpret, because their meaning is deliberately veiled and conveyed through a wealth of allusions.

We may come closest to understanding Suhrawardi's intention if we grasp two motifs together: the soul's “descent” into this world, and the “guardian angel”—the *daimon paredros*, or *agathos daimon* (the good or companion spirit)—from whom the soul separates when it descends here, and with whom it is reunited when it leaves this world, “when the hoopoe takes flight in springtime and becomes a Simorgh.” Both motifs are fundamental to Neoplatonic thought.[^EII2-345] Here doctrine becomes story, and through that story Suhrawardi seeks to suggest the meaning and role of the Simorgh. Its intervention brings the heroic epic of Iran to its fulfillment as a mystical epic. In this way, the undertaking that the *Shaykh al-Ishraq*, the Master of Illumination, carried within him all his life finds its completion.

He therefore chooses two moments from Ferdowsi's *Shahnameh* in which the Simorgh's intervention presents an especially compelling mystery for spiritual interpretation. The Archangel tells his listener the soul's spiritual history, from its beginning in this world to its final passage beyond it.

But the material of the Iranian heroic epic divides the drama—the soul's descent into this world and its final ascent back to its own world—between two characters: Zal, the hero of the epic cycle of Sistan, and Esfandiyar, the champion of the Zoroastrian faith. The latter's character was ideally suited to the purposes of the *Shaykh al-Ishraq* as the “reviver of the wisdom of ancient Persia.” From Zal's birth under the protection of the Simorgh to Esfandiyar's death in the supreme ecstasy that ends his earthly struggle, the mysterious presence of the Simorgh makes itself felt throughout.

It would take us too far afield to collect all the traditions about Zal in the Avesta, Ferdowsi, and the writers of the Islamic period, along with the many interpretations they have received.[^EII2-346] We need consider only the episode chosen by Suhrawardi: the birth of Zal, father of Rostam, the famous hero of Sistan. In Ferdowsi's epic, Zal appears chiefly as the wise adviser of the Kayanian kings. Earlier in this chapter (IV, 3), we mentioned him as one of Kay Khosrow's eight companions on the journey to the “high mountain.”

Yet Zal was among the three who heeded Kay Khosrow's warning, chose not to follow him farther, and found their way back to this world. The extraordinary feature of Zal's birth, recalled by the author of our tale, is familiar throughout the tradition. Suhrawardi, however, seems to have been the first to reveal its hidden meaning.

The disciple's question to the Archangel comes immediately after the description of the Tree of Tuba as the tree “at whose summit the Simorgh has its nest.” We saw how this deepens the preceding theme: the relationship between the “Jewel That Illumines the Night” and that same Tree of Tuba, the spiritual sun at the summit of the *Malakut*. Recall also the other passage from Suhrawardi cited above: “A Simorgh continually descends from the Tree of Tuba to earth, while the one that was there before disappears.”

There are, of course, several ways to unfold the meaning of this image. We have noted, for instance, that a Shiite mystic may read the Simorgh as a hidden symbol of the Imam and the Imamate. The interpretation proposed here seems to me both to make this deliberately veiled text intelligible and to accord with Suhrawardi's overall purpose in his books and tales.

The Simorgh's descent to earth seems to accompany the descent of the human soul. It is the guardian angel, the *agathos daimon* that, according to Iamblichus, exists as an original model or pattern even before souls descend into the world of becoming (*genesis*). Plotinus had already said (*Enneads* IV, 8, 8) that no soul, not even our own, is wholly immersed in the world perceived by the senses: “There is something in it that always remains in the intelligible world. Every soul has a lower side turned toward the body and a higher side turned toward Intellect.”

At its furthest reach, this higher soul can be understood as the personal angel who inspires our thoughts and governs our actions—until, as Iamblichus also says, through “sacred theurgy” we entrust the direction and protection of our soul to a god, with the angel acting as that god's assistant.[^EII2-347] This is, in brief, the figure we identified in an earlier analysis (Chapter III, 1, pp. 88–92): on the one hand, the personal good spirit (*agathos daimon*) of Hermes and of the Hermetic philosopher, or the “Perfect Nature,” both “father” and “child” of the soul, to which Suhrawardi dedicated his magnificent hymn; on the other, the angel Daena, a sacred manifestation of the *Xvarnah*, the divine glory of Mazdean wisdom.

In Suhrawardi, the Simorgh seems to occupy this same place. It also corresponds to the Fravarti (*foruhar*) of Mazdean thought, the heavenly counterpart of an individual living on earth. Although the Simorgh descends with each human soul, it remains distinct from that soul: its original pattern, its counterpart, its heavenly companion. It can therefore be said to care for the soul and watch over it. If the soul has remained faithful to the Simorgh, its supreme moment, the supreme vision at its departure from this world—as in Suhrawardi's interpretation of Esfandiyar—is reunion with the Simorgh, the joining into one of the two who belong together.

“When the hoopoe becomes the Simorgh,” the Simorgh “whose nest is at the summit of the Tree of Tuba,” the tree that entirely bathes it in light, then, in knowing that light, it knows itself. This interpretation would satisfy both the indications Suhrawardi gives us and those of Attar's great epic, in which the thirty birds, the *si-morgh*, discover that they themselves are the eternal Simorgh.

When the disciple asks whether it is true that the Simorgh raised Zal, the Archangel replies by recounting the circumstances of Zal's birth, familiar from the traditions about him. Zal was born with hair completely white. His father, Sam, was horrified and ordered the child to be abandoned in the wilderness. His mother, equally shaken, either could not or did not know how to oppose the order. It was winter, and no one imagined that the child could survive.

After a time, however, his inconsolable mother went in search of her son and found him in that same wilderness. To her amazement, he was still alive.[^EII2-348] By day, the Simorgh sheltered him beneath its wings. By night, a gazelle whose fawn had been taken by hunters came to feed him. What secret lay behind this? The Archangel himself had questioned the Simorgh, and received this answer: “Zal came into the world beneath the gaze of Tuba. We did not allow him to perish.”

*We did not allow him*: that is, the Simorgh and the “Tree” of Tuba, at whose summit the Simorgh has its nest. The symbolism of color immediately helps us sense that the whiteness of the infant Zal's hair marks his descent from the world of beings of light, whose color is white. The “crimson” Archangel himself tells the disciple that in his own world he is pure whiteness. More generally, in the color symbolism of Islamic spiritual philosophy—admirably explained, among others, by Qazi Sa'id Qommi—the closer a being's color is to white, the nearer it is to the spiritual world of Light and the more clearly it belongs there.

As the whiteness diminishes, passing through yellow, orange, red, then green, and finally black, the change marks an increasing distance from that world. The very sign of origin carried in Zal's hair both angers and terrifies his father, as if Sam were someone unable to accept such an origin, or someone frightened by the gravity of its consequences. The child is abandoned in the wilderness, just as the traveler in the *Tale of Western Exile* is thrown to the bottom of a well.

How can a being exiled from the world of Light survive the wilderness and loneliness of this world? How can it avoid the death a soul may suffer through what Plotinus calls “mixture with its opposite”? Yet Zal survives through the watchful care of the Simorgh. We are told that everything which continues to exist in this world does so through the Simorgh. As in the *Tale of Exile*, we encounter the symbolic alternation of day and night, whose meanings may be reversed according to the context (see Chapter VI below).

Here the Simorgh watches over Zal by day because day represents the world of Light, the soul's homeland, of which it retains an intuition and of which initiation will one day make it fully conscious. Night, in this case, represents the world of perception confined to the senses. When the symbolism is reversed, day represents the compelling evidence of sense perception, while awareness of the country beyond Mount Qaf requires the senses to fall asleep, to enter their night—as in the *Tale of Exile* or *The Rustling of Gabriel's Wings*. Here, by contrast, night is the night of the intellect. That is why it is the gazelle that cares for Zal at night: the gazelle represents the living, sensing soul, the *anima sensitiva*.

This “history” is the one human beings have known how to tell themselves—and perhaps still know how to tell—when they understand their past not as something reconstructed from the traces, archaeological or paleontological, of their outward existence, but as something that leads them, in person, back to their origin. That origin is as distant and as near today as it was for their predecessors in the remotest imaginable historical past. The tale, the *hikayat*, is essentially an act of interpretation that brings each teller, anew, to the true meaning of the story *for that person*, and in the same movement to the true meaning of that person's own being. It is an act of interpretation carried out as a sacred recitation.

We shall see this even more clearly in the *Tale of Exile*, where verses from the Quran are themselves “recited” in this way. But we can already glimpse it if we recognize the connection with the ancient Greek romance, whose meaning in the mystery religions Reinhold Merkelbach has worked to uncover through close thematic analysis. The descent of the soul into this world, its captivity here, and its eventual release form the theme of a literature so extensive that, brought together as a single body of works, it would stand as a monument and testimony to the soul's “history.” Suhrawardi's mystical tales, and with them the whole cycle of Persian mystical epic, would belong to it.

The “history” told in all these works is the only history a gnostic can truly tell (see Chapter VI, 1 below): the history of someone who knows where they came from and where they are going. Perhaps few people today can understand it, because it concerns events inaccessible to what we now ordinarily call History. It stands in stark contrast to the spiritually devastated and emptied universe of *homo oeconomicus*, the human being defined by economic life—a universe with no “polar” dimension, no origin and no final spiritual destiny, yet all the more anxious to declare itself “on the right side of history”: a history that is not its own.

We shall consider only two particularly striking examples. First is Longus's romance *Daphnis and Chloe*, which is connected with the mysteries of Dionysus. Daphnis is the initiate, the son of Dionysophanes—that is, of the god himself. His human parents are merely his foster or adoptive parents. The god has “exposed” him in this world, but does not abandon him here: he arranges a miraculous deliverance. He gives him a token of recognition that will one day establish his divine origin. Like Zal, Daphnis is fed by an animal during the time of his abandonment, in his case a goat. Even the little fawn left to the hunters in Suhrawardi's story has a counterpart in Longus: the ram that saves Daphnis and Chloe from danger, and that they sacrifice as the price of their ransom.[^EII2-349]

A second echo of Suhrawardi's story in the Greek romance appears in the work of Heliodorus, probably an Arab living in the third century of the Common Era. This is an initiatory romance associated with the cult of Helios, a solar religion that gathered the religions of the ancient world into itself, just as the romance gathered up what earlier stories had created in honor of Isis or Mithras. In this story, Chariclea, daughter of Hydaspes, king of Ethiopia, is born with an entirely white complexion—the counterpart of the white hair of the infant Zal. We are told that during her pregnancy her mother had gazed upon an image of Andromeda, and her daughter was born in Andromeda's very likeness.

Yet the mother is seized by a fear like that of Sam, Zal's father. Why is this child, whose complexion ought to be dark, unlike the others? Will her legitimacy be challenged? Will mother and daughter be condemned to death? For that reason, her mother, Persina, decides to “expose” her—as Daphnis was exposed, as Zal was “exposed in the wilderness.”

But she does not send the child away without a few treasures, including a cloth embroidered with hieroglyphs: a letter in which the mother reveals the secret of her daughter's origin, commands her never to forget it, and tells her to shape her life accordingly. We shall return later to this image of the “letter.” For now, notice that Andromeda, chained to a rock and seemingly defenseless before the dragon from which Perseus will rescue her, is herself the very image of Psyche, likewise chained to a rock.

Thus Chariclea, a new Andromeda, represents—as does the infant Zal—the fate of every human soul cast into this world and bound here, forgetting its divine ancestry until initiation awakens that knowledge. Its true homeland is the mystical land of the sun, the “East,” and all its striving must be directed toward returning there.[^EII2-350] This is the “East” in Suhrawardi's sense: the destination set before the disciple of the “Crimson Archangel,” and the destination reached at the end of Suhrawardi's *Tale of Western Exile*, just as it is reached at the end of the *Hymn of the Pearl* in the *Acts of Thomas* (see Chapter VI below).

Other examples could surely be cited in which an Iranian hero appears specifically in a Greek initiatory romance.[^EII2-351] But the examples we have placed around the story of Zal's birth already confirm the hidden meaning that Suhrawardi asks the spiritual seeker to discover. They also prepare us to understand the hidden meaning of Esfandiyar's death, the second half of this paired picture.

The protection of the soul cast into the world and the release of that soul are both the work of the Simorgh. Its protection is clear in the episode of Zal's birth. Its work of deliverance is less obvious in the course of Zal's later life, despite the protection it has promised him. Or rather, for Suhrawardi's purpose, even if the Simorgh continues to assist Zal, and even if Zal and his son appear to benefit from that assistance, its true beneficiary is another: the young Esfandiyar, who dies after a heroic battle in a final vision of the Simorgh, a vision the Simorgh itself prepares for him through Zal's intervention.

Above all, we must remember that in mystical language “to perish” always has reference to the other world. One does not “perish” *to* this world, because this world is precisely what it means to “perish” *to the true world*. Just as the Simorgh did not allow the child with the luminous hair to “perish,” it did not allow Esfandiyar to “perish,” although from an outward perspective it might appear otherwise. In truth, the one who perishes is Rostam. This, it seems to us, is Suhrawardi's spiritual interpretation of the episode from the *Shahnameh*.

To understand it, we must recall a little of the traditional story. Throughout his life, Zal retains the protection of the Simorgh. When they parted, it gave him one of its feathers, telling him that in distress or danger he need only burn a portion of it “to see the splendid being appear.” Yet the Zoroastrian religious tradition viewed Zal and his famous son Rostam with some reserve, because neither had been eager to accept Zoroaster's preaching.

By contrast, the young Esfandiyar is the very model of a knight of the Zoroastrian faith. According to the epic tradition, the immediate causes of his death cast something of a shadow upon his father, King Goshtasp (Vishtaspa in Avestan). The king supposedly compelled his son to undertake ever more difficult feats in order to postpone the day when he must fulfill his promise to hand over the throne.[^EII2-352]

Esfandiyar is eventually forced to make an impossible demand of Rostam, who resists the new faith: nothing less than that Rostam submit to being led in chains to the court of King Goshtasp. Rostam tries every possible way of reaching an agreement, but Esfandiyar cannot consent. At last the two heroes agree to settle the war through single combat, whose outcome can only be tragic. The brave Rostam is grieved at having to fight a young hero he admires; the sentiments on both sides remain entirely chivalrous. The battle goes badly for Rostam. He cannot prevail, and, seriously wounded, he is about to die.

Then, according to the epic, his father Zal appeals to the Simorgh. The bird appears, heals Rostam's wounds, and says that an agreement would be best. The Simorgh can certainly make Rostam victorious; but he must know that whoever takes Esfandiyar's life can expect happiness neither in this world nor in the next. Rostam does not consider this price too high. During the night the Simorgh therefore carries Zal to the shores of China, to a tamarisk tree. Following his guide's instructions, Zal cuts off a branch and fashions from it an arrow with two points.

Suhrawardi knew these details of the heroic tradition. Yet his tale now draws upon another source of knowledge: information that the Archangel tells his listener he has received from the Simorgh itself. This new knowledge has the power, by that very fact, to transform the past, to “break open history.” The Simorgh now seems to arrange everything so that Zal, its protégé, can both save his son Rostam from physical death and ensure that Esfandiyar, beneath the appearance of defeat, achieves the triumph of a death in ecstasy.

Through the Simorgh's care, the Iranian hero's story acquires its mystical conclusion. Simply comparing the two accounts allows us to see, almost as it happens, the elevation of meaning accomplished by spiritual interpretation. The heroic tradition says that Esfandiyar was vulnerable only in his eyes. Rostam therefore had to strike him there to inflict a mortal wound. But now that vulnerability takes on a higher meaning: it becomes the vulnerability of inward vision. For there can be an inner vision so overwhelming that it carries the seer out of this life in a supreme *ecstasy*.

Here we should recall the theory of mirrors and forms of manifestation in the “Eastern theosophy,” the philosophy of illumination, where the *Shaykh al-Ishraq* describes what we might call the laws of a spiritual optics—the conditions under which visionary perception becomes possible. Certain surfaces with the properties of mirrors can serve as the place where a form beyond the senses, belonging to the imaginal world, becomes visible (a *mazhar*, a place of manifestation). This does not mean that the form is contained within the mirror. It does not become embodied there; it is not *inside* it. It is present there “in suspension,” as the image of a person appears in a mirror placed before them.

Moreover, this form is perceived not through the external senses but through the imaginative faculty.[^EII2-353] Seen in this light, the details reported by the Archangel—those that explain the precautions Zal takes—become clear. The Simorgh possesses this power: if a mirror, or some other polished surface, is held directly before it, every “eye” that looks into the mirror is dazzled. (Recall Kay Khosrow holding the Grail, the mirror of the universe, toward the sun at the spring equinox, the season when the hoopoe takes flight to become a Simorgh.) This is why Zal dresses his son Rostam in shining armor and a gleaming helmet, and covers his horse completely with pieces of mirror.

When Esfandiyar necessarily comes face to face with Rostam in battle, the Simorgh's rays strike the armor and mirrors and are reflected into Esfandiyar's eyes, dazzling him. The two points of the tamarisk arrow wound his eyes mortally. He believes his eyes have been wounded because he has seen the arrow's two points. But what Esfandiyar actually sees with his inner sight is the two wings of the Simorgh.

We find ourselves once again in the situation encountered at the end of the “Tale of the Grail,” and to be encountered at the end of the next tale when its author exclaims, “It is I whom this story is about.” This is the situation of the *hikayat*, the mystical recitation, in which the deed recounted, the hero whose deed it is, and the person who recounts it form a threefold unity—one reality. More precisely, this unity is brought to completion at the end of the tale, when the Archangel tells his disciple: “If you are Khezr, then you too can cross Mount Qaf.”

In that case, the initiate *is* the story being told. That person is one of the many Simorghs mentioned in our tale, just as each is one of the thirty birds, the *si-morgh*, in Attar's magnificent epic. This reveals the mystical meaning of Esfandiyar's death. The Simorgh that nests in the Tree of Tuba at the summit of Mount Qaf is the divine Face as it appears to the human being; at the same time, it is that human being's own imperishable Face, the *Iman* or Angel of their being.

In this meeting face to face, the two Faces reflect one another and answer one another. A human being may glimpse this vision in advance, but cannot go beyond it without crossing the threshold. For certain apparitions always announce that the other world is near: “Whoever sees me bids farewell to the daylight of this life. You have seen the burning gaze of the Valkyrie. Now you must depart with her.”[^EII2-354]

In this central episode of *The Tale of the Crimson Archangel*, the heroic epic of Iran reaches its fulfillment as a mystical epic. This is entirely in keeping with the purpose of the *Shaykh al-Ishraq*'s “Eastern theosophy”—not only the work to which he devoted his life, but the meaning that the philosophy of *Ishraq* was to have for the whole spiritual life of Islamic Iran. In the opening chapters of this second book, we described Suhrawardi's undertaking as a return of the so-called “Hellenized” Magi to their original homeland, Iran—but an Iran that had, in the meantime, heard the call of the Prophet of Islam.

The completion of Iran's heroic epic as a mystical epic is thus one aspect of the transformation through which the wisdom of the sages of ancient Persia passes, so that it can find itself at home once again in the Persia of Suhrawardi and his successors. For Zoroastrian tradition, Esfandiyar's death was the work of Ahriman's demonic powers, acting through those who resisted the faith of Zoroaster. Now the spiritual interpretation—the *ta'wil*—of an Iranian Muslim mystic drives out Ahriman's demons, rescues the heroes from their grasp, and gives Esfandiyar's death the meaning our tale suggests.

One of our earlier publications was illustrated with an extraordinary image published some twenty years ago by Gaston Wiet. It is woven into a silk textile found in 1925 in a tomb near Tehran, perfectly preserved. What makes it especially fascinating is that a motif in the Sasanian style appears on a textile from the early Islamic period, forming an artistic link between ancient and Islamic Persia. A young man, his royal hair forming something like a halo, is being carried aloft by a great fantastic bird that holds him against its breast. Certain stylized details suggest that the bird is not simply a two-headed eagle, but the Anqa (phoenix) or Simorgh. We naturally think of Zal, son of Sam, carried away and nourished by the Simorgh.

Yet an image remains an image, and its meanings are inexhaustible for anyone who meditates on it, because they extend beyond the conscious intentions of the artist who made it. We have therefore suggested that one may discern in it a theme of individual destiny beyond death, well known in Islamic mysticism. In the present context, the Simorgh's intervention at the end of Esfandiyar's earthly life invites us to see in the Iranian artist's solemn image of ascent into heaven the fate of the hero whom the Simorgh bears skyward in a movement of apotheosis.[^EII2-355]

The purpose of the preceding pages has been to lead us to a translation of *The Tale of the Crimson Archangel*, which we can now offer without adding further notes. Our interpretation, of course, has by no means exhausted the tale's possible meanings.

But symbols cannot be “refuted.” Either we understand them or we do not. Different interpretations merely occupy different levels of understanding. Each reader must choose the level at which to stand.

##### 5. Translation of “The Tale of the Crimson Archangel”

> Glory be to Him who holds sovereign power over the two worlds. All that has been existed through His existence; all that is exists through His existence; all that will be shall exist through His existence. He is the First and the Last, the Manifest and the Hidden, and He sees all things. May prayers and blessings be upon His Messengers to His creatures, and especially upon Muhammad the Chosen One, through whom the seal was set upon Prophecy. Peace be upon his Companions and the learned teachers of religion, and may divine favor rest upon them all!
>
> One day, one of my dearest friends asked me, ‘Do birds understand one another's language?’
>
> ‘Certainly,’ I answered, ‘they do.’
>
> ‘How did you come to know that?’ my friend asked.
>
> ‘At the beginning of things, when the One who is the Maker in the truest sense wished to bring my as yet nonexistent being into existence, He created me in the form of a falcon. In the country where I then lived, there were other falcons. We spoke with one another, listened to one another's words, and understood one another perfectly.’
>
> ‘Very well,’ my friend said, ‘but how did things come to be as they are now?’
>
> ‘This is what happened. One day the hunters Decree and Destiny spread the net of Predestination. They baited it with a grain of attraction, and by this means they caught me. They carried me away from the country that had been my nest and took me to a distant land. They sewed my eyelids shut, fastened four different kinds of fetters around me, and set ten jailers to guard me. Five faced me, with their backs turned outward; the other five stood back to back with me, their faces turned away. The five whose faces were turned toward me kept me so deeply in a world of bewildered forgetfulness that I forgot my own nest, the distant country, and everything I had known there. I imagined that I had always been as I had now become.
>
> ‘After some time had passed, my eyes began to open a little, and I started to look about as far as my sight would allow. Once more I began to see things I had ceased to see, and I was filled with wonder. Each day my eyes opened a little farther, and I beheld things that astonished me. At last my eyes opened completely, and the world appeared to me as it truly was. I saw the bonds fastened around me; I saw myself held prisoner by my jailers. And I said to myself: “It seems these four fetters will never be taken off me, nor these jailers sent away, so that I might unfold my wings and fly, if only for a moment, free of every constraint.”
>
> ‘More time passed. Then one day I noticed that my jailers had relaxed their watch. “I shall never find a better opportunity,” I thought. I slipped stealthily away, and, limping along in my fetters, finally reached the road into the wilderness. There in the wilderness I saw a figure coming toward me. I went forward to meet this person and offered a greeting, which was returned with exquisite grace and courtesy. Seeing the brilliant red that suffused the stranger's face and hair, I thought I was in the presence of a young man.
>
> ‘Young man,’ I said, ‘where do you come from?’
>
> ‘Child,’ came the answer, ‘you are mistaken to address me like that. I am the eldest of the Creator's children, and you call me a young man?’
>
> ‘Then how is it that your hair has not turned white, as happens to the old?’
>
> ‘White is what I truly am. I am exceedingly ancient, a Sage whose very essence is light. But the one who captured you in the net, who bound you in all those fetters and appointed those jailers to watch you, long ago cast me too into the Dark Well. That is why you see me clothed in this crimson color. Otherwise I am entirely white, entirely luminous. Whenever something white, whose whiteness belongs to the light, is mingled with black, it takes on a reddish glow.
>
> Consider dusk and dawn. Both are white by their connection with sunlight, yet both lie between two conditions: on one side the day, which is white; on the other, the night, which is black. That is why morning and evening twilight glow crimson.
>
> Consider the moon when it rises. Although its light is borrowed, it is truly clothed in light; yet one of its faces is turned toward day, the other toward night. And so the moon appears red. Even an ordinary lamp shows the same principle. At the base its flame is white; above, it rises into black smoke; midway between, it glows red. Many other comparisons and examples could be offered to show the same law.’
>
> ‘Sage,’ I asked this time, ‘where do you come from?’
>
> ‘I come from beyond Mount Qaf. That is my home. Your own nest was once there too. Alas, you have forgotten it.’
>
> ‘And what do you do here?’
>
> ‘I am a pilgrim without rest. I travel continually around the world and contemplate its wonders.’
>
> ‘What wonders have you seen in the world?’
>
> ‘Seven wonders, to be precise. The first is Mount Qaf, your homeland and mine. The second is the Jewel That Illumines the Night. The third is the Tree of Tuba. The fourth is the twelve workshops. The fifth is David's Coat of Mail. The sixth is the Indian Sword. The seventh is the Fountain of Life.’
>
> ‘Please tell me the story of them all.’
>
> ‘First, then, there is Mount Qaf. It rises all around the world and encircles it completely; in fact, it consists of eleven mountains. That is where you will go when you have freed yourself from your bonds, for it is from there that you were taken long ago, and every being eventually returns to its original form.’
>
> ‘But how can I travel the road to that place?’ I asked.
>
> ‘The road is difficult indeed. First come two mountains, each already part of Mount Qaf. One has a hot climate, the other a cold one, and neither the heat of the first nor the cold of the second has any limit.’
>
> ‘But isn't it simple? I'll cross the hot mountain in winter and the cold mountain in summer.’
>
> ‘Unfortunately, you are mistaken. The conditions in those regions improve in no season.’
>
> ‘How far away are these mountains?’ I asked.
>
> ‘However far you travel, however long you journey, you will arrive again at your starting point. Think of a compass with one point resting at the center of a circle and the other tracing its circumference. However long it turns, it only comes back to the place from which it began.’
>
> ‘Perhaps a tunnel could be dug through these mountains, so that one could emerge on the other side?’
>
> ‘It is equally impossible to tunnel through them. But anyone who possesses the necessary Aptitude can cross them in a single instant, without digging a tunnel at all. The power resembles that of balm. If you hold the palm of your hand toward the sun long enough for it to grow hot, then pour drops of balm into your palm, the balm will pass through to the back of your hand by virtue of a natural property within it. In the same way, if you bring to life within yourself the natural power capable of crossing these mountains, you will cross both of them in an instant.’
>
> ‘How can I awaken this power within myself?’
>
> ‘I shall give you a hint, if you are able to understand it.’
>
> ‘And once I have crossed these two mountains, will it be easy or difficult to cross the others?’
>
> ‘Easy enough, provided you know how. Some remain prisoners forever within those two mountains. Others reach the third and stay there. Some reach the fourth, others the fifth, and so on up to the eleventh. The more intelligent the bird, the farther it travels.’
>
> ‘Now that you have explained Mount Qaf to me,’ I said, ‘please tell me the story of the Jewel That Illumines the Night.’
>
> ‘The Jewel That Illumines the Night,’ the Sage explained, ‘is also found in Mount Qaf—more precisely, in the third mountain. It is because the Jewel exists that the dark night becomes radiant.
>
> But the Jewel does not remain unchanged in its appearance. Its light comes from the Tree of Tuba. Whenever it stands “opposite” the Tree of Tuba, as seen from the region where you yourself are situated, the Jewel appears wholly luminous, like a shining globe. When it is no longer directly opposite the tree, but has moved closer to it, a portion of its shining disk appears dark to you, while the rest continues to glow. And the nearer it comes to the Tree of Tuba, the more the shadow spreads across its luminous part—always, of course, as seen from your own position.
>
> For the hemisphere facing the Tree of Tuba remains constantly illuminated. When the Jewel is nearest the tree, it seems to you to be completely dark, while on the side facing Tuba it is all light. Conversely, as it moves away from the tree, it begins to shine for you again—that is, when viewed from your side. And the farther it moves away, the greater its light appears to you. This does not mean the light itself is increasing; rather, more of the Jewel's surface becomes able to hold and display the light, while the region of shadow grows smaller. This continues until the Jewel again stands opposite the Tree of Tuba—that is, at its greatest distance from it. At that moment the entire body of the Jewel holds the Light for itself.’
>
> ![Fig. 1](data:image/png;base64,)
>
> *Fig. 1. *
>
> ‘An analogy will help you understand. Make a hole straight through a small sphere along its diameter, and pass a marker through the hole. Then fill a bowl with water and place the sphere at the surface, so that half of it is submerged. Suppose that, at a given moment, the water has covered every part of the little sphere ten times over as the sphere turns on itself. If someone has watched it from underneath the bowl, that person will have continually seen half the sphere submerged in water. Now suppose the observer, at first looking from directly beneath the bowl's central axis, gradually looks at it from an angle.
>
> The observer will no longer see the entire submerged hemisphere, because the farther the line of sight moves from that axis, the less of the hemisphere remains directly opposite the observer's gaze. At the same time, the observer will begin to see part of the sphere above the water. The more the gaze moves upward toward the level of the water in the bowl, the less of the submerged sphere will be visible, and the more of the part above the water will come into view. When the observer looks from exactly the level of the water, one hemisphere will be seen below the water and the other above it.
