If the gaze then moves progressively above the waterline, an ever larger portion of the sphere will appear out of the water.
>
> Finally, when the observer looks down along the bowl's central axis, the whole sphere will be visible—and visible entirely above the water. Someone may object that, looking from beneath the bowl, they could see neither the water nor the sphere. Indeed they could, we reply, provided that the bowl were made of glass or of something still more transparent. In our example of the bowl and the little sphere, it is the observer who moves around them in order to see them from different positions. But with the Jewel That Illumines the Night and the Tree of Tuba, it is they that revolve in a similar fashion around the person observing them.’
>
> ![Fig. 2](data:image/png;base64,)
>
> *Fig. 2. *
>
> — What, then, is the Tree of Tuba? I asked the Sage.
>
> — The Tree of Tuba is an immense tree. Whoever is at home in Paradise sees this tree whenever they walk there. At the heart of the eleven mountains I have told you about, there is a particular mountain. The Tree of Tuba stands within it.
>
> — Does it bear no fruit?
>
> — All the fruits you see in the world grow upon this tree. The fruits before your eyes are themselves among its fruits. If this Tree did not exist, you would never see a fruit, a tree, a flower, or a plant before you.
>
> — What connection, then, do fruits, trees, and flowers have with this tree?
>
> — Sîmorgh has her nest at the summit of the Tûbâ tree. At dawn she leaves her nest and spreads her wings over the earth. It is through the influence of her wings that fruit appears on the trees and plants spring up from the ground.
>
> — I have heard it said, I told him, that Sîmorgh raised Zâl, and that it was with Sîmorgh's help that Rustam killed Esfandyâr.
>
> — Yes, that is true.
>
> — How did it happen?
>
> — When Zâl came into the world from his mother's womb, his hair was entirely white, and so was his face. His father, Sâm, ordered that he be taken into the wilderness and abandoned there. His mother, too, was deeply distressed at having given birth to him. Seeing how repellent her son appeared, she consented to the order. So Zâl was left in the wilderness. It was winter, and it was cold. No one imagined the child could survive for long. Several days passed. His mother's resentment faded, and pity for her child stirred in her heart.
>
> “I shall go into the wilderness,” she said to herself. “I must see what has become of my child.” When she arrived, she found him still alive: Sîmorgh had sheltered him beneath her wings. When the child's eyes met his mother's, he smiled at her. She took him to her breast and nursed him. She wanted to carry him home, but then thought: “No. Until I know how Zâl has managed to stay alive all these days, I shall not go home.”
>
> So she left little Zâl where he was, beneath Sîmorgh's wing, and hid nearby. When night fell and Sîmorgh flew away from the wilderness, a gazelle came to where Zâl lay and pressed her breast to the infant's lips. After he had drunk her milk, she fell asleep beside him, keeping him safe from harm. Then his mother rose, gently moved the gazelle away, and carried her son home.
>
> — What secret lay behind this? I asked the Sage.
>
> — I myself questioned Sîmorgh about it, he answered, and this is what she told me: “Zâl came into the earthly world under the gaze of Tûbâ. We did not allow him to perish. We gave the fawn into the hunter's power, and placed compassion for Zâl in the heart of the gazelle, its mother, so that she would care for him and feed him with her milk. By day, I myself held him beneath my wing.”
>
> — And what of Rustam and Esfandyâr?
>
> — This is what happened. Rustam had not been strong enough to defeat Esfandyâr and had returned home exhausted. His father, Zâl, implored Sîmorgh for help. Now Sîmorgh has this natural power: if a mirror, or anything that serves as one, is held directly before her, anyone who looks into it is dazzled. Zâl had an iron breastplate made, with every part of its surface polished to a perfect shine, and dressed Rustam in it. He also placed a brilliantly polished helmet on Rustam's head and fixed pieces of mirror to his horse.
>
> Then he sent Rustam into the arena to stand directly facing Sîmorgh. Esfandyâr was bound to come forward to meet Rustam. As he approached, Sîmorgh's rays struck the breastplate and mirrors and flashed back into Esfandyâr's eyes. He was blinded by the glare; he could see nothing. Having glimpsed two sharp points, he imagined that both his eyes had been wounded. He fell from his horse and died at Rustam's hand. We may suppose that the two points of the arrow made from *gâz* wood, of which the stories speak, were in truth the two wings of Sîmorgh.
>
> ![Fig. 3](data:image/png;base64,)
>
> *Fig. 3.*
>
> — Do you mean, I asked the Sage, that only one Sîmorgh has ever existed in the whole universe?
>
> — No. Only someone who does not know would mistakenly think so. If a new Sîmorgh did not continually descend from the Tûbâ tree to the earth as the one already on earth disappeared—if a new Sîmorgh were not constantly arriving—nothing that exists here could endure. And just as Sîmorgh comes down to the earth, she also goes from the Tûbâ tree to the twelve workshops.
>
> — O Sage, I exclaimed, what are these twelve workshops?
>
> — First, you must know that when our King wished to set his kingdom in order, he began with our own land. Then he set us to work. He established twelve workshops, placing a number of apprentices in each. He put these apprentices to work as well, and beneath the first twelve workshops another workshop came into being. Over it our King appointed a Master (*ostâd*). He gave this Master his own particular task, and in carrying it out the Master brought another workshop into being beneath the first.
>
> Over this, in turn, the King set a second Master to work. Beneath the second workshop another appeared, entrusted to a third Master, and so it continued until there were seven workshops, each with its own appointed Master. Then the King gave a robe of honour to every apprentice in the twelve Houses. He also gave a robe of honour to the first Master and entrusted to him two of the twelve upper workshops.
>
> The second Master likewise received a robe of honour and two more of the twelve workshops. The same was done for the third. To the fourth Master the King gave the most beautiful robe of honour of all. He entrusted only one of the twelve upper workshops to him, but ordered him to keep watch over all twelve. To the fifth and sixth Masters he gave gifts equal to those received by the second and third respectively.
>
> By the time the seventh Master's turn came, only one of the twelve workshops was left. It was given to him, but he received no robe of honour. The seventh Master protested loudly. “Every other Master has two workshops, and I have only one. All of them were given robes of honour, and I was given none!” He was told that two workshops would be established beneath his own and that he would be given authority over them.
>
> And beneath all the workshops together, a field was laid out for sowing, whose care was also entrusted to this seventh Master. It was further decreed that the beautiful robe of the fourth Master would continually yield a smaller, already-worn robe for the seventh: at every moment the robe of one would in its turn become the robe of the other, just as I explained to you in speaking of Sîmorgh.
>
> — O Sage, I persisted, what is woven in these workshops?
>
> — Brocade, above all. But they also weave every kind of thing that no one has yet conceived. It is in these workshops, too, that David's coat of mail is woven.
>
> — O Sage, what is David's coat of mail?
>
> — It is the many bonds that have been fastened around you.
>
> — How is it made?
>
> — Each of the four groups of three among the twelve upper workshops produces one ring, so their combined work yields four rings. But the process does not end there. The four rings are brought to the seventh Master, who must work upon each of them. Once they are in his hands, he sends them into the field he cultivates, and there they remain for a time, unfinished. Then the four rings are linked together, forming a hard, close-woven fabric. A falcon such as you is captured, and this coat of mail is thrown over him until it encloses him completely.
>
> — How many rings are there in each coat of mail? I asked.
>
> — If you could count the drops of water in the Sea of Oman, you could count the rings in a single coat of mail.
>
> — But is there any way to be freed from it?
>
> — By the Indian Sword.
>
> — And where can that Sword be found?
>
> — In our country there is an executioner who carries it. The rule is that when a coat of mail has served its purpose for a certain span of time, and that time has run out, the executioner strikes it with his Sword. The blow breaks every ring apart and scatters them all.
>
> — Does the person wearing the coat of mail experience that blow differently from others?
>
> — There are indeed differences. For some, the blow is such that even if they had lived a hundred years and spent their whole lives considering the worst pain imaginable, whatever torments their minds might have pictured would never have approached the violence of the Sword's stroke. Others bear the blow more easily.
>
> — O Sage, I beg you, what must I do to make that suffering easier to bear?
>
> — Find the Spring of Life. Let its waters flow over your head in abundance until this coat of mail, instead of binding you tightly, becomes no more than a garment hanging freely and lightly about you. Then the Sword's blow will not harm you. For this Water softens the coat of mail (see Qur'an 34:10), and once the mail has become completely supple, the blow of the Sword no longer causes pain.
>
> — O Sage, where is this Spring of Life?
>
> — In the Darkness. If you wish to set out in search of it, put on the sandals worn by Khezr (Khadir) the Prophet, and follow the path of trusting surrender until you reach the land of Darkness.
>
> — In which direction does the path lie?
>
> — Whichever way you go, if you are a true pilgrim, you will complete the journey.
>
> — What marks the land of Darkness?
>
> — Becoming aware of the darkness. You yourself are already in Darkness, but you do not know it. When someone setting out on this path sees that he himself is in Darkness, he has understood that he was in the Night all along, and that the light of Day has never yet reached his eyes. This is the first step taken by true pilgrims. Only from this point can the ascent begin. If someone reaches this stage, then—yes—he may perhaps advance. Whoever searches for the Spring of Life within the darkness passes through bewilderment and many kinds of distress.
>
> But if he is worthy of finding that Spring, he will at last behold the Light beyond the Darkness. He must not flee from it, for this Light is a radiance descending from the heights of Heaven upon the Spring of Life. If he has made the journey and bathed in that Spring, the Sword's blow can no longer wound him. As Sanâ'î says in these verses:
>
> > Let the Sword of Love strike and wound you  
> > That you may find eternal life;  
> > For from the Sword of the Angel of Death  
> > None returns to speak of rising again.
>
> Whoever bathes in that Spring will never again be defiled. Whoever has found the meaning of True Reality has reached that Spring. When he emerges from it, he has acquired a power like that of the balm of which you place a drop in the hollow of your hand, holding it toward the sun, and which then passes right through to the back of your hand. If you are Khezr, you too can pass through Mount Qâf without difficulty.
>
> … When I had recounted these events to the dear friend who had asked me to tell him of them, he exclaimed: “So that is what you are: a falcon once caught in the net, who now goes out hunting prey. Well then, catch me! Tied to the straps of the hunter's saddle, I shall make no poor prize.”
>
> *Yes, I am that falcon whom the hunters of this world*  
> *Need at every moment.*  
> *My quarry is the dark-eyed gazelles,*  
> *For Wisdom is like the tears that seep between the eyelids.*  
> *Before me, people flee the literal sense of words;*  
> *With me, they learn to gather their hidden meaning.*

### CHAPTER VI

#### “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

##### I. The History of the Gnostic

As we have already suggested, this tale is closely connected with the one before it. “The Tale of the Crimson Archangel” ends with a condition: “If you are Khezr, you too can cross Mount Qâf”—that is, you can reach the Spring of Life. “The Tale of the Western Exile” removes the uncertainty. The spiritual seeker will prove capable of joining Khezr at the Spring of Life; or, more precisely, he will undertake Khezr's quest again, in the first person.

But the setting has changed completely. There is no longer any direct reference to the heroic epic of Iran. As we have just seen, that epic has already found its fulfilment in an epic of mystical gnosis. Now it is the gnostic himself who will *live out* his own story. He will fulfil the conditions of the threefold unity of the *hikâyat*, the mystical tale or recital, which we encountered earlier. Everything we learn in the course of the tale shows its hero to be a representative figure of mystical gnosis in Islam.

The title itself is remarkably suggestive. The founding of “Eastern theosophy” is answered by “The Tale of the Western Exile.” The entire “history” of the gnostic is contained in the tension between these two terms. It really is a history, though not history in the ordinary sense of the word—the sense usually invoked when people contrast a Christian feeling for salvation as a historical event with the Greek philosophers' understanding of the world. It is precisely because this opposition is too crude that so many judgments about gnosis miss its true nature entirely. We sometimes hear that the gnostic “flees” the world and therefore goes against “the direction of history.”

But such a judgment simply assumes what it needs to prove. To rest content with it is to presume that the very question under dispute has already been settled: what does the “phenomenon of the world” itself mean? Yet it is precisely this question that motivates the challenge voiced by gnosis. The person who feels like a stranger in this world is someone who has awakened to the knowledge that his origin and his ultimate destination lie elsewhere.

To feel entirely “at home” in this world is, for all forms of gnosis, the tragedy itself. Whoever accuses gnosis of fleeing the world would do better to say openly that he, for his part, does not believe in that *elsewhere*. And whoever accuses it of moving against “the direction of history” deliberately overlooks the gnostic's own “history.” Others claim that gnosis merely adds truths *known* to the truths *believed*. Sohrawardî's “Tale of the Exile” is enough to expose the mistake in that way of seeing things.

We have already stressed the three degrees of certainty: knowledge or theoretical certainty (*'ilm al-yaqîn*); the certainty of an eyewitness (*'ayn al-yaqîn*); and the certainty of someone who experiences the reality of what he knows because it actually takes place within him (*haqq al-yaqîn*). It is this third degree that characterizes gnostic truth. That is why the Qur'anic verses, brought by spiritual interpretation to the level of *haqq al-yaqîn*, will mark the stages of the homeward journey in this tale. A parallel could be drawn here with the spiritual interpretation practised by gnostic traditions outside Islam.

All this is far removed from the image of gnosis held by its present-day opponents, and much closer to its authentic, fundamental meaning. When the study of the texts has advanced far enough, a systematic examination of the affinities among the gnostic traditions of the “religions of the Book” will become essential (we have already alluded to this in Book I). These affinities will need to be studied until the outlines of lost continents come into view.

For now, we cannot insist strongly enough on the importance of the summaries H.-C. Puech has already published of his lectures on “Esoteric Doctrines and Gnostic Themes in the Gospel According to Thomas.”[^EII2-356] From these unusually rich and concentrated summaries, several themes emerge whose counterparts or variations can readily be found in Islamic gnosis—and, in their essentials, in the present “Tale of the Exile.” Central to them all is the theme of the “Angel,” already approached here in connection with the psalm addressed to “Perfect Nature.”

Puech's detailed analyses allow us to identify the following sequence of themes.

1) Consider the simple statement “I know myself” as it appears in gnostic writings. Its analysis leads to a fundamental distinction between the “I” that is the knowing subject and the “self” that is the object known or recognized. The first is the self I experience in everyday life, immediately, within the world I perceive through my senses: the self exposed to the demands of this world of appearances, which largely directs and determines it. The second is what I am beyond appearances and the contingent conditions of the world of coming-into-being (*genesis*). This is my real, authentic, essential self—substantial and enduring. Inward knowledge may indeed reveal it to me as if it were within me. Yet at the same time it is perceived not as a fantasy, but as something objectively real, “a being that exists and abides in itself.” It would, in fact, be better to speak of the *Self* than of the *ego*: this is our eternal archetype, “ourselves in our eternity.”[^EII2-357] Its reality is so objective that it is experienced as the “personal angel,” the “person of light,” the “personal Guide”; or it may be represented by a garment of heavenly origin, or by an image, an icon (*eikôn*), a Double or “heavenly Twin.”

We have repeatedly encountered here the saying: “Whoever knows himself [his ‘soul,’ *nafsa-ho*] knows his Lord,” together with its variations: “Whoever knows himself knows his Imam. Whoever knows his Imam knows his Lord.” The spiritual masters of Islam have meditated on this saying, turning it over and over in every possible way; we have given examples. The relationship between the reflexive *nafs* (oneself, one's soul) and the subject pronoun *man* (the one who knows) corresponds exactly to the relationship between the knowing “I” and the “self” that is known or recognized in Puech's analysis.

The correspondence is so close that in Shiite gnosis the Imam can take the place of the Self and perform the function of the “personal angel” in ancient gnosis. In Sohrawardî, this Self is represented by “Perfect Nature,” or by the initiating Angel encountered in his tales. We have already noted that for Sohrawardî and the Ishrâqîyûn—the philosophers of Eastern wisdom—the vision of “Perfect Nature” is bound up with the mystical story of Hermes.

Other Sufi masters, Najmoddîn Kobrâ for example, speak of the “Witness in Heaven,” the Guide or “invisible master.”[^EII2-358] The “person of light” (*phôteinos anthrôpos*) in the Gospel According to Thomas, and the “Light-Self” or “Living Self” of Manichaean texts, have their exact counterparts in Najmoddîn Kobrâ and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî: *shakhs min nûr*, *shakhs nûrânî*.[^EII2-359] The Ismailis know of a “form of light” that joins itself to the initiate at the moment of initiation.[^EII2-360] The “Perfect Human Being” (*Anthrôpos teleios*) is the *Insân al-Kâmil*, and so forth.

2) Self-knowledge leads to union—or rather reunion—between the apparent self (the “I” that knows) and the transcendent Self. It means becoming again “what I am, and have never ceased to be, within myself.” Yet it seems wrong to speak here of a fusion in which the two become indistinguishable. Moreover, their meeting requires more than an act of reflection: it requires a *return*. The heavenly Self retains its objective reality, like the mirror before me in which I come to know and recognize myself.[^EII2-361]

Since the mirror reveals my true “face” to me, to break it would destroy the very union it makes possible. There would be no “face” left, no knowledge “face to face.” This is also what emerges in the gnosis of the Imams from the theme of the Imam as the Face of God turned toward humanity and the Face of humanity turned toward God. The theme of *return* is essentially the theme of the birds' journey in 'Attâr, of exile in Sohrawardî's tale, and more generally of the “four spiritual journeys” in Islamic gnosis.

The theme of the *mirror* embraces the whole mystery of Sîmorgh: the eternal Sîmorgh persists, yet so do the *sî-morgh*, the thirty birds. The hoopoe herself may become a Sîmorgh, while the eternal Sîmorgh remains. In Sohrawardî's tales, the relationship between the Self of light and the lower self is expressed above all through the “two wings of the angel Gabriel”: one wing of light, and the other not exactly a wing of darkness but a wing darkened, tinged with the reddish glow of evening twilight.[^EII2-362] Every human being reflects the image of the Angel of humanity.

To free the “left wing” from darkness is not to destroy it, but to make it a wing of light once more, itself reflecting the luminous right wing. The soul as image or icon of the Angel, and the Angel as icon of the soul, is a familiar theme of Valentinian gnosis. In Sohrawardî, Perfect Nature is at once the “father” and the “child” in the spiritual world. The original relationship established by Eastern theosophy between the first lover and the first Beloved could not be abolished without abolishing the fundamental law of being, and of every being. This, as we have seen, is the meaning that Ishrâqî gnosis gives to the Qur'anic verse: “We have created all things in pairs” (51:49).[^EII2-363]

3) There is also the theme of the *personal pleroma*. For each spiritual seeker, his “angel”—the ideal reality corresponding to his transcendent Self—is his own *pleroma*, his particular fullness of being: the form of everything he is, which defines him as an individual in the complete realization of his own existence. Every such individual fullness belongs within the universal Pleroma, the fullness of the spiritual world. “To know the pleroma within oneself” and “to know oneself within the pleroma” are two ways of saying the same thing. The Angel is our pleroma: our being in its fullness.[^EII2-364]

This idea of an individual pleroma also follows from the relationship between the gnostic and his Perfect Nature. Their relationship exists within the pleroma of the angel Gabriel, the Angel of humanity (*rabb al-nû' al-insânî*), while Perfect Nature is, in turn, the angel present to each individual. This resolves the hesitation that sometimes appears among commentators as to whether the figure in question is the Angel of humanity or Perfect Nature. More than this, the dialogue between Constantine, son of Luke (Qostâ ibn Lûqâ), and his disciple 'Amalaq the Greek (see above, III, 5) may serve as an illustration of this relationship; compare also the “Personal City” discussed below in §5.

4) Closely linked to this is the theme of *spiritual ancestry*. Gnosis is knowledge that saves because it saves the person by revealing his origin. Knowing *what* one is and *who* one is cannot be separated from knowing *where* one comes from and *through whom* one exists. To know his lineage, his descent, his family is, for the gnostic, to know his true homeland: to know what he was and where he was, and to recognize the order of beings to which he belongs. In the Gospel According to Thomas, to know oneself is, by that very fact, to know that one is a “son of the living Father.”[^EII2-365]

We find all this, point for point, in Islamic gnosis. To take only “The Tale of the Western Exile,” the revelation of spiritual ancestry that drives the entire drama appears at the outset and returns solemnly at the end. The exile is the son of *shaykh al-Hâdî ibn al-Khayr*, the Yemeni.

We shall see later that this name designates the Active Intelligence, the Holy Spirit, the Angel of humanity. At the close of the tale, the Angel himself reveals to the exile, his “son,” that they share a whole succession of “ancestors.” This ancestral line is none other than the hierarchy of Angels or Intelligences in Islamic Neoplatonism and Ismaili gnosis. Here, too, we encounter the Neoplatonic idea of series or “chains” of souls proceeding from one of the gods. Proclus, we know, considered himself to belong to the “chain” of Hermes.[^EII2-366] The brothers whose family the exile belongs to in Sohrawardî's tale are represented by the “fish” playing in the “Spring of Life,” after passing through an ordeal like his own.

5) That ordeal tore them from their origin and must end with their return to it: their return “home.” Saying 49 of the Gospel According to Thomas declares: “You will find the Kingdom, for you came from it, and to it you will return.” This implies that whoever knows his beginning also knows his end, because “to discover the beginning and to discover the end are one,” since “where the beginning is, there the end will be” (Saying 18). Gnosis is precisely what reveals this identity of beginning and end, meeting at a single point.[^EII2-367]

This is the very theme of Sohrawardî's “Tale of the Exile”: “It is I who am the subject of this story; I have undergone a catastrophe.” Fallen from the world of light, from the world above or the Beyond, the exile lies imprisoned at the bottom of a well in the western city of Qayrawân, bound in iron chains.

The place to which he must return is the place from which he came. We have already quoted the command in the “Epistle of the High Towers” (*Risâlat al-abraj*): “When you are told, ‘Return,’ this implies that there is a place where you were present before. And woe to you if you take the place of return to mean Damascus, Baghdad, or some other homeland in this world!” This is, moreover, one of the central themes of Islamic gnosis, expressed through the “two arcs” of descent (*nozûl*) and ascent (*so'ûd*), the place of origin (*mabda'*) and the place of return (*ma'âd*).

The idea that the end is reached by returning to the beginning—as in the movement of the compass to which Sohrawardî referred in the preceding tale—also corresponds to the Shiite theosophical understanding of the cycle of prophecy as a cycle of descent and the cycle of the Imamate as a cycle of ascent (see Book I above). An understanding of history as a circle that closes upon itself, while offering access at every moment to a reality beyond history, necessarily belongs with the idea of preexistence. Preexistence guarantees salvation because it guarantees continuity of being on a plane higher than this world of exile and the fall.

6) The theme of *certainty*: gnosis assures the spiritual seeker that he will be saved from his present situation, and indeed cannot fail to be saved, because in truth he is already saved, here and now and for ever, since his origin and his destination are one.[^EII2-368]

This is exactly the twofold assurance of salvation that the Angel communicates, at the end of “The Tale of the Exile,” to the exile who has found his way back to him. He is saved now—so completely saved already that, until his final return, he will be able to revisit the mystical Sinai whenever he wishes, borne there by ecstatic contemplation of the heavenly symbols.

7) The theme of *preexistence* stands in relation to the theme of the Angel or of self-knowledge rather as the “answer” stands in relation to the “subject” in a musical fugue. It, too, receives an answer in turn: a certainty. Saying 19 of the Gospel According to Thomas declares: “Blessed is the one who was before coming into being.” Its answer is found in the Gospel According to Philip: “For he who is, has been and will be.” These sayings from our gnostic Gospels deserve to be inscribed in letters of gold in the ideal “Book” shared by all the gnostic traditions of the “religions of the Book.” “Preexistence implies the perpetuity of existence, permanence in Being.” To exist before becoming, to have existed before entering the world, the flesh, and chronological time: this “grounds the certainty of being, of never having ceased to be and of never ceasing to be oneself, beyond time as well as before it.”[^EII2-369] It is the certainty, we would say, that one is oneself a history which breaks open history in the ordinary sense of that word, because it is a history beyond history.

The idea of preexistence is explicit in Sohrawardî's mystical tales. It is affirmed at the beginning of “The Tale of the Crimson Archangel” and both at the beginning and at the end of “The Tale of the Exile.” Admittedly, Sohrawardî's major systematic treatises sometimes show a certain ambiguity on this point, much to the irritation of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. A particular passage near the end of the Physics of the “Book of Crossroads and Conversations” (*Mashârï wa Motârahât*) might leave us uncertain.

But we should note that these are precisely the outward, or exoteric, treatises; the inward, or esoteric, treatises written in the form of symbolic comparisons leave us in no doubt. We should add that the theme of preexistence echoes throughout Islamic gnosis. As we have said, Shiite thinkers generally accept preexistence as something taught by the holy Imams themselves. It is assumed in the spiritual interpretation of the mysterious verse about the “Covenant,” the pact made before earthly existence, when the question was put: “Am I not your Lord?” (7:171). This question keeps the believer's horizon open far beyond the moment of birth into this world.

More still: our mystical theosophers—Mollâ Sadrâ, Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î—understand this question to be repeated from world to world, at every level at which being reveals itself, in each of the forty thousand universes spoken of in certain sayings (*hadîth*) of the Imams. Of these universes, our own world, the world of Adam's descendants, is the last. By their response to that question, human beings existing before the realm of becoming have themselves determined the meaning of their passage through this changing world, and therefore also what their final return to their origin will be.

8) That is why we may say that our temporal existence is only an episode “between two eternities”; or, more precisely, that it leads from eternity to eternity.[^EII2-370] In Arabic, we would say: between *azal* and *abad*. And the theme of this return is the theme of “the gnostic meeting the Angel.” Its many variations will stand out more clearly if we take them up later (§4), after translating “The Tale of the Western Exile,” in which Sohrawardî brings together the great themes of his theosophy.

Even now, however, we should note the close kinship between Sohrawardî's “Tale of the Exile” and the “Song of the Pearl,” also known as the “Hymn of the Soul” in the *Acts of Thomas*. This text gives voice to a central theme of Iranian spirituality, particularly in the Ishrâqî school. The comparison could, of course, carry us very far. R. Merkelbach, for his part, has examined the “Song of the Pearl” theme by theme, comparing it with *Chariklea*, the romance of Heliodorus (see above, Chapter V, 4), and identifying two parallel passages in Synesius and the emperor Julian.[^EII2-371]

If the “Song of the Pearl” is to be regarded as a gnostic hymn, “The Tale of the Exile” presents itself in much the same way. Both deserve a place in the collection that may one day bring together all the scattered members—*disjecta membra*—of the vast family of gnosis. “The Tale of the Exile” could scarcely have been written differently had Sohrawardî himself first read the story of the young Iranian prince whom his parents send from the East to Egypt to recover the Pearl beyond price.

Other echoes of the Pearl motif are found in Shiite gnosis. We may think of the tradition (*hadîth*) traced back to the Imam Ja'far, according to which the “Black Stone” set into a corner of the Ka'ba was once the “White Pearl” in Paradise: Adam's “angel,” subsequently sent to this earth to help Adam himself. The Imam's entire account has the form and significance of an initiation story, leading the initiate toward the “spiritual Temple.” We have studied it elsewhere.[^EII2-372]

For the present, let us simply recall the story told in the “Song of the Pearl.”[^EII2-373] A young prince is sent by his parents, sovereigns of the “East,” his homeland, to Egypt to bring back the one precious Pearl. He removes the garment of light his parents had lovingly woven for him. He reaches the land of exile; he is the Stranger. He tries to pass unnoticed, but is recognized. He is given food that darkens his memory of his origin, until he forgets that he is a “king's son.”

Then one day a message arrives, borne by an eagle and signed by his father, his mother, and all the nobles of Parthia—that is, all the princes of the heavenly Pleroma. This distinctly Iranian way of locating them in the “East” agrees perfectly with the meaning Sohrawardî gives to “East” throughout his Eastern theosophy. The prince remembers who he is and the Pearl he was sent to recover. Then comes the “departure from Egypt,” the exodus, the great return to the East.

As in gnosis generally, and as in Sohrawardî, the West (*maghrib*) represents the world of *genesis*, of earthly coming-into-being. Here that West is Egypt; for Sohrawardî it is the city of Qayrawân. (The prophet Mânî, too, in dying, departs from Egypt, *Misraim*.)[^EII2-374] The journey eastward ends when the prince puts on again the garment of light he had to set aside as a child. As we shall recall later (§4), this is one variation of the theme of “the gnostic meeting the Angel.”[^EII2-375]

The course of “The Tale of the Western Exile” runs parallel to that of the “Song of the Pearl.” The necessity bound up with the child's future destiny requires that this child of the “East” be sent into exile,[^EII2-376] into a “West” symbolized by Qayrawân. (The city lies in the western part of the Maghreb; perhaps its name, associated here with *caravan*, evokes the life of the soul imprisoned in this world as one long pilgrimage.) It is the city “whose inhabitants are oppressors.”

The young prince is chained and thrown to the bottom of a well. By night he awakens to the other world,[^EII2-377] but by day he falls back into the depths of the well. Will he remain there? Will he forget everything? Then one night a message comes from his family in the Beyond, brought by a hoopoe. The family wonders why he has not yet set out and urges him to leave without delay.

Thus begins the journey home toward an East that cannot be found on our maps. The traveller climbs Mount Qâf, which we already know as a mountain belonging at once to the cosmos and to the inner world of the soul. He ascends as far as the mystical Sinai, dwelling place of the being who appears here as the Angel of humanity, whom the Neoplatonists call the *Nous patrikos*, the paternal Intelligence. (See also the short spiritual romance discussed below in §5, under the theme of the “Personal City,” which reproduces, theme for theme, the mystical drama just described.) We should also recall Proclus' remarkable spiritual interpretation of the “story” of Phaethon.

Like the *ta'wîl*, the spiritual interpretation practised by our mystics, Neoplatonic interpretation works at several levels of understanding. There is the so-called “historical” interpretation, which touches only the outward meaning, the *zâhir*; there is the “physical” interpretation, operating at the level of symbols; and there is the “philosophical” interpretation, which amounts to “spiritual realism.” For the story of Phaethon is the story of a soul, indeed of a whole class of souls.[^EII2-378] It is a true history, but its truth is not located at the level of external events, of the everyday empirical ego. It belongs, rather, to the level of that “Self” to which I return when “I” come to know myself.

And it is precisely when “I” make this return that “I” become the teller of the mystical tale, the *hikâyat*, as our authors themselves have described it. I tell my own story. “It is I who am the subject of this tale,” the author declares at the end of “The Tale of the Exile.” This history is not ordinary history, with the “thread of events” being spun out as the “days go by.” It is the narrator's own sacred history, his *hierohistory*. Once again we meet the question that has returned page after page throughout our study: What is history in its true sense?

What is a history that is itself truth, and that as such breaks through history in the ordinary sense, since ordinary history can reach only the self of appearances—one appearance among others? This problem lies at the heart of every spiritual interpretation of the “religions of the Book.” And because their spiritual masters have lived this experience, we find within these religions a gnosis that unveils the meaning beyond history of true history. Here we find ourselves entirely in agreement with certain recent pages by Gilbert Durand, who responds with philosophical courage and lucidity to one of those questionnaires fashionable today whose very terms already betray an impending surrender.[^EII2-379]

Since the *hikâyat* constitutes the threefold unity described above, it is fundamentally wrong to treat *hierohistory*, “Sacred History,” as though it were merely a “historical and bygone” preface to ordinary history. Gilbert Durand writes: “The term and notion of Sacred History mean, above all, *narrative*, not an undertaking in archaeological reconstruction [...] For the liturgy consists in the reading, practice, exegesis, and interpretation of the sacred Narrative. It is an *anti-history*, just as the work of art, according to Malraux, is an ‘anti-destiny’: anti-history because it calls precisely for the repeated ‘recitation’ and ‘enactment’ of the narrative, recovering its ‘meaning’ for every instant, every cycle of time, every soul, and every moment of that soul. It does so against the ‘thread’ of History, against the positivist determinism of historical facts and blind events that carry human beings and empires through ascent, power, decline, and death.”[^EII2-380]

In these words we seem to hear, expressed perfectly in the philosophical language of our time, the principle of spiritual interpretation that we have already heard from the Fifth Imam and from Sohrawardî. The power of this history that breaks through history is preserved enduringly in the “phenomenon of the sacred Book,” the source of every spiritual tradition among the “religions of the Book,” whether Bible or Qur'an.

Durand goes on: “Since the book is an originative narrative rather than a descriptive history claiming objectivity, we must reject the historical and archaeological thread in favour of an eschatological meaning”—a meaning concerned with our ultimate destiny. Whoever recites the “Book” in this way brings forth, in that very act, his own Book. Through Sohrawardî's spiritual interpretation, it is the Qur'anic verses themselves that will form the fabric of his “Tale of the Exile,” turning it into a liturgical recital.

“Recite the Qur'an,” he said, “as though it had been revealed for you alone.” The orientation of this tale, and of all his tales, toward our ultimate destiny comes from putting this principle of interpretation into practice. This is what it means to understand “sacred history”: to acknowledge the reality of the *imaginal world*, the world of real spiritual images, and to lead the truth of appearances back toward that world, against the passage of time and against death.

By contrast, those who now speak of “bringing the lives of the Saints into agreement with historical truth” have probably lost even the sense of this return. It is nothing other than the recurring act of liturgy, without which no spiritual tradition could continue to live the “Book.”

##### 2. — *Analysis of the Tale*

In this tale, which we can now read in its original Arabic and in a Persian paraphrase [^EII2-381], I propose to distinguish a prelude and three main acts, followed by a postlude or epilogue.

*Prelude.* A short introduction gives Suhrawardi, the Shaykh of Illumination, an opportunity to define his own position in relation to Avicenna. Earlier, we saw how he distinguished his own “Eastern” philosophy from the philosophy Avicenna had conceived under the same name (above, Chapter I, § 2). Now he makes a further distinction, this time concerning the mystical tale itself. Suhrawardi refers to two works from Avicenna’s trilogy of visionary tales: the *Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan* and the *Tale of Salaman and Absal*.

I have discussed Avicenna’s tales at length elsewhere and shall not return to them here [^EII2-382].

Let us simply note that Suhrawardi’s reference confirms that Avicenna did indeed compose a *Tale of Salaman and Absal*. Unfortunately, all that survives of it is the summary given by Nasir al-Din Tusi in his commentary on Avicenna’s *Isharat*. Twenty years earlier, Tusi had commented on the Hermetic version of the same story, which the great poet Jami (d. 898/1492) would later develop into an expansive poem, one of the masterpieces of Persian mystical epic. Elsewhere [^EII2-383], I have compared the Hermetic and Avicennian versions of the *Tale of Salaman and Absal*. Suhrawardi expressly declares that this tale contains the mystical secret “entrusted to the symbols of the Sages.”

Yet, for all his praise of the *Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan*, he says that it fails to shed light on the mystical stage he has in mind. He stresses the significance of that stage for the soul’s ultimate destiny by naming it in Qur’anic terms—the “Great Upheaval” or “Great Overturning” [^EII2-384]. This is hardly surprising.

The *Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan* does no more than introduce the disciple to the “East” and show him the road that leads there. The disciple must decide for himself whether to take that road, just as at the end of the *Tale of the Crimson Archangel*. Avicenna does take it in the *Tale of the Bird*.

Nevertheless, the last lines of the *Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan* contain an unmistakable allusion. As Suhrawardi quotes them, they are indeed the lines we find at the close of Avicenna’s text: “It happens that some Solitaries among humankind migrate toward Him [^EII2-385]…” Those lines become the point of departure for Suhrawardi’s own tale. The Shaykh of Illumination thus fully recognized an intention in Avicenna that others have disputed. That recognition left him all the freer to tell his own story, which he called the *Tale of the Western Exile*.

**I.** The first part of the tale (the passages I have numbered 1–14) might be called “The Fall into Captivity and the Escape.” It begins the story of the gnostic—the seeker of spiritual knowledge—in this world. That story, an episode “between two eternities,” begins with exile from the world of light, which is the East, and imprisonment in the world of material *physis*, or physical nature, which is the West. The protagonist, who also recites the story, sets out with his brother ’Âsim.

The name means “one who protects, preserves, keeps safe,” but it can also mean, in a passive sense, “the protected one,” or “the one kept safe.” We naturally think that this brother must be the “heavenly Double,” the “self of light,” the Perfect Nature, the personal Angel. He would then correspond to the brother of the young Parthian prince in the *Hymn of the Pearl*, found in the *Acts of Thomas* [^EII2-386].

But in that story the mysterious brother remains in the Kingdom while the prince is sent into the darkness of Egypt to recover the Pearl. We saw earlier (Chapter V, § 4) that whenever a human soul descends, a Simorgh descends alongside it. Here, however, we encounter two striking differences.

First, this “invisible” brother is himself held captive by the people of Qayrawân.

Second, he does not reappear until passage 12, where the message received from the world beyond mentions him and calls on him, too, to free himself and set out on the road.

The Persian commentator asks us to see in the brother “the contemplative faculty,” which belongs to the soul without involving the body. ’Âsim, he explains, is protected against every harmful or destructive force. Perhaps so.

But this is precisely the kind of commentary against which I warned earlier (Chapter IV, § 4). I would suggest another approach. To interpret a mystical tale is not to drag it back down to the familiar certainties of philosophical logic, as though explaining a symbol meant that the thing expressing it could simply disappear. This is the greatest deception in the modern enterprise of “demythologizing.”

Consider what actually happens: the hero and his brother travel from “the region beyond the river” into the Western land to hunt birds along the shores of the Green Sea. We could translate this into philosophical language: they descend from the higher world into the world of darkness so that, through knowledge, they may transform what is perceived by the senses into what can be grasped by the intellect, and thereby attain the perfection of a soul raised to the state of *Nous*, or Intellect. Certainly.

But if we hear only that explanation and put it in place of the tale, we lose the meaning of the metaphysical epic. Gnosis is gone; *hikâyat*, the living act of mystical storytelling, is gone. All that remains is a lesson in philosophy.

The two brothers reach the most distant city of this “West,” marking the soul’s farthest evening decline—the very opposite of *Ishrâq*, the illumination of dawn (*illuminatio matutina*). That city is Qayrawân, which plays the same symbolic part here that Egypt plays in the *Hymn of the Pearl*. Its inhabitants seize the brothers and bind them when they discover that the newcomers are children of the world of Light, sons of the shaykh al-Hâdî ibn al-Khayr, the Yemeni.

Since they are his “children,” it is indeed their “father” whom the exile will rejoin at the end of the tale, on the mystical Sinai at the summit of Mount Qâf. We therefore have three linked designations for the same Intellect: the Angel of humanity, the Holy Spirit, who is for human beings the *Nous patrikos* or paternal Intellect, and the Active Intellect of the Avicennian philosophers, the tenth being in the archangelic hierarchy [^EII2-387].

The name *al-Hâdî* means “the Guide.”

Let us retain that word: we shall return to it in § 4, comparing its meaning in other settings that illuminate the tale’s concern with our ultimate destiny. *Ibn al-Khayr* literally means “son of the Good.” The Neoplatonic allusion is plain. Muslim philosophers knew a work by Proclus on the “Pure Good” [^EII2-388]. At the end of the story we shall hear of the “Supreme Ancestor,” Light of Light, the one to whom all the angelic hierarchies ultimately lead, and who, like Melchizedek, has neither father nor grandfather.

Al-Hâdî proceeds from this Pure Good, the source from which being comes into manifestation: he is its “son.” Why, then, is he called “the Yemeni”? Because southern Arabia, Yemen, and the land of Sheba occupy an important place in the visionary geography of these mystical writers. *Yemen* is associated with the “right-hand side” of the valley, where the divine voice called to Moses from the Burning Bush (Qur’an 28:30). Many hadiths, or traditions of the Prophet, could be cited to illustrate this meaning.

Mir Damad, the great theologian of the school of Isfahan, was particularly fond of quoting this one: “Faith comes from Yemen; divine wisdom is Yemeni” [^EII2-389]. Yemen is thus equivalent to “East” in the Illuminationist sense. “Yemeni philosophy” stands in the same contrast to Peripatetic philosophy as “Eastern philosophy” does. Here the visionary experience even agrees with ordinary geography, since Yemen really does lie east of Qayrawân. It is worth noting, too, that the biographer of Christian Rosenkreutz, whose name gave rise to that of the Rosicrucians, sent his hero on his “quest for Knowledge” as far as the sages of Yemen [^EII2-390].

High above the deep well into which the prisoners have been thrown stands a fortified castle with many towers. It is the castle formed by the celestial Spheres, crowned by the heaven of the Fixed Stars, where the constellations of the zodiac are carried—the *abrâj*, plural of *borj*, meaning castles or high towers. The prisoners are allowed to climb to this castle and attempt a spiritual ascent through the Spheres, but only at night.

Here we meet again the symbolism of night whose ambiguity I discussed earlier (Chapter IV, § 4). It appeared in the *Tale of the Crimson Archangel*. In that story, the child Zal is with Simorgh during the day—that is, he is present in the world of light—while at night he is entrusted to the care of the *anima sensitiva*, the soul’s sensory life.

In *The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings* (above, p. 220), the prologue shows the Child, the heavenly human being, casting off his bonds as soon as night falls. These are the bonds that fetter the children of Earth: the constraints of sensory perception that keep earthly people imprisoned, asleep in their soul’s unawareness. It is, then, night *for the senses*: active Imagination and imaginative perception have complete freedom.

Yet this night of the senses is itself the dawning of the mystical day, the *Ishrâq*. The visionary opens the door of the *khângâh*, the Sufi lodge. In other words, at the threshold of awareness beyond ordinary consciousness, he opens the secret door onto the unexplored desert. It is the entrance to the world beyond the senses, the world of Mystery (*ghayb*), and the beginning of the road to the spiritual and angelic world.

When day breaks again, however—when the world of “normal” knowledge returns—the door leading outside, into the free expanse of the spiritual world, is closed, and the door onto the city is opened [^EII2-391]. That city is Qayrawân, where people go about their business while captives dwell among them, able to escape only under cover of the “night.” This is everything that passages 6–9 of the *Tale of the Western Exile* are meant to tell us [^EII2-392].

Within this symbolism, then, day can appear as night and night as day, depending on whether we look from the “Eastern” or “Western” side [^EII2-393]. The same double meaning lies at the heart of esoteric interpretation in Sufism, Ismailism, and Shiism alike. The hidden meaning (*bâtin*) is both the night of what lies concealed and the daylight of spiritual truth. The outward meaning (*zâhir*) is both the daylight of the religious Law’s literal wording and the darkness that enslaves bodies, minds, and souls.

And so the exile and his brother “climb up during the night and descend during the day” (passage 9). Day is the bottom of the well, where “darkness piles upon darkness.” Night is the sight of lightning over Yemen, the forbidden region, the Angel’s “East.”

It is from that forbidden region that the message arrives, on one particular night. A hoopoe brings it on a night of the full moon. The commentator sees the hoopoe as “inspiration of the heart” and the full-moon night as “cleansing away the stains and impurities given off by material nature.” I have no objection, provided we do not stop there.

Recall that the full-moon night was already announced as a motif in the preceding tale; it will appear again later in this one. As for the hoopoe, recall the passage in which we saw it take flight in spring and become a Simorgh (above, Chapter V, § 3). Here, in the *Tale of the Western Exile*, the liturgical recitation is already under way.

To identify itself and deliver its message, the hoopoe “recites” the Qur’anic verses in which the hoopoe from the land of Sheba—that is, from the direction of Yemen—presents itself to Solomon and tells him of Bilqis, the Queen of Sheba. The message also recalls the letter sent to the young Parthian prince in the *Hymn of the Pearl*.

Other echoes can be heard. “Hold fast to our cord,” the message commands. This is precisely what Hermes heard from his “father” when he called for help amid the dangers of his ecstatic vision (below, § 4, II). There, the cord was a “ray of light,” an illumination from the sacred world. Here it means something similar, but the image is written in a cipher that is difficult to read: “the Dragon of the heaven of the Moon in the spiritual world, which rules over the shores of the eclipse.” I believe the cipher can be deciphered as follows.

Astronomy speaks of the Dragon’s head and tail—*Tannîn* in Arabic, *Jawzahar* in Persian—as the “nodes of the Moon,” the points where the Moon’s orbit crosses the Sun’s apparent path, making eclipses possible. The ascending node, where the Moon begins to move north of the ecliptic, is the “Dragon’s head” (*ra’s al-Tannîn*), the northern node. The descending node, where it begins to move south of the ecliptic, is the “Dragon’s tail” (*dhanab al-Tannîn*), the southern node [^EII2-394].

But our subject is not astronomy. The Dragon is associated with an eclipse, while everything takes place “in the heaven of the Moon in the spiritual world.” And the Moon in the spiritual heaven is none other than the mystic himself. What we learned earlier about the “Jewel-that-Illumines-the-Night” (above, Chapter V, § 3) enables us finally to read the cipher. When the Moon is closest to the Tûbâ Tree—that is, to the Sun—it appears to us to have become wholly shadow: we can no longer see it, just as we cannot see the Grail once freed from its covering of skin.

Yet in relation to the Sun it is wholly light. That is what the return from Western exile means: an eclipse, a withdrawal from the sight of the inhabitants of the “city of oppressors,” occurring in the very measure that the mystic, disappearing from his own visible self, is completely filled with the light of the spiritual Sun. The imagery is coherent throughout. That is why the Dragon will be mentioned once more (passage 33), at a decisive moment of the Return.

The last two passages of this first part of the tale complete the message received from the “East” and give directions for the stages of the journey. These are encoded in Qur’anic verses. In the “valley of the ants” (27:18), the pious anonymous commentator sees only an allusion to covetousness.

But the first chapter of Suhrawardi’s *Language of the Ants* (*Loghât-e mûrân*) suggests something quite different. At dawn, ants emerge from the darkness of their hiding place and are astonished to see drops of dew on the plants. They argue endlessly over where the drops came from. As the sun grows warmer, however, the dew is drawn upward, for everything returns to its origin.

The Qur’anic verses cited in that work echo those “recited” here. When you reach the valley of the ants, therefore, “shake out the hem of your robe”—that is, abandon futile arguments—and recite: “To Him is our resurrection” (67:15). The commands grow more urgent: let your people perish, and your wife too—in other words, everything bound up with the desires of the flesh.

The Qur’anic verses here recall the fate of Lot’s wife, who could not be saved because she was among those who remained behind (29:31), while Sodom’s people were destroyed by a storm at sunrise (15:51–73). One must board Noah’s ark, which here, as in Shiite gnosis, is the mystical vessel of salvation. “In the name of God, let it sail and come to harbour” (11:43).

**II (passages 15–36).** The pilgrims—the exile and his brother ’Âsim—set out, reach the far edge of the shadow, and there board Noah’s ark [^EII2-395]. At that moment, the narrator tells us, “the sun was directly above our heads.” This image becomes clear if we recall what Suhrawardi says elsewhere about the “quest for the East” and the “sacred experience” (above, Chapter II, § 2). Reaching the far edge of the shadow means reaching the boundary of the sublunar material world, the limit of the “West.”

Here the “middle East” begins: the imaginal world, the proper home of visionary stories and dreams. It is the realm in which actions such as these acquire their meaning—actions intended to free the soul from the physiological apparatus of the material body. Neither these actions nor their consequences are accessible to sensory perception. They run counter to the laws of the physical world: walking on water, reaching the heavens, the folding inward of time and space, and so forth.

In short, this is entry into the world experienced by certain mystical travellers (*sâlikûn*) when, as the Shaykh of Illumination says elsewhere, the light surrounding them stands “at the zenith over certain cities of the middle East.” This is the “eighth clime,” between the West of the physical world and the East of the higher *Malakût*, the spiritual kingdom [^EII2-396].

Elsewhere we find further, converging indications of what the “hour of noon” means, when the sun stands at its highest point. At the end of his commentary on the “hadith of the White Cloud,” for instance, Qazi Sa’id Qummi explains that noon, the hour when the pilgrims’ extraordinary journey into the *Malakût* with the Imam comes to an end, signifies that they have now attained the spiritual maturity needed to enter that realm. They have reached the “equator” of human reality, the perfect balance of the *walâyat*—the spiritual authority and bond of devotion—belonging to the “Seal of the *walâyat*” [^EII2-397].

We might also recall a moment in the vision of the alchemist Zosimos. Behind the sword-bearer coming from the East, another figure appears, carrying a round object of dazzling beauty and whiteness, called “Position of the Sun at Midheaven” [^EII2-398]. This is exactly the allusion in the *Tale of the Western Exile*.

Yet its narrator has told us that he and his brother escaped from prison “during the night.” We therefore have further confirmation that the meanings of day and night are reversed when we pass from the sensory to the suprasensory world. This reversal, the appearance of a “midnight sun,” prepares us for everything that follows [^EII2-399].

What follows is a swift triumph of liturgical recitation of the Qur’an. In a handful of passages it achieves the conditions of perfect *hikâyat*, defined earlier as a threefold unity realized in the very act of recitation: the unity of the reciter, the deeds recited, and the hero whose deeds they are (above, Chapter IV, § 5, and Chapter VI, § 1).

The narrator of the *Tale of the Western Exile* is not reconstructing the historical and archaeological meaning of the Qur’an. Suhrawardi is putting his own precept into practice: “Recite the Qur’an as though it had been revealed for your own case.” As a Neoplatonist, the Shaykh of Illumination is himself proof that there is no incompatibility between the Platonic vision of the world beyond, expressed through space, and the Qur’anic or biblical vision of the world beyond, expressed through the unfolding of human history in time.

Indeed, it is precisely that other space which opens a place for this sacred history. It allows the events to remain forever ready to happen and to happen again. The result is not a chronicle but a liturgy—a liturgy in which time can be reversed within a space that time itself brings into being.

Through the liturgical recitation of Qur’anic verses, the narrator relives the drama of the prophets. His journey toward the mystical Sinai carries him from one prophet of his own being to another, folding inward from one heaven of his being to the next, until he reaches the *astrum in homine*, the star within the human being.

One after another, the narrator becomes Noah, Lot, Moses, Dhu’l-Qarnayn (Alexander), Solomon. He is Noah, separated from his son by the waters because the son was not truly of his family (passage 16). The commentator identifies this son with the vital spirit (*rûh haywânî*), while the nurse cast into the sea (passage 19) would be the physical spirit (*rûh tabî’î*).

The narrator is Lot, who knows that his people, abandoned to wrongdoing, will be destroyed the next morning, at the hour of *Ishrâq* (passage 18). He is Moses travelling with the mysterious prophet Khezr (Khadir), who initiates him (passage 20). Noah’s ark sails so boldly that it crosses the gap separating the story of Moses from that of Alexander in sura 18. Now the pilgrim reaches Mount al-Jûdî, where Noah’s ark came to rest, and faces the peoples of Gog and Magog (*Yâjûj* and *Mâjûj*, passage 21).

There he is Alexander, building a barrier to protect the human microcosm—the human being understood as a little universe—against the assaults of subhuman forces (passage 22). He can do so because he is also Solomon, at whose disposal are the spring of molten copper and the spirits who labour in his service. These allusions are obscure; they may have an alchemical meaning connected with the “resurrection body.” I would be reluctant to force an explanation on them.

Still, we should recall how often the image of a piece of iron heated until it glows recurs in different settings, the iron becoming a bearer of the fire’s properties. The image can suggest either the mystery of mystical union (*unio mystica*) or the mystery of the Imam’s being. There is another allusion to the cities of ’Âd and Thamûd, two peoples of ancient Arabia who rejected the summons of the prophets sent to them (passage 24).

Then comes a series of actions whose literal description gives an impression of magnificent incoherence. The commentator labours—or rather strains—to draw up a meticulous inventory of correspondences that are at once commonplace and unconvincing. The old psychology distinguished so many faculties of the soul that one or another can always be made to fit a given image.

Instead, I believe we should meditate on the succession of images that suggest the heavens and the Spheres being brought within the self: more precisely, the passage from the heavens of astronomy to the heavens of the microcosm, and from there to the heavens of the world of the Soul, the *Malakût*. This is what it means to leave the world of physical nature, *physis*, and ascend the mountain of Qâf, which is at once a mountain of the soul and a cosmic mountain. Such an event can only be evoked in startling, even violent images. It is the passage through darkness required by the search for the “Spring of Life.”

The “round flask decorated with circles” suggests the brain. The pilgrim now shuts the Spheres inside it (passage 25). Let passages 26–28 convey their violence without our explaining it away: they signify a break with “normal” functions in order to cross the threshold into awareness beyond ordinary consciousness and into sacred knowledge, into pure imaginative vision independent of the senses. This matters more than any minute inventory of symbols.

The fourteen coffins and ten tombs may admit several interpretations, since for a gnostic they represent the hell of the world of *physis* [^EII2-400]. The pilgrim escapes from that world, drawn toward God like the shadow that God withdraws toward Himself, making the sun its guide (passage 29). From then on, “the road is perfectly straight” (passage 30). The pilgrim alludes to his sister, who remains in darkness (passage 31). The commentator sees in her an allusion to the matter from which cosmic bodies are made.

In passage 32, the Dragon returns. We encountered it in passage 12, when the message instructed the exile to “hold fast to our cord” to ensure his return. What I recalled above about the “Jewel-that-Illumines-the-Night”—the mystic as the “Moon in the spiritual heaven”—allows us to see that the instruction has now been effectively carried out. To put the “lamp” in the “Dragon’s mouth” is to place the *astrum in homine*, to borrow Paracelsus’s expression, at the “node” where the Moon becomes invisible from the human side, while from the side of the Tûbâ Tree it is bathed in the Tree’s light (passages 32–33) [^EII2-401].

Passage 34 describes the condition in which certain zodiac constellations now appear. Astrology knows many meanings for these constellations, and a commentary might relate them to the heavens of the microcosm or the heavens of the *Malakût*. It is precisely at this moment that the “star of Yemen” appears. The commentator identifies it with the “Soul of the World” (*Nafs kollîya*), the first in the hierarchy of the celestial Souls (*Animae caelestes*), and thus immediately below the Tenth Intellect in the higher hierarchy of the intellectual Angels (*Angeli intellectuales*).

But more directly, we should keep in mind the symbolic meaning of “Yemen” explained above. Does some remnant of fear or hesitation still remain in the pilgrim? According to the commentator, that is what the sheep—or flock—mentioned in passage 35 signifies. A flash of lightning strikes it dead.

Next comes the great passage 36. It begins with an alchemical allusion—the *athanor*, or furnace, which here is the heart—and ends, quite consistently, with what is probably another alchemical image: the membrane that has enclosed the *filius Sapientiae*, the *Puer aeternus*, the eternal Child born of the Work, bursts open.

We shall return below to this alchemical symbolism. The birth that frees the heavenly Child is accompanied by the magnificent sound of the music of the Spheres. Here we should remember what Suhrawardi has written elsewhere about the effects of music, as well as Iamblichus’s account of them [^EII2-402].

Suhrawardi’s comparison may startle us, though it has a precedent in Iamblichus: the vibration or reverberation of a chain striking a rock. Presumably he felt it conveyed the intensity—the unleashed force—of this cosmic symphony, whose effects are as overwhelming as all manifestations of beauty. Under the spell of these cosmic harmonies, he feels his whole being breaking apart.

**III (passages 37–43).** The great noise has died away. The tale’s “third act” opens in peace and silence at the foot of the Sublime Mountain, where the Spring of Life and immortality wells up. The goal pursued by all mystics since Khezr has now been reached. The happy fish living in this spring need no explanation beyond what the tale itself provides (passages 37–38).

But the brief appearance of a Qur’anic verse (18:60) invites us to look more closely. In its Qur’anic setting, Moses tells his servant that he intends to journey to the meeting place of the two seas—that is, to the Spring of Life. There they lose their fish, which “takes a certain course through the sea” (18:60) and escapes. According to a tradition, it was at this very moment that Moses was destined to meet Khezr. It therefore seems that the “fish” which answers the pilgrim’s questions here (passage 38) is none other than Khezr himself.

We can go further. If we follow the symbolism found in certain alchemical contexts [^EII2-403], Khezr may here represent the pilgrim’s own *self*. In that case, this episode of the *Tale of the Western Exile* offers an exact and striking counterpart to the conclusion of the *Tale of the Crimson Archangel*, when the Archangel tells his disciple: “If you are Khezr, you too can pass.”

The Sinai at whose foot the pilgrim now stands is a mystical Sinai. It rises at the summit of Mount Qâf, and at its own summit stands the Great Rock. We have already encountered Mount Qâf several times. What, then, is this Great Rock at the summit of a Sinai that itself crowns Mount Qâf? A tradition attributed to the tenth Shiite Imam, ’Alî-Naqî, says that beyond the encircling Sphere of Spheres—that is, beyond Mount Qâf—God possesses a green Emerald whose colour is reflected throughout the sky. For our ordinary eyes, we might expect the colour to be azure blue.

But we are not speaking here of optical perception: what matters is the meaning of colours as expressions of different levels of being. Green marks the world of the *Malakût*, the world closest to ours, whose proper colour is black, or “black light” (*nûr-e siyâh*). This *visio smaragdina*, this emerald vision, is the *Malakût*: the universe of the Soul with its seventy thousand worlds [^EII2-404], the “heavenly Earth with its cities of emerald” (Jâbalqâ, Jâbarsâ, Hûrqalyâ). According to some traditions, all of Mount Qâf is made of emerald. According to others, it is the Rock (*sakhra*) forming the keystone of the heavens that is an Emerald, its colour reflected across the entire sky.

Thus, in this episode of the *Tale of the Western Exile* (passages 37–38), the whole mystical Sinai, with the Great Rock resting on its high summit, is the Angel’s place of prayer. It is the keystone of the world of the Spheres, the “heavenly gate,” and at the same time the passage to the world beyond, to Nâ-Kojâ-Âbad, the “land of No-Where.”

The “eighth clime” is pictured as lying on the convex outer surface of the Sphere of Spheres—of course, this is only a way of speaking. That is why the pilgrim prepares to climb. Here lies the boundary between the visible world and the world beyond the senses. At that boundary—as at the entrance to the Chinvat Bridge in the Zoroastrian drama of the soul after death—the earthly self meets its heavenly Self, its “Angel.”

The encounter can be reached only after bathing in the Spring of Life. That is why this ascent, like the *anagogê*, the ascent of the soul in the *Chaldean Oracles*, has the value of a “sacrament of immortality.” The emerald vision itself has other parallels, notably in the visions of auras or coloured lights described by Najm al-Din Kobra [^EII2-405].

Passage 39 describes the pilgrim’s dazzlement before the beauty of the vision. The passages that follow develop two themes.

First: who is this Great Sage, whose light is so intense that heaven and earth seem to melt beneath the force of his appearance? What is his lineage—and therefore the lineage of the exile whom he receives (passages 42–43)? Second: what is the certainty of final salvation that he promises the prisoner who has been released, but only for a time (passages 40–41)?

**1)** An answer to the first question appears even more explicitly in another of Suhrawardi’s initiatory tales, already cited here, *The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings*. The figure is indeed the Angel of Knowledge and Revelation: the Holy Spirit, whom the Qur’an identifies with the archangel Gabriel, whom the philosophers identify with the Active Intellect, and whom the *Ishrâqîyûn*, the “Eastern” sages of illumination, call the “Angel of humanity.” In the present story the Angel makes his identity clear by speaking of the hierarchy of beings above him.

There are other Sinais higher than his own. From Intellect to Intellect, Angel to Angel, Sinai to Sinai, their lineage ascends to the One who has neither father nor grandfather: the Light of Lights. In *The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings*, the terms describing this hierarchy make it resemble an initiatory brotherhood, with master and pupil, initiation, and the bestowal of a cloak [^EII2-406]. It is as though the *khosrawânî* reciter of the Grail tale wished to remind us that the brotherhood of the Grail has a heavenly origin.

The hierarchy finally reaches the exiled Child, who succeeds in rejoining his “father” at the summit of his Sinai. I noted above (pp. 262 ff.) that this is a gnostic teaching fully compatible with the *henôsis*, the union with the divine, of Neoplatonic philosophers: a chain (*seira*) of emanations connects us to the supreme God and allows us to return to Him [^EII2-407]. The exile who has been brought home now stands in relation to his Angel as that Angel stands in relation to the Angel preceding him, the exile’s “grandfather.”

Recall the Ismaili dialogue of ’Amalaq the Greek (above, Chapter III, § 5): these are different expressions of the same spiritual vision. Later (§ 4), I shall try to place the final question in its proper setting. The “fish” told the pilgrim that the Great Rock is his “father’s” place of prayer. This father is the *Nous patrikos*, the paternal Intellect, the Tenth Angel in the hierarchy of Islamic Neoplatonism.

Yet in his hymn to the Perfect Nature (above, Chapter III, § 5), Suhrawardi greeted that Nature as both his “father” and his “child.” Who, ultimately, is the gnostic’s “angel”?

**2)** The common lineage of the Angel and the one who is his “child” is disclosed in the second part of their conversation on the summit of the mystical Sinai, at the Emerald Rock. The first part of the dialogue (passages 40–41), however, perfectly illustrates the theme of certainty I examined earlier (above, p. 264). The exile is not yet free for good. For the time being, at least, he must descend once more into the “Western” prison of Qayrawân.

But he learns that from now on he may return whenever he wishes, even before the appointed time for his definitive return. In other words, he is already saved and cannot fail to be saved, for he has rediscovered his origin (above, p. 262): what he was, what he still is, and what he will never cease to be. This is what the Angel reveals when he reveals the exile’s lineage. That is why, a few lines ago, I recalled the soul’s sacred ascent, the *anagogê*. It was the central mystery of the sacramental community whose holy book was the *Chaldean Oracles* (above, Chapter II, § 1).

The ascent of the mystical Sinai, preceded by immersion in the Spring of Life, carries the same meaning in Suhrawardi’s *Tale of the Western Exile*. Similarly, in the *Tale of the White Cloud*, the Imam’s companions, whom he has led into the *Malakût* and to whom he has appeared in the radiance of his heavenly (*malakûtî*) form, have attained complete spiritual maturity [^EII2-408].

*Postlude.* The final two passages form the epilogue. “It is myself that this tale is about”—or, literally, “It is I who am in this tale.” There was scarcely any need to say so, since the whole tale is already told in the first person.

Yet these final words confirm everything we have learned about the threefold unity established in the act of mystical recitation, or *hikâyat*.

These observations call for one further discussion. Several times we have encountered traces of alchemical symbolism. Remarkably, the mysterious note brought by the hoopoe from Sheba (passage 11) closely matches the invitation addressed to philosophers by the “Philosophers’ Stone” in the *Book of Twelve Chapters* attributed to Ostanes, the Persian Magus: “This Stone calls to you, and you do not hear it; it summons you, and you do not answer. How extraordinary! What deafness has stopped your ears? What rapture has stifled your hearts?” [^EII2-409] I am certainly not suggesting that the *Tale of the Western Exile* is primarily or explicitly an interpretation of the alchemical Work (see also below, pp. 311 ff.).

But there is an underlying parallel here, similar to the one Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ’î explicitly draws between the formation of the “resurrection body” and the alchemical Operation [^EII2-410]. We also find a celebrated fourteenth-century master of Iranian Sufism, Shah Ni’matollah Wali Kermani, making annotations in his own hand in his personal copy of a work by the alchemist Jildaki [^EII2-411]. Around the turn of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the masters of the revival of Iranian Sufism, Nur ’Ali-Shah and Mozaffar ’Ali-Shah, likewise described the successive stages of mystical union (*unio mystica*) in alchemical terms [^EII2-412].

I have also just referred to the spiritual knowledge of the Shaykhi school. We seem, then, to be dealing with a persistent Iranian tradition, reaching back to the time when the alchemist Zosimos spoke of “this Stone that is not a stone… which no one can give except God alone.” It is a tradition in which alchemy’s fundamental secret was understood as “identical with the most hidden mystery of the religion of Mithra” [^EII2-413]. In Iranian Shiism, the tradition is linked to Imam Ja’far al-Sadiq and the initiatory role assigned to him in the writings attributed to Jabir ibn Hayyan [^EII2-414].

The faculty by which we perceive this correspondence between alchemical work and mystical transformation is, of course, “active Imagination”—Imagination in its true sense, capable of bringing a world into being, just as the whole of creation can be understood as divine Imagination.

Ibn ’Arabi could understand it in this way, as could Böhme or Novalis. This *Imaginatio vera*, or true Imagination, is the faculty through which we enter the imaginal world: precisely the world in which such correspondences are real, where different worlds “symbolize with one another.” It is itself the *astrum in homine*, the star within the human being, a “subtle body” that is both the instrument and the product of its own sacred work. And the birth of this psychospiritual body is the birth of the spiritual human being (recall the allusion in passage 36).

Here the hoopoe represents that faculty, while Sheba or Yemen—and ultimately the Emerald Rock—represents the world to which it gives access. The sacred creative process is an active, sustained, generative meditation. Eventually it takes the form of a dialogue with the *alter ego*, an inner conversation (*colloquium internum*) at the “Sinai of one’s own being.” Its fruit can be described as the sublimation of the Stone, its becoming volatile, its “ascent to Sinai.”

Here is another striking example. About twenty years ago, while examining the vast body of still unpublished Arabic and Persian alchemical writings, I came across a very difficult treatise attributed to the famous mystic al-Hallaj. Fortunately, it was followed by a commentary attributed to Ghazali, entitled *The Unveiling of the Mysteries of the Golden Flakes* [^EII2-415].

Both attributions are doubtful, but that does not affect what the works contain, which is what matters here. In the first part of the treatise, several of the very symbols used in the *Tale of the Western Exile* appear in the same sequence. We learn how the mystical Stone is separated from impure Earth, represented by Noah’s son swallowed by the flood (compare passage 16).

The stages of the alchemical Work—*nigredo* (blackening), *albedo* (whitening), and *rubedo* (reddening)—are announced in the same order as in Suhrawardi’s tale: the tearing open of the vessel, the passage by the island of Gog and Magog, the work of the spirits with fire, even the same Qur’anic reference (18:98) that occurs in passage 23 of the *Tale of the Western Exile*. Dhu’l-Qarnayn (“the Two-Horned,” the title traditionally given to Alexander) here represents the body undergoing the alchemical operation. One of his “horns,” or points, is whiteness, the lunar Elixir; the other is redness, the solar Elixir.

“When you know this with certain knowledge,” the text says, “you know the resurrection of the dead.” Four mountains must be climbed: those of Sâd and Nûn, two Arabic letters that here encode the Elements; then Mount Qâf; then Mount Sinai. The text also speaks of the land of the Queen of Sheba as a Holy Land where the seed of the “subtle body” of the Resurrection grows. All these parallels help us hear the different resonances, especially the alchemical ones, in the symbolism Suhrawardi employs.

From the second part of this alchemical treatise attributed, rightly or wrongly, to al-Hallaj, I shall retain only its account of the human being.
