This is not an unthinking anachronism: for this Zoroastrian Illuminationist, the chapter on Zoroaster provides precisely the right occasion to state his position toward the Islamic schools and religious groups of his own time.

One more work from the same school deserves mention: *Ayin-e Hushang* (“The Religion of Hushang,” Iran's primordial prophet). It was published by lithography in Bombay in 1296 AH/1879 CE by the Parsi scholar Mirza Bahram Rostam Nasrabadi, who supplied a lengthy preface. It is a substantial collection of four Persian treatises [^EII2-508], whose manuscripts came from the imperial library. Even a quick reading reveals the influence of *Ishraq*.

We can do no more here than draw attention to these little-known books. This Zoroastrian Illuminationist literature calls for a study of its own, which we hope to undertake elsewhere. The author of the *Dabestan* also mentions other Zoroastrian sages from Shiraz whom he knew personally. Among them were Hakim Ilahi Herbad and Hakim Mirza, both described as *Ishrâqîyûn*. Both knew the Shaykh al-Ishraq's works thoroughly, and had absorbed his teaching so completely that they made his “Book of Hours”—from which we translated two psalms above, in Chapter III, Section 5—the liturgical ritual of their own religious life [^EII2-509].

The understanding held by these Zoroastrian Illuminationists in Shah Akbar's time—of philosophy's Iranian origin in its two forms, ecstatic (*ishrâqî*) and dialectical (Peripatetic), and of the translators who disseminated learning preserved in the treasuries of the ancient Persian kings—ought to be compared with the older traditions preserved in authentic Pahlavi literature. Nor was Suhrawardi's image of the Iranian sage as a Platonist something he invented.

The historian Mas'udi (d. 346 AH/957 CE), discussing Tansar, the chaplain of Ardashir who restored the Mazdean religious establishment in the Sasanian Empire in the third century CE, already describes that eminent figure as a Platonist—or, in the terms of our texts, an Illuminationist. Tansar's own words, in his famous letter, explaining and justifying his way of life were not chosen at random. They correspond exactly to the stages that would later structure Suhrawardi's spiritual discipline [^EII2-510].

Through the distinguished spiritual figures he met in India, the author of the *Dabestan* ultimately leads us back to Iran. He tells us that he learned directly from Farzaneh Bahram that among those close to Azar Kayvan's circle, and those granted meetings with the master, was none other than Baha'oddin 'Amili, one of the most eminent figures of Iranian Shiism: the venerable *mujtahid*, or jurist qualified to exercise independent judgment, who taught Molla Sadra in Isfahan [^EII2-511].

Thus we find ourselves once more on Iranian soil, following the traces of the “community of the Book of Oriental Theosophy.” We have just seen this mystical community send out branches into India. Although distinct from Sufism, its history is nonetheless intertwined with Sufism's—perhaps most directly with the Nurbakhshiyya order. A distant great-grandnephew of the Shaykh al-Ishraq is said to have succeeded Sayyed Mohammad Nurbakhsh (d. 1464) as head of that order [^EII2-512].

As for Shiism, we have already noted more than one point of contact between Illuminationist and Imamite theosophy—indeed, something far more substantial than mere points of contact. Their interaction becomes clearer still, as we recalled earlier, when Shiite theosophers recover what they recognize as their own spiritual inheritance within the theosophy of Ibn 'Arabi. The merging of these currents would mark Iran's great intellectual and spiritual flowering under the Safavids, while in India the effects of Shah Akbar's reforms were being felt at the same time, with many Iranian thinkers taking part.

The first name that comes to mind is Mir Damad (d. 1040 AH/1630 CE), the intellectual master of the School of Isfahan, whose influence is still felt in Iran today. Without examining here how far each of his writings agrees with Suhrawardi's positions, let us note a few telling details. In answering a correspondent's question about a difficult passage in Suhrawardi's *Book of Oriental Theosophy*, Mir Damad shows a profound understanding of the text [^EII2-513]. As for the “Profession of Faith of the Philosophers,” we have elsewhere mentioned a manuscript copied in Mir Damad's own hand, ending with the highest praise for the Shaykh al-Ishraq [^EII2-514].

Finally, Mir Damad adopted the very name *Ishraq* as his pen name (*takhallos*). Readers who turn to the “Ecstatic Confessions” translated later in this work (Book V, Chapter I) will be able to appreciate the affinity between these two shaykhs. We may also recall that one of Mir Damad's pupils, Qotboddin Ashkevari, discerned in the Twelfth Imam the features of the figure whom Zoroastrian teachings about the end of time call the “Saoshyant,” the restorer who will raise the dead.

The full brilliance and range of Suhrawardi's thought become especially apparent, of course, in the work of Mir Damad's most celebrated pupil, Molla Sadra Shirazi. Molla Sadra left an immense body of writing, running to several folio volumes. An entire book would be needed to establish the place of the Shaykh al-Ishraq's writings and ideas within it. Here we shall mention only the *Glosses* Molla Sadra wrote on *The Book of Oriental Theosophy*: a work of remarkable depth, scale, and originality in its own right, without which much of Suhrawardi's book would lose its resonance.

We shall give a sample of these glosses later, after attempting to explain Molla Sadra's importance to the spiritual culture of Iran (below, Book V, Chapter II). Molla Sadra frequently uses the words *mashriq* (“east”) and *mashriqî* (“eastern”), and it is a pleasure to see his commentators—from Mirza Ahmad Ardakani Shirazi and Molla Isma'il Isfahani to Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i—carefully distinguish their meanings; their analyses invariably lead back to Suhrawardi's use of the words [^EII2-515].

Later (Book V, Chapter III), we shall also devote several pages to another outstanding master, Qazi Sa'id Qommi. His work is of the greatest philosophical interest because it shows how the Shiite understanding of the Imam intersects with a fundamental Illuminationist idea.

Even after naming two eminent masters such as Molla Hadi Sabzavari and Molla 'Abdollah Zonuzzi, who carried the philosophy of *Ishraq* into nineteenth-century Iran, we would still have to trace its presence in the writings of another forty or fifty thinkers who have sustained philosophical life in Iran over the past four centuries. Unfortunately, the work of examining those writings—which first requires reliable editions of the texts—has scarcely begun.

##### 3. — *The Religion of Transfigured Eros*

This title for our final section seems to bring together, better than any other, the teachings and intentions of the Shaykh al-Ishraq. It also prepares the way for Book III, which will deal with Ruzbehan and the “Faithful in Love.”

The theme draws together connections we have suggested, sometimes only in passing: the “story” of the gnostic; the earthly self and its heavenly counterpart; the Hermetic figure of Perfect Nature and the Mazdean or Manichaean vision of the angel Daena; the idea of Sophia in Jacob Boehme; the philosophers' Active Intelligence and the *Madonna Intelligenza* of the *Fedeli d'amore*; the emergence of the mystical epic; and more. What especially concerns us is how the austere metaphysical theme of the Active Intelligence unfolds, through imagination, into a mystical epic of love.

We can see this again in one of Suhrawardi's tales of initiation.

We must say a little about it in closing, because its dramatic setting contains, in suggestive form, everything we have tried to analyze here. It resonates with so many centuries of Iranian mystical poetry that, if we attempted to set Suhrawardi's themes alongside all their later variations, the task would have no end.

Here we shall concern ourselves only with the metaphysical foundation of the religion and mysticism of love as presented in this last tale. In doing so, we shall briefly return to all the themes we have encountered throughout this book and the questions they have raised.

Our section's title is not accidental. It is inspired by a work of the Russian philosopher Boris Vycheslavtsev, who remains little known for want of translations: his *Ethics of Transfigured Eros*, a book of the first importance for anyone investigating the role of imagination in spiritual life [^EII2-516]. Vycheslavtsev seeks to ground moral life in the proposition that “images of the imagination possess a power of transfiguration.” His inquiry is part of a broader effort to understand *transcensus*: the absolute reality of transcendence, which makes it “impossible to remain within the limits of pure immanentism” and can be fulfilled only “in the sphere of the beyond, of metaphysical being.”

Accepting the findings of depth psychology, he holds that imagination alone provides the key to the subconscious because it “raises psychic energy to a higher level.” Sublimation, on this account, corresponds to the spiritual transformation of the human being, to the divinization spoken of in Christian mysticism. By recognizing sublimation as a driving force of the soul, Vycheslavtsev can propose a new ethics, one that moves beyond moralism: “The true ethics of grace is that which is capable of transfiguring and sublimating” [^EII2-517].

Clearly, this takes us far beyond the pious but ineffective distinction between *eros* and *agape* on which so many moral theologians have insisted. We are, rather, in the current of Russian Orthodox theosophical thought that, beginning with Vladimir Soloviev, sought to recover the sacred meaning of Eros. There is also this decisive point: once imagination is granted the power to transfigure, we find ourselves on ground familiar to Ibn 'Arabi [^EII2-518]. An ethics of transfiguration and divinization corresponds to the idea of *ta'alloh*, well known in the philosophy of *Ishraq*.

We shall see that the transformation of human Eros into divine Eros is also the very heart of Ruzbehan Baqli of Shiraz's ethics (Book III, below). As for the metaphysical source of an Eros that must undergo this transformation if it is to become what it truly is, Suhrawardi attempted to suggest it in the short mystical romance to which we shall turn in closing. For us, this tale seems to express the final idea toward which the preceding discussion has been moving.

At the same time, Suhrawardi's religion of transfigured Eros, drawing on the full resources of metaphysical Imagination, brings us back to the need to recognize the distinct reality and mode of being of the *mundus imaginalis*, the imaginal world. Only in that world can the metaphysical ground of an Eros that is both transfigured and transfiguring be inwardly “seen.” Such seeing brings to life figures who are real in their own way; it is indispensable, for without it everything would remain a merely theoretical possibility. This, ultimately, is the point where Suhrawardi's metaphysics of essences meets the dramatic world of his mystical tales.

We can indicate this connection only briefly; a full treatment would demand another book.

Yet it belongs here, because the structure of Suhrawardi's mystical romance *Mu'nis al-'ushshaq* makes the connection unavoidable. Its title might best be rendered *Companion for the Faithful in Love* [^EII2-519]. Unlike the two tales translated earlier (Chapters V and VI), this one is told in the third person rather than the first. Its *dramatis personae*, or figures in the drama, are the very kind that conventional literary criticism, knowing nothing of the reality of the *mundus imaginalis*, dismisses as “personified abstractions” or “allegories.”

We must challenge that confusion and the impoverishment of meaning it brings. Our starting point should be Avicenna's understanding of *essence*. An essence, considered in itself, is simply what it is, absolutely and without qualification. It is neither the logical universal of a concept nor an individual existing in the world of the senses. The logical universal requires a negative condition: we exclude from the abstract concept of an essence everything that would prevent it from being predicated of any number of individuals.

The sensory individual requires a positive condition: we determine what must be added to the essence for it to be realized *in singularibus*, in particular beings of the empirical world. Essence, however, is not a logical universal but a *metaphysical* universal. It is a spiritual form, and there is therefore no reason why an individual being cannot have an essence of its own.

We may speak, for example, of the *Socrates-ness* of Socrates. That is neither a logical universal that other people could share nor the physical individual Socrates encountered in the sensory world. Socrates-ness is not one of the logical universals; it is the spiritual form of an individual being. Here the principle of individuation is *form*, not matter, as in Aristotelian Thomism.

Thus Socrates-ness is not abstract in the sense of a logical concept; rather, it is *separate* (*khôristos*, Arabic *mojarrad*) from what is concrete to the senses.

But it is a mistake to reserve the word “concrete” for the sensory world. There is also a concrete reality of spirit, and this is concrete in the highest degree. That is the metaphysical position underlying Suhrawardi's teaching about angels.

An absolute essence of this kind—neither a logical universal nor a sensory individual, but possessing its own unity, its own distinctive mode of individuation, and its own specific “concrete” character—is what the Shaykh al-Ishraq calls an *Angel*: the lord of a species (*rabb al-nû'*), which bears that angel's name. Each species, together with its individual members, is the “theurgy,” the creative manifestation, of its Angel.

This brings us back to the questions raised above about the sense in which each angelic being, as lord of a species, may be called universal (Chapter III, Section 3, pp. 117–118; and Chapter VI, Section 4, p. 316).

We are now confronted with a question. If such an essence stands beyond both the logical universal and the sensory individual, *how does it exist?* And once we have defined its mode of existence, *in what form can it appear to us concretely?* Can we know it as anything other than a universal concept abstracted by the intellect? If we limit ourselves to concepts, we remain trapped in the familiar dispute about universals. If the essence is merely a pure possibility, it has no actual being.

But if it truly exists—and otherwise how could we speak of what it is?—we must decisively reject any dividing line between *being* and *existing* that would reserve existence for individual things in the sensory world.

We must acknowledge a whole scale of real modes of existence above what people commonly call “reality” today. This includes, to begin with, mental existence (*wojûd dhihnî*), understood as existence in the full sense of the word. That is why Molla Sadra's metaphysics of existence may ultimately be seen as preserving, rather than destroying, the metaphysics of essence.

In what concrete spiritual form, then, can an essence reveal itself to us—an essence that Suhrawardi understands as an angelic being, individualized not by some alien material element but by its own nature, which makes it one essence rather than another? Neither as a concept nor as a thing of the senses. Its place of appearance, the “stage” on which it becomes visible (*mazhar*), can only be the *mundus imaginalis*: the world in which an Angel appears either in dreams or in contemplation while awake.

There it takes the form of the figures who animate Suhrawardi's *Companion*, and who recur throughout the Persian mystical epic: Intelligence, Beauty, Love, and Sorrow. They can also bear familiar personal names: Adam, Joseph, Zolaykha. In every case these are *proper names*. Their actions, the distinctive ways they act, show that they are more than logical concepts; and the scene of those actions is not the sensory world. To explain them as “personified abstractions” explains nothing. Once an abstraction is personified, it is no longer an abstraction. An abstract person is no person at all.

Moreover, what sort of being is involved in the *making* (*facere*) or *coming-to-be* (*fieri*) of a personification? The tragedy of a culture begins when it can understand every essence only as the logical universal of a concept. Giordano Bruno, by contrast, declares: *Intelligere est phantasmata speculari*—to understand is to contemplate images, to think through them. We might put the difference this way: with logical universals, one writes a treatise of theoretical philosophy. With concrete individuals, one writes history or an ordinary novel.

But with metaphysical universals—with pure essences appearing at the level of concrete reality proper to them, in the *mundus imaginalis*—one writes a mystical epic, a visionary narrative, a tale of initiation.

This is true whether the figures in such “romances” have ordinary personal names or names that seem, at first sight, to designate concepts. They are not concepts but real beings of the *mundus imaginalis*. The point applies equally to *The Ring of the Nibelung*, to the Grail cycle to which we have repeatedly referred, to the visions of *The Shepherd of Hermas*, to *The Romance of the Rose*, to *The Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz*, and to many other writings of this kind.

All of them deserve to be read afresh as narratives of initiation—with eyes that Western philosophy and civilization have long since closed, but that our “Eastern” theosophers have kept open to the *mundus imaginalis*.

We can now understand, too, why merely calling such works “allegories” settles nothing.

Let us take one further example: the figures who inhabit Ramon Llull's exquisite and sublime *Tree of the Philosophy of Love* [^EII2-520]. In its prologue, Llull tells us how he went into “a beautiful forest, not far from Paris, thickly wooded and full of springs.” In the middle of a lovely meadow he found a great Tree; beneath its shade sat a lady of extraordinary beauty, richly dressed.

When he greeted her, she revealed her name: “Philosophy of Love.” As the author unfolds his plan, we learn that the book will introduce a number of “ladies of love”—the roots of the Tree, such as Goodness and Greatness, eighteen in all—and also “young men of love.” The latter bear names such as *making-good* and *making-great*: in each case they represent the action, the *energeia*, proceeding from the essence named by the noun.

Each “lady of love” is thus an essence that appears to the author in its own fully “objective” reality. It is not defined by placing it within a broader class and specifying what distinguishes it, for that would reduce the essence to its logical concept. We are dealing neither with logical concepts nor with persons inhabiting the sensory world.

Each essence makes itself known through what it brings into being: it “makes essential” what it itself is. We might express this in German as *es west sein Wesen*. Goodness is that through which the good *makes good*; Greatness, that through which the great *makes great*, and so on.

In short, to give expression to an essence we must add to the noun naming it something drawn from the verb *facere*, “to make” or “to bring about.” This active dimension—*energeia*, in the Greek sense—is revealed to Llull's inward sight as a “young man of love.” That is why, throughout the book, the “young men of love” speak, act, and behave as real, concrete persons. Their concrete reality belongs precisely to the *mundus imaginalis*; without that world, we would mistakenly reduce the entire “story” to an allegory, which it is not.

Here we should recall the *Amahraspands*, the archangels of Zoroastrianism (Chapter III, Section 3), because their names also express the actions they perform. They are the “Holy Immortals,” but theirs is a holiness that acts upon and transforms what it touches: a sacred, effective energy—the *spanta* of each Amahraspand. This energy communicates being and the growth of being by bringing into existence what it itself embodies as an essence. The Amahraspands are neither conceptual abstractions nor mere “aspects” of the supreme Godhead [^EII2-521]. They are at once distinct spiritual beings and active powers.

Suhrawardi took such pains to express this by turning his metaphysics of essences into a teaching about angels. In Llull, the relation between the spiritual being and its active power, between what the noun names and what the word for action names, is the relation between the “ladies of love” and the “young men of love.” An essence becomes visible in a person who wholly embodies and gives form to what that essence is.

Neither a logical concept nor an ordinary individual in the sensory world can perform that role. If essences did not appear as “ladies of love” and “young men of love,” as the figures do in Suhrawardi's *Companion*, we would have before us only their logical concepts, not the essences themselves. This is why we must recall our earlier discussion (Chapter IV, Section 4, pp. 197 ff.) of the moment when a doctrine or theory becomes the narration of an event—the A, B, and C levels of interpretation.

If Llull uses the word *metaphor*, we must not misunderstand the direction in which it moves. *Trans-sumptio* means transposition, a carrying across. When a melody is transposed into a higher key, its accuracy or “truth” does not consist in returning it to its former pitch; it consists in preserving the structure, the *isomorphism*, between the two versions. We have used that comparison before (Book I, Chapter IV, Section 2).

In the same way, the true meaning of concrete figures in the *mundus imaginalis* is not discovered by bringing them back down to the level of a logical concept. The reverse is true. The real meaning of the logical concept becomes apparent only at the level where the essence can reveal itself: in the image that is its *mazhar*, its stage or form of appearance, and that can be perceived by metaphysical Imagination. This is why we cited the Russian philosopher's account linking *transcensus*, the movement beyond the merely given, with the transfiguring power of images.

What is ultimately at issue, then, is a kind of *space* belonging to the spiritual world, outside the locations of the senses. Within this space, imagination can “see” the spiritual world in the setting proper to its manifestation, its *mazhar*. The Arabic-Persian word means a form or place of manifestation, and in ordinary use can also mean a *theatre*. This space corresponds to the distinctive time of the *hikâyat*, the first-person visionary tale.

We have repeatedly seen how such a tale escapes the dilemma that otherwise leaves us asking whether an event is *myth* or *history*. It is the space opened up by the tale's own time. Inner vision itself bears witness to what it sees, as the surah of the Star says: “The heart did not deny what it saw” (Qur'an 53:11).

We must therefore say something about the connections between the *'âlam al-mithâl*, the *mundus imaginalis*, and some fascinating recent research, even though we must once again limit ourselves to a few preliminary observations.

I am thinking of Frances A. Yates's fine book *The Art of Memory*. The texts she examines seem to offer inexhaustible possibilities for our subject, especially because our “Eastern” theosophers have, understandably, been absent from the comparisons made so far.

The ancient *ars memorativa*, the art of memory, originally worked through two elements: places and images (*loci et imagines*) [^EII2-522]. Its method was to move mentally—or even bodily—through a building, such as a palace, church, or abbey with its outbuildings, placing striking images at successive locations. By revisiting those images in the mind, a speaker could follow the thread of a speech without faltering. This already implies that certain arrangements in space can reveal what lies hidden in the depths of the human mind.

Yet we must be precise about what is contemplated. Whatever building or landscape frames the exercise, the image itself is never a material one: it has never been physically placed there. The act is not external sensory perception but inner imaginative perception. The contents of memory are themselves inward spiritual forms, of which memory is the treasury; memory is the treasury of Imagination.

For that very reason, and because of the assumptions on which it rests, the *ars memorativa* was bound to develop between the Middle Ages and the Renaissance into a metaphysics of memory, inseparable from a metaphysics of the image and of Imagination. Such a metaphysics requires, whether openly acknowledged or not, an account of the distinctive reality of the *mundus imaginalis*.

Among those who developed this metaphysics of memory, we find several assumptions drawn from Hermeticism and Neoplatonism. The first, in one form or another, is that the soul existed before earthly life and fell from a heavenly, angelic state into a world of darkness and demonic oppression—as in Suhrawardi's tales. The fundamental act of self-knowledge is therefore an *awakening*: a recollection of what the gnostic was before entering this world.

Think here of the “Hymn of the Pearl” and the “Tale of Exile.” Such an awakening presupposes a power of memory that reaches incomparably further back than psychology ordinarily allows. It also presupposes that the Image bringing about this awakening cannot be explained by the commonplace theory that, because human beings are weak, they must clothe realities too exalted for their intellect in sensory appearances. We need instead an idea like the association of *Imago* and *Magia* found in Jacob Boehme.

In this sense the *ars memorativa* ultimately belongs to the *ars hieratica*, the sacred or theurgic art of the Neoplatonists discussed above (Chapter II, Section 1). Since the human being as microcosm reflects the macrocosm, memory becomes the memory of the “theurgic sage,” the divine human being who participates intimately in the divine powers and energies of the cosmos. Images thereby acquire, *by that very fact*, a theurgic and “transfiguring” power. We have already learned that, for Suhrawardi, each species is the theurgy, the “talisman,” of its Angel.

The same idea recurs among the Renaissance Hermeticists. It is embodied in the extraordinary *Theatrum mundi*, or Theatre of the World, constructed by Giulio Camillo and so illuminatingly explained by Yates. Reproducing the architecture of a classical theatre in miniature, according to Vitruvius's proportions, Camillo's theatre—his *mazhar*, as we might call it—unifies the contents of memory by grounding that unity in images drawn from the heavenly world. Its arrangement reverses the usual position of the audience and the spectacle.

The “performance” occupies the auditorium: images are placed in seven tiers of seats, arranged in seven “columns,” the seven pillars of the house of Wisdom. The observer, standing mentally on the stage (*frons scenae*), can take in at a glance, through contemplation of those images, the contents of all the worlds. This is something far more significant than what we ordinarily call a memory technique. As Yates writes, “the secret or one of the secrets of this theatre is that these planetary images are supposed to be talismans or to have a talismanic virtue” [^EII2-523].

These talismanic images are, of course, inward images: they reproduce the heavenly world within the inner world of imagination and make imagination receptive to celestial influences. We find this in Marsilio Ficino as well as in Giordano Bruno. For Bruno, the images of the starry world are the *Umbrae idearum*, the “shadows of ideas,” closer to true reality than the physical shadows of the lower world. In a particular and limited sense, they correspond to the *'âlam al-mithâl*. This is also how Bruno interprets Ramon Llull's *Ars*, or Art.

The *ars memorativa* is thus transformed into a mystery cult within the soul; there are inward images, even inward statues. We might say that the art of memory finds its completion in an *ars interiorativa*, an art of inward realization. Philosophy stands here at a crossroads. Wherever the full power of images and Imagination to disclose knowledge goes unrecognized, and is replaced by the logical and mnemonic arrangement of concepts, an *inner iconoclasm* is already close at hand, preceding the destruction of images in the outer world.

Indeed, the first iconoclasts opposed to the Renaissance Hermeticists and Neoplatonists were the Logicians, humanist or otherwise, who were so hostile to images that they would acknowledge no art of memory beyond the logical ordering of concepts. Where, by contrast, a metaphysics of the *mundus imaginalis* is available, spiritual realism directs us toward a *concrete* spiritual reality, toward the “transfigurations” brought about by the *imagines agentes*, the active images.

The expression *imagines agentes* is significant in itself because it parallels *Intelligentia agens*, the Active Intelligence. Just as the Active Intelligence brings the human intellect into act, so the *Imago agens*, the active Image, awakens and brings the imaginative faculty into act.

The *imagines agentes* are not “products” manufactured by imagination. They are forms of manifestation, and imagination is the place where they appear, their theatre—their *mazhar*. This theatre also reveals both the differences in style and the affinities between a particular form of inner imagination and a particular style of architecture. That architecture may be the architecture of the cosmos, as in the two Suhrawardian tales translated earlier. It may be something more limited, like the classical theatre of Vitruvius mentioned a moment ago. Or it may be a city or fortress, as it is on two occasions in Suhrawardi.

Indeed, everything suggests that Suhrawardi imagined, on the scale of the human microcosm, something corresponding to the idea of the *Theatrum mundi*: the “fortress of the soul,” whose successive floors or towers provide locations for mental images endowed with powers of memory and spiritual transformation. This fortress, described in the “Epistle of the High Towers” (above, Chapter VI, Section 6), reappears in the *Companion* we are about to discuss.

We needed to mention this way of giving space to spiritual realities, derived from the *ars memorativa*, if only to suggest the comparative studies still needed before the Shaykh al-Ishraq's work can be heard in its full resonance. Much remains to be done to understand and situate the *mundus imaginalis*, the theatre of his tales where these “transfigurations” take place—beginning with the transfiguration of Eros, as the brief account that follows will show.

The *Companion for the Faithful in Love* is chiefly concerned with a triad of these figures, commonly called “personified abstractions,” though in fact they are something quite different. Their origin takes us back once more to Avicenna's metaphysics. Neither the way they appear nor the way they act allows us to regard them as conceptual abstractions, and still less as individual people belonging to the sensory world.

Yet each has a distinct metaphysical individuality. Each is the concrete manifestation of a pure essence, appearing at the only level compatible with its nature: the *mundus imaginalis*. The short treatise opens by recalling a familiar prophetic tradition (*hadith*), already encountered in this book: “The first thing God created was the Intelligence.” This is the *Nous* of Greek philosophy, a distinct spiritual reality.

Philosophers in Islam found in this saying of the Prophet an invitation to Neoplatonic reflection. We have already recalled how, in Avicenna's account of the cosmos, the First Intelligence—whom Suhrawardi calls Bahman, the first of the Zoroastrian archangels—performs three acts of contemplation.

First it contemplates its own Source; second, its existence as made necessary by that Source, which constitutes its dimension of light; and third, its own essence, which, apart from its Source, would remain non-being, and so constitutes its dimension of shadow. From these three contemplations proceed, respectively, a Second Intelligence, the First Soul (*Anima mundi*, the Soul of the World), and the first heaven.

The Soul longs in love to be united with the Intelligence from which it proceeds. The heaven, composed of the subtlest matter and arising from the dimension of shadow, marks the ideal distance separating the Intelligence from the Soul. It is the Soul's loving longing for its Intelligence that sets this heaven in motion. Already, in this cosmic drama of the archangels, we have the first transfiguration of Eros on the scale of the universe.

At precisely this point, the *Companion* brings the drama into the world of human experience. The three beings arising from the Intelligence's contemplation now appear as three persons. They no longer bear their original names in the creation of the cosmos—Intelligence, Soul, and Heaven—but names expressing how they appear within the human soul, at the level where the religion of transfigured Eros comes into being. Their names are Beauty, Love, and Sorrow, respectively.

The three members of this triad thus correspond to Intelligence, Soul, and the Soul's Heaven. Their names are no longer common nouns but proper names, designating three pure essences. They are neither logical universals nor individuals of the empirical world. They are essences whose very nature is to act, whose power is to “make essential,” to bring into being what they themselves are. Their *energeia*, their active power, takes concrete form in three further figures whose names come from the Qur'an and the Bible: Joseph (Beauty), Zolaykha (Love), and Jacob (Sorrow). These three figures are, of course, “seen” not as characters in an anecdote about the past but as *imagines agentes*, active images of the active Imagination.

In relation to the triad whose *energeia* each embodies, they stand, in terms of their mode of being, much as the “young men of love” stand to the “ladies of love” in Ramon Llull.

The three members of the first triad appear to the Shaykh al-Ishraq in their concrete imaginal reality as three brothers (Persian has no grammatical gender, and we need not be troubled by such distinctions in our own language here). Beauty contemplates himself and discovers himself to be the most precious of all treasures.

A great tenderness fills his being; he smiles, and thousands of angels come into existence, born from that smile. His younger brother, Love, also contemplates him. The sight of Beauty drives Love beside himself: he cannot turn away and remains in Beauty's service like a slave. Whenever he tries to break free and recover his independence, the youngest brother, Sorrow, seizes hold of him.

From Sorrow's embrace, which keeps Love forever longing for Beauty without fulfillment, Heaven and Earth were born and continue to endure. For this separation, this prohibition that places Beauty beyond Love's reach, is the secret not only of the gnostic's “story,” but of the whole human race and even the entire universe. Ruzbehan of Shiraz will take up the same theme (Book III, below).

Let us briefly follow the “story” as the Shaykh al-Ishraq tells it. Its first episode gives meaning to an “event in Heaven” familiar from the Qur'an and derived from an Old Testament apocryphon, the *Life of Adam and Eve* (*Historia Adae et Evae*): the command that the angels bow down before Adam. Suhrawardi tells it in a strikingly personal epic style. On learning of Adam's existence, Beauty mounts his glorious steed and rides toward the fortress, the *Burg* (*shahrestân*), in which Adam has come into being.

Love and Sorrow follow. Beauty takes complete possession of the human form, which thus becomes his *mazhar*, his supreme form of manifestation. Love catches up with him and is once more overwhelmed. Sorrow, his companion, lifts him to his feet. He sees all the beings of the heavenly world gathered around him to offer their submission, and all of them, from a great distance, kiss the earth at Beauty's threshold. This is the meaning of the mysterious Qur'anic verse: “All the angels bowed before him” (15:30).

A second episode opens with the “story” of Joseph, who in Islamic mystical literature traditionally represents the perfect revelation of Beauty. Love and Sorrow approach him, but he turns them away with sovereign indifference. The “story” of separation now begins. Each of the two younger brothers goes his own way, and each will reveal his secret to the chosen person who will embody it most fully among human beings.

Sorrow travels to the land of Canaan. Jacob sees him enter his place of prayer and recognizes in him the mark of love. Jacob questions him, and Sorrow reveals his secret: “I come from Nâkojâ-âbâd (the Land of No-Where, the land that cannot be seen anywhere by the senses, the Eighth Clime), from the City of the Pure.” Jacob becomes his inseparable companion: he *is* Sorrow.

Love makes his way to Egypt, where the story reveals the origin of the pair formed by Joseph and Zolaykha, the archetypal lovers of the Islamic mystical epic. Seeing Love pass by her place of prayer, Zolaykha asks him, “Where do you come from? What is your name?” Love answers: “I come from the land of the Spirit (*Rûh-Abâd*). Sorrow is always near the place where I dwell. I am a solitary Sufi, always setting out, in every direction.

“Each day I complete a stage of the journey; each night I stop somewhere to rest. In the darkness of exile I am called Love (*'ishq*). In my own kingdom I am called Mihr”—the Persian form of the name Mithra, meaning both “sun” and “love.” “In the heavens I am known as the Prime Mover; on earth I appear as a beggar. I have an ancient appearance, yet my youth is eternal. I possess no outward splendor, yet my ancestry is noble. Mine is a long story…”

Love then initiates Zolaykha into his secret.

First, where is his kingdom? A road of nine stages—the nine celestial Spheres—leads to it. Beyond the vault of the nine domes rises the fortress, the *Burg*, of the soul. For we know that one must emerge from the cosmic crypt to reach the Eighth Clime, *Na-koja-abad*, the “place” of the soul's castle, which lies beyond the coordinates of sensory space.

At this point the story describes the fortress in terms that reproduce, detail for detail, the description given in the “Epistle of the High Towers.”

The places and images are arranged here according to an architecture that illustrates Sohrawardî's vision of the *theatrum mundi*—the world as a theater—as perceived by the metaphysical imagination, whose sources and implications we discussed earlier.

At the heart, or on the summit, of this fortress lies the Spring of Life. Above this *Burg*, this fortified castle, rise other castles, just as in the “Tale of Exile” another Sinai rises above each Sinai.

Then comes the second part of the initiation, answering Zolaykhâ's question: “Why did Love leave his kingdom to come all the way here?” The answer develops the “story” of the “three brothers” briefly recounted above.

Zolaykhâ gives over her entire dwelling to Love. When Joseph appears, Love puts an arm around Zolaykhâ's shoulder, and together they move toward the contemplation that ends their separation.

Zolaykhâ is Love; Beauty and Love are reunited. Meanwhile Sorrow leads Jacob to Egypt, where he is to behold Joseph and Zolaykhâ—Beauty and Love—upon the throne. Then Sorrow, Jacob, and Jacob's sons, who had sold their Joseph, bow down.

And Joseph recites the verse: “O my father, here is the meaning of the dream I once told you: Father, I saw eleven stars, together with the sun and the moon; yes, I saw them bowing down before me in worship” (Qur'an 12:4). It is Beauty “in person” who speaks through Joseph's lips.

The final chapters (X–XIII) of the *Vade-mecum*, the handbook, return to the fundamental ideas and ethical demands of this religion of love for beauty.

Let us recall these lines in particular: “It is written: If God is beautiful, he must necessarily bring forth beauty. If everything that exists, whether bodily or spiritual, seeks perfection, you will likewise find no being that does not desire the beauty of forms.

“Reflect on this, then, carefully and deeply: Beauty is what haunts the desires of all beings; every effort is consumed in the longing to be united with her. Alas, how difficult it is to reach this Beauty, whom all desire! For union with her requires a mediator, and there is no mediator but Love.

“Yet Love does not welcome just anyone. He does not make his home wherever he happens to find himself; he does not reveal himself to every gaze. If someone comes to him, ready for such happiness, Love sends Sorrow, his faithful messenger, to cleanse the dwelling and make sure that no one but Love himself crosses its threshold” (chapter X).

We can now say this: Eros becomes sacred, is transformed into a sacrament of Love, precisely insofar as it is love of Beauty. For at the very beginning of all beginnings, Beauty herself is the revelation of the holiest of holies.

Wherever Beauty ceases to appear, wherever she is denied, desecrated, and blasphemed, Eros can no longer be transfigured; Eros himself has been caricatured, degraded, and profaned. The connection is a strict one, and certain things happening in our own day make us witnesses to it.

As the prologue to the *Vade-mecum* shows us, Love is essentially *philokalia*: love of Beauty. The name *Philokalia*, as we know, is also borne by a famous collection of ascetic writings in Eastern Christianity.

To avoid confusion, and recalling what we said at the beginning about “hieratic” (sacred) wisdom and art, we prefer to propose another word: *hierokalia*, or the sense of sacred Beauty—Beauty inseparably bound, in her very essence, to what is holy.

Without this *hierokalia* [^EII2-524], there can be no religion of transfigured Eros. And such a religion is, by its nature, eschatological: it is concerned with the ultimate encounter that lies beyond earthly life.

Here we touch the deepest meaning of a conviction found in Zoroastrian faith: heavenly Beauty appears in the person of the angel Daênâ when the *eschaton* is reached, when the threshold of life after death has been crossed.

Yet the sudden appearance of absolute Beauty within earthly life is also eschatological. This happens, for example, when the mystery of Beauty is recognized as present in the beauty of another human being. Such an appearance can awaken in the one who sees it a love strong enough to break every attachment and every rule that binds us to earthly existence.

Of course, to recognize Beauty in this way, a person must already be straining with their whole being toward the vision awaited after death. The whole “story” of the gnostic now comes into play: the drama of separation from one's heavenly *alter ego*, one's other self.

The revelation of Beauty therefore brings that person to a breaking point, a “catastrophic” threshold, because it brings forward into the present what they had reason to expect only after death. This is what we mean by *hierokalia*, a word suggested to us both by Sohrawardî's *Vade-mecum* and by Rûzbehân's *Jasmine of the Faithful of Love*. It reaches infinitely further than what is commonly called, rightly or wrongly, “romantic” feeling.

In speaking of Beauty as an eschatological experience, we have just recalled the vision awaited after death by the Zoroastrian believer—a vision that also brings the gnostic's story to its conclusion. That reference was deliberate.

Throughout the mystical epic of Islamic Iran, this religion of transfigured Eros gives certain images inherited from Zoroastrianism a new power to transform the soul.

By changing them into symbols, it makes them *imagines agentes*: images that act upon us. This spiritual development accords so closely with the purpose of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, the Master of Illumination, who sought to renew the spiritual philosophy of ancient Iran, that we can best conclude with two examples.

The first comes from one of the greatest figures we have already encountered, Farîdoddîn ’Attâr (twelfth–thirteenth centuries). A poet of extraordinary and fertile genius, he created vast mystical poems in which the Iranian imagination gives brilliant expression to Goethe's words: “All that passes away is only a symbol.”

In a particularly daring *ghazal*, or lyric poem, ’Attâr cries out: “Whoever has lived in constant intimacy with the Temple of the Magi—what religious community could claim him? What ritual could bind him?—I stand beyond Good and Evil, beyond unbelief and religion, beyond theory and practice—for beyond all these, there are still many Stations [^EII2-525].”

Certainly, to transgress the Law is still to acknowledge its existence.

Yet transgression of this kind brings a person to an extreme, eschatological threshold, and one's personal experience of ultimate things is not something to proclaim in the public square.

Consider how a master of Iranian Sufism, Shaykh Safîoddîn Ardabîlî (d. 735/1334)—the very man whom the Safavid dynasty regarded as its ancestor—explained this *ghazal* of ’Attâr to his disciples.

A fire altar is truly a “fire altar” when the sacred Flame burns there without ceasing. The Temple of the Magi and the fire altar signify the world of Love. Like the sacred Flame, love for the Divine Being never dies down.

For someone immersed in that love, what meaning could religious observances and rituals have if they were tainted by the impure desire to gain paradise? If such a person must outwardly observe them, or appears to observe them, it is with an inward sincerity that has made them wholly free for God.

Good and Evil, unbelief and religion, theory and practice: all these distinctions belong to the world of the rational intellect.

But in the world of Love, which lies beyond the very “place” of this world (see the discussion of *Nâ-kojâ Abâd*, the land of No-where, above), there are many Stations.

There are the Stations of detachment that frees one from material ties (*tajrîd*), and of solitude that makes one wholly oneself (*tafrîd*); the Stations of passionate love (*’ishq*) and loving affection (*mahabbat*); the Stations of renunciation (*faqr*), contemplative spiritual knowledge (*ma’rifat*), and unification that brings all into oneness (*tawhîd*).

None of this is contained in spaces already given or imposed upon us. Beyond all their boundaries, these Stations open up the realm of Love itself: the sanctuary where the sacred Flame is worshipped, the Temple of the Magi.

There the mystical lovers, the “Templars” of transfigured Eros, perform the service of Love. There is their *qibla*, the direction toward which they turn in prayer, and they have no other worship ... So the shaykh explained.

And in the two verses he recited during this “lesson,” we can still hear Iran's enduring longing for the heavenly Vision of light and love that it proclaimed to the world: “Our religion is the service of Love; our *qibla* is Love. Whoever has neither *qibla* nor Love—that one is the unbeliever.”

This *ghazal* belongs to a whole family of passionate declarations in the poetry of the great poet of Neyshâpûr, passages in which he uses a vocabulary drawn from Zoroastrian tradition.

Read with Safîoddîn Ardabîlî's commentary, the poem offers an *’irfânî*, or mystical, interpretation of words inherited from Zoroastrianism. This spiritual phenomenon is closely related to Sohrawardî's *Ishrâq*, his philosophy of illumination; our friend Mohammad Mo’în once devoted an entire study to it [^EII2-526].

Among its most powerful *imagines agentes*, or active images, is the “great master” or “prior” of the Magi (*pîr-e Moghân*). He is the Perfect Human Being, the heavenly *Anthrôpos*; he is the *shaykh* as spiritual guide (*morshid*), or, more directly, the Imam himself in Shiite gnosis.

The “priory of the Magi” is the world of the Divine Names. The “Magus” is the true witness to the One: the one who unifies and whom the One unifies. From here unfolds an entire constellation of symbols: the “sons of the Magi,” the “Temple of Fire,” the *Môbed*, the belt (*kostî*), and so on.

Towering over them all is the image of the “wine of the Magi,” together with the image of the Grail. Sohrawardî has given us ample reason to dwell on the Grail in these pages, and perhaps it is the key to this whole language of mystical interpretation [^EII2-527].

It is from a setting dominated by this same vocabulary that we draw our second example. It comes from a vast nineteenth-century Persian mystical epic containing no fewer than seventy-six thousand couplets—roughly three times the length of Mawlânâ Rûmî's *Mathnavî*.

The poem is interwoven with prose passages and bears the title *Kanz al-Asrâr* (*The Treasury of Esoteric Knowledge*). This monumental work of Iranian Shiite Sufism unfolds in twelve books.

In Book XII we read: “An explanation of the Temple of Fire, which was nothing other than a visible form of the Divine Being's overpowering, exclusive, all-consuming Love. Zoroaster gave that Love a visible form and raised a fire altar to it.

“After the armies of Islam and the Arabs triumphed over Iran, this mystery was veiled from the Earth and withdrew into the innermost depths of the heart. Its emblem was taken up anew in the person of the royal princess (Shahrbânû, daughter of Yazdagard III), who became the mother of the Fourth Imam, Zayn ol-’Abidîn.

“Through her marriage at Yathrîb to the Prince of Martyrs (Imam Hosayn), she had entered the family of the Immaculate Ones. That is why this *hadith*, or saying, has been heard from the lips of the Prophet, prince of the Arabs and Persians: Never speak irreverently of Zoroaster, for Zoroaster was a messenger of the most loving Lord in Iran [^EII2-528].”

This lengthy text, stated as a recurring theme, is then explained over some sixty couplets. It is not our task here to assess the historical accuracy of the tradition according to which the royal princess, daughter of Yazdagard III, the last Sasanian ruler of Iran, married the Third Shiite Imam, Imam Hosayn.

This tradition belongs to Shiite religious consciousness: to the understanding Iranian Shiism has of its own history, and to the form in which it expresses that understanding. As students of religious experience, we must therefore receive it as such, seeing—and helping others see—both what it explains and what it implies.

Whatever else may be said, the tradition reveals an event that has left an indelible mark on Iran's religious consciousness. Its representation of that event is the keystone that holds together the architecture of Iran's spiritual universe.

Notice, in this connection, the importance of women in Shiite sacred imagery. Fâtima the Radiant is the link between the Prophet and the Twelve Imams.

The royal princess, daughter of Yazdagard III, establishes continuity between Zoroastrian Iran and Shiite Iran: between the religion of love symbolized by the flame upon the fire altar and the religion of love affirmed in the *walâyat*, the spiritual bond of devotion and guardianship centered on the Imams.

As for the text of the tradition, preserved and elaborated by a nineteenth-century Iranian Sufi, we cannot at present identify its source.

But the *shaykh al-Ishrâq* would surely have embraced it, so clearly does it support the conviction with which he undertook the great project of his life.

The long procession of Iranian mystics, headed by figures such as Sanâ’î, Sohrawardî, and ’Attâr, continues into the nineteenth-century Shiite Sufis. That is why their testimony seems to us the most fitting conclusion to the first two books of this work, devoted respectively to Shiism and to the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*.

Of Sohrawardî himself, let us say in closing that, for all its greatness, his work may appear to have been left unfinished, cut short by his martyrdom while he was still young. His book of “Eastern Theosophy”—*The Philosophy of Illumination*—is a great book in its ambition; in length and style, however, it is closer to a concise compendium.

Had he lived, its author would surely have expanded the outlines hastily set down on paper during his travels. Even as it stands, his work has left its mark on Iranian thought for eight centuries. It has never ceased to live in the minds of the *Ishrâqîyûn*, the philosophers of illumination, whether their earthly home was Iran or India.

But we should not imagine that life in this world was ever easy for them. All of them, even in the Safavid period, endured harassment. These members of the “family of *Ishrâq*” were solitary souls, hermits of the heart, exiles who heard “the call from the right-hand side of the valley, from within a bush” (Qur'an 28:30): the call from the “East” that rises at the heart of the “Tale of Exile.”

To call a person home from exile, that call must first awaken the exile to the knowledge that they are an exile. And in the noise and tumult of this world, nothing is more difficult.

More than once we have quoted the invocation from a psalm of Sohrawardî: “Deliver the people of Light; lead Light toward Light.” It echoes the faith of those who know that “the Darkness did not receive the Light” (John 1:5).

And it echoes the faith of those who know that the pure Islam of the true believers “began as a stranger (*gharîb*) and will become a stranger again, as it was in the beginning.

“Blessed are those who become strangers!” This famous saying of Imam Ja’far gives its full meaning to a devotion to the Shiite cause that reaches beyond every horizon of this world. It speaks to all the “strangers” who dare to accept the challenge: to go into exile from exile itself. It speaks above all to Salmân the Persian and to everyone for whom he stands.

And the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*, more than anyone, deserves to lead the procession of pilgrims who come in spirit to Salmân the Persian's tomb, there to repeat: “May I live and die, loyal friend, as you did ... you who never betrayed [^EII2-529].”

# Henry Corbin

## Within Iranian Islam

Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects

### Sohrawardî and the Platonists of Persia

Within the Islamic community, the Iranian world formed, from the very beginning, a distinct whole. Its character and calling can be understood only if we regard Iran's spiritual universe as one continuous whole, before Islam and after it. Islamic Iran has been, above all, the homeland of some of Islam's greatest philosophers and mystics.

For them, speculative thought can never be separated from the fruit it bears and its practical consequences—not in the social world, but in the whole, concrete spiritual reality that human beings nourish from their own substance beyond the boundaries of this life: their spiritual world.

The four-volume work in seven books presented here by Henry Corbin is the result of more than twenty years of research conducted in Iran itself. His method is fundamentally phenomenological, without belonging to any particular school. His aim is to encounter religious experience by allowing its object to appear just as it appears to those who experience it.

The phenomenologist must therefore become a spiritual guest of those to whom that religious reality reveals itself, and share with them the responsibility it brings. Any historical inquiry must remain within the terms of that reality rather than imposing foreign categories upon it from outside, whether dialectical or otherwise.

The first volume (Book I) sought to present some essential aspects of Twelver Shiism, or Imamism, which took root in Iran from the earliest times and became its official religion in the sixteenth century. This second volume (Book II) is devoted to the *ishrâqîyûn*, philosophers of illumination (from *ishrâq*, sunrise, the coming of light from the East), often described as “Platonists” in contrast with the Peripatetic philosophers of Islam.

At its origin stood the resolve of a brilliant young thinker, Sohrawardî, who died a martyr to his cause at the age of thirty-six (1191).

Through his writings he sought to revive the wisdom of ancient Persia, the philosophy of Light and Darkness, and to bring the Hellenized Magi home to Islamic Persia. He undertook this through the resources of spiritual interpretation (*ta’wîl*) made available to him by Islamic spirituality.

In press: Volume III: *The Faithful of Love* (Book III); *Shiism and Sufism* (Book IV); *The School of Isfahan* (Book V). Volume IV: *The Shaykhi School* (Book VI); *The Twelfth Imam and Spiritual Chivalry* (Book VII); general index.

Hvôvi remains a sacred figure of the end times: her children, the three Saoshyants or Saviours, whose successive arrivals will bring our Aeon to a close, have not yet been born. See H. S. [^EII2-89]: See *ibid.*, § 4: “Although *Magister primus* (Aristotle) was a man of great merit and eminent authority, a profound mind with perfect powers of philosophical reasoning, it is nevertheless unacceptable to praise him so extravagantly that those who were his masters are belittled—namely, the men who produced sacred books and were prophet-legislators, such as Agathodaimôn, Hermes, Asclepius, and others.” Shahrazôrî comments at length; Qotboddîn Shîrâzî does little more here than reproduce his explanation: “Agathodaimôn, that is, Seth, son of Adam (above, p. 25, n. 26); Hermes, that is, the prophet Idrîs (or Enoch); and Asclepius, the servant and disciple of Hermes, who was the father of the philosophers (*hokamâ’*) and physicians. All three were eminent prophets (*anbiâ’*) who combined the excellence of prophecy with philosophical wisdom. They were therefore capable of assembling the body of theosophical teaching (*tadwîn al-hikmat*) and initiating others into philosophy. The author names all three here either because Aristotle received wisdom from Plato, Plato from Socrates, Socrates from Pythagoras, Pythagoras from Empedocles, and so on back to the two Imams Agathodaimôn and Hermes—and the master of your master is also your master—or because Aristotle himself relied on their books and accounts of their teaching. They were therefore his masters in reality as well. Had Avicenna shown the least fairness, he would have acknowledged that Aristotle owed the sources he developed to Plato.” Both commentators go on to praise Plato with enthusiasm as a contemplator of divine Beauty, “an eminent theologian who was by no means deficient in rational dialectic, as Avicenna claimed. Moreover, most of his books have never been translated into Arabic; they have even been lost and disappeared.” See *Op. metaph. I*, pp. 304–305. This long quotation, which we have abridged, expresses a strong sense of “prophetic philosophy”: philosophy begins with prophet-sages (Empedocles, Hermes, Agathodaimôn). It also testifies to the “Platonic revival” brought about within Islam—or at least Iranian Islam—by Sohrawardî’s work.


[^EII2-90]: *Ibid.*, p. 12. Even during the *ghaybat*, the occultation or concealment of the “Pole,” the Pole remains the Pole. He does not need human recognition to be what he is; his existence fulfils a sacred and metaphysical function, not a social one. There is no need to translate this into some other conceptual framework: what the *Ishrâqîyûn* say of the “Pole” agrees literally with what Shiites say of the Imam, who is himself precisely the “Pole.” This helps explain why *ishrâqî* philosophy flourished in Shiite circles.


[^EII2-91]: On Mohammad Sharîf ibn Harawî, who translated into Persian the second part of the *Book of Oriental Theosophy* and Qotboddîn’s commentary, see *Prolegomena II*, pp. 60–61 (the translation is dated 1008 AH/1559–1600 CE). The introduction bears a clear trace of Indian Sufism (Shah Akbar died in 1605). The translator quotes a long epistle by Mîr Sayyed Mohammad Gîsû-Darâz (d. 1422), whose shrine is at Gulbarga and who is said to have converted a Bahmanid ruler, Shihâboddîn Ahmad I (d. 1421), to Shiism; see J. N. Hollister, *The Shî’a of India*, London, 1953, pp. 105 ff. The passage we have in mind states: “In speaking of power, I do not in any way mean government or visible authority, as though God’s caliph had necessarily to exercise actual rule over people in the visible world. Far from it! I mean that he possesses the qualification that makes him worthy of the *caliphate* (or Imamate), even if he is hidden in the deepest obscurity [...]. It is therefore plain that the passage concerns the Sage’s spiritual authority, not temporal power.”

Tâ-Sîn is the opening of sura 27 (the Sura of the Ant), but I do not know why the *shaykh* specifically alludes to that sura here.” Shahrazôrî, for his part, observes: “Tâ-Sîn refers to the pure Intelligences and the heavenly Souls. All the isolated letters found at the beginning of certain suras refer to those Essences that are separate from matter, just as the letters themselves stand apart. When the mystic (*sâlik*, the pilgrim) finds it easy to ascend toward the pure intellectual Essences and enter into union with the perfect Souls who belong to the Household of prophecy (*Ahl bayt al-nobowwat*)—if we agree that these are the Âl Tâsîn—then contemplation of the One becomes possible for him, provided he continues to remain what he is. In that case the author’s words are fulfilled: ‘Perhaps you will see your Lord on the broad road along which you are advancing.’ But this ascent toward the pure intellectual Essences, and the contemplation of the Being who is necessary through himself with the certainty of an eyewitness (*’ayn al-yaqîn*), cannot be achieved by theoretical knowledge, which yields only theoretical certainty (*’ilm al-yaqîn*). It can be achieved only through fully realized mystical experience (the ‘Oriental’ knowledge).”

In Mazdaism the material world is not, as in Manichaeism and Ismailism, an instrument created to save the souls of light held captive within it. Sohrawardî’s understanding of Zoroaster’s religion has a Manichaean colouring.

Christensen, *L’Iran sous les Sassanides*, second ed., Copenhagen, 1944, p. 104, n. 4, and index (Avestan *spâdhapati*; Pahlavi *spâhbat, espahbad*; Arabicized *isfahbad*). [^EII2-166]: The word *barzakh* denotes anything that acts as a screen or barrier, anything that stands “between two.” In ordinary theological usage it has an end-times meaning: the in-between world, the *mundus imaginalis* (the city of Jâbarsâ), the world and intermediate state between this life and the Great Resurrection (*Qiyâmat Kobrâ*). In Sohrawardî’s vocabulary it denotes anything that blocks light, whether in the elemental or the astral world. Etymologically, *barzakh* or *farsakh*, as a unit of distance, is thought to derive from the Greek παρασάγγης (*parasang*).

[^EII2-168]: On this cosmic drama, see our *Trilogie ismaélienne*, index under “the drama in Heaven.” In a lengthy gloss that we cannot examine here (Gloss 354 on § 126, p. 120), Mollâ Sadrâ develops the idea that acts of being, individual existences, contain a certain incapacity, weakness or deficiency in the order of “descent” (*nozûl*). Darkness arises from this deficiency as the negation of Light. This deficiency belongs to existence accidentally, not essentially. Secondary matter and material embodiment suffer from a weakness inherent in their act of existing; that weakness is their very opacity. But, according to Sadrâ, one can escape the dualism (*thanawiya*) that posits Ahriman’s necessary and demonic existence only by adopting a metaphysics of being that gives priority to *esse*—the act of existing—over essence or whatness. One can speak of a degradation in the act of existing; if instead one speaks of a degradation of essences, a dark essence will ultimately demand a dark first principle. This is the great question at the heart of Mollâ Sadrâ’s philosophy. We refer here to our edition and translation of his *Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques* (Bibliothèque Iranienne, vol. 10).

It was subsequently edited by ’Abdurrahman Badawî under the title *Ideae Platonicae*, Cairo, 1947. Its title already makes the essential distinction between the Idea as archetype at the level of intellectual intuition and Intelligence (the world of *Jabarût*), and the Idea at the level of imaginative perception and the world of the Soul (the world of *Malakût*). “Suspended” means that these image-Ideas do not inhere in matter, as, for example, a brown colour inheres in a piece of wood. Sohrawardî never confused the two; his understanding of the Platonic Ideas, however, follows a tradition different from that of the *falâsifa* (the philosophers of the Islamic Peripatetic tradition).

[^EII2-190]: Perhaps this explains why Sohrawardî did not accept Avicennian angelology’s claim that each Angel is a unique individual constituting a species in itself. Thomas Aquinas likewise held this view, and Leibniz drew inspiration from it. For Sohrawardî, an angelic being is defined not by constituting a species individually in the Peripatetic sense, but by the degree of intensity of its radiance. Intensity is thus introduced into the very category of substance. A soul may be “more a soul,” or “more intensely a soul,” than another (*Motârahât*, § 66, referring to Plato). The degree of intensity ultimately establishes an individuation just as precise as the definition by species taught by Avicennism and Thomism. It also leaves open the way of ascent from one degree of intensity to the next. We cannot pursue this comparison of angelologies further here. See also *Prolegomena II*, pp. 46 ff.

We must therefore concentrate on the figure himself and his role. His vision of the Grail’s name inscribed in the stars prepares the poem’s final resolution in book IX of Wolfram: the vision of the Grail granted to Feirefiz through his baptism. It announces an ultimate union of the Islamic world with Christendom, paralleling the vision of Princess Narkès, mother of the Twelfth Imam. We should add that if Wolfram, by turning a Hermetic story into a Christian one, was expressing his conviction that Hermetism and Christianity were closely related, then Wolfram—like the School of Chartres, which showed such keen interest in Hermetism in the twelfth century—becomes a forerunner of the Christian Hermetists of the Renaissance. This is of no small importance for the meaning of the Grail cycle in our entire spiritual culture.

Wolfram drew on Chrétien’s work while accusing him of a particular alteration. The mysterious book given to Chrétien by Count Philip of Flanders has sometimes been too readily dismissed as a literary fiction, and the importance of the *silentium mysticum*—the mystical silence observed by the hermit when teaching the secret prayer—has been underestimated. Even if we found only affinities, rather than “sources” in the historical sense, the Grail cycle would require a different interpretation from one that, through piety or habit, merely discovers the teachings of the official Church there, whether symbolically or otherwise. To label as “Cistercian” elements inseparable from a larger whole that rules out such an identification is to neglect the structure rather badly.

But is the Fisher King’s attitude toward Peredur-Parsifal hostile in a way that could justify this identification? Afrâsiyâb the Turanian was certainly Kay Khosraw’s maternal grandfather, and repeatedly tried in vain to seize the *Xvarnah* by force, “fishing” for it in mystical waters. Yet sound phenomenology does not permit us to isolate a few features of a figure in order to identify it with another. Considered as a whole, Afrâsiyâb’s figure in the Iranian tradition clearly resists identification with the Fisher King of our Grail cycle. Besides, *Peredur* hardly appears to be a “canonical text” of the Grail Quest cycle. It is actually Kay Kâûs, Kay Khosraw’s paternal grandfather, who could be compared with the Fisher King; see below.

Two passages stand out in the *Continuation* attributed to Wauchier de Denain. (1) Amid the enchantments of the forest, Perceval sees a distant glow: “It seemed to him that five candles burned so brightly and brilliantly that the whole forest was ablaze. Wondrous was the vision, for it seemed to him that the crimson flame rose as high as the clouds” (trans. S. Hannedouche; above, p. 173, n. 280; pp. 97–98). (2) Near the Fisher King’s castle, Perceval sees in the distance a leafy tree with “more than a thousand candles on it, as bright as stars.” But as night approaches, the tree turns into a chapel, and “inside he saw one lighted candle” (*ibid.*, pp. 145–146). The Grail will appear as a Light before which all earthly lights go out. All this sheds further light on the fact that several knights wear red or crimson armour, or robes the colour of fire (Galahad, Sir Bors, the hero Lug, Lancelot’s counterpart; Coyajee, *op. cit.*, pp. 109–110). This path leads us at last to the appearance of the “Crimson Archangel” at the opening of the Sohrawardian tale that bears that title; see below, chap. V, n. 328.

[^EII2-291]: See J. Marx, *La Légende arthurienne et le Graal*, pp. 85–86, 198, 305–309, 332. Jean Marx also posed with great clarity the problem of “Robert de Boron and Glastonbury” in *Nouvelles recherches*, pp. 139–152. This is a typical example of the phenomenon we are considering. Perhaps identifying Avalon with Glastonbury served Plantagenet interests, and perhaps it helped suppress King Arthur’s end-times role in favour of official Church teaching. But would that have been enough to change the *Imago Terrae*—the image of the Earth—to which we refer here, as the faculty through which a new geographical holy place is discovered or perceived? Whether or not this identification concealed the revival of a Celtic Church suppressed by the Roman Church, it did not necessarily end Arthur’s eschatological role. A *hadîth* widespread in Shiite Islam says that the bodies of prophets and Imams remain in the tomb for only three days before being carried “to Heaven.” The profound theosopher Qâzî Sa’îd Qommî warns those who might try to prove this by opening their graves: they would indeed find the body they sought. Yet the tomb is empty. For it is *another body* that is said to be carried “to Heaven,” and “this does not mean the sky above our heads.” Even if King Arthur’s and Queen Guinevere’s remains were found in their tombs at Glastonbury, their “body” (their *jism mithâlî*, imaginal body) is elsewhere, where the perception of Avalon as the Other World places them.

III*, p. 299, line 13, where the edited text reads something like: “This Grail is what lies buried beneath (what is concealed by) our old woollen cloak.” It is edifying, but hardly original; we ourselves once understood the passage this way. Yet the Istanbul Râghib 1480 manuscript (unfortunately unavailable for the published critical apparatus) has a vigorous, precise scholar’s hand, though regrettably without diacritical dots. In it, the reading of the word elsewhere interpreted as *pashmîneh* (“woollen”) becomes problematic. A few years ago, our friend Mr Mo’în and I examined this passage and read in it two Arabic words (*lohba sa-tomîtoh*) drawn from a source familiar to Sohrawardî and inserted into the Persian verse, as Persian syntax permits: “*lohba sat’mitoh*”-e mâst. The author applies the meaning of these two words to his own condition. Literally: “This buried Grail (that is, hidden treasure) is our ‘burning flame (or burning thirst) that will cause his death.’” Sohrawardî thus means: for me, this ardour or thirst that ultimately kills is the Grail concealed within me, the Grail that I myself am. Or, as we have tried to translate it, this ardour feeds on our death as it consumes our life. That is why the symbol of the Grail meets the symbol of the Phoenix here as a symbol of the *religio mentis*, the religion of the spirit.

(2) *Awâz-e Parr-e Jebrâvêl* (*The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings*), previously published and translated by us in collaboration with Paul Kraus in *Journal asiatique*, July–September 1935. (3) *’Aql-e sorkh* (*The Crimson Archangel*), translated in this volume. (4) *Rûzî bâ jamâ’at-e Sûfiyân* (*One Day in the Company of the Sufis ...*). (5) *Risâlat fî hâlat al-tifûlîya* (*Epistle on the State of Childhood*). (6) *Mu’nis al-’Oshshâq* (*The Lovers’ Vade Mecum*), which we translated under the title *Le familier des amants* (“The Lovers’ Companion”) in *Recherches philosophiques*, I, Paris, 1933. The work bears the subtitle *Fî haqîqat al-’ishq* (*On the Essence of Love*); the editor of *Op. metaph. III* preferred to reverse title and subtitle. (7) *Loghât-e Mûrân* (*The Language of the Ants*), French translation in *Hermès*, third series, III, November 1939. (8) *Safîr-e Sîmorgh* (*The Incantation of Sîmorgh*), French translation in the same issue. All these works are in Persian. (9) *Qissat al-ghorbat al-gharbîya* (*The Tale of the Western Exile*), in Arabic and Persian. We published both versions in *Op. metaph. II*; a French translation appears below, pp. 288 ff. Finally, (10) *Risâlat al-abrâj* (*Epistle of the High Towers*), in Arabic only; we published its text as an appendix to *Op. metaph. III*. We hope to publish a complete French translation of these narratives next year (“Documents spirituels,” A. Fayard). The act of “setting down this lamp” would make no sense on the glossator’s reading. Moreover, he seems completely to forget that the hierarchy of the *Angeli intellectuales* is situated in Nâ-kojâ-Abâd, beyond Mount Qâf—that is, beyond the system of the Spheres. As for the waterwheel mentioned in stanza 33, it denotes the Moon’s sphere; but the mystic himself is a moon “in the heaven of *tawhîd*” (the affirmation of divine oneness). We may recall here the Manichaean image of the Cosmic Wheel drawing up and rescuing the particles of light immersed in darkness.

First is the spiritual form (*pneumatikon eikôn*), the New Man in whom the Light-Mind (*Noûs*-Light) takes form and abides. Second is the residue of the old man within the New Man, a psychic form (*psychikon eikôn*) bound to the flesh (*sarx*). Third is the bodily form (*sômatikon eikôn*). The Maiden of Light reveals to the elect person the spiritual form—the New Man within him—by becoming his guide and drawing him upward. She enters that spiritual form, shapes and orders it within the New Man, so that it bears the seal and imprint of the limbs of the Maiden of Light who dwells in him. She is “the one called the hour of life, which is the first. But she is also the last.” We have already noted the close affinity between the Manichaean and Ismaili conceptions; see our *Trilogie ismaélienne*, index under *Form of Light*.

The title leaves no doubt: *Risâla fî’l-mabdâ’ wa’l-ma’âd ayzan ’alâ tarîq al-ramz li-ba’z Ahl al-Hind* (*Treatise on Origin and Return, Also in the Form of a Symbolic Story, by a Certain Indian Author*). I am the first to regret that this interesting epistle cannot be Avicenna’s work. Its attribution to him in the learned bibliographer’s study must be an oversight, all the more understandable if the manuscript miscellany also contains authentic works by Avicenna.

The father, Sadroddîn Dashtakî Shîrâzî (not to be confused with Mollâ Sadrâ, who was also a Sadroddîn Shîrâzî), known as Amîr Sadroddîn or Sadroddîn Kabîr (“the Great”), was among the most distinguished Iranian Imami thinkers of the ninth century AH. Murdered by Turkmens in 903/1497, he was buried in Shiraz (*Rayhânât*, II, p. 464, no. 847). His son Ghiyâthoddîn Mansûr, whom some biographers rather grandly call the “Eleventh Intelligence,” left some thirty works of philosophy and theology in Arabic and Persian. He died between 940/1533 and 949/1542–43 (*Rayhânât*, III, p. 166, no. 276). Finally there was the grandson, Amîr Sadroddîn II. One of his books is dated 961/1553–54, but the exact date of his death is unknown (*Rayhânât*, II, p. 465, no. 848). The controversy with Dawwânî, sometimes about Sohrawardî and sometimes about glosses on Nasîroddîn Tûsî, seems to have passed as an inheritance from “Sadroddîn the Great” to his son. Each of these figures deserves a monograph. See Brockelmann, *op. cit.*, II, pp. 217 and 414, supplement, pp. 306 and 593.

To put it mildly, the translation needs to be revised from beginning to end. Regrettably, a partial reprint appeared in New York in 1937—and, worse, with substantial unannounced omissions. Nothing was done to incorporate a century of Iranian scholarship. Indeed, there was little prospect of doing so: the two translators worked independently and in ignorance of one another. Their vocabularies differ, but they share the same lack of understanding of the technical terms. The result is an entirely artificial compilation. In short, a critical edition of the *Dabestân*, accompanied by a rigorous translation, is urgently needed.

[^EII2-507]: *Shârestân-e chahâr chaman* was edited in Bombay in 1279/1862–63 (according to the title page, though the last page gives 1867) by four Zoroastrian *môbeds* (priests). This important work of “Zoroastrian *ishrâqî*” literature, by Farzâneh Bahrâm, is arranged as follows. I. Cosmogony (Sohrawardî is quoted as early as p. 4); history of Iran’s prophet-kings, from Hûshang to Kay Qobâd (pp. 1–110). II. The Kayanids, from Kay Kaûs ibn Kay Qobâd to Lohrasp; the prophet Zoroaster; the *ishrâqî* theosophers; Esfandyâr, up to Dârâb (Darius) and Alexander (pp. 111–574). III. The Arsacids (*Ashkâniyân*) and Sasanians (pp. 574–663). IV. Cosmography and geography (pp. 664–798). This is the kind of work in which *Ishrâq* has been fully incorporated into the sacred history of the prophets of ancient Iran; conversely, the Avesta and the traditions are interpreted in the light of the *shaykh al-Ishrâq*’s teaching. This is why the author cannot separate his account of Zoroaster’s life and teachings from his exposition of *ishrâqî* theosophy. The lengthy discussion (pp. 230 ff.) begins by recalling that the *ishrâqî* path is a *barzakh*, an in-between way, between theoretical philosophical reflection and Sufism; it is what the Persians (*Pârsiyân*) call *gashasb* (= *ishrâq*, illumination, splendour). The author repeatedly claims to have been a pupil of Azar Kayvân, whom he greets as “*Qotb-e a’zam, Ghawth-e ’âlam wa Imâm-e zamân*” (“Supreme Pole, Helper of the World, Imam of this age”).

First comes a long introduction (21 pages) in which the editor recalls the accession of Shah Akbar, the spiritual movement he inspired, and his circle, which included representatives of every religious school. The *Dabestân* and the *Shârestân* were also published from manuscripts in the imperial library. Four treatises then make up the *Ayîn-e Hûshang* (*The Religion of Hûshang*, the prophet-king): I. *Khêshtâb* (p. 2); II. the treatise (*risâla*) of Zardosht Afshâr (p. 32); III. *Zâyendeh-Rûd* (p. 149); IV. *Zawreh* (p. 178); conclusion (pp. 178–205).
