[^EII2-527]: The origins and function of this “Mazdeanising” vocabulary would require a study of their own. Perhaps we are touching here the very heart of the questions raised by Iran’s religious destiny. Several Iranian writers have attended to the matter in the past: Shaykh Azerî Tûsî, Moh. Dârâbî, Rezâ Qolî Khân (Hedâyat); see Mo’în, *op. cit.*, pp. 53 ff., and our introduction, pp. 32 ff. When the vocabulary of *’irfân*, mystical knowledge, calls the Imam *Pîr-e Moghân*, the great master of the Magi, it brings the vision of the world offered by Sohrawardî’s work to its fulfilment. Moh. Dârâbî, a commentator on the mystical vocabulary of Hâfez of Shiraz and his poem on the Grail, defines the Grail as “an inward taste (*dhawq*) that radiates the lights of heavenly Realities upon the mystic’s heart.” We have seen that Sohrawardî’s tale refers both to the Grail of Kay Khosraw and to the Grail of Jamshîd (Jam). Whichever figure is credited with its origin, it is called sometimes the “Grail that shows the world,” sometimes the “Grail that sees the world”: two aspects of the theme of the microcosm and the Perfect Human Being. In his long poem Mahmûd Shabestarî asks: “When did the Sage give you this world-seeing Grail?” The answer: “On the very day he created the enamelled dome of heaven.” Sanâ’î (thirteenth century) uses the term for the heart. The Grail’s blaze of light is therefore the illumination of the heart. Like Sohrawardî before him, Mahmûd Shabestarî insisted that, although “many have discoursed about the Grail,” “only the soul in whom the Perfect Human Being has been born is initiated into it ... Though himself human, the Gnostic (*haqîqat-dân*) who has attained self-knowledge is himself the Grail of Jamshîd.” Let us mention other Persian Grail poems. Awhadî of Marâgha completed, in 733/1332–33, a poem of about five thousand couplets on “the Grail of Jamshîd” (*Jâm-e Jam*), which he dedicates to the reader “so that, if you desire to behold the universe, you may behold in this Grail whatever you desire” (through this Grail you will know where the King is, what his Dwelling is, and what the Path is). Earlier, Awhadî of Kermân (seventh/thirteenth century) had written *Mesbâh al-Anvâh* (*The Lamp of the Spirits*), a poem in which, following Sanâ’î, he describes his spiritual ascent through the eight “cities” or “heavens” of the Souls. The Zoroastrians are in the fourth heaven, the heaven of mystical lovers (*nafs-e ’âshiqa*), whose description joins Mazdeans and Sufis as followers of the same mystical religion of love. Finally, Hâtef Ispahânî (d. 1198/1784) composed a *tarjî’-band*, one of the masterpieces of Persian literature. Written in the manner of an oratorio, with magnificent interweaving resonances, it shows how one and the same call to unite with the One is heard in the sanctuary of the Magi, where the mystical Grail passes from hand to hand; in the bell of a Christian monastery; and in the inner mysteries of the *’orafâ*, the Gnostics. The entire first *band*, or section, is filled with traditional Mazdean vocabulary, but its dramatic setting pushes the boldness of this esoteric profession of faith to the very limit.


[^EII2-528]: See also our introduction, *ibid.*, pp. 35–36. *Kanz al-Asrâr* also bears the title *Jannat al-wisâl* (*The Paradise of Union*). We first encountered it some twenty years ago in Tehran, in a manuscript kindly lent to us by Sayyed Mohammad Meshkât. Since then, Mr Meshkât has donated it, together with his entire manuscript collection, to the Central Library of the University of Tehran (see now Dânesh-Pajûh’s catalogue, III, 4, pp. 2181 ff.). The work occupies two substantial quarto volumes (25 × 17 cm), totalling 1,187 pages, all written in a very fine hand, with five columns per page and approximately sixty lines per page. The entire work was completed in 1260/1844; the manuscript copy is dated 1314/1895–96. The lengthy passage quoted here, on Zoroaster as prophet of the religion of love, occurs in book XII, p. 1091. The recurring refrain and the *hadîth* are written in red ink, following the copyist’s practice. Who wrote this enormous rhapsody? The prologue indicates a dervish called “Ma’sûm ’Alî.” This opens several possibilities that we cannot decide here. In Mr Dânesh-Pajûh’s catalogue (pp. 2178 ff., in the notes to the descriptions of the two manuscripts of this work held in the collection) one can find the opening and closing words of each of the twelve books. One might suppose that only one such monumental work bore the title *Jannat al-wisâl* during the same period. Yet another exists, testifying to the extraordinary fertility of Shiite Sufism in Iran. This second *Jannat al-wisâl* was begun by the well-known great Iranian Sufi Nûr ’Alî-Shâh (d. 1212/1797–98); see the manuscript described by Mr Dânesh-Pajûh, *ibid.*, pp. 2182 ff. Nûr ’Alî-Shâh’s work was intended to comprise eight books (symbolising the eight gates of Paradise). Unfortunately, he died before finishing book III. His successor Rawnaq ’Alî-Shâh (d. 1225/1810 or 1230/1814–15) completed book III and composed books IV and V. Nezâm ’Alî-Shâh Kermânî (d. 1242/1826–27) then took over and wrote books VI and VII (see *Rayhânat*, IV, no. 428, p. 247). The opening and closing passages of each of these seven books, as given in the catalogue (pp. 2184–2188), show that they must be two distinct works. A comparative thematic study of these two immense poems is urgently needed, both for our understanding of Iranian Sufism and for Persian literature more generally. We understand that Mr Michel de Miras has embarked on this demanding undertaking.


[^EII2-529]: This pilgrim’s prayer at the shrine of Salmân the Persian (*Pârsî*), also called *Pûr* (*Pâk*), appears in Majlisî, *Bihâr al-Anwâr*, Tehran lithograph, 1303, vol. XXIII, p. 209. Its surrounding context includes other very beautiful prayers said by Shiite pilgrims at Salmân’s tomb.
